t: Two case reports describe spontaneous diaphragmatic rupture in EDS patients (hEDS and unspecified subtype), attributed to pre-existing muscle weakness exacerbated by increased intra-abdominal pressure from coughing or prolonged emesis.

A case report described a 49-year-old male with EDS who developed a large apical lung hernia presenting as right-sided neck swelling with coughing, diagnosed by airway fluoroscopy and inspiratory CT, and successfully treated with right thoracotomy repair.
In a cohort of 104 hEDS outpatients, pulmonary function testing was normal in the majority, with mean FEV1 101.7±16.4% and TLC 109.0±12.2% predicted.
In a cohort of 162 EDS patients, 52% had residual volume greater than 150% predicted and 19% had an RV/TLC ratio greater than 120%, indicating significant gas trapping.

In a case series of 20 EDS patients, spirometry and lung volumes were largely normal, but diffusion capacity was increased in 8 (40%) and reduced in 2 (10%), possibly reflecting hemorrhage or altered pulmonary blood flow.
In contrast to the 20-patient case series, Morgan et al. found impaired diffusion capacity in more than half of 57 EDS/JHS patients.

A 2018 FDA report found that fluoroquinolone use is associated with increased rates of aortic dissection or aneurysm, posing particular risk for EDS patients, especially those with vEDS, alongside increased tendinopathy/tendon rupture risk.

In a 2017 survey of 946 patients with EDS and HSD, those who received physiotherapist advice were 1.8 times more likely to report higher weekly training volumes than those who did not receive such advice.
Case reports describe surgical bullectomy for respiratory failure or lung transplantation for emphysema in EDS patients, with good functional outcomes reported one year post-transplant.
Cardiac dysautonomia is described as a major feature of EDS, requiring anesthesiology teams to consider tailored intra-operative fluid administration and vasopressor strategies.
Among 145 probands with type V collagen defects, 83.5% had pathogenic variants located in COL5A1.
24 of 145 probands (16.5%) with type V collagen defects had pathogenic variants in COL5A2.

85.6% of molecularly confirmed patients presented the two major clinical criteria of generalized joint hypermobility and hyperextensible skin with atrophic scarring, but significant inter- and intrafamilial phenotypic variability was observed.
Patients with COL5A2 variants often had a more severe clinical phenotype compared to those with COL5A1 variants.
Vascular complications were rare (1.4%) among individuals carrying type V collagen defects.
Among 72 probands clinically evaluated at the center, the overall molecular mutation detection rate was 82.0%.
Of the 72 clinically evaluated probands, 68.1% harbored a COL5A1 or COL5A2 defect.
13.9% of the 72 clinically evaluated probands harbored pathogenic variants in other EDS-related genes (COL1A1, PLOD1, TNXB, AEBP1), demonstrating clinical overlap with classical EDS.
Among the 72 clinically evaluated probands, 18% remained molecularly unexplained despite clinical suspicion of classical EDS.
A COL5A1 variant of unknown significance was identified in 6.9% of the 72 clinically evaluated probands.
Significant inter- and intrafamilial phenotypic variability was observed among molecularly confirmed classical EDS patients despite most sharing the two major clinical criteria.

A novel heterozygous COL3A1 variant, c.3478A>G (p.Ile1160Val), not previously reported in literature or genomic databases, was identified in the proband and, combined with functional protein data, reclassified from VUS to likely pathogenic.
Electrophoretic analysis of collagen secreted by the patient's cultured fibroblasts showed delayed mobility of type III collagen compared with an age-matched healthy control.
Densitometric scanning of the fluorogram showed a decreased amount of the α1(III) collagen chain in the patient's fibroblast culture.

Direct mRNA analysis (electrophoresis and Sanger sequencing) of the patient's fibroblasts showed no change in mRNA length and no splicing defects, contradicting the computational prediction of a cryptic splice site.
In silico analysis with Human Splicing Finder predicted that the c.3478A>G transition could activate a cryptic donor splice site, though the prediction was noted as weak.
Whole-body muscular MRI of the patient showed diffuse, slight fatty substitution mainly in the gluteus and soleus muscles bilaterally, without a selective involvement pattern or muscle edema.

The proband presented an atypical vEDS phenotype dominated by recurrent spontaneous muscle and tendon ruptures, generalized muscle pain, and only mild cardiac findings (mitral regurgitation, delayed diastolic relaxation), broadening the recognized clinical spectrum of vEDS.
Segregation analysis performed in the proband's mother was negative for the variant, partially supporting a de novo origin of the mutation (father was deceased and unavailable for testing).
At baseline, fibromyalgia patients showed reduced BOLD signal variability in the ventromedial prefrontal cortex compared to healthy controls.
At baseline, fibromyalgia patients showed reduced BOLD signal variability in the lateral prefrontal cortex compared to healthy controls.
At baseline, fibromyalgia patients showed reduced BOLD signal variability in the anterior insula compared to healthy controls.
At baseline, fibromyalgia patients showed increased BOLD signal variability in the posterior insula compared to healthy controls.
After active M1-tDCS compared to sham, BOLD signal variability increased in the left rostral anterior cingulate cortex.
After active M1-tDCS compared to sham, BOLD signal variability increased in the lateral prefrontal cortex.
After active M1-tDCS compared to sham, BOLD signal variability increased in the thalamus.
After sham tDCS, compared to baseline, BOLD signal variability decreased in the dorsomedial prefrontal cortex.
After sham tDCS, compared to baseline, BOLD signal variability decreased in the posterior cingulate cortex/precuneus.
After active tDCS compared to sham, pain reduction correlated with increased BOLD signal variability in the rACC/vmPFC.
After active tDCS compared to sham, pain reduction correlated with decreased BOLD signal variability in the posterior insula.
Melatonin levels were higher in the synovial fluid of human TMJOA patients and TMJOA rats compared with controls.

MCAS can be subdivided into clonal MCAS, in which mast cell activation is associated with a primary mast cell disorder driven by a KIT mutation (mostly KIT D816V), and nonclonal MCAS, which lacks such a mutation.

Nonclonal MCAS, lacking KIT mutation, is described as secondary (attributable to known triggers such as IgE-mediated allergy) or idiopathic (unidentified triggers) when unrelated to a primary mast cell disorder.
The clinical heterogeneity of MCAS and the molecular complexity of required diagnostic assays (e.g., KIT mutation testing) can lead to misdiagnosis, particularly outside specialized referral centers.
Applying standardized diagnostic criteria shows that in most cases the clinical presentation of MCAS also fulfills the diagnostic criteria for anaphylaxis.
Hereditary alpha-tryptasemia can be encountered in the context of anaphylaxis, MCAS, and primary mast cell disorders.
MCAS and anaphylaxis arise from spontaneous or triggered pathological degranulation of mast cells, which may be normal or pathological (increased burden, aberrant mast cells, or both).
Mast cell activation is described as one of several factors that may drive gastrointestinal symptoms in patients with IBS.
Gut microbiota alterations and malabsorption/fermentation of food substrates are cited as contributors to GI symptom generation in IBS.
Among the various diet interventions marketed for IBS, the low FODMAP (Fermentable, Oligo-, Di-, Mono-saccharide, and Polyol) diet has the strongest evidence base for effective symptom management.

In endometriotic lesions, mast cells and macrophages release proinflammatory cytokines (TNF-α, IL-1β) and IGF-1, recruiting nerve fibers and driving neuroinflammation associated with chronic pelvic pain.

In preclinical endometriosis models, mast cell stabilizers (leukotriene receptor antagonists and ultramicronized PEA) significantly reduced mast cell degranulation and TNF-α release, corresponding with reduced pain.
Despite reducing mast cell degranulation and pain, mast cell stabilizer treatment did not decrease endometriotic lesion size in preclinical models.

Clinical studies of ultramicronized palmitoylethanolamide combined with polydatin (mast cell stabilizers) suggest a beneficial effect on endometriosis-related pain, though further validation is needed before clinical adoption.
Linsitinib, an IGF-1 receptor inhibitor, inhibited activated macrophages and reduced endometriosis-associated pain and nerve growth in a preclinical model.

Peritoneal macrophage depletion using liposomal bisphosphonate or liposomal clodronate decreased endometriotic implants and systemic proinflammatory cytokine production in mouse models of induced endometriosis.
Eight weeks of melatonin administration reduced chronic pelvic pain discomfort in patients with endometriosis.

Immune modulation with T-cell regulatory drugs IL-2 and interferon-α had no impact on endometriotic lesions in clinical trials, whereas strategies targeting macrophages and mast cells produced more promising results.

Despite evidence of altered redox balance in the pelvic and follicular environment in endometriosis, supplementation with immunomodulators (e.g., pentoxifylline) or antioxidants (vitamin C and E) failed to improve pregnancy rates in endometriosis-related infertility.
Resveratrol at concentrations of 1-100 μM did not show cytotoxic effects on human intestinal mast cells after 24 h incubation.
Resveratrol dose-dependently reduced FcεRI-mediated degranulation (β-hexosaminidase release) in human intestinal mast cells, with significant effects from 10 μM and strongest inhibition at 100 μM.
Resveratrol at 5 μM or higher significantly downregulated Cxcl8 mRNA expression in FcεRI-stimulated hiMC.
Resveratrol at 25 μM or higher dose-dependently downregulated Ccl2 mRNA expression in FcεRI-stimulated hiMC.
Resveratrol at 25 μM or higher dose-dependently downregulated Ccl3 mRNA expression in FcεRI-stimulated hiMC.
Resveratrol at 25 μM or higher dose-dependently downregulated Ccl4 mRNA expression in FcεRI-stimulated hiMC.
FcεRI-mediated mast cell degranulation was totally inhibited by the STAT3 inhibitor stattic, almost totally inhibited by resveratrol, and significantly but less strongly reduced by nobiletin.
Both stattic and resveratrol inhibited expression of Cxcl8, Ccl2, Ccl3, Ccl4, and Tnf-α by almost 100% compared to stimulated controls, while nobiletin's effect was less pronounced.
Resveratrol inhibited FcεRI-induced phosphorylation of STAT3 (serine 727) in hiMC, similar to the STAT3 inhibitor stattic, whereas nobiletin's reduction was not statistically significant.
Resveratrol resulted in almost complete inhibition of FcεRI-induced ERK1/2 phosphorylation in hiMC, a stronger effect than that seen with stattic or nobiletin.
Phosphorylated ERK1/2 and phosphorylated STAT3 were detected in mitochondrial fractions of human intestinal mast cells following optimization of subcellular fractionation for low cell numbers.
Resveratrol treatment before FcεRI crosslinking inhibited activated ERK1/2 and STAT3 phosphorylation specifically within mitochondrial fractions of hiMC.
Phosphorylation of other IgE-dependently activated kinases, Akt and JNK, in hiMC was also reduced by resveratrol treatment.
WGCNA identified 594 genes overlapping between coexpression modules in T2DM and ischemic stroke, suggesting shared molecular pathways between the two conditions.
70 genes were up-regulated and 107 genes down-regulated concordantly in both T2DM and ischemic stroke, defining candidate shared disease genes.

Genes shared between T2DM and ischemic stroke were enriched for immune-related biological processes including neutrophil activation, leukocyte activation, and T cell activation, and for KEGG pathways including cytokine-cytokine receptor interaction and Th17 cell differentiation.

GSEA showed T2DM-associated genes enriched for neutrophil extracellular trap formation and bacterial invasion of epithelial cells, while stroke-associated genes were enriched for cytokine-cytokine receptor interaction and MAPK signaling.
Four miRNAs (hsa-miR-299-3p, hsa-miR-320a, hsa-miR-576-3p, hsa-miR-665) were differentially expressed in both T2DM and ischemic stroke datasets and were predicted to jointly target 134 union genes.
Seven miRNA target genes (UBE2N, TGFB3, EXOSC1, VIM, PTGS2, IL10RB, CXCL3) predicted T2DM and ischemic stroke status with an AUC greater than 0.75.
UBE2N, TGFB3, EXOSC1, and VIM were altered in the same direction in both T2DM and ischemic stroke and were proposed as candidate shared markers.
miR-576-3p emerged as the hub regulator in the constructed miRNA-mRNA network, regulating the most target genes and affecting the most KEGG pathways.
Compared with controls, T2DM patients showed significantly higher levels of activated mast cells (as well as higher neutrophils and lower CD8+ T cells) by CIBERSORT immune cell deconvolution.
Compared with controls, ischemic stroke patients showed significantly lower levels of resting mast cells by CIBERSORT immune cell deconvolution.
Among all gene-immune cell correlations examined, PTGS2 and CXCL3 expression showed the strongest positive correlation with mast cell activation levels in T2DM patients.
VIM (vimentin) expression showed a strong positive correlation with resting mast cell levels in ischemic stroke patients.

The authors note that animal models of ischemic stroke show elevated numbers of activated mast cells, and that mast cell activation can promote angiogenesis by amplifying proinflammatory monocyte responses, which may in turn promote diabetes progression and stroke risk.
The authors propose that down-regulation of resting mast cells is linked to greater risk of ischemic stroke, contrasting with elevated activated mast cells seen in T2DM.

The discussion notes that levels of miR-320a can discriminate diabetic from non-diabetic patients and are significantly reduced in stroke patients, particularly those with good prognosis, per cited prior literature.
β-caryophyllene dose-dependently reduced compound 48/80-induced systemic and cutaneous anaphylaxis-like shock in BALB/c mice.
β-caryophyllene dose-dependently inhibited mast cell degranulation in rat peritoneal mast cells (RPMCs).
Histamine release from mast cells was inhibited following β-caryophyllene treatment, consistent with reduced degranulation.
β-caryophyllene dose-dependently activated the Nrf2/HO-1 signalling pathway, as shown by western blot protein expression.
β-caryophyllene dose-dependently activated the AdipoR1/AdipoR2 (adiponectin receptor) signalling axis, linking adiponectin signalling to suppression of pseudo-allergic reactions.
BCP treatment increased circulating adiponectin (APN) levels, correlating with activation of the AdipoR1/AdipoR2 pathway.
BCP treatment reduced pro-inflammatory cytokine levels including IL-6, TNF, and IL-1β in the C48/80-induced pseudo-allergy model.
BCP treatment reduced IgE and ovalbumin (OVA)-specific IgE levels in the pseudo-allergic reaction model.
BCP reversed the C48/80-induced drop in mean arterial blood pressure (anaphylactic hypotension) in Wistar rats.
BCP dose-dependently inhibited histamine release from rat peritoneal mast cells following C48/80 stimulation.
A novel Y69H variant in the sodium channel β2 subunit (SCN2B) was identified in a patient with idiopathic small fiber neuropathy lacking other known causes.
Current-clamp analysis showed that the β2-Y69H variant induces hyperexcitability in dorsal root ganglion neurons by lowering the action potential firing threshold and increasing repetitive spiking.
The β2-Y69H variant upregulated tetrodotoxin-sensitive sodium currents in dorsal root ganglion neurons, providing a mechanistic basis for the observed hyperexcitability.
Tetrodotoxin-resistant sodium currents were not significantly altered by the β2-Y69H variant, distinguishing the mechanism from TTX-sensitive channel effects.
Ten of the 26 h-ATTR patients in this northern France cohort carried the Val30Met TTR variant.
Sixteen of the 26 h-ATTR patients in this cohort carried the Ser77Tyr TTR variant, the most frequent genotype in this northern France series.

Only about half (53.8%) of patients with h-ATTR presenting as an unexplained polyneuropathy had a family history suggestive of the disease, indicating that absence of family history should not exclude h-ATTR from consideration.

The dominant initial electro-clinical presentation of h-ATTR in this cohort was a large-fiber sensory-motor polyneuropathy (92.3% of patients), which was variably symmetric or asymmetric, length-dependent or not, and sometimes associated with nerve entrapment.
Demyelinating electrophysiological signs were observed in 70.8% of patients with h-ATTR presenting as polyneuropathy of unknown origin.

Among patients with demyelinating signs, nine (37.5% of the demyelinating-sign subgroup) fulfilled formal criteria for a definite diagnosis of chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy (CIDP), highlighting a risk of misdiagnosis of h-ATTR as CIDP.
Serum Hsa_circRNA_102682 expression was significantly lower in diabetic patients with hyperhomocysteinemia compared to those with normal homocysteine.
Serum homocysteine levels were negatively correlated with Hsa_circRNA_102682 levels in diabetic patients.
Serum creatinine levels were negatively correlated with Hsa_circRNA_102682 levels in diabetic patients.
Serum TGF-β was significantly higher in diabetic patients with hyperhomocysteinemia than in those with normal homocysteine.
TGF-β was negatively correlated with Hsa_circRNA_102682 levels.
TGF-β was positively correlated with serum homocysteine levels.
TGF-β was positively correlated with serum creatinine levels.
Serum CTGF was significantly higher in diabetic patients with hyperhomocysteinemia than in those with normal homocysteine.
CTGF was negatively correlated with Hsa_circRNA_102682 levels.
CTGF was positively correlated with serum homocysteine levels.
CTGF was positively correlated with serum creatinine levels.

ROC curve analysis indicated Hsa_circRNA_102682 had a higher diagnostic AUC (0.9735) than serum creatinine (0.8460) alone, and was similar to their combination (0.9730), for diagnosing diabetic nephropathy.
Serum creatinine values were significantly higher in the high-homocysteine diabetic group compared to the normal-homocysteine group.
Self-reported IBS (by Rome IV criteria) was significantly more common among women with fibromyalgia and myofascial pain than among those with myalgia.
In multinomial logistic regression, fibromyalgia participants were significantly more likely than myofascial pain participants to have comorbid IBS, in both crude and adjusted models.
Fibromyalgia participants were significantly more likely than myofascial pain participants to have comorbid depression, in both crude and adjusted models.
Fibromyalgia participants were significantly more likely than myofascial pain participants to report somatic symptoms disorder, in both crude and adjusted models.

The discussion states FM was significantly associated with IBS, somatic symptoms disorder, and insomnia compared with MFP, which differs from the results section statement listing IBS, depression, and somatic symptoms as the significant associations for FM vs MFP.

Myalgia participants had significantly lower adjusted odds of comorbid depression, anxiety, somatic symptoms disorder, pain catastrophizing, perceived stress, and insomnia compared to myofascial pain participants.
Total number of comorbid conditions (out of 7 assessed) was highest in fibromyalgia, intermediate in myofascial pain, and lowest in myalgia, with significant group differences.
Myalgia participants had significantly lower odds of a higher comorbidity count than myofascial pain participants (OR=0.69).
Fibromyalgia and myofascial pain groups did not significantly differ in the number of comorbid conditions.
Greater widespread pain (higher WPI) was positively associated with a greater number of comorbid conditions in ordinal logistic regression.
Longer pain duration was positively associated with a greater number of comorbidities, but this association lost significance once widespread pain was included in the model.
Being on sick leave was positively associated with a greater number of comorbidities, but this association lost significance once widespread pain was included in the model.
BMI was not significantly related to the total number of comorbid conditions.
Rates of being on sick leave were markedly higher in fibromyalgia (~50%) and myofascial pain (~30%) than in myalgia (5.1%).
Fibromyalgia participants had significantly higher self-reported BMI compared to both myofascial pain and myalgia groups.

Fibromyalgia participants reported the longest median pain duration (20.5 years), significantly longer than both myofascial pain and myalgia; myofascial pain also had significantly longer duration than myalgia.
Widespread pain index (WPI) scores were highest in fibromyalgia and lowest in myalgia, differing significantly among all three pain groups.
Nearly half of myofascial pain participants met self-reported ACR 2016 fibromyalgia criteria, far more than in the myalgia group.

A prior study cited by the authors found that myalgia and myofascial pain patients differed in salivary expression of certain metabolic, stress, and immune-related proteins, supporting the hypothesis that the two subtypes have distinct underlying mechanisms.
Myofascial pain participants reported significantly higher pain catastrophizing than myalgia participants, but not significantly higher than fibromyalgia participants.
A generalized ordinal logistic regression found a significant positive association between increased widespread pain (WPI) and a greater number of comorbid conditions.

Pain duration was positively associated with a greater number of comorbid conditions when not adjusting for widespread pain, but this association became non-significant once widespread pain was included in the multivariable model.

Being on sick leave was positively associated with a greater number of comorbid conditions before adjustment for widespread pain, but this association was no longer significant after including widespread pain in the model.
The total number of comorbid conditions was not significantly related to BMI in the ordinal logistic regression model.

Participants with MFP and FM did not differ significantly from each other in the total number of comorbid conditions, and no significant differences were found when comparing FM to MFP in the multinomial regression on number of comorbidities.

A cited prior study (Jasim et al. 2020) found that patients with myalgia and myofascial pain differed from each other in salivary expression of some metabolic, stress, and immune-related proteins, supporting the hypothesis of distinct underlying mechanisms.
Prior literature cited indicates the prevalence of fibromyalgia among TMD patients ranges widely from approximately 7% to 60%, depending on study methods and TMD diagnostic criteria used.

Exploratory fully-adjusted analysis (Supplementary Table S2) showed that associations of depression, IBS, insomnia, and somatic symptoms with pain diagnosis were modified by widespread pain (WPI), further indicating a role of widespread pain in these comorbidity associations.

The authors propose that overlapping comorbid conditions such as widespread pain, FM, some TMD cases, IBS, sleep disturbances, depression, and somatic symptoms might be better conceptualized as a single entity ('Overlapping Chronic Pain Conditions') rather than distinct disorders with separate etiologies.
Immunohistochemical staining of ascending aortic tissue from AAD patients showed LUM protein localized prominently to the intimal and medial layers.
Serum soluble LUM levels were significantly higher (3.37-fold) in patients with acute aortic dissection than in patients with coronary artery disease requiring surgery.

Lum-knockout mice showed markedly higher mortality (81.82%) than wild-type mice (26.67%) after BAPN plus angiotensin II challenge, indicating a protective role for lumican against fatal aortic dissection.
Thoracic aortic rupture occurred in 77.27% of BAPN-Ang II-challenged Lum-/- mice compared with none of the challenged WT mice.
Abdominal aortic rupture rates after BAPN-Ang II challenge were low and did not differ substantially between Lum-/- and WT mice.
Despite higher AD and rupture rates in Lum-/- mice, aneurysm dimensions measured by 7T MRI and gross morphology did not differ significantly between Lum-/- and WT mice.
BAPN plus angiotensin II challenge upregulated TGF-β and phospho-SMAD2 expression in both Lum-/- and WT mice compared with unchallenged controls.
At baseline (without challenge), Lum-/- mice had significantly higher phospho-SMAD2 levels than WT mice.
MMP2, MMP9, and NOX4 expression were significantly higher in BAPN-Ang II-challenged aortic dissection mice than in unchallenged control mice.
MMP2, MMP9, MMP14, and NOX4 levels were not significantly different between naïve unchallenged Lum-/- and WT mice, indicating Lum loss alone does not alter baseline levels of these enzymes.

Aortic Lum protein expression was significantly upregulated (2.1-fold) in wild-type mice after BAPN-Ang II challenge compared with unchallenged wild-type mice, suggesting a compensatory injury response.
Higher experiential avoidance was associated with greater lifetime odds of PTSD among deployed Gulf War veterans after adjusting for demographic and exposure covariates.
Higher experiential avoidance was associated with greater lifetime odds of depression among deployed Gulf War veterans after adjusting for demographic and exposure covariates.
Higher experiential avoidance was associated with greater lifetime odds of Gulf War Illness / chronic multisymptom illness (GWI/CMI) among deployed veterans after covariate adjustment.
Higher experiential avoidance was associated with greater lifetime odds of gastrointestinal problems among deployed Gulf War veterans after covariate adjustment.
Higher experiential avoidance was associated with greater lifetime odds of irritable bowel syndrome among deployed Gulf War veterans after covariate adjustment.
Higher experiential avoidance was associated with greater lifetime odds of arthritis among deployed Gulf War veterans after covariate adjustment.
Greater experiential avoidance was associated with higher lifetime odds of fibromyalgia in deployed Gulf War veterans after adjusting for demographic and exposure covariates.
Greater experiential avoidance was associated with higher lifetime odds of chronic fatigue syndrome in deployed Gulf War veterans after adjusting for demographic and exposure covariates.
Experiential avoidance was not significantly associated with lifetime odds of asthma or chronic obstructive pulmonary disease in this veteran sample.

Rapid correction of glycemic control (a drop of more than 2 percentage points of HbA1c over 3 months) may cause treatment-induced neuropathy of diabetes (TIND), presenting with painful neuropathy, autonomic dysfunction, gastroparesis, early retinopathy worsening and microalbuminuria.
Women and people with type 1 diabetes are at elevated risk of developing treatment-induced neuropathy of diabetes.
The patient's anti-GAD antibody level was elevated (5.7 U/mL vs normal 0–4.9), confirming autoimmune (type 1) diabetes.
The patient developed orthostatic hypotension with a substantial blood pressure drop on standing, confirmed by head-up tilt testing and abnormal autonomic reflex testing.
Autonomic reflex testing showed reduced heart rate oscillations at rest and attenuated cardiomotor response to deep breathing and Valsalva maneuver, consistent with autonomic dysfunction.
Nerve conduction studies confirmed both large and small fibre sensory neuropathy in the patient, coinciding with lancinating lower-extremity pain.
Venlafaxine was prescribed for the patient's neuropathic pain and anxiety and provided adequate pain management long-term.
A gastric emptying study confirmed markedly delayed liquid gastric emptying (half-time extrapolated to 57 minutes vs normal 6–20 minutes for 50% emptying), confirming gastroparesis.

Multiple medications for gastroparesis (metoclopramide, ondansetron, domperidone, erythromycin, nabilone, ketamine, prucalopride, haloperidol) and intrapyloric botulinum toxin injections were unsuccessful or had little effect on the patient's nausea and vomiting.
Ten months after starting treatment, the patient developed microalbuminuria (1.49 g/g vs normal <0.15) with unaffected glomerular filtration rate.

Over the following year and a half, the patient's orthostatic hypotension improved (midodrine was discontinued), retinopathy improved, and microalbuminuria returned to normal with HbA1c stabilizing between 6.1% and 7.1%.

In a 2015 retrospective review of 954 patients followed for diabetic neuropathy in Boston, up to 10% of patients had an abrupt increase in neuropathic pain or autonomic symptoms after rapid glucose correction, versus 4.3% risk among patients whose HbA1c was lowered by less than 2 percentage points over 3 months.
Treatment-induced neuropathy of diabetes occurs more frequently in type 1 than type 2 diabetes; in one study, 76 of 104 patients with the condition had type 1 diabetes.
Orthostatic hypotension is reported in 69% of treatment-induced neuropathy of diabetes cases, occurring more frequently in type 1 than type 2 diabetes.

In a small study of 16 patients with acute painful neuropathy, nausea occurred in 69% and vomiting in 56%, showing that gastrointestinal symptoms are common in treatment-induced neuropathy of diabetes.

In the Diabetes Control and Complications Trial (n=1441 type 1 diabetes patients), early retinopathy developed in 22% of patients receiving intensive insulin therapy compared with 13% on conventional therapy, occurring as early as 3 months after treatment start, though intensive control improved outcomes overall over 18 years.
In a retrospective study of 104 patients with treatment-induced neuropathy of diabetes, microalbuminuria prevalence rose from 17% at baseline to 84% at 1 year after diagnosis of neuropathy.

In a small longitudinal cohort of 26 patients with treatment-induced neuropathy of diabetes followed for 8 years, all 19 patients who maintained stable adequate glycemic control (HbA1c 6-8.5%) had gradual improvement and near-complete functional recovery of neuropathic symptoms, whereas all 7 with poor unstable control worsened.

The proposed mechanisms of treatment-induced neuropathy of diabetes include apoptosis induced by sudden glucose deprivation, formation of arteriovenous shunts causing endoneural ischemia, and regeneration of nerve fibres causing pain.
The patient had elevated ganglionic acetylcholine receptor alpha-3 subunit antibodies (75 pmol/L), supporting a diagnosis of autoimmune GI dysmotility.
The patient also had an elevated voltage-gated potassium channel antibody titer (92 pmol/L) as part of the antiganglionic antibody panel supporting AGID diagnosis.

Treatment with a 5-day course of intravenous methylprednisolone (1 g) plus oral pyridostigmine led to significant symptomatic improvement, resolution of need for gastric drainage, and tolerance of a normal diet by day 5.
A trial of metoclopramide and erythromycin (prokinetic agents) produced no improvement in the patient's GI dysmotility symptoms.

In AGID, IgG-mediated antiganglionic autoantibodies target receptors including gAChR, voltage-gated potassium channel, P/Q-type and N-type voltage-gated calcium channels, and glutamic acid decarboxylase, causing reduced neurotransmitter signaling despite preserved ganglionic structure.

The authors postulate that the patient's autoimmune GI dysmotility may be related to her chronic HIV infection, noting HIV is strongly associated with immune activation and that a subset of HIV-positive patients develop GI dysmotility including gastroparesis and intestinal dysmotility, with antiacetylcholine receptor autoantibodies implicated in some cases.
The authors note that vagally mediated HIV-associated GI dysmotility (distinct from AGID) does not respond to steroid treatment.
High antiganglionic antibody titer (greater than 0.5 nmol/L) is stated to typically correlate with more advanced disease and systemic dysautonomia in AGID.
Pooled prevalence of fatigue across included long COVID studies was 47%.
Pooled prevalence of dyspnoea (shortness of breath) across included studies was 32%.
Pooled prevalence of myalgia (muscle pain) across included studies was 25%.
Pooled prevalence of joint pain (arthralgia) across included studies was 20%.
Pooled prevalence of altered smell (anosmia) was 14% and altered taste (dysgeusia) was 7% across included studies.
The severity of acute COVID-19 (mild, moderate, severe) correlated with likelihood of ongoing symptoms at 8-12 weeks, with 59% of mild, 75% of moderate and 89% of severe cases still symptomatic.
At six months, 76% of previously hospitalised patients reported at least one persistent symptom, with a higher proportion in women who also had greater odds of fatigue or weakness.

Older age, female gender, hospital admission at symptom onset, initial dyspnoea, chest pain, abnormal auscultation findings, higher acute symptom load, and comorbidities (particularly asthma) were significantly associated with increased risk of developing persistent long COVID symptoms.
A significant association between anosmia-dysgeusia and younger age (<65) was found at 10-14 weeks in one study but was not replicated in another study's analysis at 8 weeks.
PROMIS Global Health-10 scores showed significantly lower physical and mental health t-scores and reduced ability to carry out social activities 4-6 weeks after hospitalisation compared to baseline.

Six months after hospital discharge for COVID-19-related ARDS, patients had significantly worse EQ-5D index and EQ-VAS scores compared to before infection, and only 30.8% reported no limitations in daily activities.
A quarter of patients had moderate-to-severe PTSD symptoms and 18.3% had mild PTSD symptoms at eight weeks follow-up, with over 40% reporting comorbid depression and 7.4% reporting suicidality.

PTSD occurrence and severity was significantly higher in women, in patients with severe acute COVID-19, and in those with higher acute symptom burden; inadequate social support and perceived stigmatisation were also linked to more severe PTSD symptoms.
A substantial proportion of previously hospitalised patients were unable to return to work due to long COVID: 40% within eight weeks in one study and nearly 70% at three months in another.
Cardiac MRI in college athletes 12-53 days after non-hospitalised COVID-19 infection showed evidence of myocarditis or prior myocardial injury in 46% of cases.
Cardiac MRI performed 2-3 months after COVID-19 onset showed abnormal findings in 78% of patients and myocardial inflammation in 60%, independent of severity of acute illness.

Higher admission D-dimer level was significantly associated with reduced diffusion lung capacity for carbon monoxide (DLCO <80%), suggesting D-dimer as a potential biomarker for predicting DLCO decline.

At six months, lung diffusion impairment was found in 34% of previously hospitalised patients and radiological abnormalities including fibrosis were seen in the majority of those with abnormal lung function.

MRI (diffusion tensor imaging and 3D T1-weighted imaging) of previously hospitalised COVID-19 patients suggested possible disruption to microstructural and functional brain integrity at three months, alongside reports of encephalitis, seizures, mood swings and cognitive impairment.
About one-third of previously hospitalised patients who had acute kidney injury during acute COVID-19 did not fully regain renal function by discharge or post-hospitalisation follow-up.
Two studies reported newly diagnosed diabetes mellitus in patients following hospitalisation for COVID-19, though the aetiology requires further research.

A meta-analysis of 28 follow-up studies of SARS and MERS survivors found approximately 25% had reduced lung function and exercise capacity six months after hospital discharge, with PTSD, depression, anxiety, and reduced quality of life persisting at one year.
Presence of more than five symptoms in the first week of acute COVID-19 infection was significantly associated with development of long COVID, irrespective of age or gender.
Readmission rates of previously hospitalised long COVID patients ranged from 1.4% to 15% across studies, with one study finding 15% of patients required readmission within eight weeks of discharge.
The probability of Long COVID symptoms persisting beyond 35 weeks was 91.8%, with no significant difference by test status or sex.
Severe/very severe symptom probability peaked during acute infection (<28 days), while moderate/mild symptom probability rose gradually afterward.
Participants who did not recover within 90 days had a higher and more persistent peak symptom count (17.16 at month 2) than those who recovered within 90 days (11.35 at week 2).
Nearly all respondents reported systemic (99.7%) and HEENT (100%) symptoms during their illness.
The three symptoms patients rated as most debilitating were fatigue, breathing issues, and cognitive dysfunction.
Participants experienced an average of 55.9 (±25.5) distinct symptoms over the course of their illness, out of 203 assayed.
Symptoms clustered into three groups with distinct temporal shapes (early-peaking, stable, and delayed/increasing), each spanning multiple organ systems.
On average, each respondent's illness affected 9.08 distinct organ systems.
Brain fog and cognitive dysfunction, including poor attention, executive functioning, and decision-making, were reported by 85.1% of respondents.
Memory impairments, including both short- and long-term memory loss, were reported by 72.8% of respondents.
Among respondents with memory/cognitive dysfunction who underwent brain MRI, 87% of scans showed no abnormalities despite ongoing symptoms.
Sensorimotor symptoms were the most common neuropsychiatric category, reported by 91.44% of respondents.
78.6% of respondents experienced difficulty with sleep.
Nearly half of respondents (43.4%) received a diagnosis of at least one new condition following acute COVID-19 infection.
Among respondents reporting tachycardia who could compare standing vs. sitting heart rate, 30.65% showed an orthostatic heart rate increase of at least 30 BPM, consistent with possible POTS.
6.9% of respondents reported current or recent Epstein-Barr virus infection/reactivation following COVID-19.
2.8% of respondents reported shingles (varicella zoster reactivation) since SARS-CoV-2 infection.
1.7% of respondents reported current or recent Lyme infection after COVID-19.
1.4% of respondents reported current or recent CMV infection after COVID-19.
89.1% of participants reported post-exertional malaise (worsening of symptoms after physical or mental activity), a core ME/CFS diagnostic criterion.
Symptom prevalence did not significantly differ between SARS-CoV-2 test-positive and test-negative respondents for the vast majority of the 203 symptoms assayed.
Loss of smell and taste were significantly more prevalent in SARS-CoV-2 test-positive respondents than test-negative respondents, the only symptoms differing by test status.
For 65 of 66 detailed symptoms, time-course trajectories overlapped substantially between confirmed COVID-positive respondents and those without a positive test.
A minimum of 85.9% of respondents reported experiencing symptom relapses.
Physical activity, stress, exercise, and mental activity were the most commonly reported triggers of symptom relapse/worsening.
More than a third of menstruating participants experienced symptom relapses during or before menstruation.

Among the 65.2% of respondents with symptoms for at least six months, the top remaining symptoms were systemic and neurological: fatigue, PEM, cognitive dysfunction, sensorimotor symptoms, headaches, and memory issues.
Among respondents with cognitive/memory symptoms who underwent brain MRI, the large majority showed no abnormalities, suggesting a lack of gross structural correlate for cognitive symptoms.
A large majority of respondents reported difficulty with sleep at some point during their illness.
Nearly a quarter of respondents reported hallucinations during their illness course.
Nearly half of respondents reported speech and language issues during their illness.
The majority of respondents reported headaches during their illness.
A substantial minority of menstruating respondents reported relapse of long COVID symptoms occurring during or just before menstruation, suggesting a hormonal-cycle link.
Nearly half of respondents were diagnosed with at least one new medical condition following acute COVID-19 infection.
On average, respondents experienced symptoms affecting approximately nine distinct organ systems, underscoring the multisystem nature of long COVID.
Participants reported experiencing a large average number of distinct symptoms over the course of their illness.
Patients identified fatigue, breathing issues, and cognitive dysfunction as the top three most debilitating symptoms of long COVID.

Clustering of symptom time-course shapes identified three temporal patterns: symptoms peaking early and declining, symptoms with stable probability throughout, and symptoms increasing sharply in the first two months, with each cluster spanning multiple organ systems.
Memory and cognitive dysfunction had a substantial negative impact on the ability to work, with the majority of working respondents reporting some degree of impairment.
Nearly half of unrecovered respondents were working reduced hours as a result of their illness, and about a quarter had stopped working entirely.
Among self-management strategies tried, pacing (activity management) was rated as significantly helpful by the largest fraction of respondents relative to other treatments.
Unrecovered respondents rated their current health much further from their pre-COVID baseline than recovered respondents.
Respondents who still experienced post-exertional malaise at six months had a higher symptom burden than those whose PEM had resolved or who never experienced it.
A minority of the cohort was hospitalized for acute COVID-19 illness, indicating most respondents had non-severe acute disease.
ME/CFS patients show anatomic, physiologic, and electrical abnormalities in the brain.

Elements of the immune system are chronically activated in ME/CFS patients, in some cases becoming exhausted, including chronic activation of brain innate immunity (neuroinflammation) and evidence of autoimmunity with autoantibodies targeting the central and autonomic nervous system.
People with ME/CFS have impaired cellular energy metabolism, reflected in a reduced ability of cells to generate ATP, along with associated oxidative stress/redox imbalance.
The autonomic nervous system is dysregulated in ME/CFS, with one consequence appearing to be impaired blood flow to the brain.
ME/CFS is associated with characteristic gut microbiome abnormalities, including increased pro-inflammatory bacterial species and decreased butyrate-producing anti-inflammatory species.

The U.S. National Academy of Medicine estimated in 2015, after reviewing over 9000 publications, that 836,000 to 2.5 million people in the U.S. suffer from ME/CFS, making it somewhat more common than multiple sclerosis, and classified it as a serious, chronic, complex systemic disease.
The COVID-19 pandemic appears to be producing millions of new cases of an ME/CFS-like condition, prompting more than $1 billion in NIH funding to study post-COVID chronic illnesses.

27% (10 of 37) of COVID-19 survivors developed ME/CFS-like symptoms (fatigue, sleep disturbance, pain, mood changes, subjective cognitive complaints) persisting beyond 6 months after SARS-CoV-2 infection recovery.
Sleep quality impairment (PSQI) was significantly worse in COVID-19 survivors with ME/CFS-like symptoms compared to those without.
Fatigue (measured with the Multidimensional Fatigue Inventory) was significantly more severe in ME/CFS+ than ME/CFS− COVID-19 survivors.
Pain severity (0-10 Numerical Rating Scale) was significantly higher in ME/CFS+ than ME/CFS− COVID-19 survivors.
Depressive symptoms (HADS) were significantly more severe in ME/CFS+ than ME/CFS− COVID-19 survivors, while anxiety did not differ.
Anxiety scores did not differ significantly between ME/CFS+ and ME/CFS− COVID-19 survivors.
Subjective cognitive complaints (attention, concentration, memory difficulties) were significantly worse in ME/CFS+ than ME/CFS− COVID-19 survivors.
Objective neuropsychological test scores (MoCA, Symbol Digit Test, Stroop test) did not differ between ME/CFS+ and ME/CFS− COVID-19 survivors, despite the subjective cognitive complaint difference.
Lung function (FVC, FEV1, TLC, DLCO, KCO) was within normal range and did not differ significantly between ME/CFS+ and ME/CFS− COVID-19 survivors.

Perceived baseline dyspnea (Borg scale at start of the 6-minute walking test) was significantly higher in ME/CFS+ than ME/CFS− patients, despite normal objective lung function, suggesting a functional component to dyspnea perception.

Serum neurofilament light chain (NfL) levels were normal in nearly all patients (one exception) and did not differ between ME/CFS+ and ME/CFS− COVID-19 survivors, suggesting axonal damage does not underlie ME/CFS-like symptoms.

Socio-demographic data, baseline comorbidities, and clinical/inflammatory features of acute SARS-CoV-2 infection did not differ between ME/CFS+ and ME/CFS− groups, suggesting ME/CFS-like symptom development may be independent of infection severity.
Serum thiol levels are decreased in patients with COVID-19.
Low levels of alveolar Type II cell superoxide dismutase 3 (SOD3) in the lungs of elderly individuals correlate with COVID-19 severity.
People with ME/CFS have decreased levels of α-tocopherol, a marker of oxidative stress.
Increased levels of peroxides and superoxide in ME/CFS patients correlate with severity of symptoms.
Isoprostane levels are elevated in ME/CFS patients both at rest and after exercise.
Brain magnetic resonance spectroscopy reveals elevated ventricular lactic acid levels in ME/CFS patients, consistent with oxidative stress.
ME/CFS patients show multiple biomarkers of nitrosative stress including increased inducible NOS, NO, peroxynitrite, and nitrate, particularly after exercise, compared with healthy controls.
Elevated homocysteine levels, which increase oxidative stress and cardiovascular risk, are seen in both acute COVID-19 and ME/CFS.
NOS2 is significantly up-regulated in patients with severe and critical COVID-19.
Citrulline, a product of arginine metabolism by NOS, is increased in people with ME/CFS.
COVID-19 survivors reportedly exhibit higher serum levels of H2S along with higher numbers of circulating lymphocytes.

The most extensive controlled mtDNA study using contemporary technology did not find mtDNA variants correlating with ME/CFS susceptibility, though it did find correlations between specific mtDNA haplogroups/SNPs and specific symptoms.
A deficit in Complex V (ATP synthase) activity of the electron transport chain has been identified in lymphocytes of ME/CFS patients, with compensatory up-regulation of respiratory capacity.
CD8+ T cells from ME/CFS patients show decreased mitochondrial membrane potential.
People with ME/CFS have significantly higher blood lactate levels after exercise compared with controls, indicating reduced oxidative phosphorylation and a switch to anaerobic glycolysis.
People with ME/CFS have significantly decreased plasma CoQ10 levels, which correlate inversely with fatigue, impaired concentration/memory, and autonomic dysfunction symptoms.
Increased levels of C-reactive protein and IL-6 were associated with more severe COVID-19 disease.
Impaired NK cell function is a characteristic finding in people with ME/CFS, and redox imbalance leading to increased l-kynurenine and lactate can impair NK cell function.
Inhaled nitric oxide improves oxygenation in people with COVID-19 and inhibits SARS-CoV-2 replication in vitro.
Small studies of ubiquinol and of a combination of NADH and CoQ10 reported clinical benefit, presumably in ME/CFS patients.
In two cases of acute COVID-19, therapeutically administered glutathione counteracted dyspnea and reduced pulmonary inflammation.
A screen for inhibitors of the SARS-CoV-2 main protease identified ebselen, an organoselenium compound, as a potential Mpro/NSP5 inhibitor and therapeutic agent for COVID-19.
Oral therapies directed at restoring redox balance have generally not produced dramatic improvements in conditions associated with redox imbalance.
No DTI parameter showed a statistically significant difference between ME/CFS patients meeting the broader Fukuda criteria and healthy controls, even after relaxing statistical thresholds.

ME/CFSICC patients showed significantly decreased axial diffusivity in a brainstem cluster tracking fibres from motor and premotor cortices through the midbrain to the pons, compared to healthy controls.
Mean diffusivity was significantly decreased in brainstem regions similar to the AD deficit (midbrain to ventral pons) in ME/CFSICC patients compared to controls.
The transverse eigenvalue λ2 was significantly decreased in the same brainstem cluster as MD in ME/CFSICC patients relative to healthy controls.
Mode of anisotropy was significantly decreased at a focus in the superior longitudinal fasciculus in ME/CFSICC patients compared to healthy controls.
λ3, the eigenvalue transverse to fibres, was significantly increased in the dorsal medulla near the sensory decussation in ME/CFSICC patients compared to healthy controls.
Radial diffusivity showed a group difference between ME/CFSICC and controls initially, but this lost statistical significance after correcting for multiple comparisons.
Group comparison of FA did not show any significant differences between ME/CFSICC patients and healthy controls, contrasting with two prior DTI studies that reported FA differences.

AD, MD and RD showed abnormal (opposite-signed) regression relationships with information processing score (Procinfo) in the hippocampus and parahippocampal gyrus between ME/CFSICC patients and controls.
MD and RD showed abnormal interaction-with-group regressions with information processing score in the corpus callosum, posterior cingulate and Brodmann area 36 in ME/CFSICC compared to controls.
MD alone also formed a significant abnormal interaction-with-group regression cluster with information processing score in the external capsule.
FA showed an abnormal interaction-with-group regression with SF36 physical score (Phys_all) in Brodmann Area 2 in ME/CFSICC compared to controls.
FA showed an abnormal interaction-with-group regression with sleep disturbance score (SDS) in Brodmann Area 44 (inferior frontal gyrus) in ME/CFSICC compared to controls.

MD and RD showed abnormal interaction-with-group regressions with respiratory rate in Brodmann Area 9 (prefrontal cortex) in ME/CFSICC compared to controls; RD alone also showed a cluster in the cerebellar tonsil.
PregS-induced TRPM3-like outward current amplitudes in NK cells from ME/CFS patients taking LDN were restored to the same level as healthy controls.

PregS-evoked ionic currents were significantly reduced by the TRPM3 blocker ononetin in NK cells from ME/CFS patients taking LDN, similar to healthy controls, whereas untreated ME/CFS NK cells were previously reported as ononetin-resistant.
ME/CFS patients had significantly worse SF-36 and WHODAS quality-of-life and disability scores compared to healthy controls.
Eosinophil counts differed significantly between ME/CFS patients taking LDN and healthy controls, though all values remained within normal reference ranges.
NK cell purity did not differ significantly between ME/CFS patients taking LDN and healthy controls.

ME/CFS patients self-reported improvement in cognitive symptoms (impaired thought, concentration, cognitive overload) and immune-related symptoms (sore throat, tender lymph nodes, susceptibility to colds/influenza) after starting LDN treatment.

In a prior retrospective study cited by the authors, 73.9% of ME/CFS patients administered LDN reported a positive treatment response, with improved vigilance, physical/cognitive performance, and reduced pain.
Prior literature cited by the authors reports reduced beta-endorphin concentrations in ME/CFS patients experiencing thermoregulatory dysregulation and generalized severe or long-lasting pain.

Prior independent electrophysiological studies from three ME/CFS cohorts demonstrated TRPM3 ion channel loss-of-function after stimulation with PregS and nifedipine and inhibition with ononetin in NK cells.
The authors previously reported that in vitro treatment of ME/CFS NK cells with naltrexone (NTX) for 24 hours restores TRPM3 ion channel activity.
The overall meta-analytic prevalence of CFS in Korean studies (0.77%) was very similar to that in Japanese studies (0.76%).

Korean studies showed an approximately two-fold female predominance in CFS prevalence (1.31% female vs. 0.60% male), whereas this sex difference was much less pronounced in Japanese studies (0.76% female vs. 0.65% male).

Diagnostic method (interview only vs. interview with medical tests per CDC-1994 guideline) did not appear to strongly affect the overall CFS prevalence rate in this Korea/Japan analysis, contrasting with a prior global meta-analysis finding.
CFS prevalence rates in Korea and Japan were somewhat lower than those reported in Western countries (UK and USA) using the same CDC-1994 criteria.

In a joint meta-analysis of four DNA methylation array studies, the ACE2 promoter-region CpG probe cg08559914 showed significantly decreased methylation in ME/CFS patients versus healthy controls, suggestive of increased ACE2 expression.

Four CpG probes in the ACE gene (one TSS, three gene body) showed a significant overall association with ME/CFS in the methylation meta-analysis, with methylation tending lower in patients although the disease-status main effect alone was not significant.
Pooling estimates across microarray gene-expression studies, ACE2 mRNA was significantly reduced in PBMCs of ME/CFS patients compared to healthy controls.
Pooled gene-expression estimates across microarray studies showed no significant difference in ACE mRNA between ME/CFS patients and healthy controls.

In the new German cohort, ACE2 mRNA was undetectable (below limit of detection) in a significantly higher proportion of ME/CFS patients than healthy controls, suggestive of reduced ACE2 expression in patients.
Using complete-case data from the new German cohort, ACE2 mRNA levels did not differ significantly between ME/CFS patients and healthy controls.
In the new German cohort, ACE mRNA levels did not differ significantly between ME/CFS patients and healthy controls, consistent with the meta-analysis.
Re-analysis of the Saiki et al. 2008 microarray study showed increased ACE expression in ME/CFS patients compared to healthy controls.
Re-analysis of the Gow et al. 2009 microarray study (whole blood) showed reduced ACE2 expression in ME/CFS patients, based on two ACE2 probes.
Fletcher et al. reported a large significant negative association between ME/CFS and ACE2 expression, re-analyzed by the authors as a mean log2(fold-change) of -2.396.

A targeted stress-response gene expression study found no significant difference in ADAM17 (a candidate SARS-CoV-2 co-receptor/ACE2 sheddase) expression between ME/CFS patients and healthy controls, likely underpowered.
One of the selected DNA methylation studies found decreased methylation of an ADAM17-related CpG probe in ME/CFS patients, consistent with a possible increase in this ACE2-cleaving protease.
Prior evidence cited shows an increased proportion of natural killer cells and T cells expressing DPP4/CD26, a candidate coronavirus receptor, in patients with ME/CFS.
Despite more cells expressing DPP4/CD26, the number of DPP4/CD26 molecules per cell was significantly reduced in T lymphocytes and natural killer cells of ME/CFS patients.
Across published ME/CFS genome-wide association studies, no candidate SNPs in ACE or ACE2 were reported as significantly associated with ME/CFS, and two studies found no significant SNPs overall.
In a cited clinical trial, treating ME/CFS patients with clonidine to reduce sustained arousal worsened their symptoms and increased inflammation markers.
A cited preliminary report suggested that ME/CFS patients experienced worsened symptoms following SARS-CoV-2 infection.

Fatigue severity after IMP-FITNET or face-to-face CBT delivered in routine clinical care fell within the 95% CI of the benchmark FITNET RCT, with baseline fatigue scores decreasing on average from 49.8 to 26.0.
All secondary outcomes (physical functioning, school attendance, recovery rates) in the routine clinical care cohort fell within the 95% CIs of the benchmark FITNET RCT.
Just over half (58.1%) of adolescents treated with IMP-FITNET met predefined recovery criteria posttreatment.
75.5% of adolescents with posttreatment fatigue data showed a reliable clinically significant improvement (RCI>1.96) and scored below the severe-fatigue cutoff after IMP-FITNET.
The within-treatment effect size of IMP-FITNET on fatigue severity (Cohen d=2.28) was large and fell within the 95% CI of the benchmark FITNET RCT effect size (d=2.73, CI 2.26-3.21).

The rate of clinically significant deterioration in fatigue severity after IMP-FITNET (1.2%) was not significantly different from the deterioration rate in a waiting-list control condition from a benchmark CBT study (5.7%).
The rate of clinically significant deterioration in physical functioning after IMP-FITNET (4.1%) did not significantly differ from that of a waiting-list benchmark condition (11.4%).
The proportion of adolescents lost to follow-up was significantly higher in routine clinical care IMP-FITNET (8.5%) than in the benchmark FITNET RCT (3.0%).

At baseline, adolescents referred for care in the routine clinical setting were less severely fatigued, less physically impaired, had less school absence, and had shorter symptom duration than patients enrolled in the benchmark FITNET RCT.
Adolescents who received face-to-face CBT rather than IMP-FITNET were younger, more often male, and had significantly longer symptom duration than the benchmark RCT sample.
Nearly half of adolescents completed IMP-FITNET without any face-to-face consultation, while about 42% had at least one, indicating substantial use of blended care in routine practice.
Videoconferencing was offered to 50 IMP-FITNET patients starting treatment in 2017, and nearly half (46%) used it, with an average of about 5 sessions of roughly 24 minutes each.
Therapists reported preferring face-to-face CBT over IMP-FITNET when there were family interaction problems or when the patient had psychiatric or somatic comorbidities.
Adolescents who dropped out before posttreatment assessment had significantly higher baseline physical functioning than those who completed treatment.
A meta-analysis of 11 studies (from 17 identified in the systematic review) found that HHV-6 infection is significantly associated with chronic fatigue syndrome.

The authors argue that biomedicine's emphasis on diagnosable disease and measurable biomarkers over patients' illness experience leads to functional somatic syndromes like fibromyalgia and chronic fatigue syndrome being met with clinician suspicion and biased social narratives.
The Beighton hypermobility score was significantly higher in hEDS patients than in HSD patients.
Overall clinical severity as measured by the CSS-16 questionnaire was significantly higher in hEDS patients than HSD patients.
Anamnestic bone fragility (non-traumatic fractures or low bone mineral density) did not significantly differ between hEDS and HSD patients.
Neuropathic pain detection (DN4 score) suggestive of small-fiber neuropathy did not significantly differ between hEDS and HSD patients, occurring in about half of both groups.
Suspected mast cell activation syndrome (MCAS) symptoms (flush and/or dermographism) were highly prevalent (~45%) but did not significantly differ between hEDS and HSD patients.
Spontaneous bleeding severity was significantly greater in patients with suspected MCAS compared with those without.
Spontaneous bleeding problems were significantly more severe in hEDS than HSD patients, suggesting bleeding severity could serve as an additional specific hEDS symptom.
A coordinated physical therapy management program produced similar improvement rates in hEDS and HSD patients, with no significant difference in outcome by diagnostic category at 6 or 20 months.
Family history of hypermobility was the only independent predictor of favorable evolution at end of follow-up on multivariate analysis.
Bilateral piezogenic papules of the heel, added as a 2017 diagnostic criterion feature, did not differ significantly in prevalence between hEDS and HSD patients.

In this referral cohort, 42% (61/97 included patients, though phrased as of those referred) of patients attending a hypermobility-dedicated consultation met the 2017 hEDS diagnostic criteria, indicating hEDS is not rare in this clinical setting.
Patients lost to follow-up at T1 and T2 had lower baseline CSS-16 severity scores and were more often classified as HSD than hEDS, compared with those retained in follow-up.
Dysautonomia was identified in 65% of female and 44% of male patients with hEDS/HSD.
Exercise intolerance was the most common symptom associated with dysautonomia in hEDS/HSD patients, present in 78% of cases.
Exercise capacity was limited by dysautonomia, often related to postural symptoms, in half of all patients studied.
The proportion of dysautonomic patients with sedentary lifestyle increased from 44% to 85% following the onset or significant flare of hEDS/HSD.
Dysautonomia in hEDS/HSD patients was associated with smaller cardiac chamber sizes on echocardiography, consistent with cardiac atrophy from aerobic deconditioning.
Cardiac chamber size and geometry findings in hEDS/HSD-related dysautonomia parallel prior reports of similar cardiac findings in POTS.
Skeletal craniofacial morphology in both sagittal and vertical dimensions did not differ significantly between hEDS patients and healthy controls.
Incisal relationship measures (overjet and overbite) did not differ significantly between hEDS patients and controls.
In unadjusted analysis, patients with hEDS had significantly smaller pharyngeal airway volume than healthy controls.
In unadjusted analysis, patients with hEDS had significantly smaller minimum cross-sectional area of the upper airway than healthy controls.
After adjusting for age, gender and BMI, differences in airway volume and minimum cross-sectional area between hEDS patients and controls were no longer statistically significant.
After adjustment for age, gender and BMI, minimum cross-sectional area remained near-significantly smaller in hEDS patients, suggesting a possible residual impact of hEDS on upper airway dimensions.

Prior studies cited by the authors found that obstructive sleep apnea is significantly more frequent in EDS patients compared to controls, although airway volume and minimum cross-sectional area had not previously been studied in EDS.
A 2017 patient survey by EDS Support UK found that the average time between symptom presentation and diagnosis of HSD/hEDS in Scotland was 19 years.
In the same cited 2017 survey, 87% of HSD/hEDS patients in Scotland felt their condition was not well supported by the NHS.
83% of the same surveyed patients reported no access to a medical professional knowledgeable about their condition.
The most common source of therapy referrals for HSD/hEDS patients in Scotland was rheumatology teams, reported by 95% of therapist respondents, followed by GPs (60%).
Most therapist respondents (65%) reported that referrals they received still used older terminology rather than the 2017 EDS International Classification terms.

Fewer therapists managing adult HSD/hEDS patients had access to a pain management programme (55%) compared with those managing paediatric patients (89%), though this difference did not reach statistical significance.
Therapists managing adult HSD/hEDS patients had significantly less access to a clinical psychologist (28%) than those managing paediatric patients (89%).
Overall, 80% of therapist respondents reported feeling confident in the assessment and treatment of HSD/hEDS, although 31% of occupational therapists specifically reported not feeling confident.
Nearly all therapist respondents (94.7%) were in favour of establishing a specialist centre in Scotland for training and education in the management of HSD/hEDS.
The authors cite prior work showing psychological distress is significantly higher in patients with hypermobility compared with those without hypermobility.
Cited literature indicates that fatigue, anxiety and depression have a greater impact on health than pain in this patient group, although pain has a moderate impact on disability.

Cited literature indicates HSD/hEDS patients have a higher likelihood of anxiety, depression and panic disorders, and often report guilt and low self-esteem related to poor perception of the condition by health-care providers.
Only 20% of surveyed therapists had previously received specialist external training in HSD/hEDS management, despite the majority reporting moderate confidence in assessment and treatment.
Thirty-five per cent of therapist respondents reported that more than half of their caseload consisted of HSD/hEDS patients with complex needs.
A condition-specific pain management programme for hypermobility patients developed by Rahman et al. showed substantial and continuous improvement across several outcome measures.
A pregnant woman with vascular (type IV) EDS and a prior history of cerebrovascular complications had a successful delivery at a tertiary centre through coordinated multidisciplinary management.
The overall prevalence of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome across all subtypes is estimated at 1 in 10,000 to 1 in 20,000.
The combined prevalence of EDS in adults is historically estimated at about 1 in 5000, with classical EDS at 1 in 20,000 and vascular EDS at 1 in 50,000.
Patients with EDS commonly experience a diagnostic delay of 4 to 16 years while navigating the health care system.
Chronic orthostatic intolerance syndromes, including vasovagal syncope, POTS, and orthostatic hypotension/autonomic failure, are a prevalent clinical finding in patients with EDS.
Small fiber neuropathy has been reported as a standard feature in EDS that may partly explain widespread neuropathic pain.
Disorders of gut-brain interaction, such as irritable bowel syndrome, appear to be more common in EDS patients and are often challenging to manage.
People living with EDS have high rates of depression and anxiety, similar to those with other chronic illnesses.
Emerging evidence suggests benefit of respiratory muscle training for EDS patients with significant reductions in respiratory muscle strength.

One-day Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT) workshops have been shown to reduce distress and improve engagement with meaningful activities and health behaviour in people with chronic health conditions.

The GoodHope EDS Clinic has assessed over 1,000 patients for possible EDS/HSD and continues to follow approximately 400 patients confirmed to meet criteria for EDS or Generalized Hypermobility Spectrum Disorder (G-HSD).

The authors propose that the genetic connective tissue defect in Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome increases peripheral nerve vulnerability to mechanical stress, predisposing this patient to iatrogenic nerve injury during thoracotomy.
Post-thoracotomy pain syndrome (PTPS) is reported to occur in approximately 50% of patients undergoing thoracotomy, most often due to intercostal nerve injury.

In the EDS patient, intense burning pain, allodynia, and numbness developed along the right T5 dermatome shortly after posterolateral thoracotomy, consistent with intercostal nerve injury causing PTPS.

Six months after thoracotomy, the EDS patient developed continuous involuntary jerk-like contractions of the right latissimus dorsi muscle, attributed to right thoracodorsal nerve injury from the surgery.

Surface and needle EMG confirmed semi-rhythmic bursts of continuous discharges and chronic reinnervation changes in the right latissimus dorsi muscle, supporting a peripheral (thoracodorsal nerve) origin for the jerks.
Epidural injection of ropivacaine and betamethasone at T5-T6 produced partial relief of the patient's spontaneous and evoked PTPS pain, though numbness and involuntary movements persisted.
Treatment with eslicarbazepine, levetiracetam, and clonazepam produced no therapeutic response for the involuntary latissimus dorsi jerks.

Botulinum toxin type A injections into the right latissimus dorsi muscle markedly reduced the continuous involuntary contractions, with the effect repeatedly reproduced on periodic (quarterly) re-injection.
Despite reducing the muscle jerks, BTX-A injections provided no therapeutic benefit for the patient's sensory symptoms.
Surgical revision, generally a first-line treatment for peripheral-origin jerk-like movements, was avoided in this patient because her EDS diagnosis raised concern for wound-healing complications.
At the left prefrontal cortex, the increase in HbO concentration (Δ-HbO*) from the innocuous to noxious thermal stimulus was significantly smaller in fibromyalgia patients than in controls.
At the right prefrontal cortex, the Δ-HbO* increase from innocuous to noxious stimulus did not significantly differ between fibromyalgia patients and controls.
Peak latency of HbO at the left motor cortex increased significantly more from primary to secondary thermal stimulus in fibromyalgia patients than controls, indicating slower cortical activation.

Δ-HbO (activation magnitude, not deactivation) at the left motor cortex increased less from primary to secondary stimulus in fibromyalgia patients than in controls, indicating lower cortical activation.
Fibromyalgia patients showed a significantly greater relative increase in Δ-HbO* at the left motor cortex than controls, reflecting lower post-stimulus cortical deactivation.
At the right motor cortex, fibromyalgia patients showed a marginally greater increase in Δ-HbO* than controls, suggestive of reduced cortical deactivation.

Cortical deactivation (Δ-HbO*) measured at either the left or right prefrontal cortex discriminated fibromyalgia patients from controls with at least 85% sensitivity and 80% specificity in ROC analysis.

Lower Δ-HbO* (cortical deactivation) at the left prefrontal cortex was positively correlated with greater disability due to pain and higher central sensitization symptom scores in fibromyalgia patients.

In contrast to the left side, lower Δ-HbO* at the right prefrontal cortex was inversely (conversely) associated with disability due to pain and central sensitization symptom severity, suggesting hemispheric asymmetry in PFC involvement.

A ROC analysis using the left PFC Δ-HbO* cutoff of -0.175 achieved 100% sensitivity and 98% specificity to discriminate fibromyalgia patients from controls, and yielded an AUC of 0.82 for screening severity of central sensitization symptoms.

Fibromyalgia patients showed more severe clinical symptoms (central sensitization, disability, depressive symptoms, anxiety, pain catastrophizing) and higher medication (analgesic) use compared to controls, alongside older age, higher BMI, and fewer years of education.
A dextrose concentration of at least 5% was necessary to produce antinociceptive (prolotherapy) effects in a mouse model of chronic muscle hyperalgesia.
Injection volume greater than 10 μL was required for dextrose to exert its antinociceptive prolotherapy effect.
Osmolarity of the injectant was not essential for the dextrose-induced antinociceptive effect, distinguishing it from dose and volume factors.
Activation of ASIC1a was required for dextrose-induced reduction of mechanical hypersensitivity in the mouse model of chronic muscle pain.
Both pharmacological blockade and genetic deletion of ASIC1a abolished the dextrose-induced antinociception in mice with chronic hyperalgesia.

Release of substance P from muscle afferents was required for the dextrose-induced reduction of mechanical hypersensitivity, and both pharmacological blockade and genetic deletion of substance P abolished this antinociceptive effect.
Lidocaine, used to block local neural activation, abolished the dextrose-induced antinociception, indicating a requirement for local neural activity in muscle afferents.
Intramuscular dextrose injection induced phosphorylated ERK (pERK) expression in dorsal root ganglion neurons that also expressed substance P.
Intramuscular dextrose injection induced phosphorylated ERK expression in dorsal root ganglion neurons that also expressed substance P.
The ASIC1a antagonist PcTx1 inhibited the dextrose-induced increase in phosphorylated ERK expression in DRG neurons, linking ASIC1a activity to this downstream signaling.
Mast cells lacking STAP-2 show significantly reduced IL-33-induced IL-6 and TNF-α production compared with wild-type mast cells.
STAP-1-deficient mast cells did not show a significant change in IL-33-induced cytokine production compared with wild-type mast cells, unlike STAP-2-deficient cells.
STAP-2 deficiency greatly reduced TLR4-mediated mast cell activation and cytokine production.
STAP-2 directly binds to IKKα following IL-33 stimulation, resulting in elevated NF-κB activity as the proposed mechanism of mast cell activation.
The fluoroquinolones ciprofloxacin and levofloxacin induced rapid intracellular calcium increases and CD63 degranulation marker upregulation in primary human mast cells (PBCMCs).
Of the two neuromuscular blocking agents tested, atracurium, but not succinylcholine, induced significant PBCMC activation (calcium increase) and degranulation (CD63 upregulation).
Succinylcholine did not significantly activate or degranulate PBCMCs, unlike atracurium, indicating it is not an effective MRGPRX2 agonist in primary human mast cells.

Only MRGPRX2-positive PBCMCs, not MRGPRX2-negative cells, showed significant calcium flux and degranulation in response to ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin, and atracurium, with degranulation most pronounced in cells with highest MRGPRX2 surface expression.

DsiRNA-mediated silencing of MRGPRX2 in PBCMCs reduced receptor expression by more than 70% and prevented mast cell activation and degranulation induced by ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin, and atracurium.
Sugammadex alone did not cause PBCMC activation or degranulation, while atracurium dose-dependently activated and degranulated PBCMCs via MRGPRX2.

Complexing atracurium with sugammadex at a 1:1 molar ratio markedly reduced, but did not completely eliminate, MRGPRX2-mediated PBCMC activation and degranulation, and this reduction was comparable to that produced by free atracurium at the corresponding lower concentration, indicating the effect is due to sequestration of free atracurium rather than direct receptor inhibition by the complex.

PBCMCs from rocuronium-hypersensitive patients with IgE-dependent reactions (positive specific IgE and/or BAT) showed similar MRGPRX2 expression and similar levels of MRGPRX2-mediated activation/degranulation compared to patients with IgE-independent (probably MRGPRX2-mediated) reactions.
S100A4-deficient mice showed substantially lower OVA-specific IgE, IgG, and IgG subclass antibody induction after allergic sensitization and provocation compared with wild-type mice.
Serum IL-4, IL-5, IL-13, IFN-γ, and MCP-1 were augmented after OVA sensitization/challenge in wild-type mice but not upregulated to the same extent in S100A4-/- mice.
Serum IL-6 and TNF-α levels showed no substantial regulation by asthma sensitization/challenge in either wild-type or S100A4-/- mice.

IL-10 showed a trend of higher constitutive expression in unstimulated S100A4-/- mice compared with WT, but was downregulated relative to control after allergic sensitization and challenge in S100A4-/- mice, suggesting a homeostatic role of S100A4.

S100A4-/- mice showed consistently suppressed total and differential inflammatory cell infiltration (neutrophils, eosinophils, macrophages, lymphocytes) in bronchoalveolar lavage fluid after asthma sensitization/challenge compared to wild-type mice.

S100A4-deficient mice showed almost completely suppressed cytokine/chemokine production in BALF after sensitization and challenge compared to wild-type mice, while IL-10 was the only cytokine downregulated in WT mice after provocation.
S100A4-/- mice showed compromised lung tissue inflammatory cell infiltration by histology score after asthmatic challenge compared to wild-type mice.
Challenge-induced mucin overproduction and goblet cell hyperplasia (PAS score) was suppressed in S100A4-/- mice compared to wild-type.
Fewer mast cells were recruited into asthmatic lung tissue of S100A4-deficient mice compared with wild-type mice, as revealed by toluidine blue staining.

Augmented infiltration of dendritic cells, neutrophils, and eosinophils in lung tissue after asthmatic challenge was suppressed in S100A4-deficient mice compared with wild-type mice, while alveolar macrophage infiltration was not increased by challenge in either genotype.
Provocation-induced overproduction of IL-4, IL-6, IL-13, IFN-γ, and MCP-1 in lung tissue homogenates was consistently suppressed in S100A4-deficient mice compared with wild-type mice.
T cells (splenocytes) from S100A4-/- mice showed markedly reduced antigen re-encounter-induced proliferation compared with cells from wild-type mice.
Splenocyte cultures from S100A4-/- mice produced compromised OVA-induced IL-5, IL-6, IL-10, IFN-γ, and MCP-1, with a non-significant trend toward reduced IL-4 and TNF-α.

Bone marrow-derived mast cells (BMMCs) lacking S100A4 showed decreased β-hexosaminidase release (a marker of degranulation) following IgE-crosslinking-mediated activation compared with wild-type BMMCs.
BMMCs deficient in S100A4 produced reduced levels of IL-4, IL-5, IL-6, IL-13, TNF-α, and MCP-1 in culture supernatants after IgE-mediated activation compared with wild-type BMMCs.
IL-10 and IFN-γ levels did not increase significantly after IgE-mediated activation of BMMCs, and no apparent differences were seen between WT and S100A4-/- cells for these cytokines.
In the passive cutaneous anaphylaxis (PCA) model, S100A4-/- mice showed substantially lower Evans blue dye extravasation in IgE-sensitized ears compared with wild-type mice.
Fewer degranulating mast cells (by toluidine blue morphology) were observed in IgE-sensitized ears of S100A4-/- mice compared with wild-type controls in the PCA model.

In the passive systemic anaphylaxis (PSA) model, S100A4-/- mice exhibited a less severe anaphylactic response (temperature loss) and recovered faster than wild-type mice, which sustained a low body temperature.
