Mast cells (cultured BMMCs, peritoneal mast cells, and lung tissue mast cells in asthmatic mice) express S100A4, as demonstrated by GFP reporter expression in S100A4+/+.GFP transgenic mice.

S100A4 deficiency did not affect mast cell differentiation, as indicated by the study title/figure describing that BMMC generation and phenotype were unaffected by genotype despite functional deficits in activation.
Patients with functional gallbladder disorder showed significantly increased mast cell density in the gallbladder wall compared to controls without gallbladder disease.
Mast cells preferentially accumulated in the inner muscular layer of the gallbladder wall in FGD patients.
Mast cell activation, measured by degranulation percentage on toluidine blue stain, was markedly increased in FGD patients compared to controls.

Lactic acid suppressed the early phase of MRGPRX2-mediated mast cell activation, including calcium mobilization and degranulation, in LAD2 cells, human skin mast cells, and mouse peritoneal mast cells.
Lactic acid also suppressed the late phase of mast cell activation, chemokine and cytokine release, downstream of MRGPRX2/MrgprB2 activation.
The inhibitory effect of lactic acid on degranulation and chemokine/cytokine production in LAD2 cells was pH-dependent.
Lactic acid reduced passive systemic anaphylaxis induced by compound 48/80, a known MRGPRX2/MrgprB2 ligand, in a mouse model.
Lactic acid reduced skin inflammation in a mouse model of rosacea that depends on MrgprB2 expression on skin mast cells.
Mast cell activation requires crosslinking of roughly 100-1000 FcεRI receptors, and human mast cells can be activated with as little as 0.3% antigen-specific IgE occupancy.
Different cytokine/chemokine outputs require different FcεRI receptor occupancy thresholds: MCP-1 and IL-4 need low occupancy, degranulation scales linearly, and IL-10 requires high occupancy.

Different mast cell effector functions have distinct temporal thresholds for FcεRI clustering duration: chemokines within 1-4 min, degranulation/some cytokines at 4-8 min, and cytokines like IL-2, IL-13, TNF-α, IFN-γ requiring more than 15 min of clustering.

Despite equal or greater FcεRI phosphorylation with low-affinity NP antigen, NP-induced mast cell degranulation was only one-tenth of DNP-induced degranulation, showing affinity affects downstream outcome independent of receptor phosphorylation.

Low-affinity antigen stimulation of IgE-sensitized mast cells induced more chemokine production but less degranulation, lipid mediator release, and cytokine production, correlating with a shift from LAT1- to LAT2-dependent signaling and formation of fewer, larger IgE-antigen clusters.
In vivo, low-affinity antigen (NP) injection into IgE-sensitized ear skin predominantly recruited monocytes and macrophages, whereas high-affinity antigen (DNP) recruited neutrophils.

Bi- or tri-valent antigens with epitope spacing of 4-5 nm on a rigid scaffold gave the highest mast cell activation, with activation gradually decreasing up to 7 nm (bivalent) or 10 nm (trivalent) spacing.
For intramolecularly repeated epitopes spaced less than 4 nm apart, shorter distances favored mast cell activation, in the order direct repeat > ~2.6 nm > ~3.7 nm.

Combining three IgE clones targeting the same antigen was more effective at activating mast cells than combining two, and when clones of different affinities were combined, the highest-affinity clone was the major determinant of activation kinetics.
Approximately 30% of tested IgE clones (and a similar fraction of IgG clones) were found to bind HRF, with binding mapped to the Fab region but independent of antigen specificity.
In a food-allergic mouse model, intragastric administration of HRF inhibitors significantly reduced diarrhea occurrence and body temperature drop in both preventive and therapeutic settings.
Patients allergic to hen's eggs had elevated HRF-reactive IgE levels in serum, and successful oral immunotherapy induced a sustained reduction in HRF-reactive IgEs.
Elevated circulating HRF levels have been reported in patients with atopic dermatitis, chronic spontaneous urticaria, pulmonary arterial hypertension, and acute liver rejection.
IgE binds FcεRIα with an estimated association constant of approximately 1×10^10 M-1 and an extremely slow dissociation rate (koff ~10^-5 s-1), underlying its long tissue half-life.

Omalizumab binds free IgE and blocks its binding to both FcεRI and CD23; because it does not act on FcεRI-bound IgE, reduction of IgE on mast cells takes longer (~70 days) than on basophils (~7 days), reflecting differing IgE half-lives on each cell type.

Omalizumab is efficacious across a range of allergic diseases and is approved for moderate to severe persistent allergic asthma, chronic idiopathic urticaria, and nasal polyps in the USA, and for severe pollinosis in Japan.

MEDI4212, an anti-IgE antibody with higher affinity than omalizumab, produced quick removal of free IgE in a phase I trial, but its shorter half-life relative to omalizumab led to rapid recovery of free IgE levels.
Ligelizumab, a higher-affinity anti-IgE antibody than omalizumab, failed in the treatment of severe asthma.
Ligelizumab showed superior therapeutic results in chronic spontaneous urticaria, with rapid and sustained reduction of basophil surface IgE and FcεRI levels at a smaller dose than omalizumab.

Quilizumab, targeting membrane IgE-expressing B cells, reduced antigen-specific and total IgE by up to 40%, but this did not translate into clinical improvement, failing to improve CSU and inadequately controlling allergic asthma.

DARPin E2_79 binds Cε3 outside the FcεRI binding site and accelerates dissociation of IgE from FcεRI via a 'facilitated dissociation' mechanism; tandem conjugation of another IgE-binding DARPin improved displacement activity by ~100-fold.
Llama-derived humanized single-domain antibody 026, targeting the Cε3-4 region, displaces IgE from both FcεRI and CD23 by constraining IgE in a closed conformation and via facilitated dissociation.

A Fab fragment (clone 6HD5) binding murine Cε2 reduced mast cell activation in vivo and in vitro, with suppression of passive cutaneous anaphylaxis persisting for up to 10 days after injection, without removing IgE.

Mutational studies show the N394 glycosylation site (N384 in mouse IgE) is absolutely required for FcεRI binding; substitutions such as N394T, N394Q, and disruption of the glycosylation motif (T396A) abolish mast cell activation in vitro and in vivo.

Allergic individuals show increased sialylation and reduced galactose exposure on the IgE N265 glycan (and similarly N140, N168), and experimentally induced asialylation reduces the potency of IgE to trigger degranulation without altering FcεRI or antigen affinity.
Secreted galectin-3, bound on epithelial cell surfaces, can crosslink IgE on sensitized basophils and stimulate IL-4/IL-13 release in vitro.

Galectin-9 binds IgE glycans, reducing its antigen-binding affinity, and suppresses IgE-dependent mast cell activation, shown by attenuated passive cutaneous anaphylaxis in vivo and inhibited degranulation and calcium mobilization in vitro.

A recent report found that IgE-antigen immune complexes are preferentially bound and sequestered by CD23 rather than FcεRI, whereas free IgE is preferentially bound by FcεRI, supporting IgE's role as a sensor rather than for antigen neutralization.
Omalizumab reduces free IgE bound to FcεRI on mast cells more slowly (~70 days) than IgE on basophils (~7 days), reflecting differences in receptor/cell half-life.
At extremely high, non-therapeutic concentrations (50 μM), omalizumab can facilitate dissociation of IgE already bound to FcεRI.
MEDI4212, an anti-IgE antibody with higher affinity than omalizumab, rapidly removed free IgE in a phase I trial but had a shorter half-life, leading to rapid recovery of free IgE levels.
Ligelizumab failed to demonstrate efficacy in severe asthma but showed superior therapeutic results compared to omalizumab in chronic spontaneous urticaria.
Ligelizumab produced a rapid and sustained reduction in basophil surface IgE and FcεRI levels at a smaller dose than omalizumab.
Tandem conjugation of another IgE-binding DARPin to E2_79 improved its ability to displace IgE from FcεRI by approximately 100-fold, likely by increasing avidity.
sdab 026, targeting the Cε3-4 region, uniquely displaces IgE from both FcεRI and CD23 via conformational constraint and facilitated dissociation.
A Fab fragment binding murine Cε2 suppressed passive cutaneous anaphylaxis for up to 10 days after a single injection, without removing IgE from mast cells.
Quilizumab reduced antigen-specific and total IgE by up to 40% but failed to improve chronic spontaneous urticaria and inadequately controlled allergic asthma.
AIMab7195, an anti-IgE antibody with enhanced FcγRIIb binding designed to sequester free IgE and suppress newly produced IgE, has undergone a phase I trial whose results have not yet been published.
Bsc-IgE/CD3, designed to eliminate IgE-producing B cells by linking them to cytotoxic T cells, did not affect IgE-bound cells whose IgE was already bound to FcεRI or CD23.
Mutational disruption of the N394 N-glycosylation site on human IgE (N394T, N394Q, T396A) abolishes FcεRI binding and mast cell activation in vitro and in vivo.
Retaining only the N384 glycan site on mouse IgE while disrupting all others was sufficient to preserve FcεRI binding, indicating N384 is both necessary and sufficient among the glycosylation sites.

Endo F1 treatment, which trims mouse IgE N-glycans to leave only the first GlcNAc, abolished FcεRI binding, indicating the truncated glycan is insufficient to maintain the IgE conformation required for receptor binding.
Allergic individuals show increased sialylation (and reduced galactose exposure) on the N265, N140, and N168 glycans of IgE compared to non-allergic individuals.
Asialylation of IgE reduced its potency to induce mast cell degranulation in human and mouse systems without altering IgE's affinity for FcεRI or antigen.
The co-existence of asialylated glycoproteins (not just IgE itself) attenuated mast cell activation, suggesting exposed galactose may act via galectin binding.
Secreted, cell-surface-bound Galectin-3 can crosslink IgE on sensitized basophils and stimulate IL-4/IL-13 release in vitro.
Galectin-9 binding to IgE glycans reduces IgE's affinity for its specific antigen and suppresses IgE-dependent mast cell activation both in vivo and in vitro.

IgE-antigen immune complexes are preferentially bound and sequestered by CD23 rather than FcεRI, whereas free IgE is preferentially bound by FcεRI, supporting IgE's role as a sensor rather than a neutralizer of antigen.
Around 30–50% of patients with chronic spontaneous urticaria (CSU) have IgG autoantibodies against IgE or the high-affinity IgE receptor (FcεRI) that activate mast cells and basophils.
IgE autoantibodies against dsDNA, tissue factor, IL-24, and thyroid peroxidase have been detected in subsets of CSU patients.
IL-24 is released from human mast cells in response to microvesicles derived from activated T cells, implicating IL-24 and anti-IL-24-IgE in CSU mast cell/basophil activation.
The clinical effectiveness of omalizumab (anti-IgE monoclonal antibody) supports a role for IgG anti-IgE and IgE autoantibodies in CSU pathogenesis.
Multiple coagulation markers and pro-inflammatory cytokines (D-dimer, FDP, PF1+2, CRP, substance P, TNFα, TGFβ, IL-1β, IL-6, IL-17, IL-31, IL-33) are increased in the blood of CSU patients.
MrgX2 (MRGPRX2) expression on skin mast cells is upregulated in patients with severe CSU, implicating neuropeptide-mediated mast cell activation.
Plasma levels of IL-35 and vitamin D are decreased in patients with CSU.
Heparin, which activates anti-thrombin and inactivates thrombin (FIIa), has been reported to improve CSU.
Warfarin, which inhibits production of coagulation factors FVII, FX, FIX and FII, has been suggested to be effective for CSU.
Plasma levels of prothrombin fragment 1+2, fibrin/fibrinogen degradation products, and D-dimer are proportional to the severity of CSU symptoms.
The thrombin (FIIa) generation capability of the extrinsic coagulation cascade in CSU plasma is enhanced compared to healthy donors.
PAR-2 expression on human mast cells is upregulated in urticarial lesions compared with non-urticarial lesions.
Skin mast cells clearly express PAR-1 mRNA and only marginal PAR-2 mRNA, and histamine release was not detected in response to the PAR-1 agonist TRAP-6 or the PAR-2 agonist AC55541.

HUVECs and HMVECs express high amounts of TF on their surface in response to combinations of TF-inducers (histamine, VEGF, LPS, TNF-α, IL-33, IL-1β), with synergistic induction when one Group 1 and one Group 2 inducer are combined.
Adenosine, an ATP metabolite, suppressed TF expression on vascular endothelial cells induced by TF-inducers, suggesting therapeutic potential for CSU.
TF expression is high on the surface of peripheral blood monocytes of CSU patients compared to healthy donors.
TLR ligands LPS (TLR-4 agonist) and FLA-ST (TLR-5 agonist) induced TF expression on peripheral blood monocytes in vitro, suggesting a mechanism by which infections contribute to CSU.
TF expression was demonstrated on eosinophils within CSU skin lesions.
Autoantibodies against the low-affinity IgE receptor CD23 (FcεRII), which may activate eosinophils and induce MBP release, are detected in approximately 65% of CSU patients.
IgE concentrations in CSU patients were higher compared to healthy donors.
High concentrations of IgE antibody (>1 μM) mildly activate basophils expressing IgE-free FcεRI on their surface.
Plasma C5a levels are increased in patients with CSU.

Active coagulation factors FXa and FIIa produce C5a from C5, and C5a but not C3a induces histamine release from human skin mast cells and basophils via C5aR without requiring antigen or IgE interaction.
The fibrinolysis factor plasmin also converts C5 to C5a, resulting in mast cell activation.
Plasma from CSU patients causes histamine release from human mast cell lines LAD2 and HMC-1 through an IgE-FcεRI independent mechanism.
A molecule smaller than 30 kDa present in CSU patient plasma induces histamine release from mast cells.
C5a induces TF expression in human endothelial cells, potentially linking complement activation to blood coagulation pathway activation.
Basophils express C3aR and C5aR, which are increased in CSU skin lesions, and release histamine predominantly in response to C5a.

Two doses of rituximab 375 mg/m2 given two weeks apart maintained remission of the patient's Rowell syndrome skin disease and cytopenias, with complete resolution of lesions by 3 months and SLEDAI-2K of 0 at 12 weeks.
The patient continued to have breakthrough erythema multiforme-like rash and disease progression despite treatment with hydroxychloroquine and steroids, prompting escalation to rituximab.
The patient had markedly elevated anti-Ro/SSA antibody with a speckled ANA pattern, supporting the diagnostic criteria for Rowell syndrome.
Double-stranded DNA antibody was elevated, consistent with active SLE/Rowell syndrome flare.
Complement C3 and C4 were low, consistent with active lupus/Rowell syndrome flare.
Serum ferritin was markedly elevated at presentation, raising concern for HLH/macrophage activation syndrome (termed MAS in this paper), but it halved after the first dose of intravenous steroids.

Soluble IL-2 receptor was elevated above the normal reference range but did not reach the diagnostic threshold (>2400 pg/mL) required to meet HLH/MAS criteria, supporting the decision to rule out this diagnosis.

HLH/macrophage activation syndrome was deemed less likely as the cause of the patient's pancytopenia and hyperferritinemia based on lack of hepatosplenomegaly, normal bilirubin and triglycerides, absence of persistent fevers, and ferritin response to steroids.
Rowell syndrome has been reported in the literature with a higher incidence among women than men, at a ratio of 8:1.
Among eight reported refractory SCLE cases treated with rituximab, seven showed effective results and one did not.
Rituximab has been reported to be effective for subacute cutaneous lupus erythematosus (SCLE) but ineffective for chronic cutaneous lupus erythematosus.
Direct immunofluorescence of the skin biopsy showed finely granular deposition of C3, IgM, and fibrinogen, a pattern consistent with cutaneous lupus.
The patient presented with pancytopenia (low WBC, ANC, hemoglobin, hematocrit, and platelets), attributed to an acute flare of systemic lupus erythematosus/Rowell syndrome.
PFOS increased mast cell degranulation and eicosanoid production to a similar degree as BPA in vitro.
BPA increased mast cell degranulation and inflammatory eicosanoid production at a level comparable to PFOS.
Exposure to PFOS or BPA increased serum LTC4 levels in mice, accompanying increased skin edema.
Exposure to PFOS or BPA increased serum PGD2 levels in mice, consistent with mast cell-mediated inflammation.
PFOS and BPA increased activation of the upstream kinase Fyn in mast cell signaling.
PFOS and BPA increased activation of the upstream kinase Lyn in mast cell signaling.
PFOS and BPA increased Syk/LAT activation, a key upstream signaling component in mast cell activation.
PFOS and BPA increased downstream PLCγ1 signaling activation in mast cells.
Among the three PFCs tested (PFHxS, PFOA, PFOS), PFOS induced the greatest mast cell-mediated inflammatory effects.
Both PFOS and BPA increased activation of the upstream signaling kinase Fyn in mast cells.
Both PFOS and BPA increased activation of the upstream signaling kinase Lyn in mast cells.
Both PFOS and BPA increased activation of Syk and its adaptor LAT as part of the upstream signaling cascade in mast cells.
Both PFOS and BPA increased downstream signaling through PLCγ1 in mast cells.
Both PFOS and BPA increased AKT activation as part of the downstream signaling response in mast cells.
Both PFOS and BPA increased ERK activation as part of the downstream signaling response in mast cells.
Overexpression of focal adhesion kinase (FAK) increased IgE-mediated mast cell degranulation and reduced the ability of dexamethasone to inhibit mast cell activation.
The FAK inhibitor PF-431396 reduced mast cell release of β-hexosaminidase, histamine, and inflammatory cytokines through mechanisms involving MAPK and NF-κB signaling.
CaMKII was identified as a robust FAK-associating protein in mast cells.
Inhibition of CaMKII activation with KN-93 suppressed FAK activity and its downstream signaling pathway in mast cells.
PF-431396 attenuated inflammatory responses in mouse models of passive cutaneous anaphylaxis (PCA) and active systemic anaphylaxis (ASA).
PF-431396 relieved signs of allergic disease in a mouse model of allergic conjunctivitis (AC).
Chemically denatured pullulan-conjugated Cry j 1 (Dn p-Cry j 1) showed reduced IgE-binding capacity compared to native Cry j 1 in an ELISA competition assay.
Dn p-Cry j 1 induced reduced IgE-mediated mast cell effector activation compared to native Cry j 1 in the EXiLE mast cell activation model.
In rat passive cutaneous anaphylaxis (PCA) assays, Dn p-Cry j 1 demonstrated markedly reduced in vivo anaphylactic potential compared to native Cry j 1.

The reduction in anaphylactic potential of Dn p-Cry j 1 versus native Cry j 1 in wild-type rats was of similar magnitude to the reduction seen when comparing native Cry j 1 reactions in wild-type versus mast-cell-deficient rats, implicating mast cells as central mediators of the reduced reactivity.
Skin biopsies revealed somatic small fiber neuropathy in all 21 patients with a previous diagnosis of multiple chemical sensitivity syndrome who presented with chronic pain.
Despite 18 of 21 patients reporting autonomic symptoms, skin biopsies showed sparing of autonomic innervation, indicating a dissociation between somatic and autonomic small fiber involvement.
The authors propose that chronic pain in patients with multiple chemical sensitivity syndrome may be secondary to underlying somatic small fiber neuropathy rather than autonomic nerve involvement.
Distal intraepidermal nerve fiber density was reduced in 70% of patients and neurological examination was abnormal in 62% of patients with suspected small fiber neuropathy.
Both distal IENFD and neurological examination were simultaneously pathological in 44% of the cohort, while proximal IENFD reduction with normal distal IENFD occurred in only 5% of patients.
Quantitative sensory testing (thermal thresholds) was abnormal in only 28% of patients, questioning its standalone diagnostic value for SFN.
Mechanical detection thresholds were significantly elevated in patients with suspected SFN compared with healthy controls, despite no evidence of large fiber involvement.
Applying the criterion of ≥2 pathological small fiber tests (clinical exam, QST, distal IENFD), 57% of patients were diagnosed with SFN, leaving 43% undiagnosed.
Corneal confocal microscopy showed pathological corneal nerve parameters in 53% of the sub-cohort tested.
Pain-related evoked potentials (PREP), assessing A-delta fiber conduction, were pathological in 45% of the sub-cohort tested.
QSART (sudomotor axon reflex testing) was pathological in only 9% of the sub-cohort, indicating minimal additional diagnostic value.
Adding CCM and PREP to clinical exam, QST, and distal IENFD increased SFN diagnosis rate to 89% of the sub-cohort, leaving only 11% undiagnosed.

Genetic panel sequencing of 26 pain-associated genes identified variants in 16% of patients, with over half of these located in voltage-gated sodium channel genes; pathogenicity remained unclear in all cases.

A patient in the 'pain only' group (no pathology on standard 5 tests) carried an SCN10A gene variant and showed abnormal spontaneously active bursting C-fiber activity on microneurography, the only pathological small fiber test in this case.
Reduced distal IENFD was also found in 16% of healthy controls, indicating that reduced IENFD alone does not prove SFN, while normal IENFD does not exclude it.
Impaired glucose metabolism (elevated HbA1c and/or abnormal OGTT) was newly diagnosed in 17% of patients presenting with suspected SFN.

Additional autoimmune/endocrine comorbidities (hypothyroidism, vitamin B12 deficiency, elevated autoantibody titers, and psoriasis/Hashimoto/vitiligo) were newly identified in 10% of patients presenting with suspected SFN.
Proximal skin biopsy IENFD had limited added diagnostic value but was useful for distinguishing length-dependent from non-length-dependent SFN patterns.
A regional IENFD reference range was established using 34 healthy Chinese volunteers, with lower 5th percentile values of 10.0/mm at the proximal thigh and 8.1/mm at the distal thigh.

IENFD in the proximal and distal leg was significantly lower in both the pure SFN group and the mixed DPN group compared with the non-DPN group, but did not differ significantly between the pure SFN and mixed DPN groups.
Patients with pure SFN had lower HbA1c and postprandial blood glucose levels than patients with mixed DPN, suggesting better glycemic control in the pure SFN group.
Postprandial C-peptide and insulin levels were higher in the pure SFN group than in the mixed DPN group, indicating better preserved islet function in pure SFN.
ACR, a marker of microvascular complications, was higher in the mixed DPN group compared with the non-DPN group.
25-hydroxyvitamin D levels were lower in the mixed DPN group compared to the non-DPN group.
Blood pressure and resting heart rate were higher in the mixed DPN group than in the non-DPN group.
Motor nerve conduction velocity was lowest in the mixed DPN group compared with the pure SFN and non-DPN groups, while NSS, NPRS, and SUDOSCAN readings did not differ significantly among groups.

The mixed DPN group had the highest (worst) CART scores, and the prevalence of cardiovascular autonomic neuropathy (CAN) was significantly higher in the mixed DPN group compared with both the non-DPN and pure SFN groups.
Compared with the mixed DPN group, the pure SFN group had a lower postural BP change component and a higher deep-breathing heart rate variability (max-min) component of the CART battery.

IENFD in the distal leg was negatively correlated with systolic blood pressure and ACR in raw correlation analysis, but these correlations were no longer significant after adjusting for age and diabetes duration.

CART scores were negatively correlated with distal leg IENFD, and this correlation remained significant even after adjusting for age and duration of diabetes, indicating a link between cardiovascular autonomic dysfunction and small fiber loss.
In the follow-up cohort, vitamin B12 levels increased at the final visit only in the pure SFN group, possibly reflecting supplement use.
During follow-up, the MCVs of the common peroneal and tibial nerves decreased in the mixed DPN group despite stable glucose control, indicating progression of large fiber neuropathy.

In contrast to the mixed DPN group, the pure SFN group showed an upward trend in common peroneal nerve MCV at follow-up, suggesting relative stability or improvement of large fiber function in pure SFN.
Marfan syndrome is caused by mutations in the Fibrillin-1 gene and leads to thoracic aortic aneurysm formation via elastin fragmentation and smooth muscle cell apoptosis.
NO2-OA treatment for 4 weeks significantly attenuated progressive ascending aortic dilation and wall stiffening seen by echocardiography in Fbn1C1041G/+ MFS mice compared to vehicle.
NO2-OA treatment inhibited aortic ERK1/2 activation in MFS mice, contributing to its protective effect on aortic pathology.
NO2-OA inhibited aortic Smad2 overactivation in MFS mice as part of its protective mechanism against aortic pathology.
NO2-OA inhibited nuclear factor kappa B overactivation in aortas of MFS mice.
NO2-OA treatment attenuated elastin fragmentation mediated by matrix metalloproteinase 2 in aortas of MFS mice.
NO2-OA treatment reduced smooth muscle cell apoptosis and collagen deposition in the aortic wall of MFS mice.
NO2-OA treatment reduced lethal aortic complications, including rupture or dissection, in MFS mice challenged with Angiotensin II.
Fbn1C1041G/+ MFS mice showed progressive ascending aortic dilation and wall stiffening on echocardiography over the study period, consistent with the natural disease course of Marfan aortopathy.
About half of recovered COVID-19 patients still had at least one persistent symptom at 3 months post-discharge, most commonly insomnia, chest tightness, fatigue, and cough.
Symptom prevalence declined over time, from 40.0% at 6 months to 28.4% at 12 months, with chest tightness, fatigue, and insomnia remaining the most common.
The proportion of patients with abnormal renal function fell from hospitalization to discharge but then rose again after discharge, remaining elevated through 12 months.
Cardiovascular injury (abnormal biomarkers/echocardiography) prevalence dropped at discharge but rebounded markedly, peaking at 6 months and remaining common at 12 months.
Abnormal liver function prevalence decreased over follow-up, but 7.6% of patients still had abnormal liver function at 12 months.
Electrocardiogram abnormalities including arrhythmia, ST-T change, and conduction block were present in roughly half of patients throughout the 12-month follow-up.
Higher admission cardiac troponin I independently predicted cardiovascular injury at 12 months post-discharge.
Higher admission cardiac troponin I independently predicted abnormal kidney function at 12 months post-discharge.
Higher admission total bilirubin was an independent predictor of cardiovascular injury at 12 months.
In-hospital immunoglobulin administration was an independent predictor of cardiovascular injury at 12 months post-discharge.
In-hospital high-flow nasal cannula oxygen therapy was an independent predictor of cardiovascular injury at 12 months post-discharge.
Female sex was independently protective against abnormal kidney function at 12 months post-discharge.
Higher admission blood urea nitrogen independently predicted abnormal kidney function at 12 months post-discharge.
Diabetes was an independent predictor of abnormal kidney function at 12 months post-discharge.
Chest CT abnormalities such as fibrous stripes, pleural thickening/adhesions, and enlarged lymph nodes were common at 3 months and fibrous stripes remained prevalent at 12 months post-discharge.
A small number of patients had obstructive, restrictive, or mixed pulmonary function abnormalities at 6 and 12 months, despite common CT abnormalities.
Insomnia frequency decreased over follow-up but persisted in about 6% of patients at 6 months and 4% at 12 months.
A small subset of patients experienced neurological/sensory symptoms including extremity numbness, amnesia, decreased taste, vision loss, hearing loss, and smell loss during follow-up.
All patients who had ARDS during hospitalization had fully recovered by discharge, with no recurrence of ARDS during the 12-month follow-up.

Frequencies of alkaline phosphatase, eGFR, creatinine kinase, lactate dehydrogenase, and myoglobin abnormalities decreased over time but remained persistently high, or even increased, by 12 months post-discharge.
Plasma activin B concentration did not differ significantly between ME/CFS patients and healthy controls.
No significant sex-based difference in activin B levels was found within the ME/CFS patient group.
No significant sex-based difference in activin B levels was found within the healthy control group.
Activin B levels did not change with age in either ME/CFS patients or healthy controls.
Activin B level tended to decrease as visual analogue scale (VAS) fatigue/symptom severity score increased, but this correlation was not statistically significant.
A prior Australian study (45 ME/CFS cases, 17 controls) reported significantly elevated activin B levels in ME/CFS patients compared to controls.
A follow-up study by the same Australian group (85 ME/CFS cases) later reported a significant decrease in activin B levels in ME/CFS patients, contradicting their earlier finding.

Myalgia was reported at similarly high rates in both activin B-positive (92%) and activin B-negative (96%) ME/CFS subgroups, suggesting activin B level does not influence muscle pain presentation despite its known role in muscle wasting.
The most prevalent clinical symptoms besides fatigue in the ME/CFS cohort were headache, myalgia, difficulty concentrating, and arthralgia, reported across both activin B subgroups.

Untargeted serum metabolomics found that 159 of 610 measured metabolites significantly differed between ME/CFS patients and healthy controls, with 87 elevated and 72 reduced, predominantly lipid and amino acid metabolites.

K-means clustering and PCA identified three distinct metabolic subgroups (metabotypes) within the ME/CFS cohort: ME-M1 (n=32), ME-M2 (n=38), and ME-M3 (n=13, clustering with HC), with 84% of patients falling into the two major distinct metabotypes.

The ME-M1 metabotype was characterized by markedly elevated serum non-esterified fatty acid (NEFA) and ketone body levels with reduced amino acid metabolites, indicating a lipolytic, ketogenic metabolic state.

The ME-M2 metabotype was characterized by elevated serum triglycerides (TAG) and diacylglycerols with reduced NEFA, alongside significantly increased serum pyruvate suggestive of reduced mitochondrial pyruvate oxidation.

Physical function scores (steps/24h, SF-36 Physical Function subscale, self-reported function) differed significantly between metabotypes, ranked ME-M2 < ME-M1 < ME-M3, with ME-M2 patients showing the lowest functional scores.
ME-M2 patients had significantly higher mean BMI than ME-M1 patients and a significantly larger proportion with BMI>25 compared with healthy controls.
BCAA derivatives such as isovalerylglycine were uniformly reduced in both ME-M1 and ME-M2 metabotypes compared to healthy controls, consistent with altered muscle energy metabolism.
Serum kynurenate was consistently reduced across all three ME/CFS metabotypes compared with healthy controls, implicating altered kynurenine pathway/tryptophan metabolism.
Serum glycerol, a product of triglyceride lipolysis, was uniformly elevated across all ME/CFS metabotypes, consistent with induced lipolysis resembling fasting or exercise states.

Purine nucleotide degradation products such as adenosine and xanthosine were uniformly elevated across ME/CFS subsets, suggesting energy strain and increased ATP demand similar to exercise metabolism.
The arachidonic acid derivatives 12-HETE and 12-HHTrE were uniformly lowered across ME/CFS metabotypes, potentially affecting vascular tone and blood flow regulation.
Phospholipid species (PC, PE, LPC, LPE) containing linoleic acid (18:2), an essential fatty acid and arachidonic acid precursor, were uniformly lowered in ME-M1 and ME-M2 subsets.
ME/CFS patients had slightly elevated mean insulin and leptin and reduced HMW adiponectin compared with healthy controls, an effect primarily driven by the ME-M2 subset.
Serum FABP4 was elevated similarly in ME-M1 and ME-M2 subsets, while FGF21 was significantly elevated only in the ME-M2 subset, both considered markers of metabolic/energy stress.

Complex lipidomics found 153 of 892 lipid species significantly altered in ME/CFS versus HC, with elevated diacylglycerols (DAG), triglycerides (TAG), and dihydroceramides (DCER), and reduced lysophosphatidylcholines (LPC) at the class level.

The authors reinforce, based on amino acid and pyruvate patterns, their prior hypothesis that impaired mitochondrial pyruvate dehydrogenase (PDH) function may contribute to ME/CFS pathology, especially relevant to the ME-M2 metabotype.
Morning cortisol and ACTH levels did not differ between ME/CFS patients and healthy controls, suggesting corticosteroid dysregulation is not a primary driver of the observed metabolic changes.

Endothelial dysfunction and abnormal red blood cell deformability have been reported in ME/CFS, potentially impairing exertion-triggered tissue oxygenation and blood flow, supporting a hypoxia-driven energy strain model.

At the group level, resting serum lactate was normal in ME/CFS patients, with ME-M1 showing slightly lower and ME-M2 slightly higher lactate than controls, suggesting tissue hypoxia is not a dominant factor at rest.

ME/CFS patients showed greater overall inter-individual heterogeneity (coefficient of variation) in serum metabolite levels compared to healthy controls, consistent with context-dependent, individual-specific disease effects.
A large majority of ME/CFS patients in the United States are undiagnosed, with estimates up to 91%.
Graded exercise therapy and cognitive-behavioral therapy have recently been withdrawn as first-line treatments for ME/CFS by governments and major health care organizations.
A significant percentage of people remain ill for many months after acute COVID-19 with an illness resembling ME/CFS.
The 2015 US National Academy of Medicine evidence-based clinical diagnostic criteria for ME/CFS have been adopted by the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

In patients with infection-triggered ME/CFS onset, fatigue severity correlated positively with most vasoregulative GPCR autoantibody/IgG ratios, including alpha1/2-AdR, beta1/2/3-AdR, M3/4-AChR, AT1-R, ETA-R and ETB-R, but not PAR-1/2.
Muscle pain severity in infection-triggered onset patients showed a similar positive correlation pattern to fatigue with vasoregulative GPCR autoantibody/IgG ratios, except for beta3-AdR-AAB/IgG.

SF-36 physical function scores negatively correlated with alpha2-AdR-, beta1/2-AdR- and M4-AChR-AAB/IgG ratios in infection-triggered onset patients, indicating worse function with higher AAB/IgG ratios.
Severity of cognitive symptoms in infection-triggered onset patients correlated positively only with AT1-R- and ETA-R-AAB/IgG ratios among all receptors tested.

The Bell disability score in infection-triggered onset patients showed a negative correlation with AT1-R-, ETA-R-, and alpha1/2-AdR-AAB/IgG ratios, indicating worse disability with higher AAB/IgG ratios; the ETA-R correlation remained significant after BH correction.
The immune symptom score in infection-triggered onset patients showed only an inverse correlation with PAR1-AAB/IgG ratio.
The Chalder Fatigue Score did not correlate with any AAB/IgG ratios in this cohort.

None of the significant fatigue and muscle-pain correlations found in infection-triggered onset patients were replicated in patients without infection-triggered onset, and SF-36 physical function correlations were often in the opposite direction.
In patients without infection-triggered onset, a significant negative correlation of ETB-R-AAB/IgG with the Bell disability score was found, which was not seen in the infection-triggered onset group.
In infection-triggered onset patients, gastrointestinal symptoms (COMPASS-31 domain) correlated positively with alpha1/2-AdR-AAB/IgG ratios.

In infection-triggered onset patients, pupillomotor symptoms (COMPASS-31 domain) correlated with alpha1-, beta2/3-AdR- and M4-AChR-AAB/IgG ratios; the M4-AChR correlation remained significant after Benjamini-Hochberg correction.

In patients without infection-triggered onset only, orthostatic symptoms (COMPASS-31 domain) strongly correlated with all AdR-AAB/IgG ratios (alpha1/2 and beta1/2/3-AdR), a pattern absent in the infection-triggered onset group.
In non-infection-triggered onset patients, an inverse correlation of PAR2-AAB/IgG with secretomotor symptoms (COMPASS-31 domain) was found.
Alpha1/2-AdR-, M4-AChR- and ETA-R-AAB/IgG ratios positively correlated with disease duration in the whole cohort.
Most vasoregulative GPCR autoantibody levels showed a positive correlation with total IgG and IgG subclasses, predominantly IgG1 and IgG3, replicating a previous finding by the same group.
Age was inversely correlated with total IgG levels in the ME/CFS cohort, prompting use of AAB/IgG ratios to correct for age effects in correlation analyses.

Patients with infection-triggered onset were significantly younger and had shorter disease duration than those with non-infection-triggered onset, but there were no differences in symptom severity, Bell disability, SF-36 physical function, COMPASS-31 autonomic dysfunction, or absolute autoantibody levels between the two onset groups.

After Benjamini-Hochberg correction for multiple testing, most AAB/IgG ratio correlations with fatigue, muscle pain, and cognitive symptoms, as well as the Bell score correlation with ETA-R-AAB/IgG, remained significant in infection-triggered onset patients, whereas none of the correlations in the non-infection-triggered onset group remained significant.
Graded Exercise Therapy (GET) has caused significant harm to many ME/CFS patients, sometimes progressing modestly mobile patients to a prolonged bedbound, tube-fed state.
The PACE trial supporting GET and CBT for ME/CFS is described as methodologically seriously flawed and now cited as an example of how not to conduct science.

On two-day cardiopulmonary exercise testing, the anaerobic threshold decreases on the second day in ME/CFS patients but increases in healthy sedentary controls, reflecting abnormal muscle energy metabolism underlying exercise intolerance.
Repeated electrical stimulation of isolated biopsied muscle fibres from ME/CFS patients shows metabolic impairments not seen in healthy controls.
ME/CFS patients show hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis (HPAA) disorder, with reduced circulating cortisol levels and blunted HPAA responses to physical and psychological stress.
HPA axis dysfunction in ME/CFS may be caused by an underlying autoimmune process, per cited literature.
Long-standing ME/CFS patients have significantly smaller adrenal glands than normal controls, attributed to impaired ACTH output.
Low circulating blood volume in ME/CFS is likely to contribute to Postural Orthostatic Tachycardia Syndrome (POTS), described as a common complication of ME/CFS.

ME/CFS is characterized by persistent immunological activation and chronic inflammation following an initial infectious/vaccine trigger, with the immune system failing to shut down normally, described by some as 'derailed'.
The chronic inflammatory process in ME/CFS is reported to include the brain, providing pathological support for the term 'myalgic encephalomyelitis'.
A reliable biomarker for ME/CFS is reported to be in development, described as a significant step toward objective diagnosis.
The clinical presentation of Long COVID closely resembles ME/CFS, and the two conditions may share underlying pathology.
Salivary HHV-6B DNA concentrations were on average 6.2-fold higher in severely affected ME/CFS patients than in healthy controls, significant at three of six monthly timepoints.
Salivary HHV-7 DNA loads were significantly or borderline-significantly higher in both mild/moderate and severely affected ME/CFS patients compared to healthy controls across most monthly timepoints.
The proportion of monthly saliva samples positive for HHV-6B (persistence) was significantly higher in severely affected ME/CFS patients than healthy controls.
Absolute salivary DNA loads of HSV-1 and EBV did not differ significantly between ME/CFS patients and healthy controls.
At baseline, salivary prevalence of EBV and HHV-6B differed between healthy controls and the two ME/CFS severity groups, with HHV-6B most prevalent in severely affected patients.
HHV-7 was the most prevalent and most persistently detected virus in saliva of all participant groups, being present in essentially every sample from most individuals across the 6-month study.
Co-detection of HHV-7 together with HHV-6B in saliva was significantly more frequent in severely affected ME/CFS patients than in healthy controls.
Post-exertional malaise (PEM) scores were significantly higher in severely affected ME/CFS patients than in those with mild/moderate disease, with a trend toward greater autonomic dysfunction.
Among people with ME/CFS, autonomic symptom scores were highly correlated with neurocognition symptom scores.
In severely affected ME/CFS patients whose salivary HHV repertoire fluctuated over time (pattern 1), HHV-6B DNA concentration strongly correlated with six of seven symptom domain scores.
In the same fluctuating-repertoire (pattern 1) severely affected ME/CFS subgroup, HHV-7 DNA concentration correlated with pain, neurocognition and autonomic symptom scores.
In severely affected ME/CFS patients with stable HHV repertoire (pattern 2), HHV-6B DNA concentration was negatively correlated with pain, neurocognition, and neuroendocrine symptom scores.
In the same stable-repertoire (pattern 2) severely affected ME/CFS subgroup, EBV DNA concentration was positively correlated with pain, neurocognition, and autonomic symptom scores.

During acute illness/disease exacerbation episodes in ME/CFS patients, HHV-6B DNA concentration was positively correlated with sleep dysfunction and HHV-7 concentration, but negatively correlated with PEM and pain scores.
There was no significant correlation between salivary EBV DNA concentration and anti-EBNA1 or anti-VCA IgG antibody levels in either ME/CFS or healthy controls.

Salivary HHV-6B DNA concentration was significantly higher in younger (<40 years) than older participants among healthy controls and mild/moderate ME/CFS patients, but not in severely affected patients.

Among people severely affected with ME/CFS, weak but significant correlations were found between EBV DNA concentration and pain, neurocognition and autonomic symptom scores, between HSV-1 DNA and autonomic symptoms, and between HHV-7 DNA and pain and autonomic symptoms.

The paper cites prior work suggesting HHV-6B reactivation may cause mitochondrial fragmentation and impaired energy metabolism in ME/CFS, potentially via interaction between the HHV-6B U95 early viral protein and the mitochondrial GRIM-19 protein, reducing mitochondrial membrane potential.
SNP association analysis identified an independent association signal in the HLA class I region tagged by rs4711249 in ME/CFS patients compared to controls.
A second independent association signal in the HLA class II region, tagged by rs9275582, was identified in ME/CFS patients compared to controls.

The primary HLA class II association signal localized to the HLA-DQ region, most likely driven by HLA-DQB1, particularly amino acid position 57 (aspartic acid/alanine) in the peptide-binding groove, or an intergenic SNP upstream of HLA-DQB1.

In the HLA class I region, the ME/CFS-associated SNP genotype influenced expression levels of several genes outside the classical HLA loci, including DDR1, GTF2H4, VARS2, SFTA2, and DPCR1, suggesting the causal locus may lie outside classical HLA genes.
Perceived cognitive fatigue (FIS-40 cognitive domain) improved significantly within the CoQ10 plus NADH group at both 4- and 8-week visits compared to baseline.
The psychosocial domain of FIS-40 showed a nominal improvement at 4 weeks in the active group but did not reach statistical significance.
Total FIS-40 fatigue score significantly decreased at the 4-week visit within the active group but this improvement was not sustained at 8 weeks or 4 weeks post-treatment.
Sleep duration on the PSQI showed a statistically significant between-group difference favoring the CoQ10 plus NADH group at the 4-week follow-up.
Within the experimental group, all PSQI sleep quality domains improved significantly from baseline over time.
SF-36 physical functioning scores improved significantly in the CoQ10 plus NADH group compared to placebo at both 4- and 8-week visits.
The bodily pain domain of the SF-36 improved at the 4-week visit from baseline in the CoQ10 plus NADH group.
In the placebo group, vitality scores decreased 4 weeks after treatment discontinuation.

No serious adverse events or treatment-related safety concerns were recorded, indicating that CoQ10 plus NADH supplementation was safe and well-tolerated over 8 weeks, though epigastralgia and dizziness led to some dropouts in both groups.
At baseline diagnosis, adolescents with ME/CFS reported significantly greater fatigue than healthy controls with a large effect size.
Fatigue significantly improved in the ME/CFS group from baseline to the ~2-year follow-up, while controls remained stable.
At the ~2-year follow-up, the ME/CFS group still reported significantly greater fatigue than controls, though the effect was reduced in magnitude from baseline.
At baseline, the ME/CFS group reported significantly poorer sleep quality than controls.
By follow-up, there was no significant difference in sleep quality between the ME/CFS group and controls, reflecting improvement in the ME/CFS group over time.

Sleep hygiene did not differ significantly between ME/CFS and control groups at either time point, though a significant time-by-group interaction was driven by a small decline in sleep hygiene among controls over time.
At baseline, the ME/CFS group reported significantly greater present pain severity than controls.
At follow-up, the ME/CFS group continued to report significantly greater pain than controls, although the effect was reduced compared to baseline.
At baseline, the ME/CFS group reported significantly greater anxiety than controls, but anxiety decreased over time such that by follow-up there was no significant group difference.
No significant differences in depression were found between the ME/CFS and control groups at either baseline or follow-up, nor a significant change over time.
At baseline, the ME/CFS group reported significantly poorer health-related quality of life (HRQOL) than controls, with a large effect size.
At follow-up, the ME/CFS group still reported significantly worse HRQOL than controls despite substantial improvement over time.

All ME/CFS participants met diagnostic criteria at baseline (59% severe, 41% moderate), but only 65% still met criteria at the ~2-year follow-up, with severity distribution shifting toward atypical presentations.
Pain was the most frequently endorsed diagnostic symptom among ME/CFS adolescents at follow-up, followed closely by sleep problems and autonomic/neuroendocrine/immune symptoms.

Most ME/CFS adolescents (82%) self-identified as still having ME/CFS at follow-up, and of these, 79% also fulfilled formal diagnostic criteria while 21% did not, indicating some disparity between self-perceived and criteria-based diagnosis.

None of the baseline health and psychological wellbeing variables (fatigue, sleep, pain, anxiety, depression, HRQOL) significantly predicted ME/CFS diagnostic criteria fulfilment at follow-up in logistic mixed-effects models.

Pain experienced at baseline was significantly positively correlated with ME/CFS diagnostic criteria fulfilment at follow-up, and approached significance as a predictor in regression models, though with a small odds ratio.
Healthy females had significantly higher total plasma phosphatidylcholine content compared to healthy males.
Among males, total HexCer levels were significantly increased in ME/CFS patients compared to male controls.
Among females, ME/CFS patients had significantly lower levels of PE and HexCer compared to female controls.
Among males, PE-MUFA, PI-MUFA, and TG-SFA (saturated triglycerides) were significantly higher in ME/CFS patients compared to male controls, while females showed no unsaturation differences.
AA- and DHA-containing PC and CE were elevated, whereas CAR-AA was decreased, in healthy females compared to healthy males.
Among females, AA-containing PE species were decreased in ME/CFS patients compared to female controls, suggesting selective loss of an inflammatory-lipid reservoir.
Levels of CE-AA were elevated in female ME/CFS patients compared to male ME/CFS patients.
After excluding DHA-supplement users, total CAR was significantly decreased and total Cer significantly elevated in female ME/CFS patients compared to male ME/CFS patients.
PC-DHA levels, specifically PC 40:6, PC 40:7, and PC 38:7, were significantly increased in female ME/CFS patients compared to male ME/CFS patients.
PC 40:4 increased in female controls compared to male controls but decreased in female ME/CFS patients compared to female controls.
Among males, linoleic acid-derived oxylipins 12(13)-DiHOME, 9(10)-DiHOME, 13-HODE and 9-HODE were elevated in ME/CFS patients compared to controls.
9(10)-DiHOME was decreased in female ME/CFS patients compared to female controls, the only LA-derived oxylipin lower in female patients.
NAE 14:0 was lower in male ME/CFS but elevated in female ME/CFS relative to respective controls; NAE 22:4 was lower in female ME/CFS compared to both female controls and male ME/CFS patients.
Hierarchical clustering identified CAR 5:0 increased in female ME/CFS vs female controls, and PI 36:1 and PE 36:1 increased in male ME/CFS vs male controls.
Among females, ePC 38:4, ePC 34:3, CAR 18:2, 9(10)-diHOME and HexCer 41:1 were decreased in ME/CFS patients compared to controls (cluster group B).

In males, TG and HexCer levels (cluster group B species) were significantly higher in ME/CFS patients versus controls; HexCer 41:1 changed in opposite directions between the male and female comparisons.
PC 36:5 and PC 36:6 were significantly increased in female ME/CFS versus female controls, while PC 36:2 was increased in male ME/CFS versus male controls (cluster 1 species).

Principal component analysis of the top 50 plasma lipids identified 3 components explaining 55.55% of variance; PC2 was significantly associated with headache, cognitive difficulties, and fatigue, and PC3 was associated with physical pain, headache, cognitive difficulties, and fatigue.
Headache severity, cognitive difficulties, and fatigue severity were negatively correlated with blood phospholipid levels among the top 50 identified lipids.
Most oxylipins and ethanolamides showed lower concentrations with increasing severity of headache, physical pain, cognitive difficulties, and fatigue.

Total ceramide did not reach statistical significance in this study despite a generalized ~18% increase in female ME/CFS compared to female controls, contrasting with a prior study (Germain et al.) that found significant Cer increases.

There were no overall diagnostic differences in total CAR levels between ME/CFS patients and controls, suggesting fatty acid transport into mitochondria is not a major contributor to mitochondrial dysfunction in ME/CFS.
A US multi-state telephone survey found 35% of 292 symptomatic adults had not returned to their usual state of health 2-3 weeks after testing positive for COVID-19.
An Italian hospital study found 87% of 143 post-COVID-19 acute-care patients had not fully recovered by 2 months after admission, reporting ongoing fatigue.
An Irish study of 128 post-COVID-19 patients found 52% reported persistent post-viral fatigue at a median of 10 weeks post-symptom onset, with 31% of those unable to return to work.
In the Irish post-viral fatigue cohort, 67% of those suffering persistent fatigue were female, mirroring the female bias seen in ME/CFS.
The Irish study found no correlation between acute-phase severity markers (pro-inflammatory/immune cell blood levels) and the later development of post-viral fatigue.
A UK study estimated 10% of COVID-19-positive patients remained unwell more than 3 weeks later, with a smaller proportion unwell months later.

A Wuhan cohort of 1,733 hospital-discharged COVID-19 patients found 76% had at least one persistent symptom 6 months post-onset, most commonly fatigue/muscle weakness (63%), sleep difficulties (26%), and anxiety/depression (23%).

In an international web-based survey (n=3,762) of post-COVID-19 patients at 6 months, 80% were female, with fatigue (>75%), post-exertional malaise (>69%) and cognitive dysfunction (>52%) as the most frequent symptoms.

In the same international survey, over 85% experienced stress/exertion-induced relapses, 67% were unable to work or on reduced schedule, and over 90% had not been hospitalized, indicating even mild COVID-19 can trigger ME/CFS-like illness.
A German clinical study of 42 post-COVID-19 patients found chronic fatigue in all 42, PEM in 41, cognitive impairment in 40, headache in 38, and muscle pain in 35.

Of the 42 German post-COVID-19 patients, 19 met the 2003 Canadian Consensus Criteria for ME/CFS, with severe fatigue, cognitive impairment, stress intolerance, and hypersensitivity to noise, light, and temperature.

The remaining 23 German post-COVID patients not meeting full ME/CFS criteria had similar but less severe symptoms, with PEM lasting 2-10 hours (vs >14 hours for the ME/CFS group), categorized as 'Chronic COVID-19 Syndrome'.

An Australian study of 253 patients found that three pathogenically distinct infections (Ross River Virus, Epstein-Barr Virus, and Q fever) each triggered ME/CFS in proportionally similar numbers of patients (around 12%), with similar symptom characteristics.

A 2014 Japanese PET/MRI study detected activated microglia and astrocytes within the limbic system (cingulate cortex, hippocampus, amygdala, thalamus) of ME/CFS patients, with glial activation intensity correlating with symptom severity (fatigue, cognitive impairment, pain, depression).
An MRI study correlating autonomic dysfunction (heart rate and blood pressure) in ME/CFS patients versus healthy controls found abnormalities in the brain stem and hypothalamus.
An MRI study found post-exertional malaise (PEM) in ME/CFS patients correlated with reduced cognitive function but increased brain activity in inferior/superior parietal and cingulate cortices.

An MRS/MRI thermometry study found significantly raised lactate (mitochondrial stress marker) and temperature (inflammation marker) levels in the anterior cingulate cortex and thalamus of ME/CFS patients.
A PET/MRI study of fibromyalgia found glial-cell activity elevated in the cortex relative to healthy controls, with some overlap in cingulate cortex activation similar to ME/CFS.

Low-dose naltrexone (0.5-4.5 mg/day), proposed to have anti-inflammatory properties, showed favorable but variable results in three ME/CFS case studies, ranging from life-changing improvement to reduction in some symptoms only.
A retrospective review of 101 ME/CFS patients receiving off-label aripiprazole found 74% (75/101) experienced improvement in fatigue, brain fog, unrefreshing sleep, and/or frequency of PEM episodes.

The author proposes that SARS-CoV-2 infection acts as a severe physiological stressor targeting the hypothalamic paraventricular nucleus (PVN), previously proposed as the target site in ME/CFS, switching it into an ongoing dysfunctional mode in genetically susceptible individuals.

The chemokine fractalkine and its receptor on glial cells are hypothesized to be disrupted in ME/CFS patients, potentially inducing glial-cell activation, with a fractalkine receptor inhibitor also in planned Phase 2 trials for preventing COVID-19 hyperinflammation.

Stress-induced CRH release from the hypothalamic PVN is proposed to activate glial cells and mast cells via CRH receptors, releasing neuroinflammatory mediators as a candidate 'missing link' mechanism.
SARS-CoV-2 infection provokes a surge of chemokines and pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-6, TNF, IL-1β) at the initial lung infection site, with cytokine storm severity scaling with COVID-19 severity.

Most participants in this qualitative study of an alternative, adjustment-focused CBT model reported no change in physical CFS/ME symptoms or fatigue, though some described fewer relapses and slightly improved quality of life.
Participants' acceptance of having CFS/ME appeared central to improved adaptive coping, forming a reinforcing cycle in which better daily functioning promoted further acceptance and vice versa.

Lowering personal expectations/standards was reported by participants to improve management of CFS/ME symptoms both directly and via increased acceptance, independent of any change in fatigue, contrasting with a prior study linking reduced perfectionism to reduced fatigue.

Learning tools such as problem solving and pacing, together with lowered self-expectations, helped participants approach daily life more adaptively, preventing symptom flare-ups and freeing time/energy for valued activities.

A cited Cochrane meta-analysis found CBT more effective than usual care and other psychological therapies for reducing fatigue in adults with CFS/ME, with 40% of CBT participants improving versus 26% with usual care.
A large UK M.E. Association patient survey found only 8%-35% of participants reported improvement after CBT, with 18% reporting adverse effects.
Price et al.'s Cochrane review found that CBT failed to reduce psychological distress in CFS/ME compared with usual care.
A meta-analysis by Castell et al. found that CBT produced a significantly greater reduction in depression and anxiety than control conditions in CFS/ME.

Brooks et al. found that after CBT, patients showed increased acceptance of CFS/ME and reduced perfectionism, and that increased acceptance was significantly correlated with improved fatigue, physical functioning, and work/social adjustment.

The alternative, adjustment-focused CBT model (median 6 sessions) was viewed by participants as an acceptable, time-limited approach that alleviated distress about living with CFS/ME even without improving fatigue itself.
Prior diagnoses of Lyme disease were reported by 83% of patients, but NATA/RCPA-accredited serology found no diagnostic evidence of acute Lyme disease in any patient.
38% of patients had a prior medical diagnosis of Epstein-Barr virus infection.
28% of patients had a prior medical diagnosis of chronic fatigue syndrome.
24% of patients had a prior medical diagnosis of fibromyalgia.
48% of patients had a prior history of anxiety.
41% of patients had a prior history of depression.
Fatigue was the most frequently reported symptom, occurring in 83% of patients.
Headache was reported by 72% of patients.
Arthralgia was reported by 69% of patients with Debilitating Symptom Complexes Attributed to Ticks (DSCATT).
Accredited serology testing was not diagnostic of any acute infective cause, including Lyme disease, in any of the patients tested.
Among 25 patients with available data, 92% had previously been prescribed antimicrobials for their symptoms, with 53% reporting some benefit.
Chronic fatigue syndrome was the most common diagnosis made by the hospital team, given to 31% of patients in the case series.
Migraines were diagnosed by the hospital team in 28% of DSCATT patients.
Fibromyalgia was diagnosed by the hospital team in 21% of DSCATT patients.
Only one of the 29 patients had symptoms that were not accounted for by an alternative medical diagnosis, suggesting most DSCATT presentations overlap with recognised conditions.

In a secondary psychometric analysis of PACE trial data (n=640), only 6 of 26 mediator-outcome pairs (cognitive/behavioural mediators vs physical functioning/fatigue outcomes) showed evidence of measurement overlap via cross-loading items, indicating these constructs are largely conceptually distinct.
Although all surveyed hematologists were aware of the association between joint hypermobility and bleeding, only about two-thirds reported actually evaluating patients for hypermobility.

Surveyed hematologists showed significant variation in referral patterns for genetic counseling, diagnostic evaluation, and management of nonhematologic symptoms in patients with hypermobile EDS/HSD and bleeding.
There was significant variation among physicians in what they considered the appropriate 'medical home' (primary managing specialty) for this patient population.
Surveyed hematologists identified understanding how bleeding symptoms evolve with age in patients with generalized hypermobility as a future research priority.
Surveyed hematologists prioritized development of functional diagnostic tests to identify the molecular mechanism underlying bleeding in this hypermobile population.
Surveyed hematologists identified the development of novel hemostatic agents for this hypermobile patient population as a research and treatment priority.
Genetic testing confirmed a rare autosomal recessive COL1A2 mutation, consistent with the cardiac-valvular subtype of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (cvEDS).
The patient met Beighton joint hypermobility criteria with positive Walker and Steinberg signs, elbow extension over 10°, and genu recurvatum over 10°, affecting more than 12 joints.
Transthoracic echocardiogram revealed moderate aortic regurgitation and mitral valve posterior leaflet billowing, and clinical exam detected an aortic diastolic grade III/VI murmur.

Clinical examination showed thin velvety translucent skin, large eyes, sunken cheeks, thin nose, lobeless ears, atrophic scars unrelated to trauma, and easy bruising, characteristic of cvEDS phenotype.
The patient's brother presented with the same facial and joint features, meeting family criteria consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance of cvEDS, though no consanguinity was known.

Background literature cited indicates that in EDS the average age for a first major complication is 20 years, more than 80% have had at least one complication by age 40, and mean life expectancy is shortened to 48 years.
Computed tomography angiography of the supra-aortic branches, thoracic and abdominal arteries showed no specific findings of aneurysmatic dilation despite the known risk in cvEDS.

No effective treatment for cvEDS was known, so management consisted of optimizing pain control, rehabilitation, avoidance of hard labor and weight lifting, and close outpatient surveillance for valvular worsening.
Genetic testing identified a pathogenic COL3A1 mutation confirming the diagnosis of vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome in the patient.

A previously healthy 15-year-old male with no family history of connective tissue or vascular disease developed a spontaneous innominate artery pseudoaneurysm with rupture and mediastinal hematoma while running, with no history of trauma.

Absence of aortic root enlargement combined with the young age of the vascular event favored a diagnosis of vascular EDS over other connective tissue vasculopathies such as Marfan syndrome or Loeys-Dietz syndrome.

In a review of 220 index patients and 199 affected relatives with vEDS, median survival was 48 years, with a quarter of patients experiencing first complications before age 20 and average age of first complication 23.5 years, and by age 40, 80% had at least one major complication.
High-dose vitamin C is used as a management approach in vEDS to promote collagen cross-linking and reduce morbidity/mortality, though there is no definitive treatment for the disease.
Antihypertensive agents are used in vEDS management to reduce hemodynamic stress and mitigate abnormal cellular signaling in the arterial wall.

Invasive angiographic and endovascular procedures, including stenting, are generally avoided in vEDS patients due to risk of pseudoaneurysm formation, dissection, vessel rupture, or stent migration, and low-pressure contrast injection is recommended if angiography is necessary.
Genetic testing identified a heterozygous pathogenic COL3A1 variant (c.1511) confirming a diagnosis of vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome in the patient.
Histopathology of the resected sigmoid colon showed segmental absence of the muscularis propria (SAIM), with preservation of the muscularis mucosa, most prominent near the perforation site.
Ganglion cells were abnormally located in both the submucosal plexus and within the muscularis propria, whereas they are normally found only between these layers.
A review of 220 patients with confirmed vEDS found that 40% had experienced a bowel perforation, most commonly in the sigmoid colon.
Bowel perforation in vEDS patients typically occurs later in life, with an average age of 21 years, and the sigmoid colon is the most common site of spontaneous gastrointestinal rupture.
Approximately 25% of vEDS patients will experience a major vascular/visceral complication by age 25.

A systemic review of 48 vEDS patients undergoing 102 operations found that 98% were emergent colonic perforations, with half of repeat perforations occurring on average 12 months after the first surgery.
One study found that approximately 50% of vEDS patients did not experience a second bowel perforation after their first, despite an elevated overall risk.

The patient exhibited joint hypermobility with recurrent hip dislocations, characteristic EDS facies (translucent skin, thin vermilion lips, narrow nose), and a family history of elastic skin and joint dislocation in the maternal grandmother.
Cardiology evaluation revealed mild aortic root dilation, a vascular manifestation consistent with the patient's vEDS diagnosis.

A retrospective review identified 5 pediatric SAIM patients, all born premature (25-32 weeks gestation), four with patent ductus arteriosus, suggesting an ischemic etiology for SAIM in premature infants.

Type III collagen, encoded by COL3A1, is proposed to be essential for the structural integrity, cell adhesion, and cell migration of the bowel wall, blood vessels, and uterus, and its defect in vEDS may underlie both perforation risk and SAIM via impaired cellular migration.
The JHS group reported significantly greater pain (VAS score) than both the GJH and NF groups, with no difference between GJH and NF.
JHS and GJH groups had equally elevated Beighton scores (both significantly higher than NF), confirming similar hypermobility levels between the two hypermobile groups.
During level gait, people with JHS had significantly longer stride time than both NF and GJH groups.
Gait velocity was significantly slower in the JHS group than in both NF and GJH groups.
The GJH (asymptomatic hypermobile) group had significantly greater stride length than both NF and JHS groups, the only significant difference found between GJH and NF across the whole study.
During gait, JHS participants showed significantly lower ankle joint moment than GJH and NF between ~80-90% of stance phase.
During gait, JHS had a significantly smaller hip flexor moment than NF in early stance and a significantly smaller hip extensor moment than both GJH and NF in late stance.
During gait, JHS showed lower ankle power generation and lower hip power absorption/generation than GJH and NF in late stance phase.
During stair ascent, JHS had a significantly longer stance time than both GJH and NF groups.
During stair ascent, JHS had significantly greater knee flexion than NF in early stance (0-30%).
During stair ascent, JHS ankle plantarflexor moment was lower than both GJH and NF for the entire stance phase, reaching significance early and late in stance.
During stair ascent, JHS had a significantly smaller knee extension moment than GJH near initial contact and than NF late in stance.
During stair ascent, JHS generated significantly less power at the ankle than GJH but significantly more power at the knee than NF, suggesting a compensatory 'knee strategy'.
During stair descent, JHS had significantly longer stance duration than GJH and NF, and significantly wider stride width than GJH (but not NF); velocity did not differ between groups.
During stair descent, JHS hip joint angle was more flexed than NF for most of the stance phase (0-80%).
During stair descent, JHS had a greater hip flexor moment than GJH and NF in early stance, reversing the typical extensor moment pattern seen in controls.

During stair descent, JHS had significantly lower knee power absorption than NF at approximately 55% of stance phase, but greater power absorption during mid-stance overall, consistent with a knee-favoring strategy.

Across gait and stair climbing, asymptomatic hypermobile (GJH) participants showed almost no significant kinematic or kinetic differences from non-hypermobile (NF) controls, indicating that hypermobility alone does not explain the movement impairments seen in symptomatic JHS.

Unlike a prior study (Alsiri et al.) that found reduced peak knee flexion in JHS during gait, this study found no significant differences between groups for sagittal plane joint angle, including peak knee flexion.
A novel splice-site variant in COL3A1 intron 14 (c.951+2T>G) was shown by cDNA sequencing to cause skipping of exon 14, providing the causal molecular mechanism for this patient's EDS-IV.
Dermal collagen fibrils in the patient showed variable diameters, consistent with a structural collagen defect in EDS-IV.
Cultured dermal fibroblasts from the patient showed decreased production of type III collagen, consistent with the COL3A1 splicing defect.
Screening the ToMMo whole-genome database of 8380 Japanese individuals identified 13 distinct EDS-related COL3A1 variants in the general population.
The novel COL3A1 splice variant was absent from the ToMMo database of 8380 Japanese individuals as well as HGMD, ClinVar, and LOVD, supporting its rarity/novelty and pathogenic significance.
Col5a1+/− mouse corneas were significantly thinner than wild-type corneas as measured by OCT.
After correcting for corneal thickness, optical coherence elastography showed a significantly higher E-modulus (stiffness) in Col5a1+/− corneas than wild-type.
Axial strain under ambient pressure modulation did not differ significantly between Col5a1+/− and wild-type corneas.
Col5a1+/− corneas showed increased susceptibility to premature rupture during destructive extensometry testing compared to wild-type.
Col5a1+/− corneas showed a non-significant trend towards a higher breaking load than wild-type corneas, indicating rupture was not simply due to thinner tissue.
Col5a1+/− corneas showed significantly greater stress relaxation over 100 seconds than wild-type corneas, indicating increased viscosity and reduced temporal stability.
Prony series modeling of stress relaxation showed the long-term relaxation time constant (τ3) was markedly reduced in Col5a1+/− corneas compared to wild-type, indicating faster long-term relaxation.
Stress-strain extensometry showed a trend towards a steeper curve and higher E-modulus in Col5a1+/− corneas versus wild-type, but this did not reach statistical significance.

Second harmonic generation imaging showed increased forward- and backward-scattered signal in Col5a1+/− corneas, suggesting fibril disorganization, increased fibril density, and abnormal stromal hierarchical organization compared to wild-type.
Corneal thinning in human classic EDS patients appears less pronounced than in the Col5a1+/− mouse model, with an estimated 8% reduction in humans versus ~20-26% in mice.
In a previously reported clinical cohort of classic EDS patients, spontaneous or minimal-trauma corneal rupture ('oculus fragilis') occurred in approximately 35% of patients.
A clinical case series found no signs of keratoconus in genetically-confirmed classic EDS patients, supporting the lack of association between EDS and keratoconus despite corneal thinning.
Lung herniation, the cause of a voluntarily expandable neck mass in this patient, is associated with Ehlers-Danlos syndrome type 1, likely due to underlying connective tissue weakness.
The patient's bilateral anterior lung herniation, presenting as a neck mass, was multifactorial and identified via CT imaging performed with and without Valsalva manoeuvre.
BV-2 microglia cultured for 96h with 10% FCS retain an amoeboid, macrophage-like morphology, whereas cells cultured without FCS shift to a ramified, branched morphology.
BV-2 cells grown in 10% FCS constitutively show high iNOS expression together with low CD206 expression, characterizing an activated M1-like (iNOShighCD206low) phenotype.
BV-2 cells grown in 10% FCS constitutively exhibit low expression of the M2 anti-inflammatory marker CD206, consistent with an activated cell profile.
Treatment of activated BV-210%FCS cells with 100 μM low-dose naltrexone (LDN) for 24h shifted the cells to a quiescent iNOSlowCD206high phenotype, i.e., decreased iNOS and increased CD206 expression.
Naltrexone had no major effect on iNOS/CD206 marker expression in already-quiescent BV-2øFCS cells compared to untreated controls.
Naltrexone preserved BV-2 cell viability (>96%) at doses up to 250 μM, with viability greatly reduced at 500 μM and above.

At baseline, BV-210%FCS cells were glycolytically active (low OCR, high ECAR) while BV-2øFCS cells were mostly metabolically quiescent (low OCR, low ECAR), though both had similar capacity to increase metabolic activity upon FCCP/oligomycin stress.
Stimulation of BV-210%FCS cells with LPS and IFN-γ induced a highly glycolytic phenotype (increased ECAR, decreased OCR), with IFN-γ producing a greater shift toward glycolysis than LPS.

Low-dose naltrexone (100 μM) reduced the aerobic glycolytic metabolism of BV-2 microglia cells activated by FCS/LPS/IFN-γ, reversing the hyperactive glycolytic state toward a normal or hypo-energetic, oxidative state.

Naltrexone administration increased total protein expression of p70S6K in a dose-dependent manner, with a lesser increase in the phosphorylated fraction (p-p70S6K), suggesting modulation of mTOR/S6K signaling without major stimulation of new protein synthesis.

In a cited pilot study (Parkitny et al.), 4.5 mg naltrexone administered nightly to fibromyalgia patients significantly reduced serum levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines including IL-1, IL-2, IL-12, IL-18, IFN-γ, GM-CSF, and TNF-α.
Cited prior work (Wang et al.) showed both (+)- and (−)-naltrexone isomers inhibited LPS-induced NO production in BV-2 cells across 0.1–1000 μM, with an IC50 of approximately 100 μM for both isomers.

The authors propose that naltrexone's immunometabolic effects on microglia may act via TLR-4 receptor antagonism, which is linked to reduced mTOR activity, based on known TLR-4/mTOR crosstalk in macrophages.
Ursolic acid suppressed intracellular calcium levels and inhibited degranulation in IgE-stimulated mast cells in a concentration-dependent manner.
Ursolic acid inhibited the expression and release of pro-inflammatory cytokines from IgE-activated mast cells.
Ursolic acid demonstrated anti-allergic effects by suppressing FcεRI-mediated intracellular signaling molecules in mast cells.
Ursolic acid inhibited IgE-mediated passive cutaneous anaphylaxis (PCA) reactions in a mouse model in a dose-dependent manner.
Ursolic acid inhibited ovalbumin-induced active systemic anaphylaxis (ASA) reactions in mice in a dose-dependent manner.
Trigonelline hydrochloride (TH) showed no significant cytotoxicity in bone marrow-derived mast cells (BMMCs) at concentrations up to 1 mM.
TH dose-dependently reduced IgE/antigen-induced β-hexosaminidase (degranulation marker) release from BMMCs.
TH inhibited FcεRI-triggered phosphorylation of the early signaling kinases Lyn, Fyn and PI3K in BMMCs.
TH suppressed IgE/antigen-induced secretion and mRNA expression of the inflammatory cytokines TNF-α and IL-6 in BMMCs.
TH dose-dependently decreased production of the lipid mediators LTC4 and PGD2 in activated BMMCs, accompanied by reduced phosphorylation of cPLA2 and nuclear translocation of 5-LO.
In the passive systemic anaphylaxis (PSA) mouse model, serum LTC4, PGD2 and histamine were significantly elevated in the vehicle-treated group and reduced in TH-treated mice.
TH inhibited phosphorylation of NF-κB pathway components (Akt, IKK, IκBα) and MAPK pathway components (ERK, JNK, p38) in activated BMMCs.
TH prevented nuclear translocation of the transcription factors NF-κB p65 and AP-1 (p-c-Jun, c-Jun, c-Fos) in activated BMMCs.

RNA-sequencing of TH-treated versus PBS-treated BMMCs identified 105 upregulated and 201 downregulated genes, with HIF-1α showing a notable expression difference and flagged as immune-system disease related.
In the OVA-induced asthma model, TH decreased serum IgE levels in a dose-dependent manner, with a significant inhibitory effect at the high dose (200 mg/kg).
TH-treated OVA-sensitized mice showed reduced inflammatory cell infiltration and mucus secretion in lung tissue compared to OVA-only treated mice, assessed by H&E and PAS staining.
Immunohistochemistry for c-Kit showed decreased mast cell numbers in lung tissue of TH-treated OVA-sensitized mice.

In lung tissue of OVA-sensitized mice, TH decreased Th2 cytokines IL-4, IL-5 and IL-13 (high dose comparable to dexamethasone) while IFN-γ (Th1 cytokine) showed no significant change versus OVA group.
OVA-stimulated splenocytes from TH-treated mice showed reduced IL-4, IL-5 and IL-13 production at high dose, with little effect on IFN-γ, consistent with lung tissue findings.
High-dose TH suppressed phosphorylation of ERK, JNK, p38 (MAPKs) and IκBα (NF-κB pathway) in splenocytes from OVA-sensitized mice.
Omalizumab reduces surface FcεRI expression on both basophils and mast cells.
Omalizumab-induced FcεRI downregulation occurs rapidly in circulating basophils but takes 10-20 days in tissue-resident mast cells.
Clinical trials and real-life evidence show omalizumab is safe and useful in inhibiting allergic responses as monotherapy in food allergy.
DARPins are engineered proteins that are 10,000-fold more efficient than omalizumab at dissociating IgE-FcεRI complexes in vitro, ex vivo, and in human tissue.

Self-assembled anti-IgE mRNA vaccines inhibited IgE-mediated anaphylaxis in animal models and were tested in a Phase I trial in allergic rhinitis patients, but application in food allergy remains unclear.
Covalent heterobivalent LARI molecules reduced anaphylaxis risk in experimental mouse models of peanut allergy.
