An anti-FcεRIα monoclonal antibody strongly suppressed IgE-mediated mast cell activation in a humanized mouse model of food allergy and anaphylaxis.

BTK inhibitors significantly reduced degranulation and cytokine production in human mast cells and basophils, decreased bronchoconstriction in isolated human bronchi, and prevented anaphylaxis in a humanized mouse model.
IgE from atopic individuals shows increased sialic acid content compared to non-atopic subjects, implicating sialylation in IgE allergenicity.
Neuraminidase-induced de-sialylation of IgE, in a non-FcεRI dependent manner, diminished downstream signaling in mast cells.
Dupilumab reduced peanut-specific IgE production by human B cells in vitro, with sustained inhibition after in vivo re-exposure in a peanut anaphylaxis mouse model.
A single case report described dupilumab as an efficient therapeutic option for multiple co-occurring food allergies, and it is currently in clinical trial for peanut allergy.
In a Phase II study, 73% of peanut-allergic patients treated with etokimab achieved tolerance to the target peanut dose, with reduced Th2 cytokines and peanut-specific IgE compared to placebo.
Anti-TSLP treatment (tezepelumab) successfully reduced allergen-induced bronchoconstriction and airway inflammation markers in patients with allergic asthma.
In humans, FcγRIIb transcripts are detectable in gastrointestinal mast cells but not in skin mast cells, which may explain differential tolerogenic capacity by anatomical site.
An Ara h 2-FcγRIIb bispecific fusion protein reduced allergen-specific responses in a peanut allergy mouse model.
Antibodies targeting CD200R effectively inhibited mast cell activation in mouse models and human mast cells, but no food allergy efficacy data exist yet.

CD33 ligand-coated liposomal nanoparticles suppressed mast cell activation, prevented IgE-mediated anaphylaxis, and induced short-lived allergen desensitization in ovalbumin and peanut allergy mouse models.
Engagement of Siglec-8 reduces intracellular calcium flux and FcεRI-dependent mediator release in human mast cells, while inducing a pro-apoptotic effect on human eosinophils.
Lirentelimab inhibited IgE-mediated passive systemic anaphylaxis in a humanized mouse model and showed positive clinical effects in patients with asthma and eosinophilic gastroenteritis.
Fusion proteins co-targeting CD300a and IgE on mast cells successfully reduced mast cell activation in a passive cutaneous anaphylaxis mouse model.
Multiple AIT trials using whole peanut or peanut extracts promoted tolerance to varying peanut doses in 60-80% of treated subjects.
Peanut AIT trials showed a 1-21% frequency of systemic adverse reactions, with increased occurrence at higher peanut end-goal doses.
Omalizumab administered during allergen immunotherapy reduces the risk of severe reactions and facilitates AIT.
Long-term omalizumab add-on treatment during cow's milk AIT was found not to be cost-effective, despite a higher safety profile.
An attenuated E. coli-based Ara h 1-2-3 recombinant vaccine candidate failed to promote tolerance and induced severe adverse reactions in 20% of participants.
After more than 20 years of omalizumab use, no increased risk for parasitic or neoplastic events has been observed.
Plastic caging (without added BPA) significantly increased histologically-assessed myocardial inflammation in male mice with CVB3 myocarditis compared to glass caging.
High-dose BPA (250 µg/L, EPA reference dose equivalent) in drinking water significantly increased histological myocarditis in female mice.
Plastic caging alone (without added BPA) did not significantly alter histological myocardial inflammation in female mice compared to glass caging.
Neither plastic caging nor BPA exposure altered cardiac viral gene (VP1) expression in either sex, indicating the sex-specific increase in myocarditis was not due to increased viral replication.

In females, the only immune marker significantly increased in the heart by plastic caging was the mast cell marker cKit, while other immune markers (CD45, CD11b, F4/80, GR1, CD14, CD3, CD4, CD8) were unchanged.
In males, plastic caging significantly increased cardiac gene expression of CD11b, GR1 (neutrophil marker), and CD14 during myocarditis, while CD45 and F4/80 were unaffected.
In males, BPA exposure increased cardiac CD45, CD11b, F4/80, and CD14 gene expression (all markers except GR1) compared to controls.
BPA exposure (but not plastic caging alone) significantly increased cardiac CD3 and CD4 T-cell marker gene expression in males; CD8 was unaffected.
Immunohistochemistry confirmed that plastic caging significantly increased CD11b+ and GR1+ (neutrophil) positive-stained cells in the hearts of male mice with myocarditis.
Plastic caging significantly increased cardiac cKit (mast cell marker) gene expression in female mice with myocarditis, whereas BPA exposure did not.
In contrast to females, plastic caging and BPA exposure both significantly decreased cardiac cKit gene expression in male mice with myocarditis.
Plastic caging and BPA exposure each significantly increased the number of degranulating cardiac (total and pericardial) mast cells in female mice with myocarditis.

Despite decreased cKit gene expression, plastic caging and BPA did not significantly change total mast cell number or degranulation histologically in males; males had higher baseline degranulating mast cells regardless of exposure.
Plastic caging significantly increased cardiac collagen 1 gene expression and histological fibrosis in female mice with myocarditis; BPA exposure similarly increased fibrosis.
Neither plastic caging nor BPA exposure significantly altered cardiac collagen 1 expression or fibrosis in male mice with myocarditis.
In females, plastic caging significantly increased cardiac androgen receptor (AR) gene expression without affecting estrogen receptors, while BPA exposure specifically increased ERβ expression.

In males, plastic caging significantly decreased cardiac ERα and ERβ gene expression while increasing AR expression; ERRγ was unaffected, and BPA exposure alone did not significantly alter any of the receptors in males.

In males, plastic caging and BPA exposure both significantly increased cardiac expression of complement receptor CR3 (CD11b), C4b, and the mast cell anaphylatoxin receptor C5aR1, whereas complement components were unaffected by plastic caging in females.
Plastic caging had no significant effect on cardiac complement component gene expression in female mice, in contrast to the significant increases seen in males.

Recombinant human diamine oxidase wildtype (rhDAO-WT) completely degraded a pathophysiologically relevant histamine concentration of 100 ng/mL within 15 minutes in albumin buffer and plasma, regardless of excess heparin.

In plasma from mastocytosis patients and healthy volunteers spiked with histamine, rhDAO-WT reduced both exogenous and endogenous histamine to below 1 ng/mL, an effect completely blocked by the DAO inhibitor diminazene aceturate (DIMAZ).
Wildtype recombinant human DAO was previously shown to have a very short plasma half-life (<5 min) after intravenous infusion in rats and mice, precluding its therapeutic development.

Single and double mutations in the RFKRKLPK heparin-binding motif (residues 568-575) caused DAO to elute from heparin-sepharose columns at lower salt concentrations than wildtype, confirming reduced heparin binding.

The double mutant rhDAO-R568S/R571T showed no detectable binding to high molecular weight heparin (HMWH) by ITC or BLI and only minimal binding to heparan sulfate, compared to strong binding by wildtype DAO.

Cellular uptake of DAO into SK-Hep1 cells was slightly reduced by the single mutant R568S but strongly abolished by both double mutants (R568S/R571T and R568S/K575T), reaching levels comparable to negative controls.

Across five cell lines (SK-Hep1, HUVEC, HDF, HepG2, HeLa, PODO/TERT256, HDMVEC), flow cytometry showed the R568S/R571T mutant had 67-85% reduced cellular uptake compared to wildtype, with significant reductions in every cell line tested.

Western blot analysis confirmed reduced cellular uptake, with the single mutant reduced by 29-71% and both double mutants reduced more than fivefold (to 17% and 18% of wildtype levels) in SK-Hep1 and HUVEC/TERT2 cells.

In rats, the double mutant rhDAO-R568S/R571T (and its Fc-fusion form) generated the highest area under the curve (AUC) of all tested HBM mutants, confirming markedly improved pharmacokinetics over wildtype.
In mice, the rhDAO-R568S/R571T mutant increased the area under the curve (AUC) more than 15-fold compared to wildtype rhDAO after both intravenous and intraperitoneal injection.
The R568S/R571T mutant retained enzymatic activity indistinguishable from wildtype DAO, degrading histamine equally efficiently with or without heparin excess.
After intravenous administration of HBM mutants, DAO plasma activity remained measurable for up to 28 hours, and DAO concentration and activity were highly correlated (R² > 96%).
Comparison of 87 mammalian DAO sequences showed the HBM is 68% conserved overall, with R568 the most conserved residue (89%); in primates (15 species) residues R568-P574 are 100% conserved.

In silico modeling identified R568 as critical for heparin binding (its mutation strongly decreased predicted affinity), while R571T and K575T were predicted to have lower effects; predicted affinity changes correlated with measured heparin-sepharose elution salt concentrations (R²=93%, p=0.0088).

The triple mutant reproducing the rodent HBM sequence had the lowest predicted heparin affinity of all mutants in silico, yet showed stronger actual heparin-sepharose binding than the double mutant R568S/R571T, a discrepancy attributed to limitations of the additive energy-prediction algorithm for triple mutations.

The R568S/R571T mutation abolished the fast alpha-elimination clearance phase (which removes >90% of wildtype DAO within 5 minutes) while leaving the slower beta-elimination phase (~6 hours) largely unchanged, suggesting a distinct, heparin-independent clearance mechanism for the residual phase.

In a systemic mastocytosis patient, plasma histamine rose from 10 ng/mL to 35 ng/mL over a few hours, and the patient developed severe clinical symptoms despite high-dose treatment with the H1 antagonist diphenhydramine and H2 antagonist ranitidine.

Despite treatment with histamine receptor antagonists at up to four times the approved dose plus additional medications, approximately 70% of mastocytosis patients self-identify as disabled by standard disability definitions.

In healthy volunteers, combined H1/H2 histamine receptor antagonist regimens only sufficiently blocked symptom development up to a systemic histamine threshold of approximately 6 ng/mL, only 3-4 times higher than without treatment and 20-fold below concentrations reached during severe anaphylaxis.
25-33% of chronic urticaria patients are resistant to histamine receptor antagonist treatment, illustrating a broader unmet need for histamine-targeted therapies beyond receptor blockade.
A 52-year-old man developed acute bilateral lip angioedema within hours of exposure to a Karenia brevis red tide algae bloom at a Florida beach.
Complement studies including C4, C1q, and C1 esterase inhibitor level and function were all within normal limits, supporting a histamine-mediated rather than bradykinin-mediated etiology.
Initial labs showed leukocytosis with increased neutrophils, which resolved after treatment and clinical improvement.

Initial treatment with diphenhydramine, methylprednisolone, and famotidine did not improve the patient's angioedema, and intramuscular epinephrine produced only mild improvement two hours later, but symptoms resolved with additional doses of the same medications in the ICU.

The authors propose that brevetoxins disrupt voltage-gated sodium channels causing depolarization and acetylcholine release, which can trigger mast cell degranulation and release of inflammatory cytokines and histamine, based on prior animal model studies.
Prior studies have found that red tide algae blooms are positively correlated with increased emergency department visits for asthma exacerbations and respiratory illnesses in coastal areas.
Both LUTS patients and CP1-infected mice showed increased numbers and activation of mast cells alongside elevated prostate fibrosis.

Combined treatment with the mast cell stabilizer cromolyn sodium and the H1 receptor antagonist cetirizine reduced mast cell activation, prostate fibrosis, immune cell infiltration, and inflammation, and significantly alleviated urinary dysfunction in CP1-infected mice.
Mice treated with mast cell inhibitors showed reduced phosphorylation of myosin light chain-2, a marker of prostate smooth muscle contraction, compared to symptomatic CP1-infected mice.

In one cited cohort, non-response and worsening of respiratory symptoms on aspirin therapy occurred predominantly in African-American and Latino patients, while no white, non-Latino patients worsened.
Data on sex differences in aspirin therapy outcomes are inconsistent, with one study suggesting female sex as a positive prognostic factor and another finding no gender difference.
Responders to aspirin therapy had more severe nasal symptoms on SNOT-22 and a longer interval from sinus surgery to aspirin desensitization than non-responders.
Higher blood eosinophil count and lower sputum neutrophil percentage were associated with good response to long-term aspirin treatment in AERD patients with severe asthma.
No significant changes in type 2 cytokine profile were observed in blood or induced sputum supernatant across timepoints during long-term daily aspirin therapy.

High-dose aspirin therapy paradoxically increased systemic markers of type 2 inflammation—peripheral blood eosinophilia, plasma tryptase, and urinary LTE4—independent of clinical response, despite reducing bronchial and nasal symptoms.
In responders, sputum eosinophil percentage significantly decreased with aspirin therapy while blood eosinophil count remained stable, whereas non-responders showed no changes in sputum eosinophils.
Responders to aspirin treatment were characterized by high baseline HPGD gene expression in sputum cells, suggesting it as a biomarker predicting benefit from aspirin therapy.

Higher baseline PRG2 gene expression in sputum cells, indicating greater eosinophil activity, was associated with lack of response to long-term aspirin treatment; low PRG2 expression may predict stronger benefit.

AERD patients show a selective increase in CysLT1 receptor expression on nasal submucosal inflammatory cells compared with aspirin-tolerant CRSwNP patients, and variations in its expression may contribute to heterogeneity in response to aspirin therapy.
Long-term aspirin treatment was associated with suppression of sputum IL-4 release, potentially via aspirin's inhibition of STAT6 in CD4 T cells, mediating tolerance in AERD.

Higher baseline plasma 15-HETE level, strongly correlated with eosinophilia at 4 weeks of aspirin therapy, was characteristic of AERD patients who benefited from aspirin therapy, indicating its potential as a predictive biomarker.

ALOX15 expression was significantly elevated in nasal polyps of AERD patients compared with CRSwNP patients or healthy controls, predominantly in epithelial cells, and correlated with clinical asthma severity and radiographic sinus disease.

15-Oxo-ETE, a downstream 15-LO product requiring HPGD for synthesis, was markedly higher in nasal polyp tissue of AERD patients compared with CRSwNP and control inferior turbinate tissue, and is proposed as a possible predictor of aspirin treatment outcome.

Most eicosanoids in induced sputum supernatant (PGD2, PGE2, 8-iso-PGE2, tetranor-PGD-M, tetranor-PGE-M, LTB4, cysLTs), except 15-HETE, do not change with high-dose long-term aspirin therapy and cannot predict treatment response.
Sputum cell gene expression of multiple arachidonic acid pathway enzymes and eicosanoid receptors was concluded to not be helpful in predicting response to long-term aspirin therapy in AERD.

AERD patients with a neutrophilic inflammatory phenotype based on induced sputum (associated with Th17 cytokines) are not eligible for aspirin treatment and are unlikely to respond, with a threshold of 48.5% or lower sputum neutrophils best differentiating responders.
Extracellular ATP enhanced both antigen-dependent and antigen-independent mast cell degranulation through activation of ionotropic P2X4 receptors.
P2X4 receptor activation alone did not trigger degranulation but significantly potentiated antigen-triggered mast cell degranulation.
Stimulation of the P2X4 receptor potentiated the FcεRI-mediated tyrosine kinase signaling cascade in mast cells.
Co-stimulation of mast cells with ATP together with Gi-coupled receptor agonists such as PGE2 and adenosine produced synergistic degranulation.
P2rx4 knockout mice showed impaired antigen-induced passive anaphylaxis compared to wild-type mice.
P2rx4 knockout mice showed impaired antigen-induced passive anaphylaxis responses compared to wild-type mice, confirming the in vivo significance of P2X4 receptor signaling in allergic reactions.

P2rx4 knockout mice exhibited reduced PGE2-induced increases in vascular permeability compared to wild-type mice, supporting a role for P2X4 receptor signaling in antigen-independent allergic/inflammatory responses in vivo.

In a Df-induced mouse model of atopic dermatitis, hUCB-MSC injection reduced clinical severity scores by 48% versus Df-induced mice, but co-administration with pimecrolimus prevented this improvement.
hUCB-MSC injection significantly decreased dorsal epidermal thickness by 42.7% compared with Df-induced mice, but the MSC+pimecrolimus group did not differ from the Df-induced group.
hUCB-MSC injection significantly suppressed dermal mast cell infiltration in AD-model mice, but co-administration with pimecrolimus countered this suppressive effect.
TARC and IL-22 mRNA in ear skin were reduced by either hUCB-MSC or pimecrolimus alone, but returned to Df-induced levels in the combination group.
Serum IgE level was significantly reduced by 45% following hUCB-MSC injection, but was unchanged from Df-induced levels in the MSC+pimecrolimus group.
Pimecrolimus (0.1 ng/ml-1 μg/ml) did not alter hUCB-MSC viability, proliferation, cell cycle profile, cellular morphology, or expression of MSC surface markers (CD45, CD34, CD36, CD105, CD29, CD73).
hUCB-MSC co-culture (or pimecrolimus alone) significantly inhibited ConA-induced hPBMC proliferation, but simultaneous pimecrolimus and hUCB-MSC treatment abolished this suppressive effect.
hUCB-MSCs significantly suppressed IgE/anti-IgE-induced degranulation of LAD-2 mast cells, but this suppressive effect was reduced when pimecrolimus was co-administered.
Both pimecrolimus alone and hUCB-MSC coculture decreased LAD-2 mast cell proliferation, but the combination did not show a synergistic additional decrease.
hUCB-MSC coculture suppressed TNF-α mRNA expression in LAD-2 mast cells, but no suppressive effect was seen when pimecrolimus was co-administered.
hUCB-MSC coculture decreased CD4+IL-4+ Th2 cell differentiation, but the presence of pimecrolimus restored Th2 differentiation to control levels.
hUCB-MSC coculture decreased GATA3 and STAT6 mRNA expression in differentiating Th2 cells, but pimecrolimus blocked this hUCB-MSC-induced downregulation.
hUCB-MSC coculture decreased IL-13 mRNA expression in Th2 cells, but coadministration of pimecrolimus prevented this decrease.
Pimecrolimus treatment did not alter IFN-γ-stimulated IDO-1 production by hUCB-MSCs.
Pimecrolimus treatment did not significantly alter TGF-beta secretion from hUCB-MSCs.
Pimecrolimus treatment reduced PGE2 secretion from hUCB-MSCs in a dose-dependent manner.
Pimecrolimus dose-dependently decreased COX2 mRNA (conventional PCR/qPCR), protein (Western blot) and immunostaining signal in hUCB-MSCs.

Among the five NFAT family members, NFAT1 and NFAT2 mRNA were not detected in hUCB-MSCs (though present in PBMCs/T cells), whereas NFAT3, NFAT4, and NFAT5 (and FKBP12) were expressed, with NFAT3 detected in all three hUCB-MSC donor lines.
Pimecrolimus caused dose-dependent redistribution of NFAT3 from the nuclear fraction to the cytosolic fraction in hUCB-MSCs, accompanied by a decrease in cytosolic COX2.

Ionomycin/PMA stimulation, which dephosphorylates and activates NFAT, accelerated nuclear translocation of NFAT3 and increased COX2 expression in hUCB-MSCs, demonstrating NFAT3-dependence of COX2 expression.
Pimecrolimus treatment increased phosphorylated NFAT3 levels (cytosolic, inactive form) in hUCB-MSCs under both resting and ionomycin/PMA-stimulated conditions.

Background from the authors' prior phase I/IIa clinical trial: 55% of AD patients in the high-dose hUCB-MSC group achieved a 50% reduction in EASI score, with IGA and SCORAD scores decreasing by 33% and 50% respectively.

HDGF, like FGF2 and CTGF, is rapidly released into conditioned medium from human articular cartilage within 30 minutes (largely within 5 minutes) of mechanical injury, but not from uninjured rested cartilage.

All three PCM-bound growth factors bind heparin and are eluted with 2.5M NaCl, and are released from cartilage upon heparitinase treatment, indicating they are sequestered by heparan sulfate proteoglycans.

Growth factor release upon cartilage injury occurred irrespective of tissue viability (live vs. freeze-thaw killed), temperature (4°C vs 37°C), MMP inhibition, or broad-spectrum protease inhibition, indicating a cell- and protease-independent release mechanism.
Addition of exogenous supraphysiological NaCl to cartilage displaced HDGF and CTGF from the matrix and enhanced growth factor release upon injury in a concentration-dependent manner.

Prolonged IL-1 treatment (7 days) depleted aggrecan/fixed charge density of cartilage and abrogated the injury-induced release of HDGF, CTGF, and FGF2, despite no difference in total extractable growth factor content.

Compressive loading (28% strain) of porcine osteochondral plugs caused a significant 46% increase in free sodium with a concomitant significant decrease in bound sodium fraction, measured by 23Na MRI/spectroscopy, partially restored upon relaxation.

Cyclical compressive loading of cartilage for 45 minutes induced SMAD2 phosphorylation (indicating TGFβ activation) specifically in the superficial zone (50-300 µm from surface), not seen in non-compressed explants.

Scanning acoustic microscopy revealed a region of reduced tissue stiffness 50-350 µm below the articular surface, which became more pronounced upon compression, corresponding with disordered collagen fibre alignment on polarised light microscopy.

Second harmonic generation imaging of human articular cartilage under compression (0-21% strain) showed marked volume loss and collagen fibre reorientation in the superficial zone, but no volume loss or orientation change in the deep zone.

In human osteoarthritic knee cartilage, proteoglycan (GAG) content inversely correlated with macroscopic Outerbridge disease severity score, confirming greater matrix damage is associated with reduced aggrecan content.

Biopsies from severely diseased regions of osteoarthritic joints (Outerbridge 3-4) released significantly less HDGF, CTGF, and FGF2 upon injury compared with biopsies from relatively undamaged regions (Outerbridge 0-1) of the same joint.

Despite reduced injury-induced release, more severely damaged osteoarthritic cartilage contained higher NaCl-extractable (matrix-bound) growth factor content than milder disease tissue, indicating growth factors remain present but are not mobilised.
Nos1-/- mice show complete loss of NADPH diaphorase activity and nNOS-immunoreactive neurons in the distal colon compared to wild-type C57BL/6J mice.
Total myenteric neuronal cell numbers (HuC/D+) in the distal colon were comparable between Nos1-/- and wild-type mice.
TuJ1 mRNA expression showed a non-significant 1.4-fold trend toward increase in Nos1-/- distal colon compared to wild-type tissue.
ChAT mRNA expression was similar between Nos1-/- and wild-type distal colon, indicating no compensatory change in this excitatory marker.
Substance P mRNA expression was unchanged in Nos1-/- distal colon compared to wild-type tissue.

Vip mRNA was significantly upregulated (1.43-fold) in the distal colon of Nos1-/- mice compared to wild-type controls, suggesting compensatory transcriptional upregulation of an alternative inhibitory neurotransmitter upon loss of nNOS.

Machine-learning based digital image analysis revealed significantly greater TuJ1+ neural network density (coverage) in the Nos1-/- distal colon compared to wild-type controls, despite visually similar gross morphology.

Validation of the machine-learning analysis pipeline in the Ednrb-/- mouse model (a graded ENS-loss/Hirschsprung disease model) confirmed progressively reduced network density, junction number, and branch number from ganglionic to transition to aganglionic colon regions.
Very small interganglionic (background) areas were significantly more numerous in Nos1-/- distal colon than wild-type, indicating finer network subdivision.
Small interganglionic areas (51-200 and 201-400 pixels) were significantly more numerous in Nos1-/- than wild-type distal colon.
Medium-sized interganglionic areas (401-600 and 601-800 pixels) were significantly increased in Nos1-/- distal colon compared to wild-type.
Interganglionic areas of 801-1000 pixels were comparable between Nos1-/- and wild-type distal colon.
Large interganglionic areas (>1000 pixels) were significantly reduced in Nos1-/- distal colon compared to wild-type, indicating loss of large open spaces within the network.
Total network junction number (triple and quadruple points combined) was significantly greater in Nos1-/- distal colon than in wild-type, indicating increased network interconnectivity.
Total branch number was significantly greater in Nos1-/- distal colon compared to wild-type controls.
Total branch length of the TuJ1+ network was significantly greater in Nos1-/- distal colon compared to wild-type controls.
Mean branch length was not significantly different between Nos1-/- and wild-type distal colon, indicating that increased total branching is due to more numerous, not longer, branches.

Network orientation and coherency of the TuJ1+ ENS were not significantly different between Nos1-/- and wild-type distal colon, with the apparent orientation difference attributed to a directional measurement artefact rather than a true biological effect.
The authors' prior work (cited) demonstrated reduced ICC networks in the same global Nos1-/- knockout model, supporting broader neuromuscular remodelling beyond neuronal changes alone.
miR-101a-3p expression was significantly decreased in atrial tissue of acetylcholine-CaCl2-induced AF model rats compared with sham rats.
EZH2 protein expression was significantly higher in atrial tissue of AF model rats compared with sham rats.
Lentiviral delivery of miR-101a-3p (LV-miR-101a-3p) into the right atrium significantly increased miR-101a-3p expression compared with LV-NC infected AF rats.
Overexpression of miR-101a-3p via lentivirus reduced EZH2 protein expression in atrial tissue of AF rats compared with LV-NC controls.

miR-101a-3p overexpression reversed AF-associated electrophysiological remodeling, restoring atrial effective refractory period (AERP) and reducing AF duration and inducibility compared with AF + LV-NC rats.
miR-101a-3p overexpression reduced Ach-CaCl2-induced atrial tissue injury and fibrosis as shown by H&E and Masson trichrome staining.
Ach-CaCl2-induced AF significantly increased collagen I and collagen III expression in atrial tissue, and this was reduced by miR-101a-3p overexpression.
Ach-CaCl2-induced AF significantly increased protein expression of TGF-β1, CTGF, fibronectin and α-SMA in atrial tissue, which were downregulated by miR-101a-3p overexpression.

Luciferase reporter assay confirmed that EZH2 is a direct target gene of miR-101a-3p, as luciferase activity was reduced only when miR-101a-3p mimics were co-transfected with wild-type (not mutant) EZH2 3'UTR.
Treatment of SSc-derived dermal fibroblasts with 4-octyl itaconate (4-OI) reduced secreted collagen levels by ~60% compared to vehicle.
4-OI treatment significantly upregulated the Nrf2-target gene heme oxygenase 1 (HO-1) in SSc dermal fibroblasts.
4-OI treatment significantly upregulated the Nrf2-target gene NQO1 in SSc dermal fibroblasts.

4-OI significantly increased ARE-driven luciferase reporter activity 2-fold in dermal fibroblasts, comparable to the known Nrf2 inducer sulforaphane, confirming ARE-dependent transcriptional activation.
LPS (TLR4 agonist) stimulation significantly upregulated IL-6 secretion in healthy dermal fibroblasts, and this was attenuated by pre-treatment with 4-OI.
LPS stimulation significantly upregulated MCP-1 secretion in healthy dermal fibroblasts, an effect attenuated by 4-OI pre-treatment.
Pre-treatment with 4-OI significantly reduced TGF-β1-induced ROS levels in dermal fibroblasts.
Pre-treatment with 4-OI significantly reduced TGF-β1-stimulated collagen protein levels in healthy dermal fibroblasts.
Pre-treatment with 4-OI significantly reduced TGF-β1-stimulated CCN2 (CTGF) mRNA expression in healthy dermal fibroblasts.
4-OI treatment did not increase LDH release, indicating no cytotoxic effect associated with its anti-fibrotic action.
4-OI reduced TGF-β1-induced glycolysis (extracellular acidification rate, ECAR) by over 45% in dermal fibroblasts.

In Nrf2-knockout mouse embryonic fibroblasts, the collagen-lowering effect of 4-OI and the increase in NQO1 seen in wild-type cells were abolished, indicating the anti-fibrotic effect of 4-OI requires Nrf2.
4-OI treatment caused an approximately 3-fold elevation of miR29a in SSc dermal fibroblasts compared to vehicle.
4-OI treatment did not alter expression of microRNA-155 in SSc dermal fibroblasts, unlike its effect on miR29a, suggesting specificity of the microRNA response.

Prior published work cited in this paper reports that Nrf2 is significantly downregulated in SSc dermal fibroblasts and skin biopsies, and that Nrf2-deficient mice show exaggerated skin and lung fibrosis.
A cited study found that IRG1-deficient mice (unable to generate itaconate) show exacerbated fibrosis in the bleomycin model, attributable to a macrophage rather than fibroblast-intrinsic mechanism.
Serum CTGF levels correlated positively with the rise in diastolic blood pressure in rats on the high-carbohydrate high-fat diet.
Serum fibronectin levels correlated positively with both systolic and diastolic blood pressure increases and with impaired carbohydrate metabolism.
Endothelin-1 serum levels were positively correlated with both systolic and diastolic blood pressure elevations and with fibronectin levels.
TGF-beta serum levels rose alongside fibronectin, endothelin-1, and CTGF in rats on the high-carbohydrate high-fat diet.

Arterial hypertension and histological changes in the aortic wall were most pronounced in old rats fed the high-carbohydrate high-fat diet, whereas hypertension was only transient in young rats on the same diet.
Increased aortic wall thickness correlated positively with diastolic blood pressure rise, alongside CTGF, endothelin-1 and fibronectin levels.
Among 120 patients with Marfan syndrome or Marfan-related syndrome, the prevalence of chronic periodontitis was significantly higher than in healthy controls.
A 44-year-old female with Loeys-Dietz syndrome and aggressive periodontitis was found to carry a novel TGFBR1 mutation (G188V) in the glycine/serine-rich (GS) domain encoded by exon 3.

In HEK293 cells, TGF-β-induced luciferase reporter activity was significantly elevated with wildtype Tgfbr1 but significantly suppressed with the Tgfbr1 G188V mutant, indicating loss of TGF-β signaling function.
Homozygous Tgfbr1 G188V/G188V knock-in mice underwent embryonic lethality after day 14.5, with only one homozygous mouse ever obtained live at birth.
Heterozygous Tgfbr1G188V/+ mice showed significantly reduced survival over 180 days compared with wildtype mice.
Aortic tissue from 24-week-old Tgfbr1G188V/+ mice showed distorted and fragmented elastic fibers on Elastica van Gieson staining, consistent with a vascular Loeys-Dietz-like phenotype.
mRNA levels of Tgfb1, Tgfb3, Tgfbr1, Tgfbr2, Col1a1, and Serpine1 in aortic tissue tended to be higher in Tgfbr1G188V/+ mice than WT, but the differences were not statistically significant.
TGF-β-induced Serpine1 expression, which increased dose-dependently in wildtype MEFs, was significantly reduced in Tgfbr1G188V/+ and Tgfbr1G188V/G188V MEFs.
TGF-β-stimulated phospho-Smad2 levels, which increased dose-dependently in wildtype MEFs, were lower in Tgfbr1G188V/+ and Tgfbr1G188V/G188V MEFs.
Without bacterial challenge, there was no significant difference in baseline alveolar bone resorption or periodontal tissue histology between Tgfbr1G188V/+ and WT mice at 6 or 24 weeks of age.

Expression of Tgfb1, Tgfb2, Tgfb3, Col1a1, Serpine1, and Plap-1 was significantly higher in periodontal tissue of 6-week-old Tgfbr1G188V/+ mice than in WT mice, despite no gross structural differences.
After oral Porphyromonas gingivalis administration, alveolar bone resorption was significantly greater in Tgfbr1G188V/+ mice than in WT mice, indicating increased susceptibility to periodontitis.
The number of TRAP-positive osteoclasts near the alveolar bone was significantly increased in Tgfbr1G188V/+ mice after P. gingivalis infection compared with WT mice.
Peritoneal macrophages from Tgfbr1G188V/+ mice showed significantly upregulated Cxcl10, Il6, and Tnf mRNA expression compared with WT macrophages after P. gingivalis LPS stimulation.
One third of surveyed CES patients reported ongoing bladder dysfunction at long-term follow-up.
10% of patients required ongoing use of a urinary catheter after CES.
Over a third of patients reported bowel dysfunction at long-term follow-up.
Over half of patients reported sexual dysfunction at long-term follow-up.
Nearly half of patients reported genital numbness persisting long-term.
Two-thirds of patients reported significant back pain at long-term follow-up, with a substantial minority requiring further investigation or intervention.
Quality of life among CES patients was lower than expected for their age and sex after long-term follow-up.
Half of the surveyed patients reported moderate or worse depression at long-term follow-up after CES.
Forty percent of working-age patients could no longer work due to problems attributable to CES.

Urinary and faecal incontinence, catheter use, sexual dysfunction, and genital numbness were all significantly more common in patients with CES with painless urinary retention (CESR) compared with incomplete CES (CESI).
A substantial proportion of patients required further investigation (44%) or further intervention (10%) for ongoing management of lower back pain after CES.
60.3% of patients with ME/CFS reported having had an infectious illness some time before the onset of their disease.
Mononucleosis was the most frequently reported infectious illness preceding ME/CFS onset, accounting for 30% of the reported infections.
Over 100 distinct infectious illnesses were mentioned by patients as preceding ME/CFS onset, suggesting heterogeneous infectious triggers rather than a single causative agent.
Mean age at onset of ME/CFS symptoms did not differ significantly between joint hypermobility-positive and joint hypermobility-negative patients.
Joint hypermobility status was not associated with differences in sex distribution, frequency and severity of ME/CFS symptoms, orthostatic intolerance symptoms, or comorbid conditions.
Health-related quality of life measures did not differ significantly between hypermobility-positive and hypermobility-negative ME/CFS patients, using either a Beighton cutoff of 4 or 5.
The authors conclude that although joint hypermobility is a risk factor for developing ME/CFS, it does not shape the illness's clinical presentation once present.
The authors hypothesize that ME/CFS results from CRFR2 upregulation in specific neurons of the raphé nuclei and limbic system, causing loss of homeostatic control over serotonin-mediated functions.

Acute subcutaneous CT38s treatment was associated with a statistically significant improvement in mean total daily symptom score (TDSS) across all 14 treated ME/CFS patients over 28 days pre- vs post-treatment.
Among patients whose peak plasma concentration (Cmax) stayed below 0.25 ng/ml, mean TDSS improved significantly, with all individual symptoms improving.
Among patients with Cmax above 0.25 ng/ml, mean TDSS worsened slightly but not significantly, consistent with symptom exacerbation resembling post-exertional malaise.
Among patients with Cmax < 0.25 ng/ml, TDSS improvement correlated inversely with total drug exposure (AUC) and with pre-treatment symptom severity.
Among patients with Cmax > 0.25 ng/ml, TDSS worsening correlated strongly and directly with total drug exposure (AUC), suggesting dose-dependent overstimulation.
Pre-treatment SF-36 physical and mental component scores indicated worse health status in ME/CFS patients than published US norms for patients with cancer, congestive heart failure, or diabetes.
SF-36 physical component score significantly improved from pre-treatment to pre-exit assessment in patients with Cmax below 0.25 ng/ml, but worsened in patients above this threshold.

ME/CFS patients showed significantly greater hemodynamic (heart rate and diastolic blood pressure) sensitivity to CRFR2 agonist stimulation than healthy subjects from a prior Phase 1 trial, consistent with CRFR2 pathway sensitization/upregulation.

For patients with Cmax<0.25 ng/ml, activity measures (ADL completion, PEM-avoidance, exertion level, Fitbit steps) showed non-significant trends, some favorable and some unfavorable, and were not powered to detect true effects.
Of 108 treatment-emergent adverse events (excluding treatment-day hemodynamics and flushing), 92 were recognized ME/CFS symptoms, supporting CRFR2 involvement in the disease.

One patient (ID23, dose-level D20) experienced a serious adverse event of tachycardia and hypotension during a second treatment, requiring rescue saline, attributed to a dosing protocol error and poor prediction of starting dose in a CRFR2-upregulated population.

Anecdotal long-term follow-up (up to nearly 2 years) in 9 of 14 treated patients suggested sustained improvements in sleep, brain fog, appetite, activity, and post-exertional malaise frequency/recovery.

The authors propose, citing prior animal literature, that female sex and genetic variation in threat-response genes contribute to impaired CRFR2 downregulation, potentially explaining the female predominance of ME/CFS.
Long-hauler COVID-19 patients reported an overall reduction in most symptoms over time, including unrefreshing sleep and post-exertional malaise.
Among long-hauler COVID-19 patients, neurocognitive symptoms intensified over time even as most other symptom domains improved.
Initially, COVID-19 long-haulers were more symptomatic than ME/CFS patients in the immune and orthostatic symptom domains.
Over time, long-hauler COVID-19 patients became significantly less symptomatic than ME/CFS patients across most domains, except the orthostatic domain where severity remained comparable.
The article describes chronic fatigue syndrome (myalgic encephalomyelitis) as a form of neuroimmune endocrine dysfunction diagnosed purely on clinical grounds.
The authors suggest that viral infections likely play a leading role in the pathogenesis of chronic fatigue syndrome.
Published diagnostic criteria suggest possible correlations between chronic fatigue syndrome and COVID-19 illness.
The authors propose smart peptide drugs, exemplified by cortexin, as a promising therapeutic and rehabilitative strategy for patients with chronic fatigue syndrome.
ME/CFS incidence shows two age peaks, at 10-19 years and 30-39 years, with the second peak more distinct in women than in men.

In a gender-comparison study, males with ME/CFS had a younger age of onset often triggered by infection, and reported fewer muscle, immunological, and neurovegetative symptoms with better quality of life than females, though both sexes shared unrefreshing sleep.
Individuals with inflammatory bowel disease have an increased risk of developing ME/CFS compared to the general population.
A systematic review of circulating cytokines in ME/CFS found inconclusive and contradictory results across studies.
Reduced NK cell function and cytotoxicity has been demonstrated to contribute to immune dysregulation in ME/CFS.
ME/CFS patients' NK and B cells show reduced TRPM3 expression compared to healthy controls, resulting in reduced calcium influx.
TRPM3 gene-associated single nucleotide polymorphisms have been reported in ME/CFS patients compared to controls, suggesting a genetic predisposition.
During exercise, ME/CFS patients show early activation of anaerobic metabolic pathways, suggesting impaired oxygen consumption.

In a mouse model of ME/CFS-like fatigue induced by repeated forced swimming, PDH enzyme activity was decreased compared to control mice, impairing oxidative metabolism and increasing lactate production.

EBV can decrease mitochondrial DNA replication through direct protein interactions while promoting viral DNA replication, and HHV-6B and CMV influence mitochondrial function by increasing oxidative damage, contributing to ME/CFS symptoms.

Patients with comorbid CFS and fibromyalgia show additional sleep architecture disturbances not seen in CFS-only patients, indicating the two conditions are distinct rather than part of a shared spectrum.
Despite close interrelation and shared high rates of depression, recent research indicates ME/CFS and major depressive disorder are distinct disorders that should be clinically treated separately.

CFS is associated with multiple dysregulated pathways including NF-κB signaling, oxidative stress, reduced antioxidants, mitochondrial impairment, elevated systemic/cerebral lactate, gut dysbacteriosis from Gram-negative bacterial translocation, decreased N-acetyl aspartate metabolism, and gray matter atrophy, though no established biomarker exists.
Patients with a known history of EBV showed symptomatic improvement when treated with the antiviral valacyclovir.
Acyclovir did not show improvement in patients with a known history of EBV, in contrast to valacyclovir.
Rituximab showed no difference in effectiveness compared to controls for fatigue and functional status in CFS patients.
Rintatolimod, a TLR3-activating dsRNA compound, provides symptomatic relief in 30-40% of CFS/ME patients.
Cognitive behavioral therapy may provide short-term benefit for CFS but has not been associated with symptom remission.
Graded exercise therapy has been shown to reduce fatigue and improve physical functioning in CFS patients through conditioning exercises of varying intensity.
Moderate exercise has been shown to decrease fatigue and improve sleep quality, physical function, and self-rated health in CFS.
Adaptive pacing therapy, which involves avoiding known fatigue triggers and setting daily activity goals, has shown inconsistent results for symptomatic improvement in CFS.
Traditional acupuncture techniques have been shown to effectively reduce fatigue symptoms and decrease stress and depressive symptoms in CFS.
Qigong, an exercise practice emphasizing breath-work and meditation, has been shown to reduce mental and physical fatigue as well as depression in CFS.
Probiotic treatment decreased gastrointestinal symptoms, inflammatory marker levels, and anxiety in CFS patients but failed to alter depression levels.
A randomized controlled study found that transcutaneous electrical acupoint stimulation of target points produced a significant improvement in fatigue and associated symptoms.

Pharmacological treatments decreased rates of chronic fatigue, depression, and anxiety while improving quality of life and physical performance variables such as maximal oxygen consumption, anaerobic threshold, and load time to failure.
A traditional Japanese medicine treatment (shosaikoto-based) was reported to effectively treat CFS in a single pediatric case.
Cognitive behavioral therapy may provide short-term symptomatic benefit in ME/CFS but has not been shown to induce remission.
Graded exercise therapy has been shown to reduce fatigue and improve physical functioning in ME/CFS through conditioning exercises of varying intensity.
Moderate exercise has been shown to decrease fatigue and improve sleep quality, physical function, and perceived health in ME/CFS.
Adaptive pacing therapy, based on avoidance of fatigue triggers and daily activity goals, has shown inconsistent results for symptomatic improvement in ME/CFS.
The efficacy of antidepressant pharmacotherapy in ME/CFS, despite comorbid anxiety and depression, remains unclear.
Patients with a known history of Epstein-Barr virus showed improvement with valacyclovir treatment but not with acyclovir.
Immune modulating agents targeting various immune markers have shown inconsistent results as therapy for ME/CFS.
Management with stimulants, melatonin, and acetylcholinesterase inhibitors has been inadequate for treating ME/CFS.
Traditional acupuncture has been shown to reduce fatigue symptoms and decrease stress and depressive symptoms in ME/CFS patients.
Jin's three-needle acupuncture technique (JTN), which uses more deliberate acupoint selection, is being studied for ME/CFS given its prior use for wellness promotion and depression treatment.
Qigong, an exercise form emphasizing breath-work and meditation, has been shown to reduce mental and physical fatigue as well as depression in ME/CFS.
Traditional Japanese shosaikoto-based medicine was reported to provide effective treatment for CFS in a pediatric patient case report.
Probiotic treatment showed decreased gastrointestinal symptoms, inflammatory marker levels, and anxiety, but failed to alter depression levels in ME/CFS.
Self-management interventions involving patient education and frequent self-assessment may be effective in reducing fatigue in ME/CFS.
The monoclonal antibody rituximab showed no difference in effectiveness compared to controls for fatigue and functional status in ME/CFS patients.
Rintatolimod, a Toll-Like Receptor 3 activating double-stranded RNA compound, provided symptom relief in 30-40% of ME/CFS patients.
Hypomagnesemia should be identified as an underlying cause of fatigue in some CFS patients so it can be treated appropriately with magnesium supplementation.
A randomized controlled study concluded that transcutaneous electrical acupoint stimulation of target points produced significant improvement of fatigue and associated symptoms.
Dexmedetomidine, used as an adjuvant in regional and neuraxial pain management, may have a beneficial role in treating CFS associated with chronic pain.
Lidocaine infusion, beneficial for chronic pain, is proposed as a promising multimodal approach for managing CFS given the presence of chronic pain in this population.
Neuromodulation techniques such as dorsal root stimulation and pulsed radiofrequency have been effective in various chronic pain syndromes that may be associated with CFS.

Pharmacological treatments have decreased rates of common CFS symptoms (chronic fatigue, depression, anxiety) while improving quality of life and physical performance measures including maximal oxygen consumption, anaerobic threshold, and load time to failure.
Replacing deficient lipid content and using antioxidant therapy have shown efficacy in patients presenting with moderate to severe CFS symptoms.
Nutrient supplementation such as Vitamin B12, folic acid, a multivitamin (Supradyn), NADH+coenzyme Q, and D-ribose are considered safe treatment options in CFS.

Clinical guidelines recommend specialist referral within six months for mild CFS symptoms, three to four months for moderate symptoms, and immediately for severe cases, emphasizing a holistic patient-centered approach.
Using machine learning and innovative procedures, researchers can combine biomarkers and clinical phenotypes to better examine underlying disease mechanisms for more accurate CFS diagnosis.
Children and adolescents with CFS have higher rates of school absenteeism, leading to missed educational opportunities and psychosocial experiences.

The review proposes that long COVID (post-acute/persistent COVID syndrome) may overlap substantially with myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome as defined by the International Consensus Criteria, based on symptom comparison across multiple guideline sources.

Perrin et al. hypothesized that persistent post-COVID symptoms may result from viral crossing of the blood-brain barrier via the olfactory pathway with subsequent altered cerebral microglial drainage and accumulation of proinflammatory substances, analogous to mechanisms proposed after SARS-CoV infection.
Post-mortem studies found viral RNA in different regions of the nasopharynx and brain of COVID-19 patients, supporting the plausibility of CNS viral involvement in long COVID pathophysiology.

The CDC suggests that prolonged post-COVID symptoms may reflect a persistent hyperinflammatory state, organ damage during acute infection, persistent viral activity, or an inadequate antibody response, with worse outcomes linked to poor baseline physical condition, pre-existing comorbidities, and psychological sequelae.

A review by Larun et al. of 8 studies with 1,518 participants found that exercise therapy likely has a positive effect on fatigue in adults with ME/CFS compared to usual care or passive therapies, but evidence regarding adverse effects was uncertain.

SEMERGEN guidance notes that most long COVID patients improve within 4-6 weeks with progressively increasing aerobic exercise, paralleling CDC recommendations for graded activity in ME/CFS to manage post-exertional malaise.

No approved etiological (curative) treatment currently exists for myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome; symptomatic management guidance (e.g., from UpToDate) is based on low-quality evidence, partly extrapolated from fibromyalgia treatment research.
Fatigue severity, measured with the Chalder Fatigue Questionnaire, was significantly reduced by session 4 of graded exercise therapy and this improvement was maintained at follow-up.
Work and social adjustment, measured by the Work and Social Adjustment Scale, progressively improved over therapy and reached significance at discharge, maintained at follow-up.
Physical functioning, measured by the SF-36 Physical Functioning Subscale, progressively improved over therapy and reached significance at discharge, maintained at follow-up.

Benchmarking analyses comparing this routine clinical cohort's outcomes with prior RCTs showed that effect sizes for graded exercise therapy were smaller in routine clinical practice than in RCT settings.

After adjustment for age, ethnicity, deprivation, comorbidities and year of surgery, mesh sling surgery was not associated with a significantly different 10-year incidence of autoimmune disease, fibromyalgia or ME/CFS compared with non-mesh surgery.
Unadjusted analysis found a similar cumulative incidence of the composite systemic condition outcome between mesh and non-mesh surgery groups, with a borderline non-significant hazard ratio.
A sensitivity analysis restricting the outcome to autoimmune diseases only (excluding fibromyalgia and ME/CFS) produced near-identical results to the main composite analysis.
Among women who developed a systemic condition after urinary incontinence surgery, myalgic encephalomyelitis accounted for 4.7% of first-recorded diagnoses.
Fibromyalgia accounted for less than 1.0% of the first-recorded systemic conditions among women following urinary incontinence surgery.

Older age at surgery, pre-existing comorbid conditions, and higher socio-economic deprivation were independently associated with an increased incidence of the composite systemic condition outcome, whereas ethnicity and year of operation were not.

Among the systemic conditions recorded after surgery, rheumatoid arthritis was the most common (26.0%), followed by polymyalgia rheumatica (13.9%) and psoriasis vulgaris (10.1%), with small differences in distribution between mesh and non-mesh groups.
Most of the elderly female COVID-19 survivors surveyed reported persistent symptoms in the post-recovery period.
Among post-COVID symptomatic respondents, the majority were classified as having no or possible CFS-like symptoms, with only one case meeting probable CFS criteria.
Fatigue was a commonly reported post-recovery symptom among the elderly female survivors.
Musculoskeletal symptoms were reported by roughly half of the surveyed elderly female survivors post-recovery.
Sleep problems were the most frequently reported post-recovery symptom among the elderly female survivors.
Post-recovery symptoms overall were significantly associated with stress, sadness, and sleep disturbances in the surveyed population.
Stress, sadness, sleep disturbances, fatigue, cognitive impairment, and recurrent falls were all significantly associated with CFS-like symptoms in post-COVID elderly female survivors.

In a cohort of 143 hospitalized COVID-19 patients assessed 60 days after diagnosis, only 13% were symptom-free while dyspnea, fatigue, joint pain, and chest pain were reported in 43%, 53%, 26%, and 22% respectively.
Among 279 hospitalized COVID-19 patients assessed 3 months post-diagnosis, 55% reported fatigue and 31% reported sleep disorder.
In 201 COVID-19 patients (only 18% hospitalized), assessed 140 days after diagnosis, 99% had 4 or more symptoms and 42% had 10 or more symptoms, with fatigue, muscle aches, and headache being common.

In a large Chinese cohort followed 6 months after hospitalization, 76% had at least one persistent symptom, with fatigue/muscle weakness (63%), sleep difficulties (26%), and anxiety/depression (23%) being most common, exceeding apparent pulmonary or cardiac organ signs.
Lymphopenia characterizes acute COVID-19 infection, suggesting significant impact on the immune system.
Preliminary data show high levels of autoantibodies and a strong T cell response following COVID-19, particularly in women.

In a prospective cohort of 253 patients with various viral infections followed 12 months, 12% (29/253) developed prolonged illness with disabling fatigue, musculoskeletal pain, neurocognitive difficulties and mood disturbance at six months, and 11% met diagnostic criteria for chronic fatigue syndrome.
Ten percent of Lyme disease patients develop persistent symptoms of fatigue, pain, and dysautonomia, occurring more frequently in women than men.

In a prospective series of 142 patients with laboratory-confirmed infectious mononucleosis, 12% (17 patients) reported continuing illness with fatigue and poor functional status at 6 months, with female gender being the strongest predictor of failure to recover.

In a second prospective cohort of 250 mononucleosis patients, chronic fatigue syndrome was diagnosed in 9% at 6 months by conservative criteria, with the range extending to 16-19% depending on the CFS definition applied.
In a series of 369 SARS-1 patients, chronic fatigue was reported in 40% (27% meeting CFS criteria) and 40% had active psychiatric illness three and a half years after diagnosis.
A case-control study of 22 SARS-1 patients one to three years after diagnosis reported fatigue, muscle pain, depression, and sleep disturbance in a syndrome overlapping with chronic fatigue syndrome.
A third SARS-1 study of hospitalized patients found that 20-30% of cases were unable to work 2 years after diagnosis.
A meta-analysis confirmed persistent post-infectious symptom findings for SARS-1 and extended them to MERS.

In the authors' own Nepal-based symptom-screening data of over 2500 individuals, about one quarter had not recovered from acute COVID-19 by 3 months, with significant symptom improvement by 6 months, though at least 10% remained significantly symptomatic; fatigue and pain/ache were the most common persistent symptoms.
Men appear more susceptible to acute COVID-19 infection (notably in Nepal), while in western countries more women present with long COVID.
Women develop stronger immune responses to vaccines than men, with increased antibody and T cell responses.
For symptom-defined CFS following COVID, rest and pacing of activities are essential and exercise is not helpful, as activity exceeding a patient's exertion threshold may drastically worsen symptoms.

Ivermectin has been suggested as a treatment for long-COVID with major CFS-like symptomatology, but evidence for benefit is limited and controversial, with a recent rigorous study suggesting marginal, if any, benefit.

The SARS-CoV-2 spike protein uses angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 (ACE2) as its entry receptor, and because ACE2 is expressed broadly across body tissues, the virus produces direct and indirect effects in multiple organ systems.

Acute multi-organ COVID injury involves vasculitis, endothelialitis (from ACE2 viral binding), thrombosis from cytokine/chemokine storm, and elevation of inflammatory markers including D-dimer, fibrinogen, and mast cell activity.

In high-income countries, disability figures for work, physical, and/or cognitive function at six months post-COVID range from 10-30%, with higher percentages informed by SARS-1 and organ-failure post-COVID data.
A novel heterozygous COL1A1 missense variant c.935G>T predicting p.(Arg312Leu) was identified in three affected family members and classified as pathogenic per ACMG criteria.
The variant segregated with disease status in the family, being present in all three affected members but absent in three unaffected relatives, supporting a causal role.

A different missense substitution at the same residue, p.(Arg312Cys), had previously been reported in patients with classical or vascular EDS prone to vascular complications ranging from none to arterial rupture.

All three affected family members exhibited generalized joint hypermobility, recurrent joint instability/dislocations, swan-neck finger deformity, chronic pain and fatigue, easy bruising, gingivorrhagia, and gastrointestinal/urinary symptoms.
Affected members also showed osteogenesis-imperfecta-like features including light blue sclerae (3/3), mild hearing loss (2/3), and mild osteopenia (2/3).

Cardiovascular exploration revealed no major vascular complications in the three affected patients, though minor incidental findings (mild mitral insufficiency, small thoracic aortic dilation, microfistula) were observed.

Immunostaining of dermal fibroblasts from an affected patient showed that collagen I secretion kinetics and ECM deposition were not significantly hampered by the p.(Arg312Leu) variant compared to a control individual's fibroblasts.
Co-immunostaining revealed a possibly delayed secretion of fibronectin into the extracellular matrix at 4 days postseeding in the patient's fibroblasts compared to control.

Structural modeling predicted a salt bridge between Glu309 and Arg312 in the wild-type collagen triple helix that would be disrupted by the Arg312Leu substitution, potentially destabilizing the local helical structure.
TNXB haploinsufficiency has been proposed to explain up to 5% of hypermobile EDS cases.
A variant in the LZTS1 gene has been reported as a candidate cause of hEDS in four families.

Based on major diagnostic criteria (blue sclerae, flatfeet without hindfoot deformity, generalized joint hypermobility, hyperextensible/soft doughy skin), the three patients' diagnoses were retrospectively reclassified from hEDS to COL1-related overlap disorder (C1ROD).

Residue 312 lies within the first major ligand-binding region of collagen I, so the p.(Arg312Leu) substitution may disrupt interactions with integrins α1β1/α2β1 and interleukin-2, though this remains untested.
EDS patients and controls did not differ in the accuracy of their estimates of hand location.
EDS patients and controls showed similar visually induced changes in perceived hand location after adapting reaches to altered visual feedback (visuo-proprioceptive recalibration).
EDS patients' proprioceptive-only estimates of hand position were less precise than controls' estimates.
The degree of imprecision in proprioceptive hand-position estimates could be partially predicted by Beighton score, indicating more hypermobile individuals are more likely to be imprecise.

In-depth interviews with 22 individuals with hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos syndrome revealed a prolonged, difficult diagnostic odyssey marked by dismissal of chronic pain symptoms by clinicians, worsening care satisfaction and patient-provider relationships.
Narrative analysis of patient interviews identified a 'hero's journey' framework, highlighting themes of uncertainty and integration in patients' descriptions of their diagnostic odyssey with EDS.

A 28-year-old woman with scleroderma and Ehlers-Danlos syndrome developed a painful spindle cell lipoma on the plantar aspect of the left hallux, reported as the first such case at this location in a patient with these comorbid conditions.
Pathological evaluation of the excised lesion showed strong and diffuse cytoplasmic CD34 expression, consistent with the diagnosis of spindle cell lipoma.
The lesion showed negative expression of Rb and S-100 proteins, helping distinguish spindle cell lipoma from other spindle cell tumors.
The authors note prior epidemiological studies have shown increased cancer incidence in patients with scleroderma, providing background context for this case.
A homozygous c.362dupC pathogenic duplication variant in exon 3 of the FKBP14 gene was detected in all five patients with kyphoscoliotic Ehlers-Danlos syndrome type 2.
All five patients presented with progressive thoracolumbar kyphoscoliosis of varying severity, the primary major clinical criterion of EDS kyphoscoliotic type 2.
Hearing loss (sensorineural or mixed) was diagnosed in three of five patients, consistent with literature reporting hearing loss in 73% of EDSKS2 cases.
Osteoporosis was detected radiographically in three of five patients, a minor diagnostic criterion reported to lead to fractures in 13% of cases in the literature.
Joint hypermobility was scored eight on the Beighton scale in four patients and six in one patient, with maximum score not reached due to rigid spine restricting flexibility.

Three children had congenital malformations affecting three different systems: cardiovascular (open ductus arteriosus, borderline narrowed aorta), skeleto-muscular (spina bifida sacralis dorsalis S3-S5), and genital (midshaft hypospadia).
Combined respiratory pulmonary function impairment was found by spirometry in three probands (spirometry could not be performed in the two youngest patients).
Intellectual development was normal in four of five children, while one 11-year-old girl had a slight developmental delay with IQ 80.

FKBP14-deficient skin fibroblasts show disorganisation of extracellular matrix proteins including collagen types I, III, VI, fibronectin and tenascins, along with ER cisternae enlargement and fragmentation of elastic fibers, despite normal proportion and mobility of collagen α-chains.

Lysyl pyridinoline (LP)/hydroxylysyl pyridinoline (HP) urinary excretion ratio is increased specifically in PLOD1-associated kyphoscoliotic type 1, providing a biochemical differentiator from FKBP14-associated type 2.

The c.362dupC duplication is the most common FKBP14 pathogenic variant, previously detected in 11 of 17 patients reported by Giunta et al. (2018), predominantly in Caucasian patients from the UK, Austria, Croatia, and Poland, with one Colombian patient also reported.

The same homozygous c.362dupC variant was found in five unrelated patients from different regions of Russia, suggesting either a founder effect or a recurrent mutation arising from replication slippage in the polycytidine tract.
Creatine kinase level in the detailed case (patient no. 4) was within normal reference range despite muscular weakness and Gowers' sign, arguing against primary muscular dystrophy.
Six patients with molecularly confirmed vascular Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome showed expanded, protein-filled rough endoplasmic reticulum on transmission electron microscopy of skin biopsies.
One patient with a severe form of Osteogenesis Imperfecta also showed expanded, protein-filled rough endoplasmic reticulum on transmission electron microscopy of skin biopsy.

The authors propose that assessing rough endoplasmic reticulum expansion via electron microscopy could serve as a useful additional phenotyping tool to help reclassify variants of uncertain clinical significance identified on genetic testing for vEDS and OI.
A previously undiagnosed young parturient woman was found to have vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, confirmed retrospectively by autopsy and genetic typing.
During the third period of natural term delivery, the patient developed a complete linear vertical uterine rupture presenting with haemorrhagic shock.

Following hysterectomy, the patient experienced sequential spontaneous ruptures of the iliac veins, iliac arteries, abdominal aorta, and inferior vena cava, with new bleeding sources appearing despite repeated attempts at vascular repair and ligation.
The patient, presenting with acute pleuritic chest pain, comorbid COPD, uncontrolled diabetes, and obesity, had a family history of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome noted as part of his clinical background.
Patients with vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (vEDS) showed frequent digital vascular abnormalities on transillumination, occurring more often than in controls.

Across all studied disorders (Marfan syndrome, thoracic aortic aneurysm and dissection, vascular EDS, bicuspid aortic valve with aortopathy, and arteriopathies without aortopathy), patients had significantly more digital vascular abnormalities detected by transillumination than control subjects without known vascular disorders.

Transillumination, a method previously used to detect capillary abnormalities in hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia, was adapted to detect digital vascular abnormalities in patients with aortopathies and arteriopathies.

Fibroblasts from a Desbuquois dysplasia type 2 patient carrying a XYLT1 nonsense mutation showed reduced chondroitin sulfate rather than heparan sulfate, suggesting XYLT1 loss preferentially affects CS biosynthesis.
Dermal fibroblasts from a spondyloocular syndrome patient with homozygous XYLT2 mutations showed lower GAG levels and lower XYLT enzymatic activity than healthy subjects.

Mutations in B4GALT7 cause EDS spondylodysplastic type 1, and skin fibroblasts from patients show defective DS side chains on decorin/biglycan, markedly reduced GalT-I activity, and reduced HS sulfation.
Skin fibroblasts from EDS spondylodysplastic type 2 patients with B3GALT6 mutations produced less chondroitin sulfate, dermatan sulfate, and heparan sulfate than control cells.

In spondyloepimetaphyseal dysplasia with joint laxity type 1 caused by B3GALT6 mutations, HS and HS-proteoglycan perlecan were markedly lower while CS-PG (versican) and DS-PG (decorin) levels were comparable to normal fibroblasts, suggesting selective HS impairment.

Homozygous B3GAT3 mutations causing multiple joint dislocations, short stature, and heart defects (including bicuspid aortic valve) were associated with significantly lower GlcAT-I activity and lower CS, DS, and HS levels in patient fibroblasts than controls.

A compound heterozygous B3GAT3 mutation causing pseudodiastrophic dysplasia produced markedly lower GlcAT-I activity and significantly decreased CS, DS, and HS levels compared with control cells, representing a likely complete loss-of-function.
GalNAcT activity and CS amounts were significantly reduced in fibroblasts from patients with CSGALNACT1 mutations causing mild skeletal dysplasia with joint laxity.

Reduced chondroitin sulfate in skin from a Temtamy preaxial brachydactyly syndrome patient with CHSY1 mutations coincided with up-regulated expression of NOTCH pathway genes JAG1 and HES1, implicating altered NOTCH signaling in the resulting brachydactyly.

Loss of chondroitin 6-O-sulfotransferase (C6ST1) activity and reduced 6-O-sulfated CS were demonstrated in skin fibroblasts from patients with CHST3 mutations causing spondyloepiphyseal dysplasia with congenital joint dislocations.

DSE activity in fibroblasts from an EDS musculocontractural type 2 patient was markedly decreased versus healthy controls, resulting in lower dermatan sulfate accompanied by an increase in chondroitin sulfate.

Fibroblasts from EDS musculocontractural type 1 patients with CHST14 mutations showed markedly lower D4ST activity, and produced chondroitin sulfate instead of non-sulfated dermatan on the decorin core protein.

Collagen fibrils were dispersed and disorganized in the dermis of EDS musculocontractural type 1 patients versus regularly assembled fibrils in healthy controls, attributed to the switch of decorin's GAG side chain from curved DS to linear CS disrupting collagen fibril spacing.

Homozygous EXTL3 mutations causing immunoskeletal dysplasia with neurodevelopmental abnormalities resulted in mislocalized mutant protein outside the Golgi apparatus and markedly lower HS levels in patient fibroblasts than healthy controls.
HS chains from HS2ST1-mutant patient fibroblasts lacked 2-O-sulfation of GlcA/IdoA residues with compensatory increased N- and 6-O-sulfation, and showed decreased FGF2-induced ERK1/2 activation.

Recombinant UGDH mutants (p.Ala44Val, p.Ala82Thr) causing developmental and epileptic encephalopathy showed altered oligomerization (dimer/monomer vs wild-type hexamer) and Vmax reduced to below 50% or undetectable, in 36 cases from 25 families.

Missense, nonsense mutations, and deletions in BGN cause thoracic aortic aneurysms and dissections with joint hypermobility and connective tissue features, and TGFβ signaling is up-regulated in patients, resembling Loeys-Dietz syndrome.

Compound heterozygous PAPSS2 mutations cause hyperandrogenism, premature pubarche, and hyperandrogenic anovulation in addition to short stature and skeletal dysplasia, likely resulting from low serum dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate with increased androgen.
A SNP (rs17077540) located 75 kbp upstream of DSEL was associated with recurrent early-onset major depressive disorder, and DSEL (unlike DSE) is predominantly expressed in the brain.

A patient with SLC35A3 mutations causing a neuroskeletal disorder with autism had a shorter CS side chain on serum bikunin (CS-PG) compared with a control subject, without changes in keratan sulfate biosynthesis.

GORAB knockout mice showed a reduction specifically in dermatan sulfate (not CS or HS) in skin and cartilage, suggesting the mechanism underlying gerodermia osteodysplastica caused by GORAB mutations in humans.
Both siblings carried novel compound heterozygous ZNF469 mutations (a nonsense and a frameshift variant), each predicted likely pathogenic, confirming a diagnosis of BCS-1.
Both siblings with BCS-1 had a significant fracture history beginning in the neonatal period and continuing until adolescence, with the fracture rate falling after skeletal maturity.
Bone density at the lumbar spine and femoral neck was in the osteopenic range in both siblings with BCS-1, while forearm bone density was normal.
Bone biopsy of the older sibling showed increased trabecular bone volume (30.2% vs normal 22.5±3.5%) but reduced cortical thickness (687 μm vs normal 909±98 μm).
Cortical bone porosity was markedly low (1.3% vs normal 6.3±0.6%) in the bone biopsy of the older sibling with BCS-1, a feature potentially linked to fracture propensity.

Bone turnover markers, plasma calcium, phosphate and vitamin D concentrations were normal in both siblings, and bone apposition rate on tetracycline labelling was normal, indicating no abnormal bone turnover despite the fracture phenotype.

Both heterozygous carrier parents had significant fracture histories (mother 11 fractures between ages 4-59; father two wrist fractures and a femoral fracture) despite having higher bone density z-scores than their affected children, suggesting fracture predisposition may not be directly linked to bone density but to bone quality.

A 28-gene bone fragility next-generation sequencing panel found no pathogenic variants in the older sibling, arguing against blended or modified inheritance and supporting ZNF469 mutations as the likely cause of the bone phenotype.
Heterozygous ZNF469 mutations have previously been associated with reduced central corneal thickness, based on prior literature cited in the discussion.
A review by Dhooge et al. estimated that bone fragility may affect 16% of patients with Brittle Cornea Syndrome, recommending ZNF469/PRDM5 screening be added to bone fragility gene panels.

Mutation in either ZNF469 or PRDM5 is proposed to cause downregulation of genes encoding extracellular matrix molecules including fibrillar collagens, connective tissue components, and molecules regulating cell migration and adhesion.

Prior work cited in this paper found elevated brain and/or spinal cord TSPO (glial marker) levels across multiple chronic pain conditions including chronic low back pain, fibromyalgia, migraine and Gulf War illness.
In the primary somatosensory cortex representation of the back/leg, 11C-PBR28 PET signal (a marker of TSPO/glial activation) was higher in radicular compared to axial chronic low back pain patients.
Functional connectivity between the primary somatosensory cortex (back/leg region) and the thalamus was higher in radicular versus axial chronic low back pain patients.
11C-PBR28 PET signal in the primary somatosensory cortex back/leg region and functional connectivity to the thalamus were positively correlated with each other.

11C-PBR28 PET signal in the primary somatosensory cortex back/leg region was positively correlated with 'fibromyalgianess' scores (degree of nociplastic pain/pain centralization) across the combined patient groups.
Functional connectivity between the S1 back/leg region and thalamus was positively correlated with fibromyalgianess scores across groups.
Statistical mediation analysis showed that fibromyalgianess mediated the association between 11C-PBR28 PET signal and S1-thalamus functional connectivity across groups.
Patients who develop VITT show high titers of IgG antibodies against PF4-polyanion complexes despite never having been exposed to heparin.
VITT occurred in healthy individuals under 60 within 5-20 days after the first ChAdOx1 nCoV-19 vaccination at a rate of 6.5 events per million.
Mortality from cerebral venous thrombosis in Janssen/Vaxzevria vaccine recipients was higher than expected, at a rate of 0.37 events per million.
Preclinical models show adenoviral particles are engulfed by platelets expressing CAR, triggering platelet activation (P-selectin exposure) and platelet-leukocyte aggregate formation.
Mast cells express the adenoviral receptor CAR and are efficiently infected by adenoviral vectors, suggesting mast cells could be integrally involved in VITT development.

Mast cell activation syndrome (MCAS) is characterized by somatic mutations in multiple mast cell regulatory genes driving chronic aberrant constitutive and reactive mast cell activation with excessive inflammation and aberrant heparin release.
MCAS prevalence estimates in the literature vary widely, from as rare as 0.1% to as prevalent as ~17% of the population.
Natural IgG antibodies capable of binding PF4/heparin complexes are detectable in 4.3-6.6% of the general population, usually associated with chronic bacterial infections such as periodontal disease.

Combining the frequency of natural anti-PF4/heparin antibodies with the frequency of MCAS, the authors calculate that the probability of an individual having both conditions is roughly 1 in 200,000-400,000, and when restricted to the subset with strong local inflammatory reaction (20%), this narrows to about 1 in 1-2 million, matching observed VITT frequency.
IL-6 is proposed as an early inflammatory event after adenoviral vector exposure, based on prior data showing IL-6 increased in all patients receiving AVV therapy for OTCD genetic syndrome.
A platelet activation threshold of 7.6% distinguishes asymptomatic individuals from those at risk of a HIT-like pro-thrombotic reaction.
Platelets express high levels of ACE2, and purified SARS-CoV-2 Spike protein may directly activate platelets through ACE2 interaction, potentiating the prothrombotic cascade.

MCAS is proposed to be intimately involved in the pathogenesis of both severe acute COVID-19 and COVID-19 'long-haul' syndrome via ACE2/Spike protein interactions, and altered mast cells interacting with neo-synthesized Spike protein could further contribute to VITT development.

Most vaccinated individuals developing thrombotic events up to VITT are young fertile women, with contraceptive estrogen use, recent surgery, and female-predominant autoimmune antiphospholipid/antiplatelet antibody production proposed as contributing risk factors.

MCAS can, in some instances, drive the development of pathogenic autoantibodies that trigger true autoimmune diseases, providing a potential mechanism for MCAS patients to produce pathogenic anti-PF4/heparin antibodies contributing to the rarity of VITT.
Activated platelets release PF4 that can complex with natural heparin released by basophils and mast cells upon IL-33 activation from damaged endothelia, proposed as a step in the VITT cascade.
The pentapeptide FRKKW and hexapeptide WNKWAL activate human LAD2 mast cells via MRGPRX2 at a potency similar to the PAMP-12 positive control peptide.

Peptide activators of MRGPRX2 can be generalized to a structural motif Xa-(Y)n≥3-Xb, where Xa is an aromatic residue, Xb is a hydrophobic residue, and Y is a minimum 3-residue sequence containing at least one positively charged residue among otherwise uncharged residues.
Artificial peptides WKKKW and FKKKF, designed from the derived Xa-(Y)n≥3-Xb motif, activated LAD2 mast cells similarly to PAMP-12 controls, confirming the structural rule.

Tested peptides showed a graded ranking of MRGPRX2 activation potency in LAD2 cells: FRKKW = WKKKW = FKKKF > PAMP-12 = WNKWAL > YKKKY > FRKKANKWALSR = FRKKWNKAALSR > KWKWK > FRKK = WNKWA > KYKYK > NKWALSR = YKKY = WNK.
CTMCs were detected in the blood of 96% of patients with advanced systemic mastocytosis.
CTMCs were present in 100% of patients with smoldering systemic mastocytosis.
CTMCs were detected in 45% of patients with indolent systemic mastocytosis.
CTMCs were detected in only 7% of patients with bone marrow mastocytosis.
CTMCs were systematically absent in the blood of patients with cutaneous mastocytosis and MC activation syndrome.
The number of MC-committed CD34+ precursors progressively decreased across the disease spectrum from MCAS, CM, and BM mastocytosis to ISM, SSM, and advanced SM.
Presence and higher number of CTMCs in blood were associated with more adverse disease features and poorer-risk prognostic subgroups per the International Prognostic Scoring System for advanced SM.
CTMC presence and number were associated with poorer-risk subgroups as defined by the Global Prognostic Score for mastocytosis.
