Presence and higher numbers of circulating tumor mast cells in blood were associated with significantly shortened progression-free survival in patients with systemic mastocytosis.
Presence of circulating tumor mast cells was associated with significantly shortened overall survival in patients with systemic mastocytosis.
The authors conclude that CTMCs represent a novel candidate biomarker of disseminated disease in systemic mastocytosis, strongly associated with advanced SM and poorer prognosis in indolent SM.

Increased germline copy number of TPSAB1 is described in association with elevated basal serum tryptase and clinical features compatible with mast cell activation syndrome (MCAS), defining the condition hereditary alpha tryptasemia (HαT).
Approximately 29% of people carry no alpha-tryptase alleles without clinical manifestations, with a higher frequency (up to 45%) in Caucasians and lower frequency in other ethnic backgrounds.
The upper limit of normal basal serum tryptase (11.4 ng/ml) is exceeded in approximately 5% of Caucasians at baseline.

A cohort study found increased germline TPSAB1 copy number to be more prevalent in patients with mastocytosis than in the general population (17.2% vs. 4.4%), suggesting a link between the two conditions.

In Case 1, qPCR genetic testing found a duplication of TPSAB1 in the proband and mother, but not the father, alongside elevated basal serum tryptase (13–17.6 ng/mL over serial measurements) and a clinical diagnosis of MCAS.

The Case 1 mother, also carrying TPSAB1 duplication, presented with multi-system involvement including chronic diarrhea, autonomic dysfunction (recurrent syncope, hyperhidrosis), skin flushing, juvenile osteoporosis with vertebral fracture, lymphadenomegaly, and recurrent first-trimester miscarriage.
In Case 2, genetic testing revealed a quadruplication (four copies) of TPSAB1 in the proband and mother but not the father, with fluctuating elevated basal serum tryptase (15.8–19.8 ng/mL).
The Case 2 proband developed a solitary cutaneous mastocytoma with a positive Darier sign on the right wrist, in the context of TPSAB1 copy number gain.

The two described cases contradict a hypothesized linear gene-dosage relationship between TPSAB1 copy number, basal tryptase level, and clinical severity, since the patient with fewer copies and lower tryptase had more severe disease than the one with more copies and higher tryptase.

Heterotetramers composed of alpha- and beta-tryptase, but not homotetramers, activate protease-activated receptor-2 (PAR2) on smooth muscle, neurons, and endothelium, proposed as a mechanism linking increased alpha-tryptase dosage to connective tissue and vascular manifestations such as joint hypermobility and hypotension.
Alpha/beta-tryptase tetramers cleave the alpha subunit of the mechanosensory receptor EMR2, increasing mast cell susceptibility to vibration-triggered degranulation.

Patients with mastocytosis, venom allergies, or idiopathic anaphylaxis who also carry TPSAB1 copy number gain have more severe anaphylaxis manifestations, suggesting HαT may act as a disease-modifying rather than disease-causing factor.

Hereditary alpha tryptasemia is associated with increased numbers of small intestinal mast cells throughout the mucosa and submucosa, including superficial villi, proposed as a mechanism for the gastrointestinal manifestations of HαT.
Autonomic dysfunction, including postural tachycardia syndrome and hypotension, is reported as a clinical feature of hereditary alpha tryptasemia.
Joint hypermobility is reported as a clinical feature associated with hereditary alpha tryptasemia.
GV14 acupuncture significantly increased CO2 reactivity (cerebral vasomotor reactivity) of the basilar artery compared with baseline.
GV14 acupuncture significantly increased CO2 reactivity in the right middle cerebral artery compared with baseline.
GV14 acupuncture significantly increased CO2 reactivity in the left middle cerebral artery compared with baseline.
GV14 acupuncture significantly increased the corrected blood flow velocity at 40 mmHg CO2 (CV40) in the basilar artery.
CV40 of both middle cerebral arteries showed no statistically significant change after GV14 acupuncture despite an increasing trend.
Mean blood pressure and heart rate did not change significantly before versus after GV14 acupuncture, suggesting the CBF effects were not mediated by systemic hemodynamic changes.
Treatment with 4-cis-8-trans- and 4-cis-8-cis-4,8-sphingadienine stereoisomers inhibited IgE-mediated degranulation of RBL-2H3 mast cells in vitro.
Intradermal administration of 4-cis-8-trans- and 4-cis-8-cis-sphingadienine ameliorated ear edema in a passive cutaneous anaphylaxis (PCA) mouse model.
4-trans-8-trans- and 4-trans-8-cis-sphingadienine stereoisomers did not inhibit RBL-2H3 degranulation nor ameliorate PCA-induced ear edema.
None of the four 4,8-sphingadienine stereoisomers altered the amount of bound anti-TNP IgE on RBL-2H3 cells after sensitization, indicating their effect is not via modulation of IgE binding.

The authors conclude that a cis double bond at the C4-position of 4,8-sphingadienine confers anti-allergic activity by inhibiting the downstream signaling pathway that follows IgE binding to mast cells, rather than by preventing IgE binding itself.
IBS was most strongly associated with mast cell activation syndrome, with an odds ratio of 16.3 in database analysis.
IBS was also significantly associated with urticaria, idiopathic urticaria, non-malignant mastocytosis, and mast cell malignancy, with odds ratios ranging from 4.5 to 9.9.
Up to 4% of IBS patients had a comorbid mast cell disorder, and patients with IBS were at least 4 times more likely to have a mast cell disorder than the general population.
Patients in the IBS+MCD overlap cohorts were predominantly female, and the overlap was seen across all IBS subtypes (IBS-C, IBS-D, IBS-M).
Comorbid mood disorders and migraines, along with more thorough endoscopic evaluation, were more common in the IBS+MCD overlap cohorts than in patients with IBS alone.

The paper's title indicates that itch experienced in lichen simplex chronicus is associated with a localized form of small fiber neuropathy, but no abstract or further detail was provided to characterize the finding.
Injection of mesenchymal stem cell (MSC)-derived exosomes significantly reduced bleomycin-induced dermal fibrosis in a mouse model of systemic sclerosis.
MSC-derived exosome treatment significantly reduced the amount of collagen deposited in lesional skin of the bleomycin-induced fibrosis model.
MSC-exosome treatment reduced the number of alpha-smooth muscle actin (α-SMA)-positive myofibroblasts and CD68-positive macrophages in lesional skin.
In vitro, MSC-derived exosomes reduced expression of type I collagen and TGF-beta receptor 1 in fibroblasts.
MicroRNA profiling of MSC-derived exosomes identified several microRNAs with potential antifibrotic activity.

All three PPAR isoforms (alpha, delta, gamma) showed reduced nuclear immunohistochemical expression in lung tissue of transgenic (TG) mice compared to wildtype (WT) littermates, particularly near vessel walls.

Of 25 PPAR-pathway genes showing a trend of differential expression between TG and WT tissues/explants, 72% (18/25) were downregulated in TG mice, and of 9 genes reaching statistical significance, 89% (8/9) were reduced in TG.
High-dose lanifibranor (100 mg/kg) significantly reduced bleomycin-induced lung fibrosis (Ashcroft score) in transgenic mice compared with vehicle.
In wildtype mice, lanifibranor treatment did not reduce bleomycin-induced histological lung fibrosis compared with vehicle.

Lanifibranor at 100 mg/kg produced a dose-dependent, significant reduction in new lung collagen deposition (measured by Sircol assay) in bleomycin-treated transgenic mice, reducing excess collagen formation by 50%.
Mean arterial blood pressure (MABP) did not differ significantly between the 6 treatment groups in the SU5416 haemodynamic experiment.

Transgenic (TG) mice developed numerically elevated right ventricular systolic pressure/mean pulmonary arterial pressure compared with wildtype mice following SU5416 administration, consistent with prior published studies, though this did not reach statistical significance in the current smaller cohort.
Lanifibranor did not attenuate the elevation of right ventricular systolic pressure/pulmonary hypertension induced by SU5416 in transgenic mice.
High-dose lanifibranor (100 mg/kg) prevented right ventricular hypertrophy (Fulton index) that otherwise develops in transgenic mice after SU5416-induced pulmonary hypertension.
Lanifibranor did not reduce endovascular/endothelial proliferative lesions (pulmonary arteriolar obliteration) in SU5416-treated transgenic mice compared with vehicle.
Genes involved in fatty acid oxidation (Cpt1b and Fabp4), which are repressed by PPARγ agonism in cardiac protection mechanisms, were found to be downregulated in the transgenic mouse model.
Transcutaneous electrical acupoint stimulation (TEAS) reduced the incidence of postoperative paralytic ileus after colorectal surgery compared to sham stimulation.
TEAS decreased the odds of postoperative paralytic ileus by 32% relative to sham treatment.
TEAS shortened recovery times to first flatus, first defecation, resumption of normal diet, and return of bowel sounds after colorectal surgery.
TEAS treatment significantly increased median serum acetylcholine levels at 72 hours postoperatively compared to sham.
TEAS treatment significantly increased median serum interleukin-10 levels at 72 hours postoperatively compared to sham.
TEAS treatment significantly decreased median serum interleukin-6 levels at 72 hours postoperatively compared to sham.
TEAS treatment significantly decreased median serum inducible nitric oxide synthase levels at 72 hours postoperatively compared to sham.
Anti-RNPC3 antibodies are associated with more severe gastrointestinal disease in systemic sclerosis patients.
Anti-nicotinic acetylcholine receptor (gAChRα3) autoantibodies were significantly higher in SSc patients with GI disease compared to SSc patients without GI manifestations.
Anti-muscarinic-3 receptor autoantibodies may contribute to GI dysmotility in SSc by inhibiting contraction of smooth muscle cells.
Gastrointestinal (esophageal) involvement is the most common internal organ complication of systemic sclerosis, affecting over 90% of patients.
There is no difference in the degree of GI involvement between diffuse and limited forms of systemic sclerosis, despite the diffuse form having greater skin/muscle involvement.
A screening questionnaire study of dysphagia-related disability in SSc found mild disability in 74% of patients and moderate to severe disability in the remaining 26%.
Esophageal dysmotility, confirmed via manometry, is found in about 70%-75% of SSc patients, characterized by decreased peristaltic amplitude and decreased LES tone.
The prevalence of esophageal reflux (GERD) in SSc patients is 34.8%, based on large retrospective studies.
A case-control study found hiatal hernia in 16 of 25 SSc patients compared to only 3 of 25 control patients.
Erosive esophagitis develops in 30%-60% of SSc patients across a collection of studies, with one study reporting 24.2% mild-to-moderate and 3.6% severe erosive esophagitis.
Esophageal strictures are found in 17%-29% of SSc patients, and a diagnosis of SSc increases the odds of developing strictures with an odds ratio of 12.
Barrett's esophagus has been found in up to 37% of SSc patients and is more likely to develop in patients with limited SSc.
Esophageal adenocarcinoma incidence is higher in SSc patients with Barrett's esophagus (0.7% per year) compared to Barrett's esophagus patients without SSc (0.45% per year).

Candida esophagitis, the most common cause of infectious esophagitis (incidence up to 88%), is likely to occur more in SSc patients due to esophageal stasis and use of acid suppression/immunosuppressive therapy.
Sjogren's syndrome, causing xerostomia via salivary gland loss, is seen in 17%-29% of SSc patients and may worsen GERD by reducing bicarbonate buffering of refluxed acid.
Between 5% and 81% of SSc patients suffer from concurrent myopathies (Scleroderma Polymyositis Overlap), depending on the definition of muscle involvement used.

Dysphagia is reported in up to 36% of patients with myositis, with pharyngeal manometry showing globally weak pressure generation, absent hypo-pharyngeal constrictor activity, and abnormal UES contractility correlating with post-swallow residue and aspiration risk.
In a study of 30 SSc patients, hand dexterity was reduced to 68%-80% and grip force was reduced to 46%-65% compared to healthy individuals, with finger flexion/extension most impaired.
Gastroparesis has been reported in 50%-67% of SSc patients exhibiting GI symptoms, and about 27% of gastroparesis patients suffer from concomitant moderate to severe GERD.
Proton pump inhibitors are effective in relieving GI symptoms in SSc, and are more effective than H2-receptor antagonists.
Baclofen may decrease the incidence of transient LES relaxations, thereby reducing the number and length of reflux episodes.
The diameter of the esophagus in SSc patients correlates with progression of interstitial lung disease, as measured by diffusion capacity of the lung for carbon monoxide (DLCO).
A history of childhood abuse and neglect is described as making a substantial contribution to irritable bowel syndrome in adults.
A history of childhood abuse and neglect is described as making a substantial contribution to chronic fatigue syndrome in adults.
A history of childhood abuse and neglect is described as making a substantial contribution to fibromyalgia in adults.
At least one in ten US adults reports a significant history of childhood maltreatment, indicating exposure to child abuse or neglect is common and endemic.
Adults with a history of child maltreatment have a shortened life expectancy compared to those without such history.

Patients with familial dysautonomia, who lose unmyelinated sensory nerve axons, have an increased predisposition to osteoporosis, illustrating the role of sensory nerves in maintaining bone homeostasis.

A 68-year-old woman with undifferentiated connective tissue disease and meningococcal epiglottitis with septicaemia was found to have low C2 levels and reduced classical pathway complement activation, with C2 gene sequencing confirming type 1 C2 deficiency.

C2 deficiency is usually hereditary, inherited in an autosomal recessive manner, and is often asymptomatic, though some patients develop infections with encapsulated bacteria and/or autoimmune diseases, particularly systemic lupus erythematosus.
Among 616 lung transplant recipients with no prior gastroparesis history, 17.4% developed a new diagnosis of delayed gastric emptying within 3 years of transplant.
Black race was significantly associated with increased odds of a new gastroparesis diagnosis after lung transplantation on multivariable analysis.
Age, sex, history of diabetes, connective tissue disease, transplant type, diagnosis group, renal function, and body mass index were not significant predictors of post-transplant gastroparesis.
A new diagnosis of gastroparesis was significantly associated with increased risk of chronic lung allograft dysfunction (CLAD) after lung transplantation.
Gastroparesis was not significantly associated with overall post-transplant mortality.
Intra-PVN microinjection of the selective nNOS inhibitor NPLA attenuated exercise-induced hyperthermia compared to vehicle-treated rats.
Heat dissipation sensitivity (Hsen) was increased in NPLA-treated rats compared to vehicle controls.
Heat storage was lower in NPLA-treated animals compared to vehicle-treated animals.
There was no significant difference in tail skin temperature or in the heat dissipation threshold (Hthr) between NPLA-treated and vehicle-treated rats.
Despite altering thermoregulatory variables, intra-PVN nNOS inhibition with NPLA did not affect running performance on the treadmill compared to vehicle-treated rats.
Psychosocial manifestations were the most common post-acute symptom category, with a pooled prevalence of 28% across the included cohorts.
Fatigue or weakness was the single most prevalent post-acute COVID-19 symptom overall, affecting nearly half of patients.
Memory impairment was reported in over a third of post-acute COVID-19 patients as a leading neurological symptom.
Anxiety or depression was reported in about a third of post-acute COVID-19 patients.
Dyspnea affected about a third of post-acute COVID-19 patients as a leading cardiopulmonary symptom.
Cardiopulmonary and neurological systems showed similar overall symptom prevalence in post-acute COVID-19 patients, each around 15%.
Musculoskeletal symptoms, including myalgia and joint pain, were present in roughly 13% of post-acute COVID-19 patients.
Gastrointestinal symptoms had the lowest prevalence among the affected organ systems in post-acute COVID-19 patients.
Overall pulmonary function abnormalities were present in one-fifth of post-acute COVID-19 patients across seven studies with lung function data.
Impaired diffusion capacity (DLCO <80%) was the most common lung function abnormality, observed in nearly half of tested post-acute patients.
Airflow obstruction (FEV1/FVC <70%) was relatively uncommon among post-acute COVID-19 patients and reported in only three studies.
Severe COVID-19 patients were more likely than non-severe patients to develop musculoskeletal, cardiopulmonary, and psychosocial manifestations post-acutely.
Joint pain, dyspnea, palpitation, and anxiety or depression were significantly more prevalent among severe COVID-19 cases compared to non-severe cases in the post-acute phase.
Fatigue or weakness, the most common post-acute symptom overall, did not differ significantly in occurrence between severe and non-severe COVID-19 patients.
Severe COVID-19 patients were more than twice as likely to have persistent abnormal pulmonary function in the post-acute phase compared with non-severe patients.

Lung volumes and diffusion capacity (TLC, FEV1, FVC, DLCO all <80% predicted) were significantly more likely to be abnormal in severe versus non-severe COVID-19 patients, with TLC showing the strongest association.
FEV1/FVC <70%, indicating airway obstruction, showed no significant difference between severe and non-severe COVID-19 groups in the post-acute phase.

The discussion cites prior work proposing that a subset of COVID-19 patients may develop chronic fatigue syndrome (CFS) similar to that following SARS and MERS, potentially via SARS-CoV-2 invasion of olfactory neurons causing lymphatic congestion and toxin accumulation in the CNS.

The authors note that joint disorders in prior SARS follow-up were presumed related to high-dose steroid therapy rather than direct viral effect, suggesting a similar consideration for musculoskeletal findings in COVID-19 patients treated with glucocorticoids.
Nearly two-thirds of ME/CFS patients had a reduction or deficiency in at least one measured immune parameter.
About a quarter of ME/CFS patients showed signs of immune activation or inflammation via elevation of at least one immune parameter.
IgA levels were below normal in 6.5% of ME/CFS patients, exceeding the expected general population deviation.
Total IgG levels were decreased in 6.5% of ME/CFS patients.
IgM levels were below norm values in 4.9% of ME/CFS patients, with a significant sex difference (more frequent in one sex, p=0.02).
IgG3 was the most frequently reduced IgG subclass, found in 8% of ME/CFS patients.
IgG4 was reduced in 4.9% of ME/CFS patients, with an age-group difference in isolated deficiency rates.
Reduced MBL levels (<50 ng/mL) were the most frequently reduced humoral immune parameter, found in 32.1% of ME/CFS patients.
Reduced C3c levels were found in 16% of ME/CFS patients, the second most frequently reduced parameter.
Unclassified antibody deficiency (recurrent/severe infections plus immunoglobulin/subclass deficiency) was diagnosed in 17.6% of ME/CFS patients.
Isolated IgG3 subclass deficiency was diagnosed in 5.7% of ME/CFS patients, the most common isolated subclass deficiency.
Selective IgA deficiency, a rare disorder with EU prevalence ~0.001%, was diagnosed in 2.7% of ME/CFS patients, a rate the authors note is unstudied in this population.
MBL deficiency (with recurrent/severe infections) was diagnosed in 6.9% of ME/CFS patients, higher than the ~4% reported in the general Caucasian population using a similar cutoff.

The most common combination of humoral and cellular immune parameter reduction was immunoglobulin reduction together with reduced CD3-CD16+CD56+ NK cell counts (n=8), and n=6 when restricted to unclassified antibody deficiency.
Elevated CD8-CD57+ NK cell counts were found in 23 patients and showed above-average deviation from expected general population frequency by 95% CI analysis.
Elevated CD4+ T-cell levels were detected in 12 ME/CFS patients.
Elevated IgG2 was the most common immunoglobulin increase, found in 13 patients, and showed above-average deviation from the expected general population rate as well as a sex difference (p=0.01).
74% of ME/CFS patients tested positive for EBV antibodies (IgG or IgM), slightly lower than the 88.3% seropositivity reported in a similarly aged healthy reference cohort.
A history of frequent recurrent infections was reported by 60% of all ME/CFS patients, and 17.2% recalled having had acute mononucleosis (EBV infection).
Elevated complement C4 was rarely observed, found in only 3 ME/CFS patients, and elevated C3 in only 1 patient.

Across nearly all immune parameters, no significant differences were found between male and female patients or between age groups (18-40 vs 41-80 years), suggesting immune alterations occur independent of sex and age.
42.8% (107/250) of ME/CFS patients had complement C1q levels above the normal laboratory reference range.
8.8% of ME/CFS patients had decreased C1 inhibitor levels below the normal reference range.
ME/CFS cases with elevated C1q had higher red blood cell counts than cases with normal C1q levels.
Total protein levels were higher in the elevated-C1q ME/CFS cluster compared with the normal-C1q cluster.
Complement C3 levels were higher in the elevated-C1q ME/CFS cluster compared with the normal-C1q cluster.
Complement C4 levels were higher in the elevated-C1q ME/CFS cluster compared with the normal-C1q cluster.
IgG3 subclass levels were lower in the elevated-C1q ME/CFS cluster compared with the normal-C1q cluster.
IgG4 subclass levels were lower in the elevated-C1q ME/CFS cluster compared with the normal-C1q cluster.
C1 inhibitor concentrations were lower in the elevated-C1q ME/CFS cluster compared with the normal-C1q cluster.

Unbiased hierarchical and k-means clustering of symptom scores identified three ME/CFS subgroups (severe, moderate, mild) that differed significantly in total FIS-40, total COMPASS-31, total PSQI, physical functioning, and bodily pain scores.
Hemoglobin levels differentiated only the moderate symptom-severity cluster from the severe and mild clusters, with unclear physiological meaning.
Neutrophil counts differed between the severe and mild symptom-severity clusters, being increased in severe ME/CFS.
Cholesterol levels differed between the severe cluster and both moderate and mild clusters, with no difference between moderate and mild.
HDL cholesterol levels differed between severe and moderate clusters but not with the mild cluster.
Complement C3 differed between severe and mild clusters and between mild and moderate clusters, but not between severe and moderate, suggesting C3 may distinguish mild cases from more severe ones.
60.4% of ME/CFS cases showed abnormal vitamin D values, mostly reflecting deficiency.
55.6% of ME/CFS cases had elevated LDL cholesterol values above the normal reference range.
26.4% of ME/CFS cases had elevated total cholesterol above the normal reference range.
Platelet mean volume was abnormal in a substantial proportion of ME/CFS patients, showing both increases and decreases relative to reference ranges.
Stratifying ME/CFS cases by elevated vs normal C1q levels showed no significant symptom score differences except a non-significant trend toward higher bodily pain in the high-C1q group.

The proportion of cases with elevated C1q increased with symptom-severity cluster: 33% in mild, 35% in moderate, and 39% in severe cases, though this trend was not statistically significant at the individual symptom level.
No correlation was found between C1q levels and disease chronicity status in ME/CFS cases.
Only a few ME/CFS cases showed positive self-antigen (autoimmune) reactivity across the panel of ten autoimmunity-related tests performed.
Myalgia was more prevalent in ME/CFS patients (96%) than in non-ME/CFS fatigue patients (73%), making it one of the differentiating symptoms.
Arthralgia occurred in 86% of ME/CFS patients and was identified as one of the symptoms tending to differentiate ME/CFS from non-ME/CFS fatigue patients.
Sleep disturbances, assessed using the Athens Insomnia Scale, were present in 53% of ME/CFS patients, lower than the 79% reported in some prior literature.
Fibromyalgia was the most common comorbidity in ME/CFS patients, present in 20% of cases, among an overall comorbidity prevalence of 66%.
EBV infection history was reported as a comorbid/prior infectious factor in 5% of the ME/CFS cohort.
ME/CFS patients with at least one comorbidity showed the highest individual fatigue pattern scores, suggesting comorbidities are associated with a more severe disease course.

Most ME/CFS patients (93%) could not identify similar fatigue symptoms in first-degree relatives, suggesting limited association between fatigue and positive family history in this cohort, contrary to some prior studies.
A large majority (82%) of patients in both ME/CFS groups had reduced their workload or become unemployed due to fatigue.
Among ME/CFS patients using pharmacological treatment for fatigue symptoms, NSAIDs were the most commonly used drug class and were reported as effective by 90% of users.
In the ME/CFS group without comorbidities, younger age was correlated with identification of more current symptoms.
Male sex was associated with identification of more consequences of fatigue than female sex, in both the non-ME/CFS and ME/CFS-without-comorbidities groups.
In the ME/CFS group without comorbidities, younger age and shorter fatigue duration were each correlated with higher pain VAS scores.
In the ME/CFS with comorbidities group, increasing age correlated with longer fatigue duration and with identifying more potential causes for fatigue.
None of the ME/CFS patients reported using supplements or cognitive behavioural therapy as fatigue management strategies.
Choline and related compounds were found decreased in plasma across all reviewed ME/CFS metabolomic studies.
Ceramide levels were altered (both increased and decreased across studies) in the plasma of ME/CFS patients.
Carnitine levels were reported dysregulated in plasma of ME/CFS patients in more than one study.
Plasma glucose was found decreased in ME/CFS patients relative to controls in two independent studies.
ATP levels were reduced in plasma of ME/CFS patients, consistent with the disease's characteristic lack of energy.
The amino acids lysine and tyrosine were found increased in plasma of ME/CFS patients in more than one study.
Urinary creatinine was found dysregulated (both increased and decreased across studies) in ME/CFS patients versus controls.
Urinary alanine was found dysregulated (both increased and decreased) in ME/CFS patients across independent studies.
Urinary urea was persistently decreased in ME/CFS patients across two independent studies, the most significant urine finding.
Phosphocholines, particularly phosphocholine 16:0, were increased in plasma/serum of fibromyalgia patients across two studies.
Glutaric acid was dysregulated (increased and decreased in different sample types) in fibromyalgia patients across two studies.
Taurine was increased in both plasma and urine of fibromyalgia patients across two studies, indicating increased amino acid metabolism.
A substantial proportion (30%-70%) of patients diagnosed with FM also meet diagnostic criteria for ME/CFS and vice versa, indicating high comorbidity.
Peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) cultured with plasma from ME/CFS patients behaved differently than those cultured with healthy control plasma, suggesting a disease-specific plasma factor.
Unpublished preliminary data indicated that cellular oxygen consumption of a muscle reporter cell line was increased upon addition of ME/CFS patient plasma.

Long-chain and short-chain acyl cholines (e.g., palmitoylcholine, linoleoylcholine, arachidonoylcholine) were markedly reduced in ME/CFS plasma and are proposed to negatively regulate acetylcholine expression, potentially explaining brain fog and low blood pressure.
In contrast to plasma findings, brain choline levels measured by imaging were found increased in different brain regions of ME/CFS patients compared with controls.

The authors hypothesize that induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs), owing to their heightened sensitivity to nutritional/metabolic and osmotic environmental cues, could serve as a bioassay sensor for ME/CFS and FM plasma factors, though no prior study has directly tested this.
Only 27% of doctors reported prior formal teaching on ME, 70% had some clinical experience of ME patients, and 23% had neither teaching nor experience.
The vast majority of doctors admitted not knowing how to diagnose ME and lacked confidence managing ME patients.
Doctors' self-reported confidence in diagnosing ME was significantly associated with their confidence in managing ME patients.

All six respondents who expressed confidence in diagnosing or managing ME believed the illness was at least partly psychological, none chose the correct diagnostic criteria, and all endorsed graded exercise therapy as treatment.
The large majority of doctors incorrectly believed ME is at least partly psychological/psychosomatic, with only a small minority correctly identifying it as purely a physical illness.

Doctors who had received prior formal teaching or clinical experience with ME patients were paradoxically less likely to correctly understand ME as a physical illness than those with no teaching or experience.
Doctors generally answered general epidemiology and chronicity questions about ME correctly, averaging 82.3% correct across a range of propositions.
About a third of doctors incorrectly endorsed the statement that children with ME miss school because parents support the sick role and this should be discouraged.
Most doctors incorrectly classified ME as belonging to the category of 'medically unexplained symptoms' and did not know the difference between ME, CFS, and post-viral fatigue syndrome.
Almost all doctors erroneously endorsed the notion that ME patients need to think positively and build up strength through exercise, with only two respondents correctly disagreeing.
Most doctors selected a careful history as central to diagnosing ME, but only about half selected the fully correct diagnostic combination excluding a psychiatric history.
Most doctors incorrectly believed six months of fatigue is required for a diagnosis of ME, contrary to the International Consensus Criteria which allow diagnosis without waiting six months.
A significant proportion of doctors did not recognise post-exertional malaise as an essential diagnostic requirement for ME.
Only just over half of doctors correctly recognised that psychiatric features are not part of the diagnostic criteria for ME.
Only a small minority of doctors selected the fully correct diagnostic combination of post-exertional malaise and multi-system symptoms without psychiatric features.
Most doctors underestimated the level of disability of ME patients relative to other serious illnesses, with only just over a third correctly recognising comparable disability.
Nearly half of doctors overestimated the ability of ME patients to remain in work.
Nearly all doctors recognised that children with ME can miss long periods of school, most recognised ME as painful, but only a quarter knew ME can be fatal.

Only a minority of doctors recognised that ME can affect all seven commonly involved body systems (nervous, cardiovascular, endocrine, musculoskeletal, gastrointestinal, immune, and cellular metabolism).
Almost all doctors believed graded exercise therapy (GET) is a suitable treatment for ME, and a majority believed cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) is also suitable.
Most doctors were amenable to further education on ME after an introductory lecture, with only a small minority declining.

A reanalysis of the PACE trial (the largest GET trial in ME/CFS), cited in the discussion, found recovery rates of about 10%, close to natural recovery rates, rather than the 22% recovery rate originally reported by PACE trial authors.

A 2011 review of eight patient surveys, cited in the discussion, found that around half of respondents reported GET made their health worse, and other surveys found the majority of patients responded negatively to GET.
Cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT), cited in the discussion, was found beneficial to only a minority of ME/CFS patients.
Cited literature indicates widespread employment loss among ME/CFS patients across multiple countries, considerably higher than doctors in this audit appreciated.

Reanalysis of the PACE trial, the largest graded exercise therapy trial for ME/CFS, found recovery rates close to 10%, only slightly above natural recovery rates, rather than the 22% recovery rate originally reported.

A 2019 Cochrane review of eight reports concluded exercise therapy probably had a positive effect on fatigue in ME/CFS, but a subsequent reanalysis found this conclusion was flawed due to non-reporting of harms, and that GET appeared ineffective and unsafe.
A 2011 review of eight patient surveys found that 51% of respondents reported that graded exercise therapy had made their health worse.
An analysis of primary and secondary patient surveys found that 54-74% of patients responded negatively to graded exercise therapy.
Cognitive behavioural therapy was found to be of benefit to only 8-35% of ME/CFS patients according to an American clinicians' report.

A large UK study using the UK CFS/ME National Outcomes Database found that 50.1% (998 of 1991) of patients had lost employment because of illness, with estimated UK annual productivity costs of £102.2 million.
A Spanish community-based study found that 63% of ME/CFS patients were unable to work.
Another Spanish report from the same research group found that 58.6% (636 of 1116) of people with ME/CFS were unemployed.
A Norwegian study of hospital patients found that 45% (43 of 92) of ME/CFS patients were unemployed.
Patient evidence suggests adverse outcomes occur in 20% of ME/CFS cases treated with CBT.
In a survey of ME patients' experience in Italy, Latvia and the UK, only 1.4% (1 of 70) of UK respondents who had undergone graded exercise therapy reported it as effective.
Research cited indicates increased mortality among ME/CFS patients from cardiovascular disease, cancer and suicide.
A recent paper highlighted considerable risk to life from malnutrition among patients with very severe ME.
The direct costs of ME/CFS to the UK are estimated at £3.3 billion per annum.
ME/CFS is stated to be more than twice as common as multiple sclerosis and is the single greatest cause of long-term school absence in children.
Central sensitisation, defined by enhanced temporal summation and inefficient conditioned pain modulation, was present in 84% of CFS cases compared to none of the healthy controls.
Central sensitisation, defined by enhanced temporal summation and inefficient conditioned pain modulation, was present in 95% of FM cases compared to none of the healthy controls.
Pressure pain thresholds were significantly lower in CFS cases than in healthy controls.
Pressure pain thresholds were significantly lower in FM cases than in healthy controls.
FM cases showed a significantly different cold-induced pain threshold compared to healthy controls, indicating altered thermal pain processing.
FM cases showed a significantly different heat-induced pain threshold compared to healthy controls, indicating altered thermal pain processing.
Unlike FM, CFS cases did not differ significantly from healthy controls in cold- or heat-induced pain thresholds.
Brain creatine concentration in the anterior cingulate cortex was significantly lower in CFS patients compared to healthy controls.
Brain glutathione concentration in the anterior cingulate cortex was significantly lower in CFS patients compared to healthy controls, consistent with increased oxidative stress.
Brain myo-inositol concentration in the anterior cingulate cortex was significantly lower in CFS patients compared to healthy controls, potentially reflecting glial dysfunction.
Glutamate concentration in the ACC showed a trend toward lower levels in CFS patients but did not reach statistical significance.
Glutamine concentration in the ACC did not differ significantly between CFS patients and healthy controls.
Absolute GABA concentration in the ACC showed a trend toward higher levels in CFS patients that did not reach significance.
When expressed as a ratio to NAA (to control for possible water dilution effects), GABA/NAA was significantly higher in CFS patients than controls.
NAA concentration in the ACC did not differ significantly between CFS patients and healthy controls.
Within CFS patients, higher NAA levels in the ACC correlated moderately with longer duration of fatigue symptoms.
There was no significant correlation between fatigue severity ratings and any of the measured ACC neurochemicals in CFS patients.
CFS patients had substantially higher fatigue scores, and modestly increased depression and anxiety scores compared with healthy controls.
A history of viral infection preceded the onset of CFS symptoms in 17 of the 22 CFS patients studied.

Antidepressant medication use (mainly SSRIs) was significantly more common in CFS patients than in healthy controls, but adding this as a covariate did not materially change the neurochemical findings.
Most classical EDS cases are caused by alterations in COL5A1 or COL5A2, most commonly COL5A1 haploinsufficiency from an unstable transcript of one allele.
Kyphoscoliotic EDS is caused by mutations in PLOD1 or FKBP14, whereas the molecular basis of hEDS remains unidentified.
cEDS patients frequently report gastrointestinal symptoms including nausea, vomiting, GERD, and constipation at substantial rates.
Pelvic organ prolapse, pregnancy, and menstrual cycle complications including infertility are far more common in EDS (particularly hEDS) patients than in the general population.
hEDS patients commonly show autonomic dysfunction manifesting as tachycardia, POTS, vasovagal syncope, neurally mediated hypotension, or orthostatic hypotension.
In a case series, all 28 hEDS patients studied reported pain, with a mean severity score of 8/10 across EDS types.
In a larger EDS cohort, 90% of 273 patients reported pain and 93% reported joint hypermobility, with hEDS showing the highest pain severity scores.
Pain prevalence increases sharply with age in hEDS, rising from ~30% in children to over 80% in patients over 40, even when Beighton scores become negative.
Skin biopsies from EDS pain patients show decreased intraepidermal nerve fiber density, supporting a neuropathic contribution to their pain.

A single family carried a COL3A1 Gly637Ser point mutation (typically seen in vEDS) but presented an hEDS-like phenotype without the vascular fragility, with reduced/altered collagen organization inherited autosomal dominantly.

A heterozygous missense LZTS1 mutation was found in all affected members of a multigenerational Belgian hEDS family and in none of the unaffected members, though its role in connective tissue biology is unclear.

Truncating TNXB mutations/deletions causing Tenascin-X deficiency occur in patients meeting cEDS criteria, while TNXB haploinsufficiency is found in an autosomal dominant hEDS form lacking easy bruising and skin hyperextensibility.
Reduced serum tenascin-X levels were found only in a minority (5-10%) of patients diagnosed with hEDS/Benign Joint Hypermobility Syndrome.
A contiguous gene deletion syndrome (CAH-X) involving TNXB exon replacement by TNXA and 21-hydroxylase (CYP21A2) deficiency causes co-occurrence of congenital adrenal hyperplasia and hEDS.

High alpha-tryptase levels linked to TPSAB1 gene mutations were found in patients with hEDS-like symptoms (connective tissue abnormalities, autonomic dysfunction, GI, allergic and cutaneous symptoms), though not all such patients met hEDS diagnostic criteria and elevated basal tryptase is common in the general population.
Proteome profiling of hEDS patients' dermal myofibroblasts identified 183 differentially expressed proteins spanning metabolism, cytoskeleton, translation, and other cellular processes.
Multiple miRNAs (miR-378-3p, miR-224, miR-23) are altered in hEDS and contribute to decreased SFRP2 mRNA and aberrant Wnt/β-catenin signaling implicated in hEDS pathogenesis.
Serum analysis of JHS patients (a common EDS comorbidity) showed higher levels of complement-related proteins C1R, vitronectin, C9, and C4BPA compared to controls.
Exome analysis of a single classical EDS type I patient revealed three heterozygous mutations in TTR, FBN1, and CACNA1A genes.
Analysis of hEDS fibroblasts showed increased expression of complement factor D, which has been proposed as a predictive biomarker of joint pain in osteoarthritis.
Transcriptome analysis of hEDS skin fibroblasts showed increased expression of aquaporin 9 (AQP9), a marker of chronic inflammation also seen in IBS, psoriasis and rheumatoid arthritis.
Functional analysis of JHS/hEDS fibroblasts showed IL6 gene downregulation, suggesting its dosage could serve as a tool for studying disease follow-up.

Elevated serum prolactin is associated with various pain conditions (migraine, RA, osteoarthritis) and may modulate nociceptor activity, suggesting a possible role in EDS-related chronic pain, though this link is speculative for EDS specifically.

SELENBP1 is upregulated in blood and brain of schizophrenia patients and is proposed as a schizophrenia biomarker; the authors hypothesize it may be worth investigating in EDS patients given their psychiatric comorbidities, though no EDS-specific data are presented.

In patients with homo- or compound heterozygous CHST14 mutations (musculocontractural EDS type 1), dermatan sulfate was absent from urine, suggesting this absence as a non-invasive diagnostic biomarker.

Urinary lysyl-pyridinoline and hydroxylysyl-pyridinoline crosslink analysis is a fast, non-invasive diagnostic test for kyphoscoliotic EDS (EDS VIA) caused by PLOD1-related lysyl-hydroxylase deficiency.

The paper reports on the prevalence of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (alongside Marfan syndrome and osteogenesis imperfecta) among patients with hidradenitis suppurativa, but no abstract text with specific results was provided.
Adults with ADHD had significantly higher odds of generalised joint hypermobility (GJH), as measured by the Beighton scoring system, compared to non-ADHD controls.

Adults with ADHD had an even stronger association with symptomatic GJH (GJH plus musculoskeletal symptoms and/or skin abnormalities, a proxy for hypermobility spectrum disorders/EDS) than with non-specified GJH alone.
A novel missense variant in MAP3K7 (c.467A>T, p.Asp156Val) was identified in the first reported Asian male with cardiospondylocarpofacial syndrome.
The reported CSCF case exhibited a mixed phenotype overlapping with Ehlers-Danlos syndrome and Noonan syndrome, suggesting phenotypic overlap between these conditions and CSCF.
The study radiographically captured the progressive process of carpal fusion in a CSCF patient for the first time.
Pathogenic variants in COL3A1, the gene encoding type III collagen, underlie vascular EDS and predispose patients to blood vessel rupture.
In a mouse model exhibiting vEDS traits, treatment with the beta-blocker celiprolol significantly improved thoracic aorta biomechanical strength.
Specifically designed small interfering RNAs (siRNA) can effectively and selectively silence the pathogenic variant COL3A1 allele.
Intracellularly expressed lysyl oxidase has been shown to regulate and enhance the transcription rate of the wild-type COL3A1 promoter, aiming to boost normal allele expression.
The embryonic transcription factor Nanog was shown to upregulate wild-type COL3A1 expression by activating the transforming growth factor-beta pathway, thereby increasing type III collagen synthesis.
Fibromyalgia patients and matched controls showed no significant difference in T lymphocyte reactivity to Borrelia burgdorferi sensu stricto full antigen.
T lymphocyte reactivity to a mix of Borrelia OspA antigens from three species did not differ significantly between fibromyalgia patients and controls.
T lymphocyte reactivity to lymphocyte function antigen-1 (shared epitope) did not differ significantly between fibromyalgia patients and controls.
Mast cells are hypothesized to mediate microglial activation in fibromyalgia via production of IL-1β, IL-6, and TNF-α, contributing to musculoskeletal pain and central sensitization.
A cited study found that about one-third of FMS patients with xerostomia tested positive for Sjogren's syndrome biomarkers, with most positive for one or more tissue-specific autoantibodies.
CCL1 (eotaxin-1) and CCL2 (eotaxin-2), chemoattractants for inflammatory cells, were found to be elevated in patients with FMS, supporting a mast cell role in pathogenesis.

Stress-induced HPA axis activation (CRH-ACTH-glucocorticoid cascade) with resultant mast cell degranulation is proposed to sensitize peripheral and central nociceptors and increase pro-inflammatory cytokines in FMS.
It is hypothesized, but not yet proven, that reduced endocannabinoid system activity underlies fibromyalgia pathophysiology.
Recent studies found nabilone superior to placebo, showing significant reductions in visual analog scale (VAS) pain scores in fibromyalgia patients.

A study of cannabinoids for non-cancer pain that included FM patients concluded cannabinoids can be used for neuropathic pain but should not replace first-line therapy; results were inconclusive for FM specifically since the study was not exclusive to FM.
Nabilone and dronabinol showed improvement in pain and anxiety across several RCTs and meta-analyses, with the THC:CBD ratio determining overall treatment effect.

In an experimental study of 38 patients, adding medical cannabis for a minimum of six months to standard analgesic therapy produced greater improvement across FIQ, VAS, ODI, and lumbar range of motion than analgesic therapy alone.

In a 20-patient study of four inhaled cannabis varieties, none showed an effect greater than placebo on spontaneous or electrical pain overall, though more subjects on Bediol showed a 30% decrease in pain scores versus placebo, pressure pain threshold increased significantly with Bedrocan and Bediol, and Bedrolite (high-CBD, low-THC) showed no analgesic activity.

In a 367-patient study of medical cannabis for fibromyalgia over six months, pain intensity dropped from a median of 9.0 to 5.0 (p<0.001), with 81.1% of patients achieving treatment response and mostly mild adverse effects (dizziness, dry mouth, GI symptoms).

In a 102-patient study of adjunctive medical cannabis treatment (MCT) with Bedrocan and Bediol, 50% showed moderate improvement in anxiety and depression, and concomitant analgesic therapy was reduced or suspended in 47% of patients, with only one-third experiencing mild adverse events.

A double-blind, placebo-controlled RCT of 17 women over eight weeks found that THC-rich cannabis oil produced a significant decrease in FIQ score compared to placebo, indicating a well-tolerated, low-cost therapy improving symptoms and quality of life.

In a study of 751 chronic pain patients (132 with FM, 17.6%), medical cannabis treatment over 12 months showed improved pain scores and was not associated with increased adverse event frequency, but rather decreased frequency of headaches, fatigue, anxiety, and nausea.

A retrospective open-label case series of 38 patients with 12-month follow-up found MC may be a useful alternative for FMS patients unresponsive to conventional therapy, though limited by non-serious adverse effects (mental confusion, dizziness, nausea/vomiting, restlessness/irritation).
Due to unclear pathophysiology and lack of a single defining symptom, approximately 75% of fibromyalgia patients remain undiagnosed.
Fibromyalgia affects approximately 5% of the population and is described as a classical centralized pain syndrome/sensory-processing disorder.

In fibromyalgia patients, an fMRI study by Gracely et al. found that less than half the stimulus intensity was needed to evoke a BOLD response in pain-processing brain areas compared with healthy controls, indicating central augmentation of peripheral stimuli.
The central hypersensitivity seen in fibromyalgia may extend beyond pain to other sensory modalities such as auditory perception and smell.
Migraine, tinnitus, and dizziness are common comorbidities in fibromyalgia patients.
Similar to patients with visual snow syndrome, tinnitus, and PPPD, fibromyalgia patients report triggers such as stress, trauma, or environmental changes associated with symptom onset and flares.

Repetitive mechanical stimulation produces excessive temporal summation at lower stimulus intensities/frequencies and more pronounced painful after-sensations in fibromyalgia patients compared with healthy controls, suggesting a lack of pain inhibition.
Wagner et al. demonstrated a specific and significantly more expansive BOLD response to painful stimuli in the bilateral insula, secondary somatosensory cortex, and thalamus in fibromyalgia patients.
In fibromyalgia, there was reduced connectivity between the somatosensory cortex and other regions but increased connectivity between the somatosensory cortex and the bilateral anterior insula.

Structural imaging showed total gray matter volume decrease in fibromyalgia in one study, and widespread regional gray matter decreases in the cingulate, insular, medial frontal/prefrontal cortices, parahippocampal gyri, thalamus, and pons across other studies.

Sleep disturbances, including insomnia, abnormal sleep architecture, and sleep fragmentation, are well known in fibromyalgia and have also been reported in tinnitus and migraine, but no literature was found on this topic in VSS and PPPD.
Cognitive symptoms such as decline in memory and mental alertness ("brain fog") are reported in about 50% of fibromyalgia patients and are frequent in visual snow syndrome as well.

The concept of "thalamocortical dysrhythmia," evidenced by reduced alpha and increased theta EEG power over certain cortical areas, has been proposed as the neuronal correlate of visual snow syndrome, fibromyalgia, and tinnitus.
Tinnitus is more prevalent in patients affected by fibromyalgia than in the general population.
Migraine affects about 15% of the population and is characterized by a predisposition to recurrent headache attacks with a migrainous phenotype.
In migraine, sensory thresholds reach their minimal (most sensitive) point during the ictal phase, but hypersensitivity to multimodal stimuli persists even interictally.
An MRI study by Karsan et al. demonstrated hyperperfusion of the hypothalamus, anterior cingulate cortex, midbrain, and limbic areas before the onset of nitroglycerine-triggered migraine attacks.

In consecutive fMRI scans over 30 days, hypothalamic activity in response to trigeminal nociceptive stimulation and hypothalamic functional connectivity to spinal trigeminal nuclei increased during the preictal phase of migraine.

MRI studies in migraine show structural gray and white matter volume alterations (VBM and DTI) in widespread cortical areas including sensory areas, prefrontal cortex, cerebellum, brainstem, insula, and anterior cingulate cortex.
Interictal functional studies in migraine revealed alterations in the default mode network, dorsal attention network, salience network, and visual cortex.

The anterior cingulate gyrus and insula, components of the salience network, appear to be affected across visual snow syndrome, fibromyalgia, tinnitus, and PPPD, and this network is also implicated in depression and anxiety pathophysiology.

The authors hypothesize that migraine constitutes a risk factor for the development of other persistent perceptual disorders including fibromyalgia, tinnitus, and PPPD, potentially via shared thalamocortical and salience-network dysfunction.

Optic nerve head blood flow area (ONH-BFA) measured by OCTA was significantly higher in both mild-moderate and severe fibromyalgia patients compared with healthy controls, with no difference between the two FMS severity groups.
Average RNFL thickness was significantly lower in the severe FMS group compared with both the mild-moderate FMS group and healthy controls.
Inferotemporal quadrant RNFL thickness was significantly reduced in the severe FMS group compared with the mild-moderate FMS group and controls.
Inferonasal quadrant RNFL thickness was significantly reduced in the severe FMS group compared with the mild-moderate FMS group and controls.
Nasal-superior quadrant RNFL thickness was significantly higher in healthy controls than in both mild-moderate and severe FMS groups.
ONH-BFA showed a weak positive correlation with fibromyalgia disease severity as measured by FIQ score.
Average RNFL thickness showed a weak positive correlation with fibromyalgia disease severity (FIQ score).
Inferotemporal RNFL thickness showed a weak positive correlation with fibromyalgia disease severity (FIQ score).
Inferonasal RNFL thickness showed a weak positive correlation with fibromyalgia disease severity (FIQ score).

Fatigue assessment scale scores in LC participants rose significantly after COVID-19, reaching levels approaching those of MCAS patients.
Self-rated quality of life scores dropped markedly in LC participants after COVID-19 infection and were significantly lower than in MCAS patients prior to treatment.
Antihistamine use among LC participants increased substantially after COVID-19 infection compared to before, tracking increased mast cell activation symptoms.

The authors hypothesize that Long-COVID may often arise from SARS-CoV-2-driven provocation of primary or secondary mast cell activation syndrome (MCAS), potentially via cytokine-storm-induced somatic mutations, direct viral activation of mast cells/microglia, viral dysregulation of MC-controlling genes, autoantibodies against MC immunoglobulin receptors, or increased Toll-like receptor activity.

Clinicians reported observing improvement in Long-COVID patients using combinations of mast cell-directed therapies including antihistamines, cromolyn, quercetin, luteolin, low dose naltrexone, montelukast, and vitamins C and D, though this was not formally tested in this study.

Kounis syndrome is markedly underreported in patients under 20 years old compared to older adults, likely reflecting underdiagnosis in pediatrics.
Antibiotics and insect bites are reported as the most common triggers of Kounis syndrome across the literature.
The patient carried a pathologic CYP1B1 mutation underlying his congenital glaucoma, unrelated to the cardiac event.
The patient developed acute bradycardia and hypotension approximately 30 minutes after induction with midazolam and sevoflurane, without overt allergic symptoms.
Serum CK-MB, troponin, and NT-proBNP were elevated during the acute cardiac event, consistent with myocardial injury and left ventricular dysfunction.
Inflammatory markers, eosinophil count, electrolytes, and liver/kidney function were normal, arguing against systemic infection or overt eosinophilic allergic reaction.
Echocardiography revealed global left ventricular hypokinesia and dilatation with an ejection fraction of 34%, while right ventricular function was preserved.
Cardiac MRI showed anterior LV wall oedema (high T2 signal) without late gadolinium enhancement, consistent with reversible ischemic myocardial injury rather than myocarditis or fibrosis.
The patient achieved complete ECG normalization and cardiac functional recovery within 72 hours, with biomarker reduction by discharge on day 6, without specific drug therapy.
Coronary CT performed 10 days after onset excluded lumen obstruction, dissection, or anatomical variants, but revealed myocardial bridging of a segment of the LAD coronary artery.
Skin prick testing for midazolam and sevoflurane was negative, though this does not rule out hypersensitivity given known test limitations.
Using the Naranjo adverse drug reaction probability scale, there was a probable causal association between anesthetic drug administration and onset of the cardiac event.
Allergic reactions to sedative/analgesic drugs during pediatric pre-procedural sedation occur at an incidence of about 1:4,219, with midazolam being the third most commonly implicated drug.
Isoflurane has previously been reported as a precipitating factor for acute coronary vasospasm in both an adult and a young child.

In anaphylaxis cohorts, skin manifestations are present in the majority (84%) of cases, followed by cardiovascular (72%) and respiratory (68%) involvement, meaning cutaneous signs can be absent in a substantial minority.
In Kounis syndrome cohorts, rash occurs in a minority of cases, while chest pain and anaphylaxis are more common presenting features.

Cardiac MRI criteria for Kounis syndrome type 1 show the interventricular septum as the most commonly involved myocardial region, followed by the LV lateral wall, differing from the anterior wall involvement seen in this patient.

Active and resting mast cell states in the tumor microenvironment were significantly associated with prognosis in lung adenocarcinoma using CIBERSORTx-based immune infiltration analysis of TCGA-LUAD data.
CCNA2, identified as a key target of Fuzheng Kang'ai Formula, was found to be an independent prognostic factor in lung adenocarcinoma with a hazard ratio of 1.41.

BCL2L2, ACTL6A, and ITGAV were identified as downstream targets of CCNA2 via protein-protein interaction analysis and were experimentally validated by qRT-PCR in A549 lung cancer cells, supporting a mechanism by which Fuzheng Kang'ai Formula binds CCNA2 to inhibit tumor growth.
TLR7 mRNA expression in HMC-1 mast cells remained stable and was not significantly changed by imiquimod (TLR7 agonist) treatment.

Transmission electron microscopy revealed that imiquimod-treated HMC-1 cells had increased vesicles, lipid droplets, and ribosomes compared to untreated control cells, indicating an activated cellular state.

RNA sequencing identified 218 differentially expressed genes between untreated and imiquimod-treated HMC-1 mast cells (fold-change >2, p≤0.05), with 25 transcripts showing log2 fold-change greater than 2 upregulation.

Gene Ontology analysis showed that genes involved in cell migration, cell surface receptor signaling, cell adhesion, antiviral defense response, and carbohydrate metabolism were negatively regulated (downregulated) in imiquimod-stimulated HMC-1 cells.

Genes involved in angiogenesis, positive regulation of angiogenesis, and vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) production were highly enriched among positively expressed biological process categories in imiquimod-stimulated HMC-1 mast cells.
Muc22 (mucin family gene) expression was upregulated in imiquimod-treated HMC-1 mast cells, confirmed by RT-qPCR.
Ern2, a positive regulator of mucin gene expression, was upregulated in imiquimod-treated HMC-1 mast cells, confirmed by RT-qPCR.
Rps17, encoding a ribosomal protein, was upregulated in imiquimod-treated HMC-1 mast cells, consistent with the observed ultrastructural increase in ribosomes.
Epha1, a gene involved in cell migration, adhesion, and angiogenesis, was upregulated in imiquimod-treated HMC-1 mast cells.
Kcnt1 expression was upregulated in imiquimod-treated HMC-1 mast cells and is expected to contribute to promoting inflammatory processes such as immune cell activation and migration.
Nlrp3 was upregulated in imiquimod-treated HMC-1 mast cells and is expected to increase vascular permeability via production of active IL-1β.
Ccl4 expression was upregulated in imiquimod-treated HMC-1 mast cells, expected to contribute to inflammatory immune cell activation and migration.
Il12rb2 was the most highly upregulated gene by both RNA sequencing and RT-qPCR in imiquimod-treated HMC-1 mast cells, suggesting TLR7 signaling enhances IL-12 responsiveness in mast cells.
In perfusion-fixed baseline ileum tissue, female mice had significantly more ACK2-immunoreactive mast cells per crypt-villus axis than males.
ACK2-IR mast cells from baseline female ileum sections were significantly larger in size than those from males.
There was no sex difference in the baseline percentage of ACK2-IR mast cells located within 1 µm of a VIP-immunoreactive neuronal fiber in perfused ileum.
No sex difference was found in the percentage area labeled with VIP-immunoreactivity across the crypt-villus axis at baseline.

Neuronal drug treatments (VIP, VPAC antagonist, TTX) did not significantly alter ACK2-IR mast cell counts compared to vehicle, though there was a sex-by-treatment interaction driven by VIP treatment lowering the percentage of mast cells near a VIP fiber specifically in females.

Without LPS challenge, there was no sex difference in the percentage of mast cells heavily immunoreactive for VIP.
After LPS challenge, the percentage of ACK2-IR mast cells heavily immunoreactive for VIP increased significantly in females but remained largely unchanged in males, regardless of treatment.

Preliminary EdU proliferation data suggested male ileum slices had more proliferating (EdU+) mast cells in crypts in response to LPS challenge than female slices, suggesting local proliferation may drive the male mast cell count increase.
Mice exposed to intranasal Alternaria extract for 6 weeks developed eosinophilic airway inflammation with mucus overproduction and airway remodeling compared to PBS-treated control mice.
RNA-Seq of central airway tissue identified 403 upregulated and 108 downregulated genes in Alternaria-exposed mice relative to control mice.

Gene ontology analysis showed that keratinization and defense response to other organisms functions were downregulated in Alternaria-exposed mouse airways.

Gene set enrichment analysis showed positive enrichment of mast cell activation, T-cell receptor complex, immunological synapse, antigen binding, and immunoglobulin receptor binding pathways in Alternaria-exposed mouse airways relative to control.
GSEA showed negative enrichment of keratinization and cornification pathways in Alternaria-exposed mouse airways relative to control.

In vitro exposure of human airway epithelial cells (16HBE14o-) to Alternaria validated downregulation of epithelial keratinization-related genes SPRR1A, SPRR1B, and KRT6B, confirming the RNA-Seq findings from the mouse model.
Patients 1 and 2 showed markedly elevated serum C3a during acute anaphylaxis compared to the normal reference range, indicating complement activation.

Patient 3 displayed elevated Th2-associated cytokines (IL-4, IL-33, IL-10, TNF receptor I, and MCP-1) during acute anaphylaxis, a cytokine profile associated with severe anaphylactic reactions.
Serum C3a and most cytokine levels decreased in all three patients 4-5 weeks after the anaphylactic reaction compared to acute-phase levels, consistent with resolution of the pseudoallergic process.
Anti-BNT162b2 IgG levels did not increase in any of the three patients 4-5 weeks post-anaphylaxis, which the authors postulate may be related to corticosteroid treatment received.

All three patients required treatment with intramuscular adrenaline and moderate-to-high-dose corticosteroids (7-9 days) to manage protracted, recurrent pseudo-anaphylactic reactions to the BNT162b2 vaccine.

Substance P(+) IENFs show 40-60% colocalization with TRPV1, and their denervation causes loss of thermal response ability due to low IENF density.
P2X3(+) nonpeptidergic nociceptors, sensitized by TRPV1-depleting neurotoxins, mediate mechanical allodynia via burst ATP release from denervated skin and injured DRG tissue.
Downregulation of PAP, which is highly coexpressed with P2X3(+) (up to 87%) and about 50% with TRPV1, correlates with development of mechanical allodynia.
TRPV1 activation on spinal GABAergic interneurons mediates mechanical allodynia via disinhibition of long-term depression in the spinothalamic tract.

NGF has paradoxical effects on neurotrophin receptors, upregulating TrkA (peptidergic-dependent) while downregulating Ret (nonpeptidergic-dependent) receptor.
Activation of Ret receptors mediates both thermal and mechanical noxious sensations, whereas TrkA receptors have no effect on mechanosensation.
ATF3 is upregulated in DRG neurons following nerve injuries and noxious stimuli and is preferentially expressed by small-diameter nociceptors, reflecting susceptibility to neuropathic pain.

TNFα-deficient mice exhibit fewer nonpeptidergic Ret(+) neurons, indicating Ret/TNFα signaling is required for neurotoxin-induced neuropathy via a TRPV1-independent pathway.
TNFR2 is reported as a major responding effector mediating TRPV1-dependent inflammatory pain.

The NGF inducer 4-methylcatechol suppresses neuropathic behavior, enhances neuroregeneration, induces GDNF synthesis, and normalizes upregulated Ret(+) neurons.

Using serial TNSr assessment, 37 of 43 patients (86.0%) treated with taxanes were diagnosed with taxane-induced neuropathy (TIN) 3 months after enrollment.
Clinical features including BMI, age, chemotherapy interval, and cumulative taxane dose did not differ significantly between patients who developed TIN and those who did not.
Nine patients (20.9%) already had abnormal neuropathy symptoms or signs (sensory, autonomic, tendon reflex, or vibration abnormalities) before chemotherapy began, per baseline TNSr.
In the TIN group, sensory symptoms were the most frequent finding after chemotherapy, reported by 24 of 37 (64.9%) patients on TNSr_F.
Autonomic symptoms were common in the TIN group, with 20 of 37 (54.1%) patients experiencing more than one autonomic symptom post-chemotherapy.
By patient-reported EORTC-CIPN20 at follow-up, 18 of 25 (72.0%) patients reported hand sensory symptoms such as tingling, burning, or prickling pain.
By patient-reported EORTC-CIPN20 at follow-up, 17 of 25 (68.0%) patients reported autonomic symptoms.
The EORTC-CIPN20 sensory symptom scores were significantly correlated with both the TNSr_F sensory symptom scores and pin sensation scores.
Nerve conduction velocities and amplitudes of all tested sensory and motor nerves were significantly reduced after taxane chemotherapy compared to before treatment.

Despite significant reductions in NCS values after chemotherapy, only 3 patients (8.1%) had sural sensory nerve action potential amplitudes that fell outside the normal range, suggesting most large-fiber nerve conduction values remained clinically normal.
No patients in this cohort reported motor symptoms or motor weakness following taxane chemotherapy, contrasting with a prior study using NCI-CTCAE that found considerable motor impairment in TIN.
It is postulated that taxanes interrupt axonal transport and damage mitochondria, causing axonal damage that underlies TIN.

The pattern of pure sensory neuropathy with neuropathic pain and without motor impairment observed in this cohort is suggested to be typical of small fiber neuropathy, with prior evidence that taxanes damage small nerve fibers first, potentially via interaction between skin nerve endings and epidermal basal keratinocytes.
