A case-control study found that CFS patients had lower FreeT3 and total T3, decreased peripheral conversion of T4 to T3, normal/high-normal total T4, and lower protein binding of thyroid hormones.

Women with CFS have a significantly greater probability of earlier menopause onset due to hysterectomy/oophorectomy and endometriosis-related pelvic pain compared to controls, and the resulting decline in estrogen may contribute to chronic fatigue and sleep disorders via immune effects.
A large meta-analysis of 94 studies showed antidepressants were approximately 3.5 times more effective than placebo in treating chronic pain in CFS patients.
Fluoxetine has shown the ability to improve symptoms and immune function in CFS patients.
Bupropion was found effective for treating fatigue and depression in nine fluoxetine-resistant CFS patients.

Data from eight randomized clinical trials concluded that physical/exercise therapy improves exhaustion, sleep quality, and health status of ME/CFS patients in the long term, contradicting the notion that patients always feel worse after exertion.
Fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) was reported to produce positive outcomes in CFS patients, though further evidence and safety data are needed.
After 18S RNA sequencing of stool from 49 ME/CFS patients and 39 healthy individuals, Mandarano et al. reported a nonsignificant difference in eukaryotic diversity between groups.
Levels of the lncRNAs NTT and EMX2OS in PBMCs were associated with more severe ME/CFS, and NTT positively correlated with IFNGR1, suggesting an NTT/IFNGR1 axis in disease pathogenesis.
Up-regulation of miR-150-5p is seen in T-cell and B-cell maturation/differentiation and influences release of pro-inflammatory cytokines in ME/CFS.
Across 15 case-control studies, patients with ME/CFS or fibromyalgia showed a small to moderate increase in pain after standardized aerobic exercise testing compared to healthy controls.

The magnitude of post-exercise pain increase was moderated by the timing of pain measurement, with delayed measurement (8-72 hours post-exercise) showing a larger effect than measurement taken immediately (0-2 hours) after exercise.

Graph theoretical analysis of resting-state qEEG source connectivity showed that patients with ME/CFS differed significantly from healthy controls in the baseline organization of the cortical autonomic network (CAN).

In patients with ME/CFS, cognitive, affective, and somatomotor symptom cluster ratings were associated with alterations in CAN topology, with the specific relationship depending on the EEG frequency band examined.
SIPS patients had significantly lower SF-36 scores than healthy controls, with physical functioning, role-physical, general health, vitality, and social functioning scores each below 20.

Compared with the general ME/CFS population and with RituxME trial participants, severely ill SIPS patients had substantially lower physical functioning scores (PF <15, mean 13.3±12.8 vs >30 in RituxME arms).

Role limitations due to emotional problems (RE) and mental health (MH) were much less impacted in SIPS patients, similar to the general ME/CFS population, distinguishing the disease from clinical depression.
SIPS quality-of-life scores correlated most positively with Congestive Heart Failure (r=0.63) and most negatively with Clinical Depression (r=-0.33) among comparator medical conditions.
Severely ill patients reported significantly greater fatigue, sleep disturbance, sleep-related impairment, pain behavior, and pain interference than controls on PROMIS instruments.
SIPS patients showed significantly worse sleep quality, more sleep disturbances, and worse Global PSQI compared to controls; 20% of patients had probable Restless Leg Syndrome.

All severely ill patients had fatigue, sleep disturbance, and post-exertional malaise, and either cognitive impairment (100%) or orthostatic intolerance (79%) or both, meeting IOM ME/CFS diagnostic criteria.
100% of patients had significant pain and 89% had sensory sensitivity to light, noise, vibration, odor, taste, and touch.

Fatigue and pain were the most troublesome symptoms reported by severely ill patients (85% and 65%, respectively), with fatigue and post-exertional malaise ranked as the single most troublesome symptom by 50% and 20% of patients.
SIPS patients had a median of only 912 daily steps, significantly lower than healthy controls and published US population norms, confirming severely limited mobility.

Overnight sleep monitoring showed abnormal sleep architecture in most patients: 75% had abnormally high awakening frequency, 65% had abnormally long wake time after sleep onset, and 50% had reduced sleep efficiency.
EEG sleep staging showed 70% of patients had below-normal Stage R (REM) percentage and 90% had above-normal Stage N1 percentage, consistent with frequent awakenings.

SIPS patients had significantly more difficulty identifying emotions (94% vs 40% of controls outside normal range, p=0.005) and more attention problems (81% vs 40%, p=0.043) than controls, with slower reaction times to happiness and anger.
No significant difference was found between SIPS patients and controls in memory and maze cognitive test scores, nor in EEG signals recorded during cognitive testing.
Severely ill ME/CFS patients showed significantly lower morning salivary cortisol levels than controls and a flattened diurnal cortisol decline.
Severely ill patients had a significantly higher cholesterol/HDL ratio than controls (FDR<0.1).
Severely ill patients had significantly lower blood albumin levels than controls (FDR<0.1).
Severely ill patients had significantly lower total bilirubin levels than controls (FDR<0.1).

No significant differences were found between patients and controls in CBC with differential/platelets, lymphocyte subsets, NK cell function, comprehensive metabolic panel, standard lipid panel, acylcarnitine profile, urinalysis of organic acids, hormone panel, vitamin panel, and other selected chemistry analytes/disease biomarkers.

No significant differences were detected between severely ill patients and healthy controls in IgG/IgM antibody and antigen tests for HHV6/7, HSV1/2, EBV, CMV, parvovirus B19, Borrelia burgdorferi, Bartonella species, and Mycoplasma pneumoniae, showing no evidence of active/acute infection driving severe illness.

Symptom frequencies remaining after six months in a large long-COVID cohort showed striking similarity to symptom patterns in the severely ill ME/CFS patients, supporting shared post-viral illness mechanisms.
Reserpine-treated mice showed significantly increased immobility time in the forced swimming test compared to controls, indicative of depression-like behavior.
High-dose Myelophil (100 mg/kg) and imipramine (10 mg/kg) significantly reduced immobility time in reserpine-treated mice, indicating antidepressant-like efficacy.
Marble burying behavior, reduced in all reserpine groups on day 11, was restored to normal only in the RES+MYP100 group by day 22.
Total distance traveled in the open field test, reduced by reserpine, was significantly increased by MYP and imipramine treatment in a dose-dependent manner.
Mechanical hypersensitivity (paw withdrawal to von Frey stimulation), increased by reserpine, was reduced by MYP and imipramine, with MYP100 showing greater analgesic effect than IMI10.
Thermal hypersensitivity (reduced hot plate latency) caused by reserpine was significantly improved by MYP and imipramine treatment.
Fatigue-like behavior on the rota-rod test (reduced latency to fall) caused by reserpine was reversed only by the high-dose MYP100 treatment.
Reserpine administration increased c-Fos positive cell counts in multiple brain regions (M2, IL, PrL, striatum, Cg1, CA1, CA3, PVN, DMPAG, DRL) related to depression, pain and fatigue.
MYP treatment reduced reserpine-induced c-Fos overexpression across all affected brain regions including motor cortex, striatum, cingulate cortex, hippocampus, PVN, DMPAG and DRL.
Reserpine administration significantly decreased 5-HT1AR positive cells in multiple brain regions including motor cortex, infralimbic cortex, striatum, CA1, and dorsal raphe subregions.
MYP treatment restored 5-HT1AR expression in most affected brain regions except cingulate cortex 2, PVN, and lateral hypothalamus.
Reserpine significantly decreased 5-HT1BR positive cells in M1, striatum, cingulate cortex, CA1, dentate gyrus, posterior hypothalamus, NTS, and lateral PAG regions.

Reserpine administration significantly increased TGF-β1 positive cells across multiple brain regions including motor cortex, PVN, hippocampal subfields, substantia nigra, dorsal raphe subregions, and NTS.
MYP treatment significantly reduced the reserpine-induced elevation of TGF-β1 across all affected brain regions.

Cells double-positive for TGF-β1 and Iba1 (microglial activation marker) were prominently increased across all hippocampal subregions (CA1, CA2, CA3, DG) in reserpine-treated mice, and this was reduced by MYP100 treatment.
Striatal dopamine release, decreased by reserpine, was prominently increased after MYP treatment as measured by in vivo microdialysis.
Striatal serotonin concentration was significantly lower in reserpine-treated mice than controls, and recovered non-significantly after MYP treatment.
TH-expressing fiber density in the striatum and TH-positive cell counts in the substantia nigra were significantly reduced by reserpine, and both were reversed by MYP100 treatment.
Striatal D1DR and D2DR expression were decreased after reserpine administration and increased following MYP treatment.
mRNA expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines TNF-α, IL-6, iNOS, and COX-2 was significantly increased in the spleen of reserpine-treated mice and reduced after MYP treatment.
Hepatic antioxidant enzyme mRNA (HO-1, SOD, catalase, GPx) was decreased in reserpine-treated mice and increased after MYP treatment.

A cited clinical study found that 3-month MYP administration in severe ME/CFS patients significantly changed pain range, a fatigue questionnaire score, and related biomarkers (referenced background, not primary data of this study).

All 30 participants (adolescents, parents and healthcare professionals) said that acceptance and commitment therapy (ACT) would have value as an additional treatment option for adolescents with persistent CFS/ME.
Ten of twelve interviewed adolescents said they would be willing to try ACT as a treatment for their CFS/ME.
Two participants who had already received ACT considered it more acceptable than CBT-f, describing it as gentler and kinder, particularly for managing pain and fatigue.
Healthcare professionals were concerned that parents might misunderstand ACT's concept of 'acceptance' as meaning patients should just tolerate their symptoms rather than actively move forward.

All interviewed healthcare professionals felt it would be feasible to deliver ACT in clinical practice, as it was no more difficult than existing psychological therapies already informally used, though formal ACT-specific training would be needed.

Healthcare professionals disagreed about when ACT should be offered, with some favouring introduction only once patients are 'stuck' after initial treatment and others favouring offering it from the start of care.
Seven of the ten adolescents who said they would try ACT also stated they would consent to participate in a randomised controlled trial of ACT.

Paediatric CFS/ME is reported to have a prevalence of 0.55% across community, primary care and hospital populations, and can be severely disabling with fatigue, chronic pain, postural instability and cognitive dysfunction.
Despite specialist treatments (CBT-f, activity management, graded exercise therapy), at least 15% of children with CFS/ME remain symptomatic after one year of treatment.
A cited feasibility study in 40 adults with CFS/ME found that ACT resulted in sustained improvements in CFS/ME-related disability at 6 months.

A separate feasibility study of group-based ACT in adolescents with functional somatic syndromes found that 90.5% completed the therapy and all would recommend it to a friend, consistent with this study's acceptability findings.
Some parents felt ACT's cognitive defusion approach (stepping away from rather than challenging thoughts) sounded 'scary' or 'confrontational' for younger or more timid children.
Some adolescents and parents were reluctant to accept randomisation in a future RCT, expressing a treatment preference for either ACT or treatment-as-usual, which could affect trial engagement.

The review notes that both the 1918 H1N1 influenza virus and SARS-CoV-2 are neurotropic and may cause chronically debilitating neurological conditions, including encephalitis lethargica and myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome respectively.
Post-exertional malaise (PEM) was present in 75.45% of the CFS cohort, with similar prevalence in males (80%) and females (73.33%).
Unrefreshing sleep was highly prevalent, reported by 89.09% of the total sample.
Impaired memory or concentration was highly prevalent, reported by 87.27% of the total sample.
Tender cervical or axillary lymph nodes was the least prevalent Fukuda symptom, reported by only 34.55% of the sample.
New-onset headache was more prevalent in females (57.33%) than males (40%), representing the most prominent sex difference in symptom prevalence.
PEM was positively correlated with the co-occurrence of impaired memory or concentration.
Both PEM and impaired memory/concentration presence were associated with more severe fatigue as measured by CFQ and FIS scales.
PEM presence was positively correlated with multi-joint pain co-occurrence.
PEM presence was negatively correlated with tender lymph node presence, indicating patients rarely reported both together.
PEM presence was negatively correlated with muscle pain presence.
Sore throat was positively correlated with higher heart rate.
Sore throat was positively correlated with orthostatic intolerance severity and with total Compass-31 score, indicating a link to subjective autonomic nervous system disturbance.
Sore throat was negatively correlated with left ventricular ejection time (LVET).
Length of CFS symptom history was not significantly related to any Fukuda symptoms after FDR correction and was therefore excluded from the network analysis.

The paper cites prior literature reporting that TRPM3, a non-selective calcium channel, has significantly reduced expression and function in NK cells of CFS patients, proposed as a mechanism for pain, cognitive, and cerebellar symptoms.

A novel homozygous nonsense variant in TNXB (c.8488C>T, p.(Gln2830*)), predicted to cause a truncated protein or nonsense-mediated decay, was identified in a Saudi male with classical-like Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.
The same TNXB variant was found in a heterozygous state in the proband's father and sister, both of whom presented with milder EDS/heritable connective tissue disorder symptoms.
The TNX-deficient patient exhibited rare neurological manifestations including ophthalmoplegia and a myopathic pattern on electromyography, along with hand weakness, that are atypical for EDS.

TNX-deficient EDS patients can present with clinical and electrophysiological features such as frontal baldness, ophthalmoplegia, and myotonia that clinically mimic myotonic dystrophy type I, highlighting a diagnostic overlap clinicians should recognize.
At post-treatment, the waitlist control group reported significantly higher fatigue than the self-selected PPI (S-PPI) group.
At post-treatment, the S-PPI group reported higher life satisfaction than the waitlist control group.
At post-treatment, the S-PPI group reported higher positive affect than the waitlist control group, and also higher positive affect than the A-PPI (assigned) group.
At post-treatment, pain disability scores did not differ significantly among the A-PPI, S-PPI, and waitlist groups.
Negative affect did not differ significantly between groups at post-treatment or at any timepoint.

Overall, a MANOVA on change scores across five outcome variables (fatigue, pain disability, positive affect, negative affect, life satisfaction) showed a significant difference among the three groups (A-PPI, S-PPI, waitlist) at post-treatment.
At 1-month follow-up, the MANOVA on change scores remained significant across the three groups for the combined five outcome variables.
At 1-month follow-up, the S-PPI group had significantly higher life satisfaction and positive affect than both the waitlist and A-PPI groups.
The reduction in fatigue observed post-treatment in the S-PPI group was not maintained as a statistically significant group difference at 1-month follow-up.
At 1-month follow-up, pain disability was significantly higher in the A-PPI (pre-assigned) group compared to the S-PPI (self-selected) group.
Overall satisfaction with the 5-week online programme was high, with more than three-quarters of participants rather or very satisfied.

Participants who dropped out of the study had received less physiotherapy, orthosis, and psychotherapy, took more painkillers, had more psychiatric comorbidities, and scored higher at baseline on pain disability and negative affect than completers.
Participants experienced a long delay to EDS diagnosis, averaging over two decades from symptom onset to diagnosis.
Nearly half of the EDS sample reported psychiatric comorbidities, with a quarter of those having both mood and anxiety disorders.
The large majority of the recruited sample had hypermobile EDS, with smaller proportions of classical, vascular, and other subtypes.
Among the ten positive psychology themes, "Spot the Positives" was rated most enjoyable and "Hope Quest" least enjoyable by participants who completed them.
In FMS patients, higher situational cognitive distraction was associated with lower pain catastrophizing, which in turn was associated with no antidepressant use.
Higher cognitive distraction predicted lower total pain severity (PRI-T on MPQ) in FMS patients via reduced catastrophizing.
A serial mediation chain showed cognitive distraction reduced catastrophizing, which reduced fibromyalgia impact (FIQR), which was associated with no use of analgesics overall.
The same serial mediation chain (cognitive distraction → lower catastrophizing → lower FIQR) predicted no antidepressant use.
The serial mediation chain (cognitive distraction → lower catastrophizing → lower FIQR) also predicted no anxiolytic use.
The pain-reducing effect of cognitive distraction (via lower catastrophizing) was strongest in FMS patients with mid-range to lower extraversion scores (introverts).
The pain-reducing effect of cognitive distraction via catastrophizing was found in FMS patients with mid-range to lower psychoticism scores.
The pain-reducing effect of cognitive distraction via catastrophizing was found in FMS patients with mid-range to higher neuroticism scores.
Higher Externally Oriented Thinking (EOT, an alexithymia facet) was associated with lower depressive symptoms, which mediated lower likelihood of antidepressant and anxiolytic use in FMS patients.
Higher EOT was associated with lower total chronic pain severity (PRI-T), mediated by decreased depressive symptoms.
A serial mediation chain (EOT → lower depression → lower fibromyalgia impact) predicted no analgesic and no antidepressant use.

The pain-reducing effect of EOT via decreased depression was strongest in FMS patients with mid-range to higher extraversion scores (extraverts), contrasting with the introvert-specific effect of situational cognitive distraction.

The pain-reducing EOT-depression pathway was found in FMS patients with mid-range to higher psychoticism scores, contrasting with the lower-psychoticism specificity of the cognitive distraction pathway.
The pain-reducing EOT-depression pathway was also found at higher neuroticism scores, at the same level identified for the cognitive-distraction pathway.

In contrast to its effect on sensory/affective pain, higher EOT (via lower depression) was associated with an increase in the cognitive/evaluative pain subscale (PRI-E), at higher extraversion and psychoticism.

In healthy participants without chronic pain, situational cognitive distraction reduced retrospectively-assessed acute pain intensity, but only in those with higher catastrophizing scores (>15), demonstrating a 'competition' mechanism.

In healthy participants, greater retrospective acute pain intensity (lower SF-36 body pain scores) was associated with higher catastrophizing, which in turn was associated with higher use of cognitive distraction, supporting a 'positive feedback' developmental mechanism.

In healthy participants, higher acute pain intensity (VAS) predicted higher EOT scores, specifically in those with higher depressive symptom severity (>18), supporting a 'positive feedback' developmental mechanism for EOT.

In FMS patients, an initial direct negative effect of the 'ignoring pain' coping strategy on pain intensity disappeared once situational cognitive distraction was included in the model, indicating cognitive distraction as the primary mechanism.

Unlike EOT, the Difficulty Identifying Feelings (DIF) and Difficulty Describing Feelings (DDF) facets of alexithymia mediated the relationship between pain severity and higher trait/implicit anxiety in both FMS and healthy groups.
Somatic KIT D816V mutation causes constitutive activation of the KIT tyrosine kinase receptor, driving mast cell proliferation/survival and the development of clonal systemic mastocytosis.
The KIT D816V activating mutation is found in the large majority of adult systemic mastocytosis cases.
In childhood-onset mastocytosis, KIT D816V is present in only 40% of cases, other KIT mutations in 35%, and wild-type KIT in 25%, contrasting with the adult pattern.
Next-generation sequencing panels identified 10 additional recurrently mutated genes with prognostic significance in systemic mastocytosis, most commonly TET2, SRSF2, ASXL1, and RUNX1.
In a 70-patient trial, SRSF2 or ASXL1 mutations were independent risk factors for worsened overall survival, with outcomes further influenced by the number of S/A/R genes mutated.
Among patients lacking S/A/R panel mutations, EZH2 mutation identified a subgroup with worse progression-free and overall survival, suggesting added prognostic value over the S/A/R panel alone.
TET2 mutation has also been implicated as a poor prognostic factor in systemic mastocytosis.
In a 39-patient trial, advanced SM (ASM) patients were far more likely than indolent/smoldering SM patients to carry additional non-KIT mutations and to have higher overall mutational burden.
In a 150-patient trial, non-KIT mutation frequency was highest in patients with SM-associated hematologic neoplasm (SM-AHN) compared with only 14% in indolent SM.
Anaphylaxis occurs in up to 49% of mastocytosis patients in one trial and is most commonly observed in indolent systemic mastocytosis.
Bone marrow mastocytosis (BMMC) shows a markedly higher anaphylaxis incidence (>90%) than indolent SM (20-49%) or the general population (0-2%).

Hereditary alpha-tryptasemia (HαT) is an autosomal dominant condition, present in ~5% of the general population, causing elevated basal serum tryptase (>8 ng/mL) via increased pro-alpha-tryptase synthesis (extra TPSAB1 copies) rather than mast cell activation.

In a cohort of 101 patients with hereditary alpha-tryptasemia, 80% were female, mean tryptase was 17.2 ng/mL, over half presented with unprovoked anaphylaxis, and omalizumab reduced urticaria/anaphylaxis in over 90% of patients.

Within hereditary alpha-tryptasemia, dysautonomia, joint hypermobility, and diarrhea are more refractory to omalizumab therapy than allergic symptoms like asthma, rhinitis, urticaria, and food allergy.
Midostaurin, a multikinase/KIT inhibitor, achieved a 60% overall response rate (45% major response) in advanced systemic mastocytosis, including similar responses in mast cell leukemia patients.

Avapritinib, a selective KIT D816V inhibitor FDA-approved for advanced systemic mastocytosis, showed a 75% overall response rate in the interim PATHFINDER trial analysis, with no difference between treatment-naive and previously treated (including midostaurin-treated) patients.
Nilotinib and dasatinib show limited efficacy in systemic mastocytosis, with response rates of 22% and 33% respectively.
Omalizumab significantly improves symptom control and quality of life in patients with recurrent anaphylaxis related to mast cell disorders.

Among 351 Hymenoptera-allergic patients with normal serum tryptase, KIT D816V mutation was detected in blood in 28 patients, predominantly those with more severe anaphylactic reaction histories, suggesting KIT mutation is a more sensitive biomarker than tryptase in this setting.
Nearly all patients with systemic mast cell disease and Hymenoptera venom allergy experience subsequent systemic reactions, most of which are severe if immunotherapy is not given.

Mast cell sarcoma is a rare, highly malignant mast cell neoplasm with poor prognosis (<2 year survival), KIT D816V present in only about one-fifth of cases, and resistance to most conventional therapies.
The authors note that a role for mast cell activation is invoked in joint hypermobility syndromes and postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (POTS), but without much concrete supporting data.

Compared with patients with mast cell disorders, idiopathic anaphylaxis (IA) patients showed evidence of activated T cells and CD19+CD23+ B cells in peripheral blood, though this may be confounded by concomitant glucocorticoid use.
A combination of serum tryptase and urinary 11β-PGF2α helped avoid misdiagnosis of MCAS in a group of 25 patients.

In a retrospective review of 342 SM patients, KIT D816V prevalence did not differ significantly across SM variants, but indolent SM patients had superior survival compared with non-indolent SM subtypes.
In patients with aggressive systemic mastocytosis, midostaurin achieved an overall response rate of 60%, with 45% showing a major response (complete resolution of at least one organ dysfunction).

The selective KIT D816V inhibitor avapritinib showed an interim overall response rate of 75% in the phase II PATHFINDER trial for advanced systemic mastocytosis, regardless of prior midostaurin treatment.
Nilotinib showed limited efficacy in systemic mastocytosis with a reported response rate of 22%.
Dasatinib showed limited efficacy in systemic mastocytosis with a reported response rate of 33%.
Mast cell sarcoma is a rare, highly malignant disorder with KIT D816V mutation found in only about one-fifth of patients and poor prognosis of less than two years survival.

In a trial of 70 patients, mutations in SRSF2 or ASXL1 were independent risk factors for worsened overall survival in systemic mastocytosis, with survival further affected by the number of mutated genes in the SRSF2/ASXL1/RUNX1 panel.
Among patients without S/A/R panel mutations, EZH2 mutation identified a subgroup with worsened progression-free and overall survival, suggesting added prognostic value beyond the S/A/R panel.
TET2 mutation has also been implicated as a poor prognostic factor in systemic mastocytosis.

In a retrospective review of 342 patients diagnosed with systemic mastocytosis, KIT D816V mutation prevalence did not significantly differ across SM variants, but indolent SM patients had superior survival compared to non-indolent subtypes.

In a trial of 39 patients with KIT D816V-mutated systemic mastocytosis, 89% of aggressive SM patients had at least one additional non-KIT mutation compared with only 25% of indolent/smoldering SM patients, and advanced SM had higher mutational burden.
In a larger trial of 150 patients with systemic mastocytosis, non-KIT mutation frequency was highest in SM with associated hematological neoplasm compared with only 14% in indolent SM patients.

Selb et al. found KIT D816V mutation in peripheral blood of 28 of 351 Hymenoptera-allergic patients with normal serum tryptase, predominantly in those with more severe anaphylactic reactions, suggesting KIT mutation may be a more sensitive biomarker than tryptase.

According to Vos et al., 97.5% of patients with systemic mast cell disease experienced subsequent systemic reactions to Hymenoptera stings, with 90% of these reactions being severe in the absence of immunotherapy.
Bone marrow mastocytosis is associated with a markedly higher incidence of anaphylaxis (>90%) compared to indolent systemic mastocytosis (20–49%) and the general population (0–2%).

In a study of 101 patients with hereditary alpha-tryptasemia (80% female, average tryptase 17.2 ng/mL), omalizumab was effective in decreasing urticaria and anaphylaxis in over 90% of patients, while dysautonomia, joint hypermobility, and diarrhea were more refractory to therapy.

In hereditary alpha-tryptasemia, dysautonomia, joint hypermobility, and diarrhea are more refractory to standard therapy (antihistamines/omalizumab) than allergic symptoms such as asthma, rhinitis, urticaria, and food allergy.

The authors note that joint hypermobility syndromes and postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (POTS) are conditions in which a role for mast cell activation is proposed but lacks concrete supporting data.

Grammar and coworkers showed that idiopathic anaphylaxis patients had evidence of activated T cells and B cells in peripheral blood compared to patients with mast cell disorders, though it is unclear if this is primary or an epiphenomenon of concomitant glucocorticoid use.
An unpublished gene expression profiling study found that idiopathic anaphylaxis patients had activated genes regulating mast cell and basophil degranulation.

A combination of serum tryptase and 11β-PGF2α measurement helped avoid misdiagnosis of MCAS in a study of 25 patients, suggesting 11β-PGF2α may be a superior marker to tryptase alone, though assays are difficult to perform.

Hymenoptera venom allergy prevalence associated with systemic mast cell disease is estimated as high as 7.9%, exceeding the prevalence observed in the general population, though it is notably absent in aggressive systemic mastocytosis with increased mast cell load.

Alpha/beta tryptase tetramers formed in hereditary alpha-tryptasemia cleave and activate the EMR2 (ADGRE2) and PAR2 (F2RL1) receptors, contributing to vascular leakage, edema, urticaria, angioedema, and anaphylaxis.

Complement can activate mast cells to express chymase and tryptase via complement receptors, which in turn can further activate complement, forming a paracrine mast cell activation loop in inflammation.
Clonal hematopoiesis of indeterminate potential mutations were classified as myeloid or lymphoid and each subtype was associated with risk of lineage-specific hematologic malignancies.
Autosomal mosaic chromosomal alterations were analyzed in 420,969 individuals and classified into myeloid and lymphoid subtypes, each associated with risk of lineage-specific hematologic malignancy.

An integrated analysis combining somatic alterations with peripheral blood count parameters stratified risk of incident myeloid and lymphoid malignancies, suggesting utility for clinical risk identification.
CIBERSORT immune deconvolution of synovial tissue showed that OA samples had a higher proportion of resting and activated mast cells compared with normal synovium.
ZNF160 expression was positively correlated with activated mast cell infiltration and negatively correlated with resting mast cell infiltration in OA synovial tissue.

The 18 OA hub genes identified by combined WGCNA and differential expression analysis were functionally enriched in biological processes including mast cell chemotaxis and migration, alongside protein auto-ADP-ribosylation and positive chemotaxis induction.
LPS stimulation of mast cells increased production of dimeric TCTP (dTCTP) and its secretion during degranulation.

Extracellular dTCTP released from mast cells increased pro-inflammatory molecule production, including IL-8, by airway epithelial cells, acting in a paracrine manner without affecting mast cell activation itself.

dTBP2 (a dTCTP inhibitor peptide) selectively blocked the dTCTP-mediated signaling network from mast cells to epithelial cells and decreased IL-8 production through induction of IkB and nuclear export of p65.
In an in vivo model, dTBP2 efficiently attenuated LPS-induced severe airway inflammation, decreasing immune cell infiltration, IL-17 production, and dTCTP secretion.
Frailty index was higher in old mice compared with young mice, with no difference between old male and old female mice.
Endothelium-dependent dilation (EDD) in the middle cerebral artery and mesenteric artery did not differ between old male and old female mice.
In the middle cerebral artery, frailty index was inversely related to endothelium-dependent dilation among old female mice but not old male mice.
In the mesenteric artery, frailty index was inversely related to endothelium-dependent dilation among old male mice but not old female mice.

A higher frailty index was associated with a greater improvement in endothelium-dependent dilation following the superoxide scavenger TEMPOL, in the MCA for old female mice and in the mesenteric artery for old male mice.
Frailty index was negatively related to extracellular superoxide dismutase (Sod3) gene expression in the mesenteric artery.
Frailty index was positively related to interleukin-1β (Il1b) gene expression in the mesenteric artery.
In old male mice, a higher frailty index was associated with a greater improvement in mesenteric artery endothelium-dependent dilation following treatment with the superoxide scavenger TEMPOL.
Frailty index was negatively related to mesenteric artery gene expression of extracellular superoxide dismutase (Sod3), suggesting reduced antioxidant capacity with greater frailty.
Frailty index was positively related to mesenteric artery gene expression of interleukin-1β (Il1b), suggesting increased proinflammatory signaling with greater frailty.

Small nerve fibers appear to be the most vulnerable structures in diabetic neuropathy, with damage detectable even in patients with impaired glucose tolerance before overt chronic hyperglycemia develops.

In animal models of type 1 and type 2 experimental diabetes with neuropathy, an increased inflammatory response with macrophage/T cell infiltration and elevated soluble cytokines was observed in the sciatic nerve, with intraepidermal small nerve fibers as a predominant site of axonal degeneration.

Hyperglycemic ob/ob mice (type 2 diabetes model) showed increased sciatic nerve macrophage infiltration associated with loss of myelinated and unmyelinated nerve fibers and axonal damage, indicating overt neuropathy.
Elevated serum concentrations of inflammatory biomarkers including CRP, IL-6, and IL-18 were found in humans with type 2 diabetes.
Biomarkers of inflammation have been shown to be associated with diminished cardiac autonomic function in type 2 diabetes.
In a prospective clinical study of an elderly diabetic population, systemic biomarkers of inflammation were linked to the onset and progression of neuropathy over 6.5 years of follow-up.

An increased expression of inflammation-associated genes was observed in macrophages from dorsal root ganglia of diabetic neuropathy patients, accompanied by downregulation of multiple DRG-neuronal genes, suggesting a role in pain hypersensitivity.

Clinical studies showed diabetic patients with or without neuropathy had increased total oxidative status and oxidative stress index together with low total antioxidant status compared with healthy individuals.
Serum total antioxidant capacity was significantly decreased in patients suffering from diabetic neuropathy.

Patients with recently diagnosed type 1 and type 2 diabetes showed evidence of systemic oxidative stress despite good glycemic control, suggesting impaired extracellular antioxidative defense against superoxide plays a role in early diabetic neuropathy development.
Epidemiological studies found that high serum ferritin and decreased transferrin levels were associated with a higher risk of type 2 diabetes, pre-diabetes, or gestational diabetes.

In a rat model of type 1 diabetes, a low-iron (rather than high-iron) diet led to reduced sensory nerve conduction velocities in the sciatic nerve and mitochondrial damage in numerous dorsal root ganglion neurons, without lowering systemic iron levels.

Low dietary iron load caused more pronounced neuropathy abnormalities than high-iron load in ob/ob mice (metabolic syndrome) and db/db mice (type 2 diabetes), replicating findings from the type 1 diabetes rat model.
In high-iron fed diabetic mice, blood glucose and HbA1c concentrations were decreased rather than increased, contrary to prior expectations of iron overload worsening glycemia.

In db/db mice, pro-inflammatory M1 macrophages were reduced while anti-inflammatory M2 macrophages were increased in the sciatic nerve of animals on a high-iron diet compared with those on a low-iron diet.

A retrospective study at a large diabetes center found that 11% of diabetic neuropathy patients had treatment-induced neuropathy in diabetes (TIND), accompanied by an HbA1c decrease of more than 2 percentage points over the prior 3 months, regardless of antidiabetic therapy type.

In a BB/OKL rat model mimicking TIND via rapid insulin-induced HbA1c reduction, animals showed greater abnormalities in motor and sensory nerve conduction velocities, increased sciatic nerve macrophage infiltration, and a reduced number of CGRP-positive nerve fibers compared with animals with a milder HbA1c decrease.

A clinical study in obese children and adolescents demonstrated extended autonomic nervous system dysfunction affecting several organs, with dysfunctional parasympathetic and sympathetic activity resembling that seen in normal-weight diabetic children and adolescents.
Leptin-deficient ob/ob mice showed pathological changes in sciatic nerve fibers and their endoneural microvessels, especially distally, even in the absence of overt diabetes.

A clinical study found stabilization and improvement of autonomic neuropathy correlating with improved weight status and metabolic risk factors following a lifestyle intervention combining exercise, nutritional counseling, and psychological support.
Aerobic, resistance, and especially combined exercise training in humans may improve inflammation-linked biomarkers, suggesting an anti-inflammatory effect of these interventions.
Large-fiber neuropathy was detected by nerve conduction studies in 43% of ATTRv/asymptomatic gene carriers.
Large-fiber neuropathy by nerve conduction studies was found in 70% of ATTRwt patients.
Quantitative sensory testing revealed a mixed small and large fiber impairment in all ATTRv/asymptomatic gene carriers.
Quantitative sensory testing revealed a mixed small and large fiber impairment in 78% of ATTRwt patients.
Autonomic function tests (SSR, QSART) were pathological in the majority of ATTRv patients.
Autonomic function tests were pathological in over 50% of ATTRwt patients.
Skin punch biopsies showed reduced intraepidermal nerve fiber density (IENFD) in all ATTRv/asymptomatic gene carriers tested.
Skin punch biopsies showed reduced IENFD in over 80% of ATTRwt patients biopsied.
Two ATTRwt patients showed a pure small fiber neuropathy phenotype on skin biopsy without accompanying large fiber involvement.

After excluding patients with relevant co-morbidities that could independently cause neuropathy, 44% of ATTRwt patients still exhibited large and/or small fiber neuropathy attributable to amyloidosis itself.
Comprehensive nerve fiber testing led to new diagnosis of peripheral nervous system disease manifestation in three ATTR gene mutation carriers, directly changing their clinical management.
Gastric electrical stimulation is proposed to work by activating vagal afferent nerve endings and inducing the vago-vagal reflex via the nucleus tractus solitarius (NTS) in the brainstem.

Single- and multi-unit recordings from gastric neurons in the nucleus tractus solitarius showed highly orientation-selective responses to gastric electrical stimulation across a range of stimulus amplitudes.
The strongest NTS neuronal responses occurred when the applied stimulation current flowed parallel to the vagal intramuscular arrays and the underlying smooth muscle fibers.
Under physiological conditions, the largest proportion of NRG1-positive neurons in the caecum myenteric, outer submucous and inner submucous plexuses also expressed nNOS (~30-32%).
Galanin (GAL) showed the lowest baseline co-localization with NRG1 among all substances tested in the caecum, ranging from ~20-22% of NRG1-positive neurons.

Oral administration of low and high doses of BPA increased the degree of co-localization of NRG1 with nNOS, VIP, SP and GAL in all types of enteric plexus in the caecum, with greater effects at the higher dose.
High-dose BPA caused the clearest increase in NRG1/GAL co-localization in the caecal myenteric plexus, rising from ~20% to ~35% of NRG1-positive neurons.
High-dose BPA markedly increased NRG1/SP co-localization in the caecal inner submucous plexus, from ~22% to ~38% of NRG1-positive neurons.
In the ascending colon inner submucous plexus, high-dose BPA increased NRG1/VIP co-localization from ~21% to ~46% of NRG1-positive neurons, the most pronounced change observed in that segment.
In the descending colon, GAL showed the highest baseline co-localization with NRG1 among all substances tested, unlike other intestinal segments where nNOS or VIP predominated.
High-dose BPA produced the largest change in the descending colon myenteric plexus, increasing NRG1/GAL co-localization from ~30% to ~47%.

Low-dose BPA had minimal or non-significant effect on NRG1 co-localization patterns in the descending colon for several neuron populations, including SP in all plexus types and nNOS in the myenteric and outer submucous plexuses.

The authors propose that the high degree of NRG1 co-localization with nNOS and VIP suggests NRG1 may participate in inhibitory regulation of intestinal motility, since both VIP and NO are the principal inhibitory factors reducing smooth muscle activity.

Because all substances co-localizing with NRG1 (nNOS, VIP, SP, GAL) have previously described neuroprotective effects, the authors conclude NRG1 in porcine enteric neurons likely has neuroprotective functions.
Cortistatin levels are inversely correlated with fibrogenic activation in damaged skin and dermal fibroblasts in this scleroderma model.
Cortistatin-deficient mice exposed to bleomycin developed a thicker, more fibrotic dermal layer, enlarged epidermis, and increased inflammatory infiltration compared with wild-type mice.
Cortistatin deficiency enhanced dermal collagen deposition in bleomycin-treated skin.
Cortistatin deficiency increased expression of connective tissue growth factor (CTGF) in bleomycin-induced skin fibrosis.
Cortistatin deficiency was associated with loss of skin microvessels in the bleomycin model of scleroderma.
Cortistatin-deficient mice were more predisposed to develop pulmonary fibrotic disease and increased mortality following dermal bleomycin exposure.
Cortistatin-deficient mice showed loss of dermal microvessels following bleomycin challenge compared to wild-type mice.
Cortistatin deficiency increased predisposition to pulmonary fibrotic disease as a complication of bleomycin-induced dermal fibrosis.
Cortistatin-deficient mice exhibited increased mortality following bleomycin challenge relative to wild-type mice.
Exogenous treatment with cortistatin mitigated the exacerbated dermal and pulmonary fibrotic pathology seen in the bleomycin-induced scleroderma model.
The authors conclude cortistatin acts as an endogenous brake on skin inflammation and fibrosis, such that its deficiency may serve as a marker of poor prognosis in scleroderma.
Daily subcutaneous bleomycin injection for 28 days significantly increased dermal thickness in C57BL/6J mouse skin compared to saline-treated controls.

Skin levels of MRI-1867 were markedly lower in bleomycin-fibrotic skin (0.12 µM) than in healthy control skin (15 µM) after a single oral dose, indicating compromised drug exposure in fibrotic tissue.
Skin levels of the endocannabinoids AEA and 2-AG were higher in bleomycin-induced fibrotic skin compared to normal skin, indicating upregulation of the local endocannabinoid system.

In wild-type C57BL/6J mice, chronic MRI-1867 administration failed to reduce bleomycin-induced increases in skin endocannabinoids, consistent with inadequate CB1R engagement due to poor skin drug exposure.
Bleomycin treatment significantly increased P-glycoprotein protein expression in mouse skin, as shown by immunohistochemistry.
Skin exposure to MRI-1867 was markedly higher in Mdr1a/b(-/-)-Bcrp(-/-) triple knockout mice than in wild-type mice, reaching 8.8 µM at the 10 mg/kg dose compared to 0.12 µM in wild-type mice.
In KO mice, chronic MRI-1867 dosing produced dose-dependent increases in serum and skin drug levels, reaching a maximum skin concentration of ~26 µM at 30 mg/kg, with no further increase at 60 mg/kg.

In Mdr1a/b(-/-)-Bcrp(-/-) mice, daily bleomycin injections for 28 days significantly increased skin hydroxyproline content, dermal thickness, and endocannabinoid levels, confirming induction of skin fibrosis in this genotype.

Chronic oral MRI-1867 (30 mg/kg) for the final 14 days of a 28-day bleomycin regimen significantly reduced bleomycin-induced increases in hydroxyproline content, dermal thickness, and endocannabinoid levels in Mdr1a/b(-/-)-Bcrp(-/-) mouse skin.
At an equipotent 10 mg/kg dose for CB1R antagonism, MRI-1867 significantly reduced bleomycin-induced dermal thickness and hydroxyproline content and was significantly more effective than rimonabant.
Rimonabant (10 mg/kg), a brain-penetrant CB1R antagonist, did not significantly reduce bleomycin-induced dermal thickness compared to vehicle, unlike MRI-1867 at the same dose.

MRI-1867 showed dose-dependent antifibrotic efficacy: 1 mg/kg had no significant effect, 3 mg/kg significantly reduced dermal thickness but not hydroxyproline content, and 10 mg/kg significantly reduced both.

Both rimonabant and MRI-1867 at 10 mg/kg significantly and comparably reduced bleomycin-induced increases in skin endocannabinoids, indicating similar CB1R target engagement despite MRI-1867's superior antifibrotic efficacy.

A cited study found no significant differences in the frequencies of three ABCB1 gene SNPs between systemic sclerosis patients and controls in a Polish population, although one haplotype was more frequent in patients without demonstrated functional consequence.
Genetic polymorphism in IRF5 is associated with increased risk of systemic sclerosis, while reduced IRF5 expression is associated with improved survival in patients with the disease.
A cited prior study found that genetic deletion of IRF5 protected mice from bleomycin-induced skin and pulmonary fibrosis, suggesting IRF5 as a potential therapeutic target in scleroderma.
A cited prior study showed that genetic deletion of CB1R protected mice from bleomycin-induced skin fibrosis and reduced infiltration of T cells and macrophages in lesioned skin.

MRI-1867 was previously shown to increase upper gastrointestinal motility in mice via peripheral CB1R inverse agonism, suggesting potential benefit for the GI dysmotility/constipation common in systemic sclerosis patients.

In lung tissue from patients with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, expression of the efflux transporters P-gp and BCRP was similar to control lung samples, suggesting the bleomycin-induced upregulation seen in the mouse model is not part of human IPF pathology.
Nanocurcumin supplementation significantly increased Treg cell frequency compared with both baseline and placebo in Behçet's disease patients.
FoxP3 mRNA expression increased considerably in the nanocurcumin group compared with baseline and placebo.
TGF-β mRNA expression increased considerably in the nanocurcumin group compared with baseline and placebo.
IL-10 mRNA expression increased considerably in the nanocurcumin group compared with baseline and placebo.
miRNA-25 expression increased considerably in the nanocurcumin group compared with baseline and placebo.
miRNA-106b expression increased considerably in the nanocurcumin group compared with baseline and placebo.
Serum TGF-β levels significantly increased in the nanocurcumin group compared with baseline and placebo.
Serum IL-10 levels increased significantly in the nanocurcumin group compared with baseline and with the placebo group.
Disease activity was significantly lower in the nanocurcumin group compared with the placebo group after the 8-week trial.

A novel heterozygous TGFB3 missense variant (c.730G>A, p.Glu300Lys, referred to as E244K) was identified in a patient with recurrent coronary artery fistulae and features overlapping Loeys-Dietz syndrome type 5, and was considered likely pathogenic based on combined genotype and phenotype evidence.

The patient with the TGFB3 variant had recurrent coronary artery fistulae (LIMA-to-PA, RCA-to-PA, LAD-to-PA, and right ventricle-to-PA) that recurred after both coiling and surgical ligation, ultimately requiring a bovine pericardial patch to prevent further recurrence.

The patient also exhibited additional connective tissue and vascular features consistent with a TGFB3-related Loeys-Dietz spectrum disorder, including spontaneous right vertebral artery dissection, tortuous carotid arteries, persistent joint laxity, and atrophic scars.
Pharmacological activation of TGF-β1/SMAD signaling with the agonist SRI-011381 increased α-SMA protein expression and staining compared with the inhibitor (SB-431542) and nanofiber conduit groups.
Western blot analysis showed TGF-β1, TβRI, Smad2 and p-Smad2 protein levels were all highest in the agonist group and lowest in the aligned nanofiber conduit group in Part I.

Immunohistochemistry showed markedly higher, disorderly proliferation of Collagen I and Collagen III with epineurium erosion in the control and TGF-β1/SMAD agonist groups compared with the SB431542 inhibitor and aligned nanofiber conduit groups.
Aligned nanofiber nerve conduits reduced α-SMA and Collagen I/III proliferation and prevented neuroma formation to a similar degree as pharmacologic TGF-β1/SMAD inhibition.

In Part II, co-administration of the TGF-β1/SMAD agonist SRI-011381 with the aligned nanofiber conduit did not block the conduit's suppressive effect on α-SMA, collagen, or TGF-β1/SMAD pathway protein levels, with no significant difference between conduit-alone and conduit+agonist groups.

Scanning electron microscopy showed that Schwann cells cultured on aligned nanofiber material exhibited extensions oriented along the fiber alignment direction, indicating better promotion of linear Schwann cell growth compared with non-aligned nanofiber material.
A previous study by the same group (cited here) found a strong positive correlation between autotomy (pain-related behavior) scores and α-SMA expression levels in traumatic neuroma tissue.

A previous study by the same group (cited here) reported that traumatic neuroma formation was significantly inhibited and expression of the pain marker c-fos was significantly lower in the nerve conduit group compared with the no-capping group, with no autotomy occurrence.
Ten years after a giardiasis outbreak, fibromyalgia prevalence was significantly higher among those exposed to Giardia than among unexposed controls.
The elevated unadjusted odds of fibromyalgia in Giardia-exposed participants (OR 2.91) was no longer significant after adjusting for IBS and chronic fatigue (OR 1.05).
Among participants without chronic fatigue, those with irritable bowel syndrome had over six times higher odds of fibromyalgia than those without IBS, regardless of Giardia exposure status.
Among participants without IBS, those with chronic fatigue had nearly five times higher odds of fibromyalgia than those without chronic fatigue.
High concentrations of pirfenidone (750 and 1000 μg/mL) significantly reduced viability of GO orbital fibroblasts after 24h treatment.
Pirfenidone pretreatment attenuated TGF-β1-induced upregulation of CTGF, fibronectin, and α-SMA in a dose-dependent manner in GO orbital fibroblasts.
In four independent GO patient-derived orbital fibroblast cultures, pirfenidone (500 μg/mL) significantly abolished TGF-β1-induced upregulation of CTGF, fibronectin, and α-SMA.
Pirfenidone pretreatment significantly abolished TGF-β1-induced upregulation of collagen type I in GO orbital fibroblasts.
Pirfenidone pretreatment significantly abolished TGF-β1-induced TIMP-1 protein expression in GO orbital fibroblasts.
Pirfenidone pretreatment restored MMP-2/-9 enzymatic activities that had been suppressed by TGF-β1 in GO orbital fibroblasts.
Pirfenidone inhibited TGF-β1-induced phosphorylation of p38 and JNK in GO orbital fibroblasts, suggesting these MAPK pathways are molecular targets of pirfenidone's antifibrotic action.
A novel 0.248 Mb interstitial deletion at chromosome 1q41 encompassing the entire TGFB2 gene was identified in the propositus and both his sons, confirming a diagnosis of Loeys-Dietz syndrome type 4.
The chromosomal deletion also removed the RRP15 gene, whose function in humans is unknown, in addition to TGFB2.

Comparison of six reported 1q41 deletions encompassing TGFB2, ranging from 6.5 Mb to 0.25 Mb, suggests that smaller deletions involving fewer additional genes correspond to a more representative/classic LDS4 clinical phenotype.
The propositus displayed marked joint hypermobility with a Beighton score of 8/9, alongside a systemic features score of 8, initially supporting a Marfan syndrome diagnosis.
The propositus's aortic root aneurysm progressed from 47 mm to 50 mm over approximately 8 years, ultimately requiring valve-sparing aortic root replacement (David procedure) at age 41.

Targeted NGS analysis found no pathogenic variants in FBN1 or other Marfan/LDS-related genes (TGFBR1, TGFBR2, TGFB3, SMAD3) in the propositus, prompting subsequent array-CGH testing that revealed the TGFB2 deletion.
At 40 years old, CT angiography revealed mild ectasia and tortuosity of the iliac arteries in addition to aortic root ectasia, a feature atypical for Marfan syndrome and suggestive of LDS type 4.

Ectopia lentis, a hallmark of Marfan syndrome, was absent in the propositus and in the original TGFB2 mutation cohort described by Lindsay et al., though a single recent case report described an LDS4 patient with ectopia lentis.

Both sons of the propositus carry the same TGFB2-encompassing deletion but showed normal aortic root dimensions at ages 3 and 6, suggesting age-dependent penetrance of vascular manifestations in LDS4.

The youngest son of the propositus, a carrier of the TGFB2 deletion, presented with a supraventricular arrhythmia (atrial flutter) with hemodynamic impairment at birth, successfully treated with DC-shock.

Deletions of the entire TGFB2 gene account for less than 15% of TGFB2 mutations, with haploinsufficiency (via deletions, nonsense, splicing, and frameshift mutations) being the primary disease mechanism underlying LDS4.
IBS is reported (from prior literature) to co-occur in 46.2% of people with fibromyalgia.
Fibromyalgia is reported (from prior literature) to occur in 12.9% to 31.6% of patients diagnosed with IBS.
None of the 73 highly-cited or high-impact-journal physical therapy clinical trials in fibromyalgia considered IBS as a comorbidity within their participant selection (inclusion/exclusion) criteria.
Only two of the 73 trials excluded participants for unspecified 'concomitant somatic disorders' without naming IBS or any other visceral condition specifically.

Over half (54.7%, 40/73) of the fibromyalgia physical therapy trials excluded participants with cardiac, pulmonary, or kidney disease due to concerns these visceral conditions would limit the exercise intervention, but did not similarly exclude for IBS.
Seven of the 73 trials excluded participants with some visceral pathologies but did not specifically exclude for IBS.
Four studies acknowledged that comorbid conditions could worsen fibromyalgia symptomatology in general terms, without naming any specific visceral pathology such as IBS.
Prior IBS has been identified elsewhere as the strongest predictor for new-onset development of fibromyalgia.

A proposed shared mechanism for FM-IBS comorbidity is dysregulation of the brain-gut axis producing generalized hyperalgesia (central sensitivity), increasing excitability of central nociceptive pathways and inhibiting descending pain modulation.
ME/CFS prevalence in Spain is estimated at a minimum of 0.1% of the population, though reported ranges vary widely (0.0052% to 6.40%) depending on study methodology.
ME/CFS affects women more frequently than men at a ratio of approximately 4:1, occurring at any age between 11 and 69 years, mostly in Caucasian populations.
Voxel-based morphometry (VBM) studies of gray and white matter show some regional differences but no significant differences overall compared to controls.

Using diffusion tensor imaging (DTI), Zeineh et al. (2015) proposed the arcuate fascicle as a potential biomarker for diagnosis and monitoring of ME/CFS, though this has not been replicated by other groups.

Functional connectivity (BOLD) studies show variations in neural activity at rest and after slight activity, either increased or decreased, in brain areas involved in executive and control functions such as anterior/posterior cingulate cortex, insula, and parietal/prefrontal cortex.
Arterial spin labeling (ASL) studies show a decrease in regional cerebral perfusion in ME/CFS patients.
MR-spectroscopy studies report an intraventricular increase of lactate in ME/CFS patients, possibly reflecting anaerobic metabolism.
Alterations in oxidative metabolism with a decrease in glutathione have been reported, suggesting mitochondrial function compromise in ME/CFS.
7.0-Tesla MRI studies reported a decrease in GABA in the anterior cingulate cortex with elevation of glutamate and glutamate+glutamine in the putamen in ME/CFS patients.

The neuronal viability marker N-acetylaspartate (NAA/Cr ratio) is decreased in the prefrontal cortex of ME/CFS patients, an area involved in cognitive control, and may help define a subgroup with higher pain scores.
Positron emission tomography (PET) has demonstrated neuroinflammation (encephalitis/myelitis) in ME/CFS patients but lacks neuropathological correlation.
PET-based studies of serum muscarinic acetylcholine receptor antibodies concluded that they do not alter cognitive function in ME/CFS.

MRI studies measuring cerebral perfusion indicated that high resting cerebral perfusion is associated with greater severity of dizziness symptoms, potentially reflecting brain stem neurovascular regulation alterations in response to orthostatic stress.
Autonomic dysfunction, including palpitations, orthostatic intolerance (hypotension, tachycardia), urinary frequency, and thermoregulation alterations, appears in 90% of ME/CFS patients.
Heart rate variability studies show a sympathetic/parasympathetic imbalance with increased LF/HF ratio, indicating sympathetic predominance that may explain physical and mental fatigue in ME/CFS.
Studies point to reduced nocturnal parasympathetic activity together with increased sympathetic activity in ME/CFS patients.
Yamamoto et al. (2004) reported decreased density of serotonin transporters (5-HTTs) in the anterior cingulate cortex of ME/CFS patients using PET.
Cleare et al. (2005) reported a marked decrease in 5-HT1A receptors in the hippocampus of ME/CFS patients using PET.

Several studies report the presence in serum of autoantibodies against acetylcholine, norepinephrine, and serotonin receptors in at least a subgroup of ME/CFS patients, raising the possibility of an autoimmune subtype.

Recent publications did not find an increase in the frequency of autoantibodies against NMDA (autoimmune encephalitis-related), LRP4, ACHR, MuSK (myasthenia gravis-related), or the mitochondrial membrane in ME/CFS patients.

Unlike multiple sclerosis or Parkinson's disease where physical exercise/rehabilitation is a mandatory treatment pillar, ME/CFS patients' chronic status deteriorates or worsens significantly if physical exercise is incorporated into treatment.
A mathematical re-analysis and a historical study of survivor accounts jointly invalidate the 1970 McEvedy/Beard claim that the 1958 Royal Free ME/CFS epidemic was 'epidemic hysteria'.

ME/CFS is described as a multi-system disorder involving HPA axis dysregulation, autonomic sympathetic sensitization, orthostatic intolerance with reduced cerebral blood flow, abnormal cortisol/circadian rhythms, increased pro-inflammatory cytokines, altered muscle anaerobic threshold, post-exertional malaise, central sensitization, and grey/white matter brain changes.
Blood test results differed between ME/CFS patients and healthy controls, with creatine kinase and creatinine levels reduced in ME/CFS patients.

Dysfunctional ß2-adrenoreceptor autoantibodies, arising from an infection-triggered autoimmune process, have been implicated in ME/CFS, and a pilot study of immunoadsorption therapy targeting these antibodies showed promising results.

A literature review found that between one-third and one-half of GPs did not accept ME/CFS as a genuine clinical entity, with a similar proportion of patients dissatisfied with the primary care they received, consistent across geography and over recent decades.
One study found that 89.1% of participants with Long COVID experienced post-exertional malaise, considered the defining symptom of ME/CFS.
A German study found that approximately half of all Long COVID patients fulfilled the diagnostic criteria for ME/CFS.

A systematic review of twenty-one studies (Wong and Weitzer) reported substantial symptom overlap between Long COVID and ME/CFS, including fatigue, reduced daily activity and post-exertional malaise, and some shared pathophysiological features.

Biological abnormalities common to both Long COVID and ME/CFS include redox imbalance, systemic inflammation and neuroinflammation, impaired ability to generate ATP, and a general hypometabolic state.
Based on overlapping biological and clinical features, the authors propose a new taxonomic category, 'post-active phase of infection syndromes' (PAPIS), encompassing both Long COVID and ME/CFS.

In a postal questionnaire study of 24 adult ME/CFS patients, illness negatively affected patient quality of life (especially physical health) and there was a significant correlation between patients' and family members' quality-of-life scores.

A comparative survey found that the impact of ME/CFS on net household income and quality of life was similar across Italy, Latvia and the UK, though differences emerged in medical/social care patterns and societal attitudes.

A study of ME/CFS patients found that those with more severe illness were more likely to have comorbidities, most frequently fibromyalgia, chronic hepatitis and Lyme disease; symptoms including fatigue, myalgia, arthralgia and sleep disturbance were more common among ME/CFS patients than non-ME/CFS fatigue patients, and 90% had used NSAIDs.
Of seventy UK ME/CFS patients surveyed who had undergone graded exercise therapy (GET), only one reported any positive benefit from it.

A systematic review of ten economic evaluations from RCTs found mixed cost-effectiveness evidence: three studies suggested CBT may be cost-effective (context-dependent), and two trials suggested GET may be cost-effective.

In Latvia the number of undiagnosed ME/CFS patients may be five times greater than diagnosed patients, with estimated direct medical costs for undiagnosed patients over €15 million/year before COVID-19, rising to about €17 million.

A review of twelve studies (including seven RCTs) of mind-body interventions in ME/CFS found general improvements in fatigue severity, anxiety/depression, quality of life, and physical/mental functioning, though findings were considered provisional.

A EUROMENE review of prevention strategies concluded primary prevention is of limited value due to insufficient knowledge of modifiable risk factors, with the notable exception of occupational exposure to agricultural chemicals such as organophosphates, while secondary prevention via reduced diagnostic delay would improve outcomes and cost.

An online survey of 499 respondents fulfilling the Canadian Consensus Criteria (with post-exertional malaise) found German ME/CFS patients were medically underserved, reporting low satisfaction with care and geographic/financial barriers to accessing services.
The ME/CFS patient cohort showed a strong female predominance of nearly 4 women to every 1 man.
Nearly all measured clinical variables (fatigue, pain, dysautonomia, sleep, neuroendocrine, anxiety/depression) were significantly worse in ME/CFS patients than in healthy controls.
Cognitive function scores did not significantly differ between ME/CFS patients and controls, unlike all other clinical variables.
Fibromyalgia was the most frequent comorbidity in ME/CFS patients, affecting the majority of women and nearly half of men.
The vast majority of ME/CFS patients reported poor sleep quality, with only a small minority reporting sleeping well.

Only 16 of 84 ME/CFS patients formally met criteria for orthostatic intolerance syndrome despite near-universal dysautonomic symptoms on COMPASS-31, a much lower rate than the ~90% incidence reported by another study.
Orthostatic intolerance syndrome was more frequent among men than women in the ME/CFS cohort.
Nearly two-thirds of ME/CFS patients experienced slight neuroendocrine manifestations such as sweaty hands, night sweats, cold extremities, or temperature dysregulation.
Primary hypothyroidism was the most frequent endocrine comorbidity, occurring almost exclusively in women.
About one third of ME/CFS patients had clinically significant anxiety and depression scores on the HAD questionnaire.
The HAD questionnaire detected substantially more depression than had been previously clinically diagnosed, suggesting underdiagnosis of depression in ME/CFS patients.
Women with ME/CFS reported significantly higher pain perception than men when pain was measured quantitatively.
Women with ME/CFS scored significantly better than men on the MoCA cognitive test.
Over half of ME/CFS patients showed reduced sustained attention capacity on the Toulouse-Piéron test despite normal general cognitive (MoCA) scores.
Most ME/CFS patients had markedly reduced functional autonomy, being unable to work and needing occasional help with daily activities, with average Karnofsky scores of 54 in women and 62 in men.

Hierarchical cluster analysis using Gower's distance and Ward's method identified five distinct ME/CFS phenotypes based on fibromyalgia status and severity of anxiety/depression, dysautonomia, neuroendocrine, and immune features.

Preliminary unpublished data from post-COVID patients evaluated in the authors' Dysautonomia Unit showed a similar autoantibody profile against alpha/beta adrenergic, muscarinic, and angiotensin receptors, linked mainly to POTS.
Most ME/CFS patients could not identify a trigger for their illness; among those who could, chronic stress was cited more often than an infectious episode.
Fatigue onset in this cohort was progressive over months to years in 75% of patients, contrasting with a prior report describing acute onset after infectious convalescence.
The clinical course of ME/CFS in this cohort was reported as continuously worsening in most patients, contrasting with a fluctuating course described in another series.
Illness duration and time to diagnosis did not significantly differ between women and men with ME/CFS.
The direct and indirect economic costs of ME/CFS in the United States have been estimated at 18-24 billion dollars, underscoring the societal burden of the disease.
The patient, previously diagnosed with chronic fatigue syndrome and fibromyalgia, was found on combined anterior pituitary function testing to have ACTH deficiency with a normal pituitary MRI.
Physiologic-dose oral hydrocortisone replacement therapy improved the patient's general fatigue.
A secondary workup using a growth hormone-releasing peptide-2 test revealed that the patient also had growth hormone deficiency.
Growth hormone replacement therapy improved the patient's muscle pain and depression, symptoms previously attributed to fibromyalgia/CFS.
The authors propose that combined ACTH and GH deficiency should be considered as a differential diagnosis when evaluating patients presenting with chronic fatigue syndrome-like symptoms.

Serum IL-6 (z-scores) was significantly higher in COVID-19 patients than in healthy controls, with levels highest in patients with SpO2≥76% and somewhat lower (but still elevated vs controls) in those with SpO2<76%.
CRP levels were significantly elevated in COVID-19 patients compared with healthy controls and were further increased in patients with lower SpO2.
IL-10 was significantly elevated in COVID-19 patients versus controls.

Soluble RAGE levels were significantly increased in COVID-19 patients compared to controls, and were the strongest and most consistent biomarker predictor across all regression models of depression, anxiety and physiosomatic scores.

Serum soluble ACE2 was significantly increased in COVID-19 patients versus controls, but was not independently associated with depression, anxiety or physiosomatic symptoms once the immune-response latent vector was accounted for.
Serum albumin was significantly reduced in COVID-19 patients compared with controls and progressively lower with worsening SpO2.

Serum magnesium was significantly lower in COVID-19 patients, especially those with SpO2<76%, but showed no independent association with any neuropsychiatric symptom domain after accounting for the immune response.

Serum calcium was significantly lower in COVID-19 patients and was a recurring significant negative predictor of depression, anxiety and physiosomatic (FF) symptom scores in multiple regression models.

Chest CT abnormalities (total CCTA, crazy-paving, and other CT abnormalities) were significantly greater in COVID-19 patients with SpO2<76% than in those with SpO2≥76%, and this difference survived FDR correction.

Depression (total HDRS), anxiety (total HAM-A), and physiosomatic/ME-CFS-like (FF) symptom scores, plus cognitive impairment and insomnia composite scores, were all significantly higher in COVID-19 patients than in healthy controls, with total HDRS and melancholia further increasing with lower SpO2.

Total HDRS, FF, and HAM-A scores showed significant positive correlations with CCTAs, CRP, IL-6, IL-10, sRAGE, and ACE2, and significant inverse correlations with SpO2, albumin, magnesium, and calcium.
Multiple regression showed that SpO2 (inversely), sRAGE (positively), and CCTA (positively) together explained 72.6% of variance in total HDRS depression score.
IL-6 (positively) and calcium (inversely) together explained 39.5% of variance in key (core) depressive symptoms.
CCTA and IL-10 (both positively) explained 43.3% of variance in physiosomatic HDRS symptoms.
SpO2 (inversely), sRAGE and IL-6 (both positively) jointly explained 64.3% of the variance in total FF (ME/CFS-like) score.
sRAGE (positively) and SpO2 (inversely) explained 46.2% of the variance in the fatigue subscore of the FF scale.
sRAGE and GGO (both positively), and SpO2 and calcium (both inversely), together explained 68.0% of variance in total HAM-A anxiety score.

PLS-SEM path analysis showed that combined 'immune response' and 'pneumonia' latent vectors explained 70.0% of the variance in the physio-affective (PA) core (comprising key depression, key anxiety, and physiosomatic HDRS/HAM-A/FF symptoms).

The immune response latent vector explained 29.2% of the variance in melancholia and 9.7% of variance in cognitive symptoms, indicating that immune activation mediates the effects of pneumonia on these specific symptom domains.
COVID-19 pneumonia latent vector and BMI together explained 28.7% of the variance in insomnia symptoms.

The COVID-19 pneumonia latent vector (CCTAs and lowered SpO2) explained 62.0% of the variance in the immune response latent vector, and had significant specific indirect effects on the physio-affective core, melancholia, cognitive symptoms, magnesium, and ACE2, all mediated through the immune response.

A second PLS model combining pneumonia and immune indicators into one 'infection-immune-inflammatory (III) core' explained 70% of variance in the physio-affective core, 31.1% in melancholia, 30% in insomnia (shared with BMI), and 8.8% in neurocognitive impairments; lowered magnesium and increased ACE2 were spin-offs of this core but not linked to neuropsychiatric symptoms.
A synthesis of 13 qualitative studies identified four overarching categories of factors contributing to diagnostic delay in hEDS/HSD: disease, patient, provider, and system factors.
Lack of a confirmatory diagnostic test for hEDS/HSD was cited as a key disease-related factor contributing to delayed diagnosis.
Patient-level factors contributing to diagnostic delay included psychological and emotional responses, consulting multiple providers, and receiving multiple prior diagnoses.
Provider-level factors contributing to diagnostic delay included limited clinician knowledge of hEDS/HSD and negative attitudes toward patients.
System-level factors contributing to diagnostic delay included silo-based health care systems and bureaucratic barriers.
Hypermobility predicts elevated trait and state anxiety even in non-clinical populations, without necessarily meeting formal anxiety disorder thresholds.
Among psychiatric conditions, hypermobility is most strongly linked to panic disorder and agoraphobia.

In Col3a1m1Lsmi/+ mice, thoracic aortic tensile strength was improved by celiprolol and doxycycline but not by losartan or bisoprolol.
