MyoD mRNA expression showed no significant difference between Chst14-/- and Chst14+/+ mouse muscle.

Cytokine/chemokine array analysis showed reduced expression of stromal cell-derived factor 1 (SDF-1), complement component C5a, interferon-γ (IFN-γ), and IL-1β in Chst14-/- mouse muscle compared to wild-type.
IL-1ra, the antagonist of IL-1, was slightly increased in Chst14-/- mouse muscle compared to wild-type, suggesting an altered cytokine/chemokine balance.
Chst14-/- mice showed a higher fibrotic area in muscle by sirius red staining compared to Chst14+/+ mice.
TGF-β1 protein expression was upregulated in Chst14-/- mouse muscle compared to Chst14+/+, consistent with enhanced fibrosis.

Collagen type III protein expression was upregulated in Chst14-/- mouse muscle compared to Chst14+/+, consistent with enhanced fibrosis, though the authors also note this may relate to a loose collagen meshwork phenotype.
Collagen type I protein expression showed no significant difference between Chst14-/- and Chst14+/+ mouse muscle.
A review of 27 original studies identified polymorphisms in 29 genes implicated in the pathophysiology and clinical presentation of fibromyalgia.
Most (73.33%) of the genes identified as related to fibromyalgia were also associated with psychological disorders such as anxiety, depression, schizophrenia, and obsessive-compulsive disorder.
40.00% of the fibromyalgia-related genes were also associated with pain sensitivity and/or migraine.
Genes related to different pain syndromes and altered pain thresholds were identified among the FM-associated genes, with some polymorphisms linked to susceptibility to fibromyalgia.
Involuntariness in the sense of agency during hypnosis was predicted by responsiveness to control, ideomotor, and dissociation suggestions.
Effortlessness in the sense of agency was predicted by responsiveness to control and ideomotor suggestions, as well as by age.
Hypnotizability was associated with main clinical pain outcomes in fibromyalgia patients.
Alterations in the sense of agency were not associated with clinical pain outcomes in fibromyalgia patients.
Chronic mast cell activation and immune activation have been implicated as underlying mechanisms in the development of abdominal pain in IBS.
Mast cells release increased levels of mediators including histamine, which sensitizes enteric nociceptors and drives visceral hypersensitivity in IBS.
A local break in oral tolerance to food antigens leads to IgE-mediated mast cell activation causing food-induced abdominal pain, demonstrated in preclinical models and IBS patients.
IBS is the most frequently diagnosed functional gastrointestinal disorder, affecting up to 25% of the global population.
MRGPRX2 is a mast cell receptor activated by basic peptides and small proteins, driving degranulation and resulting in allergic or neurologic inflammation, pain and itch.
SHP-1 phosphatase normally opposes FcεRI-Syk signaling but is reversibly inhibited by hydrogen peroxide generated during mast cell activation, permitting sustained Syk activity.

NOX2 is the predominant NADPH oxidase in mast cells and generates extracellular superoxide upon FcεRI activation; inhibiting this initial superoxide burst suppresses antigen-stimulated mast cell degranulation.
Induction of heme oxygenase-1 (HO-1) in mast cells opposes degranulation, partly because the bilirubin it generates inhibits NOX2-dependent NADPH oxidase activity.

Activation of AMP-activated kinase (AMPK) suppresses the association of Lyn and Syk with the FcεRI receptor complex, inhibiting mast cell degranulation, possibly via phosphorylation of the receptor's beta chain.
Cyclic GMP-dependent protein kinase G II (PKGII) can phosphorylate and activate SHP-1, providing a possible mechanism by which cGMP elevation inhibits mast cell degranulation.

Endogenous H2S generation and H2S-releasing drugs suppress mast cell degranulation through multiple complementary mechanisms including AMPK stimulation, Nrf2/HO-1 induction, and cGMP promotion via sGC activation and PDE5 inhibition.

Berberine inhibits mast cell degranulation in vitro by suppressing Syk phosphorylation, consistent with its role as an AMPK activator, and confers protection in rodent models of allergic rhinitis and passive cutaneous anaphylaxis.
Lipoic acid, a phase 2 (Nrf2) inducer, has been found protective in rodent models of anaphylaxis, lessening histamine release.

In a controlled clinical trial, ingestion of broccoli sprout extract (BSE) improved allergic rhinitis symptoms, and another clinical study found BSE ameliorated the nasal allergic response to inhaled diesel exhaust particles.

Melatonin promotes Nrf2 expression and Sirt1-mediated AMPK activity while antagonizing NF-kappaB signaling, showing efficacy against ovalbumin-induced allergic rhinitis in rats and suppressing mast cell degranulation provoked by water avoidance stress.
Nrf2 activation has recently been shown to also inhibit MRGPRX2 signaling that mediates pseudo-allergic mast cell activation, in addition to suppressing FcεRI signaling.

Paeoniflorin, a bioactive component of peony flower extracts, has demonstrated mast cell stabilizing action in cell cultures and rodent allergy models, with potential to inhibit both FcεRI and MRGPRX2 signaling.

Oral spirulina or its protein phycocyanin (bound to phycocyanobilin) alleviated symptoms and reduced histamine release in rat anaphylaxis models induced by ovalbumin or compound 48/80, and stabilized mast cells with reduced symptoms in ovalbumin-induced allergic rhinitis.

Small clinical trials with modest oral doses of spirulina found symptomatic benefits in allergic rhinitis, and oral spirulina decreased interleukin-4 production by ex vivo-stimulated peripheral blood mononuclear cells.

At supraphysiological (high-dose) concentrations, biotin can directly activate soluble guanylate cyclase mimicking nitric oxide/carbon monoxide effects, but its impact on mast cell activation has not yet been studied.
Supplemental NAC boosts endogenous H2S production because cysteine is the preferred substrate for CBS and CSE, and may also counter oxidative inhibition of SHP-1 via increased glutathione synthesis.
Taurine has been found to induce CBS and CSE expression in vascular tissue and to alleviate ovalbumin-induced allergic rhinitis in mice, though its effect on mast cells specifically is unclear.

Benifuuki green tea, rich in O-methylated EGCG, has shown clinical effectiveness in seasonal allergies (Japanese cedar pollinosis), attributed to the superior pharmacokinetics of O-methylated EGCG compared to EGCG.

EGCG and O-methylated EGCG stabilize mast cells in vitro via high-affinity binding to the 67 kDa laminin receptor, an interaction associated with down-regulated cell surface expression of FcεRI, inhibition of calcium ionophore-induced degranulation via blocked myosin II regulatory light chain phosphorylation, and inhibition of NADPH oxidase assembly.

The review describes solar urticaria as an immunologically mediated photodermatosis in which cutaneous mast cells are activated by specific wavelengths of solar radiation, producing itch, erythema, and wheals.
Historic passive transfer experiments support a 'photoallergy' model in which solar radiation alters a putative chromophore, leading to mast cell activation through an IgE-dependent mechanism.

The authors note that the classic photoallergy/IgE model fails to account for several passive transfer observations and subsequent clinical/photobiological findings, prompting a call to reformulate solar urticaria pathogenesis in light of contemporary mast cell biology.

IgE-mediated and non-IgE-mediated (silver nanoparticle, compound 48/80) degranulation mechanisms produced differing effects on mitochondrial activity and glucose uptake in murine bone marrow-derived mast cells.
Non-IgE-mediated degranulation (silver nanoparticle and compound 48/80) depleted mast cells' glycolytic reserve, an effect not seen with IgE-mediated degranulation.
Compound 48/80-induced (non-IgE) degranulation further inhibited mast cells' ability to maximize mitochondrial respiration, an effect not observed with IgE-mediated degranulation.
Fuel flexibility among the three primary mitochondrial nutrient sources was eliminated in activated mast cells, with the loss being most pronounced in non-IgE-mediated degranulation.
IgE-mediated mast cell degranulation upregulated metabolite concentrations related to the TCA cycle and glycolysis compared with non-IgE-mediated treatments.
SFN incidence was 1.3 per 100,000 person-years in Olmsted County and increased over the 20-year study period.
The prevalence of SFN was estimated at 13.3 per 100,000 in the study population.
Patients with SFN did not self-identify as substantially disabled, with only a slightly higher modified Rankin Scale score than controls.
Patients with SFN had significantly higher overall comorbidity burden (Charlson Comorbidity Index) than matched controls.
Myocardial infarction was substantially more common in patients with SFN than in matched controls.
The majority of SFN cases were idiopathic, with the remainder attributed to diabetes and rarer causes including Sjögren disease, amyloidosis, Fabry disease, lupus, postviral, and Lewy body disease.
Foot ulcers occurred in a subset of SFN patients, predominantly those with underlying diabetes.
A substantial proportion of SFN patients progressed to develop large fiber neuropathy over several years of follow-up.
Autonomic severity, as measured by the Composite Autonomic Severity Score, was low at onset and changed minimally per year in most SFN patients.
Neuropathy Impairment Scale scores were low at onset overall but showed marked variability in yearly change, with rapid worsening confined to specific severe etiologies.
Myocardial infarction after symptom onset was more common in SFN patients than in matched controls.
The majority of SFN cases had no identifiable underlying cause and were classified as idiopathic.
Diabetes was the identified cause of SFN in 15% of cases.
Sjögren disease was identified as the underlying cause in 2% of SFN cases.
AL-amyloidosis was identified as the underlying cause in 1% of SFN cases.
A small proportion of SFN cases were attributed to Sjögren disease as the underlying etiology.
AL-amyloidosis was identified as the cause of SFN in a small subset of patients.
Hereditary transthyretin amyloidosis was identified as the cause of SFN in a small subset of patients.
Fabry disease was identified as the underlying cause of SFN in a small subset of patients.
Lupus was identified as the underlying cause of SFN in a small subset of patients.
A postviral etiology was identified in a small subset of SFN cases.
Lewy body disease was identified as an associated condition in a small subset of SFN cases and was among the etiologies with the fastest impairment progression.
A minority of SFN cases had a multifactorial etiology rather than a single identifiable cause.
Foot ulcers occurred in 17 patients with SFN, and the majority of these patients also had diabetes.
All 17 subjects had laboratory-confirmed small fiber neuropathy associated with elevated TS-HDS IgM autoantibodies.

Therapeutic plasma exchange (TPE), delivered as a loading course of 3-5 procedures over 2 weeks with a mean of 9 procedures per subject, was associated with symptomatic improvement or slowed disease progression in 71% (12/17) of patients with TS-HDS-associated SFN.
TPE was associated with adverse events in about 15% of procedures, with vasovagal reactions being most common, and 53% of patients experienced at least one adverse event.
The most common symptom reported among the 17 TS-HDS antibody-positive SFN patients was lower extremity paresthesia, occurring in 88% of subjects.
Salivary mast cell chymase activity was elevated in chronic periodontitis patients.
Salivary bradykinin levels were elevated in chronic periodontitis patients.
Salivary HMWK levels were elevated in chronic periodontitis patients.
Salivary lactoferrin levels were elevated in chronic periodontitis patients.
In vitro, mast cell chymase cleaved HMWK to generate bradykinin, defining a novel chymase-dependent bradykinin generation cascade distinct from the factor XII or tryptase cascades.
Bradykinin treatment promoted proliferation and cell cycle progression in primary gingival fibroblasts.
Bradykinin stimulation increased intracellular expression of NF-kappaB in gingival fibroblasts.
Bradykinin stimulation increased intracellular expression of focal-adhesion-kinase (FAK) in gingival fibroblasts.
Bradykinin stimulation increased intracellular expression of transforming-growth-factor-beta (TGF-beta) in gingival fibroblasts.
Bradykinin stimulation increased intracellular expression of P38 in gingival fibroblasts.
Bradykinin stimulation increased intracellular expression of P53 in gingival fibroblasts.
The authors propose MC-chymase as a potential therapeutic target and salivary biomarker for chronic periodontitis.
The patient and her mother carried two novel pathogenic compound heterozygous CYP11B1 variants causing 11β-hydroxylase deficiency congenital adrenal hyperplasia.
The patient showed increased androstenedione and other androgen levels, prompting suspicion of 11β-hydroxylase deficiency.
The patient exhibited a poor cortisol response to the ACTH stimulation test, consistent with impaired cortisol synthesis.
Prior molecular testing of the CYP21A2 gene (the most common cause of CAH) was negative in the patient, ruling out 21-hydroxylase deficiency before CYP11B1 testing was pursued.
The proband's mother, previously diagnosed with CAH at age 10, was treated with methylprednisolone.

In a study of 78 type 1 diabetic patients using a 13C-spirulina breath test, about half had normal gastric emptying, nearly half had slow emptying, and a small fraction had rapid emptying, with delayed emptying linked to GI symptoms and hyperglycemia duration.

In a case-control study of 12 type 1 diabetics with GI manifestations versus 12 healthy controls, diabetic patients had a significantly higher frequency of distention-evoked GI contractions that correlated with disease duration.

A large questionnaire study of 15,000 subjects found that poorly controlled diabetes was associated with a higher prevalence of upper and lower GI symptoms regardless of diabetes duration or treatment.
In a study of 129 type 1 and type 2 diabetic patients, scintigraphy showed 36% had delayed gastric emptying and 22% had rapid gastric emptying.
A community-based study in Olmsted County found that the risk of developing delayed gastric emptying (gastroparesis) was higher in type 1 diabetes compared to type 2 diabetes.
In 1,101 diabetic subjects, upper GI symptoms were independently associated with self-reported glycemic control and HbA1c levels rather than diabetes duration or type.
Diabetic autonomic neuropathy causing stagnation of intestinal contents is cited as a contributor to small intestinal bacterial overgrowth (SIBO).
An Italian multicenter study screening children and adolescents with type 1 diabetes found a higher prevalence of biopsy-proven celiac disease.
The HLA-DR3/DQ2 haplotype is expressed in over 90% of celiac disease patients and about 55% of T1DM patients, compared to up to 25% of the general population.
ELISA-based detection of IgA anti-tissue transglutaminase antibody (TTG IgA) is described as having high sensitivity and specificity for diagnosing celiac disease.
Introducing gluten to infants either before three months or after six months of age is associated with a higher incidence of type 1 diabetes.
NAFLD affects around 33% of the general Western population and up to 75% of obese patients with insulin resistance.
Hepatic triacylglycerol deposition in NAFLD derives mainly from circulating free fatty acids (59%), followed by de-novo lipid synthesis (26%) and dietary fat intake (14%).
In a cross-sectional study of 277 hospitalized diabetic patients using Fibrotest and FibroScan, 15.5% had severe liver fibrosis, particularly elderly diabetics with prior diabetic foot ulcers.
In 220 type 1 diabetic adults not on vitamin D or calcium supplements, NAFLD prevalence was 29.5% and showed no association with blood vitamin D or calcium levels.
In a prospective study of 293 NASH patients on a 52-week calorie-restricted diet, 25% achieved resolution of hepatic steatosis and 19% showed fibrosis regression on repeat biopsy.

In 756 patients undergoing Roux-en-Y gastric bypass or laparoscopic adjustable gastric banding, achievement of metabolic control and weight reduction correlated with normalization of ALT and reduced HbA1c.
Autoimmune gastritis (AIG) and pernicious anemia (PA) are three to five times more prevalent in T1DM patients than the general population, affecting 5-10% (AIG) and 2-4% (PA).
Colonoscopy is described as the gold-standard screening test for colorectal carcinoma, with the highest reported sensitivity for carcinomas.
Fecal elastase-1 levels below 200 µg/g stool and below 100 µg/g stool indicate mild and severe pancreatic exocrine insufficiency, respectively.
Full-thickness gastric biopsies from patients with gastroparesis show increased numbers of pro-inflammatory macrophages.
Full-thickness gastric biopsies from patients with gastroparesis show decreased numbers of resident macrophages.

Diagnostic characterization of gastroparesis uses gastric emptying measurement, a functional luminal imaging probe, and high-resolution antral duodenal manometry to assess motor function at the gastroduodenal junction.

Management of gastroparesis includes nutritional support, dietary modification (including reduced solid food particle size), prokinetic and anti-emetic pharmacological agents, and interventions such as gastric electrical stimulation and pyloromyotomy.
Proximal tubule-specific Zeb2 knockout mice had significantly lower plasma creatinine and blood urea nitrogen than wild-type mice after ischemia-reperfusion injury.
Zeb2 knockout mice showed milder tubular injury, reduced neutrophil infiltration, and fewer fibrotic changes at 3-14 days post-IRI compared with wild-type mice.
Expression of fibrotic proteins including collagen type IV, alpha-smooth muscle actin, fibronectin, and CTGF was reduced in Zeb2-cKO mice compared to WT after IRI.
Zeb2 expression was upregulated in proximal tubular cells of wild-type mice after ischemia-reperfusion injury.
Zeb2 siRNA knockdown reduced TGF-beta-stimulated mRNA and protein expression of collagen type IV, alpha-SMA, fibronectin and CTGF in cultured renal tubular cells.
Human patients with AKI-to-CKD transition exhibited high Zeb2 expression in renal tubules on renal biopsy.
Hypoxia and CoCl2 treatment upregulated Zeb2 promoter activity and mRNA/protein expression in cultured renal tubular epithelial cells, suggesting hypoxia regulates Zeb2.
In both the 2018 and 2020 samples, the CSS group had a higher proportion of women than the non-CSS group.
The CSS group had a lower education level and a higher number of comorbid diseases than the non-CSS group in both 2018 and 2020.
Prevalence of osteoarthritis, skin diseases, neurological diseases, and obesity was significantly higher in the CSS group compared to the non-CSS group in both 2018 and 2020 samples.
Pulmonary disease was more prevalent in the CSS group in 2020, and cardiovascular disease was more prevalent in the CSS group in 2018.
Higher self-reported COVID-19 stress (worry and stress) was associated with more severe somatic (pain/fatigue) symptoms during the pandemic peak, even after adjusting for covariates.
In the 2020 sample, having a CSS was the strongest independent predictor of greater somatic symptom (pain/fatigue) severity.
Lower psychological flexibility (FIT-60) was independently associated with more severe somatic symptoms during the 2020 pandemic peak.
The interaction between COVID-19 stress and CSS group status was not significant, indicating the stress-symptom severity association was not stronger in people with CSS than without.
Contrary to the study hypothesis, the 2018 (pre-pandemic) sample reported more severe somatic symptoms than the 2020 (pandemic peak) sample.
In the combined 2018/2020 analysis, having a CSS remained independently associated with greater somatic symptom severity.
Across both 2018 and 2020 samples, lower psychological flexibility was the single strongest predictor of greater somatic symptom severity.

A significant but trivial group by psychological flexibility interaction showed that higher flexibility buffered symptom severity slightly more in the non-CSS group than the CSS group (effect size difference d=0.17).

Ad hoc analyses excluding participants with osteoarthritis or inflammatory rheumatic disease still showed no significant interactions, confirming the main null findings were not driven by diagnostic overlap.
During the pandemic peak, a higher proportion of the CSS group than the non-CSS group reported being worried about infection and reported increased stress relative to normal.
Plasma NFL levels increased significantly from baseline to 1-year follow-up in patients with MSA.
Baseline plasma NFL levels were significantly associated with the severity of motor symptoms in patients with MSA.
Baseline plasma NFL levels were significantly associated with motor progression over the 1-year follow-up in patients with MSA.
Baseline plasma NFL levels were not significantly associated with cognitive progression in patients with MSA.
16S rRNA sequencing of stool from 43 ME/CFS individuals versus 36 healthy controls showed altered gut microbiota composition and imbalance in microbial diversity.
A striking decrease in relative abundance and diversity of Firmicutes and a higher number of Bacteroidetes was detected in ME/CFS, often accompanied by an increase in Enterobacteriaceae.

Nagy-Szakal et al. reported an increase in Alistipes and decrease in Faecalibacterium in ME/CFS cases with IBS comorbidity, while ME/CFS without IBS showed a rise in unclassified Bacteroides (but not Bacteroides vulgatus), compared to matched controls.
18S rRNA sequencing analyzing eukaryotic diversity in ME/CFS versus controls reported insignificant differences, contradicting other dysbiosis findings.
Serum IgA and IgM levels against LPS of enterobacteria are significantly higher in ME/CFS cases than controls and correlate with disease severity.
Raised IgA response to commensal bacteria and enhanced inflammation were reported in 128 ME/CFS cases compared to healthy volunteers.
Combining a leaky gut diet with anti-inflammatory and anti-oxidative substances produced significant improvement, suggesting a new therapeutic approach for ME/CFS.
An increase in oxidative stress and a decrease in antioxidant levels in resting conditions have been reported in ME/CFS cases compared to controls.
Elevated urinary 8-OHdG, a marker of oxidative DNA damage, was shown to correlate with malaise and depression in ME/CFS.
High levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines including IFN-γ, IL-4, IL-5, TGF-α and IL-1 are detected in ME/CFS, similar to IBS.
Enhancement of 92 circulating inflammatory markers in ME/CFS individuals resembles the inflammatory marker analysis obtained in Q fever fatigue.
Administration of Bifidobacterium infantis 35624 to 48 ME/CFS cases reduced the systemic pro-inflammatory markers CRP, TNF-α and IL-6.
An 8-week treatment using four probiotic mixtures in ME/CFS replicated promising results seen with probiotics in other diseases.
Preliminary evidence suggests a significant drop in anxiety, associated with eubiosis reestablishment, when Lactobacillus casei strain Shirota is administered daily for 2 months in ME/CFS cases.
Improvements in neurocognitive functions were noted among ME/CFS-diagnosed individuals receiving L. paracasei spp. paracasei F19, L. acidophilus NCFB 1748 and B. lactis Bb12.
Eicosapentaenoic acid found in omega-3 rich fish oil has been found to alleviate symptoms in ME/CFS cases.
In a study of 34 ME/CFS participants who received FMT, 41% showed persistent relief after 11-28 months, while 35% reported only little or late relief.
A 70% response rate was obtained when 13 non-pathogenic bacteria were administered via colonoscopy in 60 ME/CFS individuals, with 58% maintaining response without recurrence at 15-20 years follow up.
NADH, probiotics, high cocoa polyphenol rich chocolate and Coenzyme Q10 all proved capable of improving fatigue in ME/CFS-diagnosed cases, though replication in larger samples is needed.

Integration of Sarcodon imbricatus or a mixture of Angelica gigas, Cnidium officinale, and Paeonia lactiflora proved effective in restoring oxidant/antioxidant homeostasis and reducing fatigue in ME/CFS mouse models.
Increased levels of lipopolysaccharide derived from Enterobacteriaceae are detected in ME/CFS, hypothesized to mediate intestinal inflammation and permeability.

The metabolite 4-hydroxyglutamate, part of the glutamate metabolism pathway with implications for brain function, was reported elsewhere to be elevated in ME/CFS patients and is used here as an example query in the portal's Results File Explorer tool.
The authors argue that cognitive behavior therapy, when properly delivered following thorough clinical assessment, can safely improve fatigue and function in CFS/ME.
The authors argue that graded exercise therapy, when appropriately applied, is among the best evidence-based options for improving fatigue and function in CFS/ME.

Informants who received individualized educational adaptations that worked (e.g., extended deadlines, fewer tests, adjusted progression plans) reported more regular school attendance than those who did not.
Informants who were disbelieved by teachers or did not receive promised adaptations reported low self-esteem, resistance to attending school, and risk of school dropout.

Overambitious school attendance plans and difficulty recognizing their own limitations led some informants to overestimate their capabilities, resulting in worsened fatigue, post-exertional malaise, and increased school absence.
Most informants described online teaching during the COVID-19 pandemic as helpful, allowing them to participate on equal footing with peers and improving contact with teachers and peers.
Some informants preferred physical school attendance over online teaching, finding it easier to follow lessons and ask questions of teachers in person.

Informants reported a broad symptom burden including fatigue worsened by overexertion, insomnia/unrefreshing sleep, headache, joint and muscle pain, sensory hypersensitivity (light, sound, smell), neurocognitive difficulties (memory, concentration), and autonomic, neuroendocrine and immune manifestations, which fluctuated over time.
Most informants found a healthcare-provider-recommended daily activity plan (pacing) with fewer activities useful, though two informants said it did not work for them.
Some informants used assistive devices such as noise-cancelling headphones, special sunglasses, or a wheelchair to manage symptoms.

Two participants who attended special education schools received comprehensive adaptations and reported satisfaction with their school situation, valuing atmosphere, alternative tasks, and close contact with teachers.
All informants reported missing social contact with peers, with socialising made difficult by both fatigue and school absence, contributing to loneliness.
Fewer negative experiences regarding school adaptations were reported among the most recently diagnosed informants compared with those diagnosed years earlier.
Informants who focused on their fatigue and lost abilities reported feeling depressed, whereas focusing on remaining abilities and staying positive-minded improved how they felt.

In a 4-week period before the interview, 10 of 18 informants attended more than half of classes while 5 of 18 did not attend school at all, though 3 of these 5 maintained contact with school personnel and received home assignments.
The study sample reflected the known female predominance of CFS/ME, with 13 of 18 informants being female.
Over half of patients evaluated for suspected mast cell activation disease had at least two of hEDS/HSD, mast cell activation disease, and immunoglobulin deficiency.
Among 974 patients with suspected mast cell activation disease, 46% received a confirmed MCAD diagnosis.
Immunoglobulin deficiency was present in 43% of the cohort of patients evaluated for suspected MCAD.
hEDS/HSD co-occurred with immunoglobulin deficiency (with or without MCAD) in 19.3% of the cohort, representing 45% of all patients with immunoglobulin deficiency.
10% of the cohort had both hEDS/HSD and mast cell activation disease.
21% of the cohort had both immunoglobulin deficiency and mast cell activation disease.
A small subset (0.7%) of the cohort had immunoglobulin deficiency and hEDS/HSD without mast cell activation disease coded.
Nearly one-fifth of the cohort (181 patients, 19%) had the full triad of hEDS/HSD, MCAD, and immunoglobulin deficiency co-occurring together.
Most patients with these overlapping comorbidities (hEDS/HSD, MCAD, Ig Def) were female, comprising 74% of the affected group.
Approximately 75% of individuals with Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome are reported to suffer from cervical dystonia.
Cervical dystonia is described as particularly problematic and difficult to treat in hypermobile patients, where it can worsen myeloradiculopathy or atlantoaxial subluxation.

Across the three hypermobile EDS patients, low-dose OnabotulinumtoxinA injection produced an average 16-point improvement in TWSTRS score, exceeding the 8-point threshold for minimally important clinical change, with no reported adverse effects.

In Case 1 (28-year-old female with hypermobile EDS and left torticollis/right laterocollis), TWSTRS improved from 56.25 to 36.25 one month after 100 U of low-dose OnabotulinumtoxinA injected into multiple myofascial sites.
In Case 2 (34-year-old male with hypermobile EDS and right torticollis), TWSTRS improved from 49 to 15 one month after 82 U of low-dose OnabotulinumtoxinA.
In Case 3 (49-year-old female with hypermobile EDS and left torticollis/right laterocollis), TWSTRS improved from 50 to 29.5 one month after 94 U of low-dose OnabotulinumtoxinA.
Sternocleidomastoid deep fascia thickness decreased after OnabotulinumtoxinA injection, suggesting the toxin may alter fascial tissue properties beyond direct muscle effects.

Total OnabotulinumtoxinA doses used (82-100 U) were lower than standard dosing yet appeared no less effective, possibly due to proximity of selected myofascial injection points (Centers of Coordination/Fusion) to neuromuscular endplates.
Nearly two-thirds of women with EDS or HSD reported experiencing dyspareunia (painful intercourse).
Half of women with EDS or HSD screened positive for probable vulvodynia, substantially higher than the estimated 8% rate in the general U.S. female population.
6.5% of women with EDS or HSD reported comorbid irritable bowel syndrome.
40.0% of women with EDS or HSD reported comorbid fibromyalgia.
56.4% of women with EDS or HSD reported comorbid temporomandibular joint dysfunction.
6.7% of women with EDS or HSD reported comorbid migraine.
1.7% of women with EDS or HSD reported comorbid interstitial cystitis.
10.2% of women with EDS or HSD reported comorbid mast cell activation syndrome.
Nearly half of participants with dyspareunia also reported ovarian cysts, fibroids, or abdominal/pelvic scars.
26.5% of participants with dyspareunia reported comorbid endometriosis.
19.3% of participants with dyspareunia reported a history of genital lacerations.
The estimated rate of vulvodynia in women with EDS or HSD (50.0%) appears substantially higher than the estimated 8% rate in the general U.S. female population.

Median arcuate ligament syndrome (MALS) and superior mesenteric artery syndrome (SMAS), both abdominal compression syndromes, were found at a surprisingly high prevalence in a cohort of hEDS and HSD patients presenting with gastrointestinal and other painful complaints.

In hEDS/HSD patients with abdominal compression syndromes, symptoms significantly reduced or ceased after decompressive surgery, suggesting compression syndromes may be a primary, treatable pathology rather than solely functional GI dysfunction.

Compression syndromes also occur in the retroperitoneum and pelvis (nutcracker syndrome and May-Thurner syndrome), causing chronic pelvic congestion syndrome, which the authors link to hypermobility-related pathology.

The authors recommend that functional ultrasound duplex examination, performed by experienced practitioners, can be used to identify abdominal compression syndromes in hEDS and HSD patients presenting with pain in the 'belt' area.
Patients with hEDS had greater thickness of the deep fascia of the sternocleidomastoid muscle compared with non-hEDS subjects with chronic pain.
There was no significant difference in thickness of the iliac fascia between hEDS and non-hEDS subjects.
There was no significant difference in thickness of the iliotibial tract between hEDS and non-hEDS subjects.

Non-hEDS subjects with chronic pain showed a higher strain index (indicating softer fascia and relatively stiffer muscle) compared with hEDS subjects and with non-hEDS subjects without pain, suggesting hEDS fascia does not undergo the same softening seen in typical myofascial pain.
Persons with EDS had a higher overall prevalence of prescription claims for immunomodulator and antiinflammatory drugs compared with matched controls.
Persons with EDS had 1.3 to 4.2 times higher odds of prescription claims for 5 out of 6 IMD drug classes compared with matched controls.
Biologic agent prescription claims were not significantly different between persons with EDS and matched controls.
Peripubertal increases in NSAID prescription claims were observed among female persons with EDS.
Peripubertal increases in oral and injectable steroid prescription claims were observed among female persons with EDS, supporting the hypothesized hormonal influence.
Periodontal EDS (pEDS) is defined by early-onset, rapidly progressing periodontitis with a mean onset age of 14 years.
Without periodontal treatment, individuals with pEDS experienced complete tooth loss at a mean age of 20 years (range 14–48).
A child with cEDS and a pEDS-specific gingival/periodontal phenotype was found to carry both a pathogenic COL5A1 mutation (causing cEDS) and a de novo C1R mutation (causing pEDS).
A case of vEDS with severe periodontitis was found to carry two pathogenic variants, one in COL3A1 (causative of vEDS) and one in C1R.
Two independent prospective case–control studies totaling 23 vEDS patients found a decreased prevalence of periodontitis compared to controls, contrary to assumptions of increased risk.

A study comparing hEDS to healthy controls found no significant differences in caries, tooth fractures, tooth number, enamel defects, mucosal abnormalities, crown/root morphology, or pulp calcifications, but found significantly higher plaque indices in hEDS.

In two case-control studies of 23 vEDS patients versus 96 healthy controls, the most frequent dental abnormalities were pulp shape modifications (75%) and root abnormalities such as root fusion (50%) and excessive root length (69%), considered biological variation rather than pathology, with no significant difference in caries or tooth fractures.
Classical EDS (cEDS) may be associated with abnormal dentinogenesis resulting in shortened or bulbous root anomalies, which can be misinterpreted as localized periodontitis.
Calcification of the dental pulp (pulp stones/obliteration) is a common finding in classical EDS, usually without causing pulp disease but potentially complicating root canal treatment.

Dentinogenesis imperfecta with abraded teeth, thin enamel, large pulp caves, and curved roots has been reported in osteogenesis imperfecta/EDS overlap syndrome and in single individuals with arthrochalasia (aEDS) and spondylodysplastic EDS (spEDS).
Crown malformations and tooth discolorations indicating enamel irregularities were reported in single individuals with kyphoscoliotic (kEDS), dermatosparactic (dEDS), and arthrochalasia (aEDS) EDS.
One of the earliest reports described gingival fragility and high translucency in 11 patients with EDS.
A particular gingival phenotype with generalized thinness and translucency of the gingiva was described for vEDS.
Lack of attached gingiva leading to severe gingival recession and tissue fragility has been identified as a pathognomonic feature of periodontal EDS (pEDS).
Severe and generalized gingival hyperplasia, nodular, fragile, and inflamed, has been described in children with dermatosparactic EDS (dEDS).
Absence or hypoplasia of lingual and/or inferior labial frenula was documented in 90% of EDS cases compared to 1.8% in controls, appearing characteristic of at least classical and hypermobile EDS.
EDS patients reported nearly three times more often a nonresponse to local anesthetics during dental procedures compared to unaffected individuals, suggesting reduced anesthetic effectiveness.
A questionnaire-based analysis in hEDS patients supported lower efficacy of dental anesthetics, and articaine was the agent with the highest reported success rate.
A case series of five female patients with hEDS or cEDS showed no dental implant pathology after 12 years, indicating no evidence of reduced implant success in most EDS types.

Severe and rapidly progressing peri-implant disease was shown in a case series of three individuals with periodontal EDS (pEDS), with one case requiring explantation as early as 5 years after implantation.

A study clinically assessing physical oral health alongside self-reported quality of life in EDS patients found that objectively good oral health often co-occurred with low self-reported oral health-related quality of life, driven by pain, malocclusion, temporomandibular joint disorder, anxiety, and insecurity.
Vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, caused by mutations in the type III procollagen gene COL3A1, was confirmed by genetic testing in this patient.
The patient developed acute spontaneous left lower extremity compartment syndrome without preceding trauma, in the setting of vEDS, requiring emergent four-compartment fasciotomy.

Imaging identified a left tibioperoneal trunk (TPT) dissection with a 4.28 x 1.75 cm pseudoaneurysm, along with a left common iliac and external iliac artery aneurysm and dissection, in the vEDS patient.

Endovascular stent graft placement (PK Papyrus covered balloon-expandable PTFE stent graft) successfully excluded the TPT pseudoaneurysm with preserved distal three-vessel runoff and continued stent patency at 1 month follow-up.
In prior reports of vEDS patients, stent grafts and coil embolization used to treat enlarging or ruptured infrapopliteal aneurysms had complications including stent graft occlusion at 1 month.

Standard vEDS management recommendations include serial surveillance imaging (MRA of the neck/head, and chest/abdomen/pelvis imaging annually), use of beta-blockers such as celiprolol to reduce arterial shearing force and possibly prevent dissection/aneurysm, avoidance of pregnancy in female patients due to high complication rates, and genetic counseling.
Genetic testing confirmed a heterozygous COL3A1 gene mutation in the patient, establishing the diagnosis of vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.

Vascular EDS results from qualitative and quantitative abnormalities in type III collagen synthesis, a major component of vessel walls, skin, joint capsules, uterus, and gastrointestinal tract including the colon.
Life expectancy in vascular EDS is reduced to a mean age of 45-50 years due to spontaneous vascular rupture or colonic perforation.
In vascular EDS, the first complication may occur before age 20 in 25% of cases, and 80% of patients have a risk of complications before age 14.

Sigmoid colon perforation was the presenting complication in this patient, occurring before molecular diagnosis, consistent with the pattern that sigmoid perforation is the most frequent colonic complication in vascular EDS often preceding genetic diagnosis.
Without adequate therapeutic management, 47% of patients with a colonic perforation in vascular EDS are at risk of early recurrence within 20 months of the first perforation.

A meta-analysis of 109 operations in 51 EDS patients found significantly higher recurrence after colo-colic anastomosis compared to ileo-rectal anastomosis (55% vs 7%), with better survival after total colectomy.

Preventive total colectomy with ileorectal anastomosis or definitive ileostomy is recommended to limit immediate complications such as suture loosening, anastomotic leakage, digestive/cutaneous/vascular fistulas, and intra-abdominal hemorrhage, which occur at a high rate (66%).
The patient underwent total colectomy with ileo-rectal anastomosis as a preventive measure after confirmed diagnosis, with uneventful postoperative and long-term follow-up.

Histological analysis of the resected bowel showed moderate congestive interstitial colitis with numerous eosinophilic polynuclear cells exceeding 40 per field, suggestive of eosinophilic colitis, without granulomatous lesions or other signs of inflammatory bowel disease.

Physical examination revealed classic vascular EDS morphotypic features including thin loose skin, hypoplasia of the ear lobule, 'Madonna face' appearance (pinched nose, horizontal lips, prominent cheekbones, sunken dark-circled eyes), and acrogeria of the hands.
Any idiopathic colonic perforation in a young adult without prior colonic pathology should prompt genetic screening for vascular EDS.
Recent studies suggest that endometriosis and premature rupture of membranes may occur less frequently in EDS patients than previously believed.
Knowledge of an EDS diagnosis enables anticipatory obstetric/gynecologic planning, which reduces morbidity from hemorrhage and tissue injury.
Most participants in this mixed cohort of bleeding disorder and Ehlers-Danlos syndrome patients reported improvement in bleeding after LNG-IUS insertion.

LNG-IUS expulsion occurred in a subset of patients within the first three weeks post-insertion despite use of hemostatic agents.

In a single-blind pilot study of 10 women with fibromyalgia, quantitative sensory testing showed improved pressure and heat pain thresholds during LDN 4.5 mg treatment compared to placebo.
In a double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover RCT of 31 women with fibromyalgia, LDN 4.5 mg was significantly better than placebo in reducing pain.

In an 8-week single-blind non-controlled pilot study of 8 women with fibromyalgia all receiving active LDN 4.5 mg, 17 of 63 measured pro-inflammatory cytokines showed significant reductions from baseline.
A prior dose-response study by the same group testing LDN doses of 0.75–6 mg found an effective dose in 50% (ED50) of 3.88 mg and an effective dose in 95% (ED95) of 5.40 mg.

A proposed mechanism of LDN analgesia is opioid receptor antagonism that triggers feedback-mediated upregulation of opioid receptor expression in the CNS, possibly improving endorphin signaling.

A second proposed mechanism of LDN is an anti-inflammatory effect via inhibition of Toll-like receptor 4 (TLR4) on astrocytes and microglia, potentially suppressing the pro-inflammatory cytokine cascade implicated in chronic pain.

Treatment of HMC-1 human mast cells with a TLR7 agonist increased expression of inflammatory cytokines, establishing a TLR7-driven mast cell activation model.
T-MSC-derived exosomes significantly reduced expression of inflammatory cytokines in TLR7 agonist-treated HMC-1 mast cells.
T-MSC exosomes were found to contain microRNAs that target inflammatory cytokines, suggesting a mechanistic basis for their anti-inflammatory effect on mast cells.
In a mouse model of repeated TLR7 agonist injection, T-MSC exosome treatment inhibited the increase in the number of dermal mast cells.
T-MSC exosome treatment also inhibited the increase in dermal CD14-positive cells in TLR7 agonist-treated mice, indicating broader anti-inflammatory effects beyond mast cells.

A 3-week broad-spectrum antibiotic regimen (streptomycin, neomycin, polymyxin B, bacitracin) in drinking water significantly reduced total fecal bacterial load and shifted bacterial sub-population structure in rats, whereas control rats showed no change over the same period.
Antibiotic-treated rats showed a 3.5-fold increase in cecal weight (normalized to body weight) compared to controls, consistent with a gut dysbiosis phenotype.

Middle cerebral arteries from antibiotic-treated (dysbiotic) rats developed significantly greater spontaneous myogenic tone than arteries from control rats, despite comparable maximum diameters between groups.

L-NAME-mediated vasoconstriction (a measure of basal NO production) was significantly blunted in middle cerebral arteries from antibiotic-treated rats compared to controls, indicating reduced basal endothelial NO release.

Endothelium-dependent dilation to luminal ATP was significantly attenuated at the two highest concentrations in middle cerebral arteries from antibiotic-treated rats compared to controls, implicating impaired NO- and EDH-mediated dilation.

Smooth muscle sensitivity to an exogenous NO donor (MAHMA NONOate) was comparable between control and antibiotic-treated middle cerebral arteries, indicating that smooth muscle NO sensitivity was not compromised by dysbiosis.
Densitometric analysis of cerebral artery homogenates showed a significantly reduced eNOS-P/total eNOS ratio (a surrogate for eNOS activity) in antibiotic-treated rats compared to controls.

Maximum diameter of middle cerebral arteries (measured in calcium-free PSS) was comparable between control and antibiotic-treated rats, indicating the observed functional differences were not due to differences in vessel size.
Fenebrutinib at 150 mg daily and 200 mg twice daily produced dose-dependent, clinically meaningful reductions in CSU disease activity (UAS7) compared with placebo at week 8.
Fenebrutinib reduced UAS7 weekly itch and hive component scores in a dose-dependent manner compared with placebo at week 8.
Fenebrutinib produced a dose-dependent increase in the proportion of patients achieving well-controlled disease (UAS7 ≤ 6) at week 8 compared with placebo.
Fenebrutinib increased the proportion of patients with complete response (UAS7 = 0) at week 8 in a dose-dependent manner.
Fenebrutinib showed near-maximal efficacy as early as week 4, with treatment effects on UAS7 similar to those at week 8.
Fenebrutinib reduced the median time to achieve the minimally important difference (MID) in UAS7 compared with placebo.
Post-hoc analysis showed marked increases in well-controlled patients within the first week of fenebrutinib treatment compared with placebo.

At 200 mg twice daily, fenebrutinib improved disease activity similarly in patients with and without markers of type IIb autoimmunity (BHRA+, IgG-anti-FcεRI+, low IgE), and at lower doses BHRA+ and IgG-anti-FcεRI+ patients showed greater improvement than marker-negative patients.
Among patients positive for IgG-anti-FcεRI autoantibodies at baseline, fenebrutinib substantially reduced these autoantibody levels at week 8 across all dose levels compared with placebo.
Fenebrutinib did not cause obvious reductions in total serum IgG subtypes including IgG1 and IgG3, suggesting the autoantibody reduction was not due to a broad effect on total antibody levels.
Greater reductions in IgG-anti-FcεRI autoantibody levels were correlated with greater decreases in disease activity (UAS7) at week 8.

The most common adverse events with fenebrutinib were urticaria, nasopharyngitis and headache, with no serious AEs in cohort 2 and a similar proportion of AE-related discontinuations compared with placebo.

Grade 2 and 3 liver transaminase elevations occurred between weeks 4 and 8 in a limited number of patients in the 150 mg daily and 200 mg twice daily fenebrutinib groups; these were asymptomatic, reversible, and did not meet Hy's law criteria for drug-induced liver injury.
Dose-dependent increases in mean creatinine occurred in fenebrutinib arms starting at week 1 and continuing through week 8, compared with placebo.

Two of three serious adverse events in the cohort 1 200 mg twice daily fenebrutinib arm (periorbital cellulitis and increased hepatic enzymes) were treatment-related and led to treatment withdrawal; severe urticaria was reported in four cohort 1 patients after fenebrutinib cessation.

Both substance P and PAMP(9-20) activate MRGPRX2 on mast cells, triggering release of inflammatory mediators, but with differing magnitude and composition of mediators released.

Site-directed mutagenesis showed that residues G165E, D184N, W243R, and H259Y of MRGPRX2 were necessary for substance P to activate the receptor.
Only D184N and W243R residues of MRGPRX2 were important for PAMP(9-20)-induced receptor activation, a smaller subset of sites than required for substance P.
The downstream signaling pathways activated by substance P and PAMP(9-20) differed in the phosphorylation level of PKC.
Substance P activates MRGPRX2-induced histamine release, which may contribute to allergic airway inflammation.
PAMP(9-20)-induced MrgprB2 activation releases more tryptase and fewer monoamines compared to other MRGPRX2/MrgprB2 activators.
