Beaded axons were strongly associated with more severe dry eye symptoms, occurring in 87.5% of patients with OSDI scores >13 compared to 44.44-50% in patients with lower OSDI scores.
Neuroma-like images were more frequent (75%) in patients with high dry eye symptom scores (OSDI>13) compared with 33.33-55% in patients with lower OSDI scores.
Dendritic cell presence appeared independent of OSDI symptom severity (44-50% of patients across all OSDI groups), but was more frequent in younger patients under 35.

Corneal neuroma prevalence increased with the time elapsed since COVID-19 diagnosis, suggesting worsening or chronic progression of the neuropathy over months, while dendritic cell prevalence was also higher in patients examined longer after infection.
Corneal neuromas coincided with a history of anosmia in 46.15% of affected patients, suggesting shared trigeminal/olfactory sensory nerve involvement in COVID-19.
Corneal nerves have been reported to express ACE2 and TMPRSS2 receptors, potentially rendering them susceptible to SARS-CoV-2 infection and contributing to nerve damage.

NRP1 and NRP2, expressed on corneal sensory nerve endings, are proposed alternative SARS-CoV-2 receptors independent of ACE2, potentially explaining viral neuroinvasion and generation of small fiber neuropathy and dendritic cell recruitment in the cornea.

Molecules such as CD209, CD26, CD30 and CD66, expressed on dendritic cells, have been identified as SARS-CoV-2 receptors, which the authors propose may explain dendritic cell recruitment to the cornea regardless of symptom status.

A separate study by Bitirgen et al. also found reduced CNFD/CNFL and increased dendritic cell density in COVID-19 patients, but restricted to a subset with persistent long-COVID neurological symptoms, partially corroborating the present study's findings even though the present cohort excluded formally diagnosed long-COVID patients.

Gambini et al. reported prevalence of dry eye disease symptoms and indicators (OSDI, Schirmer test) in a cohort of 64 COVID-19 patients, supporting the present study's findings of DED symptoms after COVID-19 infection.
Skin biopsy confirmed small fiber neuropathy (reduced intraepidermal nerve fiber density) in 6 of 13 patients with post-SARS-CoV-2 paresthesias, all of whom had both neuropathy symptoms and signs.
Two of the six patients with skin biopsy-confirmed SFN also showed autonomic dysfunction on autonomic function testing.

Among seven patients with normal skin biopsies, six had no clinical neuropathy signs while one exhibited signs and abnormal autonomic function testing, indicating some patients had clinical SFN features despite normal biopsy.

Two patients with markedly reduced intraepidermal nerve fiber densities had severe or moderate COVID-19, while most other patients (with mild COVID-19) had less severe or absent nerve fiber loss, suggesting a possible link between COVID-19 severity and nerve fiber pathology.
All 13 patients developed new-onset paresthesias within 2 months following SARS-CoV-2 infection, with acute onset in seven and co-existing autonomic symptoms in seven.
Symptomatic treatment for neuropathy controlled paresthesias in 77.8% (7 of 9) of treated patients.
A prior double-blind RCT of IVIg in idiopathic SFN patients showed a statistically nonsignificant improvement in neuropathic pain compared to placebo.

Proteomic screening identified 11 autoantibodies significantly different between SFN patients and healthy controls in the main cohort, and 131 in the validation cohort, of which 9 were reproducible across both cohorts.
Anti-MX1 autoantibodies were significantly elevated in SFN patients compared to healthy controls in both main and validation cohorts.
Anti-DBNL autoantibodies were significantly elevated in SFN patients compared to healthy controls in both main and validation cohorts.
Anti-KRT8 autoantibodies were significantly elevated in SFN patients compared to healthy controls in both main and validation cohorts.
Anti-MX1 was elevated in idiopathic SFN patients compared to healthy controls with the highest fold change, but only reached statistical significance in the main cohort.
Anti-MX1 fold change was significantly higher in idiopathic SFN than in secondary SFN, suggesting MX1 may help differentiate SFN subtypes.
MX1 has been reported to interact with the TRPC6 channel and potentiate calcium influx, a mechanism proposed to link elevated anti-MX1 to neuropathic pain in iSFN via TRPC6 signaling.
Anti-LIN28A autoantibody was one of 9 proteins reproducibly and significantly elevated in SFN and iSFN patients compared to healthy controls.
Anti-METTL3 autoantibody was one of 9 proteins reproducibly and significantly elevated in SFN and iSFN patients compared to healthy controls.
Anti-MIF (macrophage migration inhibitory factor) autoantibody was one of 9 proteins reproducibly and significantly elevated in SFN and iSFN patients compared to healthy controls.
In prior literature cited by the authors, KRT8 gene expression was found to be downregulated in CIDP patients compared to controls and Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease groups.
Positive autoimmune blood test markers (ANA ≥1:80, high ESR, anti-ENA, or ANCA) were present in 29.3% of SFN patients in the main cohort.

Hyperspectral imaging spectral difference measurements significantly distinguished T2DM patients with sudomotor dysfunction (ESC ≤60 μS) from those with normal sudomotor function (ESC >60 μS), whereas traditional neuropathy examinations could not.
Hyperspectral imaging waveform reflectance in the 1400-1600 nm range progressively increased with greater severity of diabetic neuropathy.

All four HSI-derived spectral measurement methods achieved an AUC of at least 0.8 for detecting abnormal electrochemical skin conductance, indicating good diagnostic accuracy for early small-fiber neuropathy.
In the MIRE-treated cohort, IENFD increased from 0.90 ± 0.73/mm2 at baseline to 1.71 ± 1.11/mm2 at 3 months, a change of similar or lesser magnitude than that seen in the sham group.
In the sham (placebo) cohort, IENFD also increased over the study period, from 0.60 ± 0.89/mm2 at baseline to 2.17 ± 0.98/mm2 at 3 months, a numerically greater increase than in the MIRE cohort.
MIRE therapy produced a significantly greater reduction in pain (VAS) than sham therapy after 3 months.
MIRE therapy led to a significantly greater improvement in quality of life (Norfolk QoL-DN) than sham therapy after 3 months.

The authors concluded that MIRE therapy provides symptomatic and quality-of-life benefit in painful diabetic peripheral neuropathy despite not increasing IENFD over short-term use, suggesting the symptomatic effect is not mediated by nerve fiber regeneration.
Perineurial injection of a miR-21-5p inhibitor reversed mechanical and heat hypersensitivity induced by the spared nerve injury (SNI) model in mice.
miR-21-5p inhibitor-treated SNI mice showed a reduction of the SNI-induced increase in CCL5 expression.
miR-21-5p inhibitor-treated SNI mice showed a reduction of the SNI-induced increase in CCL17 expression.
miR-21-5p inhibitor-treated SNI mice showed a reduction of the SNI-induced increase in IL-12ß expression.
Bioinformatic analysis identified several predicted and experimentally validated miR-21-5p targets that interact with the chemokine CCL5.
YWHAE gene expression was lower in mice after SNI plus perineurial scrambled oligonucleotide injection compared to naïve mice, but this reduction was not affected by miR-21-5p inhibition.
miR-21-5p inhibitor treatment further increased the SNI-induced elevation of TGFβ beyond the injury-alone increase.
Systemic miR-21-5p expression was higher in patients with small fiber neuropathy compared with other patient groups studied.
Systemic miR-21-5p expression was lower in patients with nerve lesion compared with other patient groups studied.
White blood cells from patients with small fiber neuropathy showed higher systemic expression of pro-inflammatory mediators compared to healthy controls.

The authors conclude that CCL5 is a miR-21-5p-dependent mediator common to both the mouse SNI neuropathic pain model and human small fiber neuropathy, supporting translational relevance of the miR-21-5p/CCL5 axis.
Patients with ulcerative colitis showed significantly lower gray matter volume than matched healthy controls in the left middle frontal gyrus and left anterior insula.
No brain regions showed significantly higher gray matter volume in UC patients compared to healthy controls.

Patients with IBS showed significantly lower gray matter volume than controls in seven clusters including left postcentral gyrus, left precuneus, right lateral orbital gyrus, right inferior/middle temporal gyrus, and right inferior occipital gyrus.

Patients with IBS showed significantly higher gray matter volume than controls in 12 clusters including bilateral temporal pole, bilateral superior frontal gyrus, left middle cingulate gyrus, left middle frontal gyrus, left inferior frontal gyrus, left occipital pole, and right superior parietal lobule.

In UC patients, greater GI symptom severity was associated with reduced gray matter volume in the right superior frontal gyrus, an inverse pattern compared to the positive correlation seen in controls.
In IBS patients, greater GI symptom severity was associated with reduced gray matter volume in the right occipital pole, contrasting with a positive correlation in controls.
No significant interaction was found between chronic stress and gray matter volume comparing UC patients to controls, at either corrected or uncorrected thresholds.

In IBS patients, higher chronic stress was associated with lower gray matter volume across 10 clusters spanning angular gyrus, temporal pole, frontal regions, postcentral gyrus, thalamus, and occipital gyrus, an inverse pattern relative to controls.
Both UC and IBS patients reported significantly greater GI symptoms, including abdominal pain (especially lower abdominal pain), compared to matched healthy controls.

IBS patients, but not UC patients, reported significantly higher chronic stress (TICS) levels than their matched healthy controls, despite both patient groups reporting greater overall psychological distress (HADS total).
In a female-only subsample analysis, the previously observed GMV differences between UC patients and controls were not confirmed, suggesting a possible sex effect or reduced statistical power.

ROI-based cross-disease comparisons indicated that GMV alterations were largely disease-specific, particularly for IBS, with only a small subset of brain regions showing overlapping alterations between UC and IBS.
OT protein was localized by double immunofluorescence to neuron cell bodies and nerve fibres in cultured enteric neurons and in mouse colon cross-sections.
Direct stimulation of cultured enteric neurons with LPS or IL-4 for 24h caused no significant change in OT or OTR mRNA expression or OT secretion compared with control.
M1 (LPS-polarized) macrophage-conditioned supernatant significantly decreased OT and OTR mRNA and protein expression in cultured enteric neurons compared with control.
M2 (IL-4-polarized) macrophage-conditioned supernatant significantly increased OT and OTR mRNA and protein expression in cultured enteric neurons compared with control.
The suppressive/stimulatory effects of M1/M2 macrophage supernatant on OT mRNA were also confirmed in enteric neurons from female (ovariectomized) mice, excluding a menstrual-cycle confound.
M1 macrophage supernatant contained significantly elevated TNF-α, IL-6 and IL-1β, whereas M2 supernatant contained significantly elevated TGF-β.
Direct treatment of cultured enteric neurons with IL-6, TNF-α or IL-1β dose-dependently decreased OT and OTR mRNA expression and reduced OT release.
Direct treatment with TGF-β increased mRNA levels of OT and OTR in cultured enteric neurons.
IL-10 treatment of cultured enteric neurons did not affect OT or OTR mRNA expression.
Receptor antagonists tocilizumab (IL-6R), R-7050 (TNF-R) and LY2109761 (TGF-βR) each reversed the corresponding cytokine's effect on OT/OTR expression, confirming receptor-dependent signaling.

Blocking IL-1β, IL-6 and TNF-α receptors reversed the M1-supernatant effect on OT expression, while blocking TGF-β receptor reversed the M2-supernatant effect, confirming these cytokines mediate the macrophage-supernatant effects.
IL-6 and TNF-α increased STAT3 phosphorylation and decreased OT/OTR protein expression; this inhibitory effect was reversed by the STAT3 inhibitor stattic.
IL-1β did not affect STAT3 phosphorylation but upregulated phosphorylated NF-κB (p-p65) and decreased OT/OTR expression; this was reversed by the NF-κB inhibitor Bay11-7082.
TGF-β treatment upregulated phosphorylated Smad2 and Smad3, increasing OT/OTR expression; the Smad3 inhibitor SIS3HCl blocked this increase.

During the inflammatory phase (weeks 1–2) of DSS-induced colitis, colonic M1 markers (IL-1β, TNF-α, IL-6, CCL2, iNOS) and M1-phenotype macrophages (F4-80+/iNOS+) increased while OT and OTR mRNA expression significantly decreased.

During the recovery phase (week 3 onward) of DSS-induced colitis, colonic M2 markers (TGF-β, CD206, Arg1, Chil3) increased, coinciding with a significant rise in OT and OTR mRNA and colon explant OT protein and neuron density.

Oral D-mannose feeding for 7 days decreased colonic iNOS (M1 marker) while increasing M2 markers (CD206, Arg1, Ym1, Chil3, TGF-β, IL-10) and increasing OT and OTR expression in the colon; effect also confirmed in female mice.
D-mannose applied directly to cultured enteric neurons (without macrophages) did not affect OT or OTR mRNA expression, indicating the in vivo effect requires macrophages.
Systemic macrophage depletion with clodronate liposomes significantly reversed (abolished) the D-mannose-induced upregulation of colonic OT and OTR expression.
D-mannose treatment inhibited Peg3 expression in colon LMMP while increasing OT expression; the Smad3 inhibitor SIS3HCl abolished the D-mannose-induced suppression of Peg3.

M2 macrophage supernatant and TGF-β (but not M0/M1 supernatant or IL-6/IL-1β/TNF-α) reduced Peg3 mRNA/protein expression in cultured enteric neurons; blocking Smad3 with SIS3HCl attenuated both the Peg3 downregulation and the OT/OTR upregulation induced by TGF-β, indicating Peg3 mediates the M2/TGF-β effect on OT/OTR.
ANA positivity, titre height, and staining pattern were similar between schizophrenia patients and healthy controls.
Anti-dsDNA antibodies and hypocomplementemia (low C3/C4) were absent in both schizophrenia patients and healthy controls.
Schizophrenia patients had a significantly higher frequency of positive lupus anticoagulant compared with healthy controls.
Anticardiolipin (IgG/IgM) and anti-beta-2-glycoprotein I (IgG/IgM) antibody frequencies were comparable between schizophrenia patients and controls.
BMS-986187 acts as a delta opioid receptor (DOR)-selective positive allosteric modulator with agonist activity that shows probe dependence on the co-applied orthosteric agonist in the mouse colon.
BMS-986187 augmented the inhibitory effect of DOR agonists on neurogenic contractions of the mouse colon.
BMS-986187 enhanced reflex-evoked internalization of DOR in myenteric neurons.
BMS-986187 significantly increased DOR endocytosis in myenteric neurons in response to the weakly internalizing agonist ARM390.
BMS-986187 reduced the generation of complex motor patterns in the isolated intact mouse colon.
BMS-986187 reduced fecal output in a novel environment stress mouse model of IBS-like symptoms.
BMS-986187 reduced diarrhea onset in the castor oil model of IBS-like symptoms in mice.

The authors conclude that selective allosteric modulation of endogenous delta opioid receptor signaling can suppress colonic motility without causing constipation, suggesting DOR PAMs as a therapeutic strategy to normalize GI motility in conditions such as IBS.
Among patients waiting to see their GP, 14.3% met criteria for restless legs syndrome.
Nearly half of patients with RLS reported their symptoms as moderately to very distressing.
The large majority of patients with RLS were not using any medication for their condition.
The proportion of patients with RLS was significantly higher among those who also reported irritable bowel syndrome compared to those without IBS.
The proportion of patients with RLS was significantly higher among those reporting chronic fatigue compared to those without chronic fatigue.
The proportion of patients with RLS was significantly higher among those reporting chronic muscle and back pain compared to those without it.
The ERS1 patient carried a homozygous FAM20A c.358C>T mutation resulting in a null (undetectable) protein in gingival fibroblasts.

The ERS2 patient's FAM20A p.F252del mutation, located at the homodimerization interface, did not abolish protein stability but caused abnormal accumulation of FAM20A in the cis-Golgi rather than its normal vesicular/secretory localization.
Proteomic and mRNA analyses of ERS-derived gingival fibroblast secretomes suggested upregulation of the TGFβ signaling pathway compared to controls, confirmed by increased phospho-SMAD3 activation.
Exogenous TGFβ1 treatment (5 ng/mL, 6h) further amplified the pro-fibrotic/pro-calcific gene expression profile of ERS-derived gingival fibroblasts.
Collagen type VIII alpha 1 (COL8A1) was more than 15-fold increased in conditioned media from ERS gingival fibroblasts compared to controls.
HAPLN1, a cross-linking protein stabilizing hyaluronan-proteoglycan interactions, was overexpressed more than 12-fold in ERS-derived gingival fibroblast conditioned media.
Pentraxin 3 (PTX3) mRNA was dramatically decreased (~5-fold) and its protein was under-represented in ERS-derived gingival fibroblasts/secretome compared to controls.
Annexin A2 and Annexin A5, calcium-binding proteins involved in calcification and fibrosis regulation, were under-represented in the ERS gingival fibroblast secretome relative to controls.
Netrin-1 immunoreactivity was markedly stronger and more extensively distributed along fibroblast processes in ERS gingival tissue than in control gingiva.
COL6A immunoreactivity was patchy but strongly decorated the disorganized collagen fibers in ERS gingiva, and COL6A2/COL6A3 mRNA and protein abundance were higher in ERS fibroblasts than controls.
MMP2 protein (secretome) and mRNA levels were 3-fold increased in ERS gingival fibroblasts compared to controls, and further increased after TGFβ1 exposure.
DKK3, a Wnt modulator and TGFβ1 target, was 3.8-fold overexpressed in ERS gingival fibroblasts, suggesting perturbed TGFβ-Wnt signaling crosstalk.

The ratio of p-SMAD3-positive nuclei to total nuclei was significantly increased in untreated ERS gingival fibroblasts compared to untreated control fibroblasts, and TGFβ1 exposure caused a tenfold increase in this ratio in control cells.
Serpine1 protein was decreased 2-fold in ERS gingival fibroblast conditioned media compared to controls, despite mRNA being inducible by TGFβ1 in both groups.

Label-free LC-MS/MS proteomics identified 534 proteins after filtering, of which 109 were differentially regulated between ERS and control gingival fibroblast secretomes (69 more abundant, 40 less abundant), with 50 classically secreted proteins (38 over- and 12 under-represented) selected for detailed analysis.
Meta-analyses cited in the review show cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) produces a small to moderate, replicated effect on symptoms in functional somatic syndromes.
A review of CBT for IBS found that in four of five studies, cognitive change mediated the effect of treatment on symptom severity.
A review of CBT for CFS identified three illness perception types (fatigue as aversive, activity as dangerous, symptom preoccupation with fatigue) that may perpetuate CFS symptoms.
In a study of 104 fibromyalgia patients, over two-thirds reported they could not understand the cause of their pain at all, indicating an absence of clear dysfunctional illness beliefs to target.
In a study of 66 CFS patients, half of the sample believed stress had contributed to development of their illness, showing complex non-physical illness attributions.
A qualitative study of nine adolescents with CFS found that three participants held a multi-causal illness understanding combining physical and psychological origins.
In an RCT of CBT versus relaxation training for CFS, CBT was superior and 70% of those who completed CBT achieved a good outcome.
In the same CBT RCT for CFS, widespread physical illness attributions did not change with treatment and did not predict improved outcomes.
A rigorously conducted fibromyalgia mediator study found avoidance behavior, mindful non-reactivity, and catastrophizing cognitions/worry were each related to successful treatment outcome.
Time-lagged analysis of the same fibromyalgia mediator study showed that only prevention of avoidance behavior, not cognitions/worry, acted as a probable causal agent in reducing pain.

A study of Emotional Awareness and Expression Therapy for FSS patients found two emotional processes (impoverished emotional experience/alexithymia-like traits, and unprocessed/intrusive emotions) were associated with reductions in somatic symptoms.
Marfan syndrome is caused by mutations in the FBN1 gene on chromosome 15q21.1, which encodes fibrillin-1, leading to abnormal microfibril structure and multi-organ manifestations.
A case-control study found MFS patients had significantly increased odds of death from respiratory causes compared to age- and gender-matched controls.
Mutated fibrillin-1 reduces LTBP binding to microfibrils, resulting in failure to sequester TGFβ and increased bioavailability of free TGFβ with overactivation of downstream signaling cascades.
Congenital chest wall deformities including pectus excavatum and carinatum occur in up to 70% of MFS patients and can restrict chest wall movement, causing restrictive lung physiology.
Scoliosis is the most common spinal deformity in MFS, affecting more than 50% of patients, though only 10-20% require interventional treatment.
Severe kyphoscoliosis (Cobb angle >70 degrees) is associated with impaired lung function, though decline in forced vital capacity can occur at scoliotic angles as low as 55 degrees.
One longitudinal study found that severity of hyperkyphosis was associated with a decline in pulmonary function in women with MFS but not in men.

In an Italian case series of MFS patients referred to a center-of-excellence, 44% had an obstructive spirometry pattern, diffusion impairment, and/or hyperinflation suggestive of emphysema, only 37% had normal spirometry, and only 19% had restrictive measures despite 45% having moderate-to-severe rib cage abnormalities.
In a case series of two lung biopsies and three autopsies of MFS patients, distal acinar (paraseptal) emphysema was found in all patients examined.

TGFβ was found to be elevated in lung tissue of smokers with COPD, in mice with FBN1 gene mutation, and in mouse lungs after cigarette smoke exposure, supporting a shared pathogenic mechanism for emphysema in MFS.
Lifetime incidence of spontaneous pneumothorax in MFS is estimated at 4-14%, with recent estimates trending toward ~4%, substantially higher than annual general-population incidence.
Recurrence risk of secondary spontaneous pneumothorax in MFS may exceed 50%, and in one MFS case series 25% of patients with pneumothorax had already experienced a second or third recurrence.

In a small cohort of 10 children with MFS undergoing methacholine challenge, 37.5% showed large airways obstruction and 7 of 10 showed small airways obstruction, compared to about 7% positivity in the general population.

Loeys-Dietz syndrome patients, who share TGFβ pathway dysregulation with MFS, show elevated eosinophil counts, IgE, and TH2 pathway cytokines associated with asthma severity, suggesting a shared mechanism that could explain increased asthma risk in MFS.
A Korean study of 79 adult MFS patients found bronchiectasis on CT in 28%, bronchiolectasis in 13%, and bronchiolitis in 4%, with low overall NTM disease burden over a median 65-month follow-up.
Prevalence of sleep apnea in MFS patients ranges from 32% to 64%, much higher than age- and sex-matched general population rates.
A case-control polysomnographic study of 61 MFS patients versus 26 matched controls found mild OSA in 32.8% vs 11.5% and moderate OSA in 18% vs 0%, respectively.
Aortic root diameter was positively correlated with obstructive sleep apnea diagnosis in the MFS case-control cohort.
In two randomized controlled trials, losartan alone or as add-on therapy significantly reduced the rate of aortic root dilation in children and adults with MFS compared to β-receptor blocker alone.

Long-term follow-up of the COMPARE trial (median 8 years, 94% of original cohort retained) showed continued losartan use was significantly associated with reduced incidence of aortic dissection and death compared to patients without losartan.
In murine models, positive effects of losartan are seen with haploinsufficient FBN1 mutations rather than dominant-negative mutations, suggesting mutation-type-dependent drug efficacy.

In a Fbn1mgR/mgR mouse model, lung tissue became over 85% less elastic than wild-type mice by 3.5 months of age; losartan treatment attenuated this lung tissue degradation to levels comparable to wild-type controls.
Lower levels of vocational training were associated with a higher risk of functional somatic disorders across all FSD delimitations studied.
Being unemployed was associated with a higher risk of functional somatic disorders regardless of FSD delimitation.
Living alone was associated with a higher risk of functional somatic disorders regardless of FSD delimitation.
Lower subjectively evaluated social status was significantly negatively associated with FSD, i.e. lower perceived social status corresponded to higher FSD risk.
The associations between lower social position and FSD persisted after multiple adjustments and appeared strongest for the more severe FSD subtypes.
Premature spillage, an oral-phase dysphagia sign, was far more common in MSA (75.4%) than in PD (15.8%).
Piecemeal deglutition, another oral-phase sign, was markedly more frequent in MSA (75.4%) than PD (1.8%).
Pharyngeal residues were common in both diseases, occurring in about half of MSA patients (50.9%) and PD patients (47.4%), suggesting pharyngeal-phase involvement is not distinctive of MSA.
Penetration/aspiration occurred in 28.1% of MSA patients, described as less frequent than oral-phase symptoms but still a substantial pharyngeal-phase risk.
MSA patients had greater risk of oral-phase disturbances as disease severity increased, with an odds ratio of 3.15.
Patients with MSA showed significantly higher intraindividual interswallow variability compared with PD patients.
The standard Swallowing Disturbance Questionnaire cutoff, validated in PD, was not sensitive enough to identify dysphagia in MSA patients on endoscopy.
A newly developed Swallowing Disturbance Questionnaire subscore for MSA, with a new cutoff, achieved 85% sensitivity and 100% specificity for identifying dysphagia in MSA.

A newly developed Swallowing Disturbance Questionnaire subscore tailored for MSA achieved 85% sensitivity and 100% specificity for identifying dysphagia on endoscopy, outperforming the original PD-validated cutoff.

The authors hypothesize that dysfunction of the beta-2 adrenergic receptor, potentially caused by autoantibodies, polymorphisms, and stress-induced desensitization, is central to ME/CFS pathophysiology.
A cited study found altered endothelial dysfunction-related microRNAs in the plasma of ME/CFS patients.
ME/CFS patients have a reduced absolute cerebral blood flow (CBF) compared to healthy individuals.
During head-up tilt testing, end-tilt cerebral blood flow reduction was 7% in healthy controls versus 26% in ME/CFS patients.
In severe ME/CFS patients, cerebral blood flow decreased 24.5% simply from changing position from supine to sitting.
fMRI studies show consistently sluggish signals in ME/CFS suggesting abnormal neurovascular coupling with disturbed local blood flow regulation.
Neuroradiological MRI signs of intracranial hypertension were present in 83% of ME/CFS patients studied.
ME/CFS patients show a higher prevalence of perineural (Tarlov) cysts in the spinal cord compared with healthy people, attributed to increased cerebrospinal fluid pressure.

Bradykinin, one of the vasodilator mediators spilling over from skeletal muscle, is proposed as the most potent opener of the blood brain barrier, potentially explaining moderate intracranial hypertension and neurological symptoms in ME/CFS.

Prolonged illumination of the pupils in ME/CFS patients revealed abnormal pupillary reflexes: rhythmic contraction and dilatation in three-quarters of patients, and paradoxical dilation after initial contraction in others.
Hypervigilance and sympathetic hyperactivity are present in ME/CFS patients.

The presynaptic α2-adrenergic autoreceptor, which normally inhibits norepinephrine release, shows desensitization in ME/CFS, hypothesized to enhance catecholamine release and drive arousal, sympathetic overactivity, and autonomic dysregulation.
Hypocapnia and hyperventilation are frequently found in both ME/CFS and POTS.

In POTS patients, blood pressure does not fall during head-up tilt (maintaining cerebral perfusion pressure), yet middle cerebral artery blood flow velocity is reduced, associated with hyperventilation, indicating the CBF decrease is due to cerebrovascular resistance/vasoconstriction rather than hypotension.
In post-Covid-syndrome, hyperventilation has been identified as a cause of dyspnea, occurring early during exercise and resulting in impaired ventilatory efficiency.
Patients with whiplash injury, who frequently also suffer from ME/CFS, present with hyperventilation.
Baseline NK cell cytotoxic activity was significantly reduced in ME/CFS patients compared with healthy controls across all effector-to-target ratios tested.
Overnight IL-2 stimulation significantly increased NK cell cytotoxic activity from baseline in both ME/CFS and healthy control groups, abolishing the between-group difference.
Pharmacological agonism (naltriben) or antagonism (NS8593) of TRPM7 did not significantly alter NK cell cytotoxic activity compared with IL-2 stimulation alone, within or between groups.
In ME/CFS patients, TRPM7 co-localization with actin was significantly increased following TRPM7 antagonist (NS8593) treatment compared with TRPM7 agonist (NTB) treatment.
ME/CFS patients showed significantly greater TRPM7 co-localization with actin than healthy controls under TRPM7 antagonist (NS8593) treatment.
No significant differences were found in TRPM7 co-localization with actin between ME/CFS and healthy controls following IL-2 stimulation alone or IL-2 plus TRPM7 agonist (NTB) treatment.
TRPM7 co-localization with PIP2 significantly increased after TRPM7 antagonist (NS8593) treatment compared with TRPM7 agonist (NTB) treatment in both healthy control and ME/CFS cohorts.
ME/CFS patients reported greater impairment across all SF-36 domains and most WHODAS domains (except school/work participation) compared with healthy controls.

ME/CFS patients showed statistically significant hypoperfusion in the limbic system, including the anterior cingulate cortex, left anterior ventral insular area, pallidum, and caudate nucleus, compared to healthy controls.
Cerebral perfusion in the identified limbic regions was reduced by approximately 34% in ME/CFS patients compared with healthy controls.
In ME/CFS patients, reduced rCBF in a cluster within the anterior cingulate cortex was significantly associated with lower EQ-VAS self-rated health scores.
The association between reduced limbic rCBF and fatigue severity scale (FSS) scores showed a trend but did not reach statistical significance.

Although the voxel-wise analysis detected a cluster overlapping the left insula, the ROI-based (AAL) analysis found no significant difference in average rCBF for the entire left insula ROI between ME/CFS and HC.
Model-driven AAL ROI-based analysis confirmed hypoperfusion clusters overlapping bilateral putamen and pallidum regions, consistent with the voxel-wise findings.
The patient tested positive for antinuclear antibody, raising suspicion of an underlying autoimmune process.
The patient's Chlamydia pneumoniae IgG titer was markedly elevated, leading the treating physician to suspect a post-infectious process contributing to her ME/CFS.
Mycoplasma pneumoniae IgG was borderline elevated and later became the primary suspected chronic infection contributing to the patient's ME/CFS.
The patient had low serum T4 consistent with significant, long-standing hypothyroidism.
The patient's serum iron was below the normal range at initial workup.
The patient had low free lambda light chains with an increased kappa-to-lambda ratio, suggesting immune dysregulation.
Elevated blood ammonia levels, combined with a long history of antibiotic use, led to suspicion of intestinal Candida overgrowth.
CRP levels rose to high values at two points during treatment, coinciding with periods of paradoxical worsening.
Salivary gland ultrasound findings and dry eyes/mouth led to a diagnosis of Sicca syndrome with suspected underlying Sjogren's syndrome.
The patient carried the HLA DQ2+ genotype and was noted to have gluten intolerance.
Initiation of thyroid hormone treatment for hypothyroidism coincided with resolution of the patient's longstanding congenital neutropenia, psychogenic polydipsia, and amenorrhea.
The patient repeatedly experienced Jarisch-Herxheimer-type reactions (symptom worsening) following nearly every treatment change, interpreted as evidence of an unresolved chronic infectious process.

After antibiotic treatment began, Mycoplasma pneumoniae IgG titers rose while Chlamydia pneumoniae IgG titers fell, leading the physician to view Mycoplasma pneumoniae as the more probable contributor to the patient's ME/CFS.
Non-detectable aldosterone levels were identified as contributing to the patient's severe orthostatic intolerance and hypotension, prompting treatment with licorice root and later Fludrocortisone.

EFT and EMDR sessions targeting infection/toxin-related themes produced severe adverse reactions in the patient, including joint pain, headaches, excessive yawning, and flu-like symptoms, taking days to stabilize.

LED light therapy (blue, red, green) was initially intolerable (causing severe migraines within 1-2 minutes) but became a daily treatment of up to 6 hours/day as tolerance improved, coinciding with the patient's overall recovery.

After 2.5 years on a revised protocol combining herbs, thyroid medication, and non-invasive therapies (EFT/EMDR/light), the patient improved enough to move out of her parents' home and resume graduate school after being bedridden with ME/CFS for 4.5 years.
A cited study found no significant differences in antibody/antigen serology tests against common viral and bacterial pathogens between patients with severe ME/CFS and healthy controls.
A cited meta-analysis reported that Lyme disease serologic tests are falsely negative in 40.5% of cases, highlighting diagnostic challenges relevant to the patient's tick-bite history.

A cited study indicates that spontaneous recovery from ME/CFS rarely occurs after 15 months of illness, supporting the interpretation that this patient's improvement was treatment-related rather than spontaneous.

Graded exercise therapy is contraindicated for ME/CFS patients because it can cause detrimental effects related to mitochondrial dysfunction, low oxygen uptake, abnormal autonomic responses, and immunological abnormalities, consistent with the patient's post-exertional malaise.
Serum FABP-2, a marker of increased intestinal permeability, was significantly higher in ME/CFS patients than in healthy controls.
Serum IL-17A was modestly but significantly increased in ME/CFS patients compared with controls.
No significant differences were found between ME/CFS patients and controls in serum IL-4, IL-10, IL-18, or IFN-γ levels.
Serum tryptophan tended to be lower in ME/CFS patients than in controls but did not reach statistical significance.
Serum serotonin levels were significantly lower in ME/CFS patients than in controls.
No difference in serum melatonin levels was found between ME/CFS patients and controls.
ME/CFS patients had significantly lower serum levels of kynurenine than controls.
ME/CFS patients had significantly higher serum levels of 3-hydroxykynurenine, a neurotoxic kynurenine metabolite, than controls.
No significant differences were seen between ME/CFS patients and controls for serum quinolinic acid or kynurenic acid.

In Study 1, a double-blind RCT of high-dose (2 g/kg) IV IgG vs placebo in 49 adults with severe ME/CFS, 43% of IgG recipients were classified as 'responders' at 3-month follow-up compared with 12% of placebo recipients, a statistically significant difference.

Patients classified as 'responders' (in either the IgG or placebo arm of Study 1) showed a significantly greater improvement in CD4 helper T-cell count (37% increase) compared with non-responders (3% decrease).
Among Study 1 IgG recipients, percentage improvement in quality-of-life score was positively correlated with improvement in CD4 count (r=0.4, p<0.05).
Eight of ten IgG 'responders' in Study 1 relapsed within one year of the final infusion, but further IgG therapy produced an identical remission of symptoms and improved function in each case.

Study 2, a lower-dose (1 g/kg) RCT in 30 adults, found no significant difference between IgG and placebo on most measures except a slight relative improvement in social functioning in the placebo group, leading the authors to conclude IV IgG is unlikely to be of clinical benefit.

Despite Study 2's overall negative conclusion, IgG recipients showed a significant improvement in health perceptions score (MOS SF) rising from 8.5 to 20.5 (a 141% increase), described by the authors as of 'small magnitude'.

Following IgG treatment in Study 2, IgG1 deficiency resolved in all 12 patients with baseline deficiency, whereas IgG3 normalized in only 6 of 18 patients, consistent with IgG3's shorter half-life (7 days vs 22 days for IgG1).

Study 3, an RCT in 70 adolescents with ME/CFS, found significantly greater functional improvement with IV IgG than placebo at 6-month follow-up (mean functional score increase 40.2 points vs 26.2 points), with 25% of IgG recipients vs 12% of placebo recipients returning to full function.

In Study 3, adolescents with impaired cell-mediated immunity (CMI) at baseline benefited more from IgG (mean 6-month functioning score 65.4) than similarly impaired placebo-treated patients (39.3), while those with normal CMI improved regardless of treatment arm.

In Study 3, severity of headache and duration of nausea following infusion were sensitive (but not specific) predictors of clinical improvement, suggesting these adverse effects may be linked to IgG's mode of action.

Study 4, a dose-ranging RCT of IV IgG (0.5, 1, or 2 g/kg) vs placebo in 73 adults, found all groups including placebo improved significantly on Karnofsky performance scores, with no significant between-group difference, leading to the published conclusion that IV IgG is ineffective.

In Study 4, all treatment groups (including placebo) showed a significant linear increase in absolute CD8 (suppressor/cytotoxic T) cell counts across baseline, pre-final-infusion, and 3-month follow-up.
A 2021 paper on immune-related pathogenesis reported that several immunoglobulin genes are significantly increased in ME/CFS patients compared with controls.
Pilot work presented in 2020 found that autoimmune-associated small-fibre polyneuropathy (aaSFPN), a condition known to respond to IV IgG, may occur in a substantial proportion of ME/CFS patients.
A single ME/CFS patient with aaSFPN treated with two IV IgG infusions experienced a dramatic reduction in levels of all four relevant autoantibodies along with favorable symptom reduction.

Historical evidence cited includes demonstration of enteroviral RNA in muscle tissue and enteroviral antigen in serum of ME/CFS patients, supporting a hypothesis of failed clearance of viral antigens as a disease mechanism.

A case series of five severe paediatric-onset ME/CFS patients treated with intramuscular or IV immunoglobulin in clinical practice (1990-2006) showed near-total recovery in all cases with no treatment failures.

A 2013 report on ME/CFS patients treated at the Aviano National Cancer Institute CFS Unit found that combined antiviral and immunological (immunoglobulin) therapies had the highest response rate (75%), described as superior to other treatment approaches.
A 2003 UK case series reported successful IV immunoglobulin therapy in 3 cases of Parvovirus B19-associated chronic fatigue syndrome.

Across the four RCTs, adverse events commonly took the form of transient exacerbation of ME/CFS symptoms and occurred at similar rates in IgG and placebo groups, suggesting attribution to participation effort rather than IgG itself, though headache was more common with IgG.

At baseline in Study 1, two-thirds of participants had reduced cutaneous delayed-type hypersensitivity responses and 82% had abnormal cell-mediated immunity as evidenced by DTH and/or T-cell lymphopenia.

At baseline in Study 3, 21% of adolescent ME/CFS patients tested were anergic and 31% hypoergic on DTH testing, compared to normative data indicating only 5% of healthy children are hypoergic and none anergic.

Conditioned media from hEDS fibroblasts (hEDS-CM), but not control CM, induced disorganization of FN-, collagen I-, and tenascin-ECM and myofibroblast conversion (αvβ3 integrin patches, nuclear Snail1/Slug, α-SMA stress fibers) in healthy control fibroblasts, in a time-dependent manner.

Western blot of pooled CM showed distinct degradation fragments of collagen I, fibronectin, and tenascins in hEDS-CM, whereas only intact protein forms were detected in control CM, indicating increased proteolytic activity.

LC-MS/MS secretome profiling of hEDS vs control fibroblast CM identified 656 total proteins, 112 present in ≥65% of samples per group, and 32 significantly changed proteins (21 up-regulated, 11 down-regulated, FDR-adjusted p<0.05).
Secretome profiling showed higher levels of secreted fibronectin in hEDS compared to control fibroblasts, suggesting FN and its fragments are key molecular triggers in disease pathogenesis.

PANTHER classification of the secretome DEPs identified matrix-remodeling enzymes MMP1 and TIMP2 among significantly changed proteins, indicating an unbalanced MMP/TIMP-mediated ECM proteolysis in hEDS fibroblasts.

GO enrichment analysis of hEDS secretome DEPs identified extracellular matrix organization, collagen fibril organization, platelet degranulation, cell adhesion, and ECM disassembly as the most perturbed biological processes.
KEGG pathway analysis of hEDS secretome DEPs showed enrichment of ECM-receptor interaction, focal adhesion, PI3K-Akt signaling, and ER protein folding/redox balance pathways.
Doxycycline treatment of hEDS fibroblasts restored a fibrillar FN-ECM network in a dose-dependent manner, becoming significant at 25 µM after 48h and comparable to control at 50-100 µM.
Doxycycline treatment caused dose-dependent disappearance of the alternative αvβ3 integrin FN receptor from the cell surface of hEDS fibroblasts after 48 hours.
Doxycycline treatment for 4 days restored significant tenascin and collagen I ECM deposition in hEDS fibroblasts, comparable to control fibroblasts at 100 µM.

Doxycycline (100 µM) partially reversed myofibroblast differentiation of hEDS fibroblasts, reducing but not eliminating α-SMA stress fibers (at 6 days) and Snail1/Slug nuclear localization (at 8 days), leaving residual cytoplasmic Snail1/Slug and α-SMA microfilaments.
Supplementing hEDS-CM with 50 µM doxycycline abolished its ability to degrade ECM and induce myofibroblast differentiation in control fibroblasts, which maintained proper ECM organization instead.

Many of the dysregulated proteins in the hEDS secretome are predicted to localize to extracellular vesicles, suggesting EVs may mediate intercellular transmission of ECM components, matrix-modifying enzymes, and RNA cargo in disease pathogenesis.

The PAR4 agonist AYPGKF-NH2 promoted pro- and anti-inflammatory cytokine production in HMC-1 mast cells, mimicking thrombin's effect.
The authors developed an engineered HEK cell line expressing MRGPRX2 to screen peptide libraries for receptor activation using calcium flux imaging as an alternative to using mast cells.

PAMP-12, an endogenous proadrenomedullin N-terminal 12 secretagogue, is known to bind MRGPRX2 with high specificity and affinity and was used as the basis for a truncation and alanine-scanning peptide library.
LL-37 and other endogenous peptides such as defensins and degraded albumin fragments are cited as known ligands of MRGPRX2.
Most mast cell activation signatures, except unstimulated, repeated FcεR1-stimulated, and IFN-γ-stimulated signatures, were enriched in sputum transcriptomes of participants with severe asthma.

A FcεR1-IgE-stimulated mast cell signature and a single-cell signature from asthmatic bronchial biopsies were highly enriched in eosinophilic asthma and in the TAC1 molecular phenotype, with elevated expression of related genes and pathways.
IL-33- and LPS-stimulated mast cell signatures showed greater enrichment scores in neutrophilic and mixed granulocytic asthma and in the TAC2 molecular phenotype.
Subjects with high IL-33/LPS mast cell signature enrichment exhibited neutrophil activation along with NF-κB and IL-1β/TNF-α pathway activation.
The IFN-γ-stimulated mast cell signature had the greatest enrichment in TAC2 and TAC3 molecular phenotypes, which were associated with responses to viral infection.
Findings on mast cell signature enrichment patterns in severe asthma phenotypes were replicated in an independent ADEPT asthma cohort.
Fabry's disease is an X-linked inherited multisystem disorder caused by deficient activity of the lysosomal enzyme α-galactosidase.
Neuropsychiatric manifestations of Fabry's disease reported in the literature mainly include small fiber neuropathy, cerebral microangiopathy, and depression.
In this reported patient, a psychotic episode associated with thalamic ischemic stroke was the first manifestation leading to diagnosis of Fabry's disease.
The authors recommend including psychiatric evaluation and screening as well as brain MRI in the routine initial workup of patients newly diagnosed with Fabry's disease.
Biallelic SORD mutations were identified in 5 of 78 patients with unclarified CMT2/dHMN (6.4%) and in 5 of 485 total hereditary neuropathy patients (1%).

The c.757delG (p.A253Qfs*27) variant was the most predominant SORD mutation, found in homozygous or compound heterozygous states in 5 affected patients, with a heterozygous carrier frequency of 0.46% in 650 healthy Chinese controls.
Three novel missense SORD variants (p.P244L, p.A259V, p.L284P) were identified in compound heterozygous state with c.757delG in three patients and classified as likely pathogenic per ACMG criteria.

Patients with biallelic SORD mutations presented with pure motor axonal neuropathy of childhood/adolescent onset, characterized by symmetrical distal lower-limb muscle wasting, decreased/absent deep tendon reflexes, and foot deformities, with mild-to-moderate progression (mean CMTNS 12.2).

Electrophysiological studies showed reduced compound muscle action potential (CMAP) most pronounced in the peroneal nerve, with normal motor nerve conduction velocity (MCV), consistent with a pure motor axonal neuropathy.

In a patient with numbness and a positive pinprick test, sympathetic skin response (SSR) and contact heat evoked potential (CHEP) testing showed prolonged latency and decreased amplitude on the affected side, indicating small fiber impairment despite normal sensory nerve action potential (SNAP) and sensory conduction velocity (SCV).

Two patients (1 and 5) with minor sensory involvement had normal sensory nerve action potential (SNAP) and sensory conduction velocity (SCV) in median, ulnar, and sural nerves despite subjective numbness and pain.

Muscle MRI in a patient with SORD-related neuropathy showed slight fatty infiltration and edema in the anterior tibial and extensor hallucis longus muscles and distinct fatty infiltration in the gastrocnemius muscle, while lumbar nerve root/plexus morphology was normal.

Prior mechanistic work (cited) demonstrated complete loss of SORD protein and increased intracellular sorbitol in patient-derived fibroblasts with SORD nonsense variants, implicating polyol pathway dysregulation as the mechanism of SORD-related neuropathy.
Aldose reductase inhibitors epalrestat and ranirestat (cited from prior literature) rescued synaptic degeneration and motor deficiency caused by loss of SORD orthologs in a Drosophila model.

Detection rates of biallelic SORD mutations varied across cohorts/studies: 6.4% (this study), similar to INC cohort findings, 7.5% (3/40) in CMT2 and 1.4% (3/215) in CMT overall in one study, and 13.8% (4/29) in unclarified CMT2/dHMN in another.
Combined Notch and TGF-beta signaling in mouse bone marrow-derived mast cells synergistically upregulates mucosal mast cell markers mMCP-1, mMCP-2, and CD103 more than either pathway alone.
Notch and TGF-beta-mediated transcription of mucosal mast cell marker genes both depend on the TGF-beta signaling transducer SMAD4.
Notch signaling markedly upregulates mMCP-1 and mMCP-2 expression through epigenetic deregulation of their promoter regions, but does not affect the CD103 gene promoter.

Forced expression of a constitutively active Notch2 intracellular domain in bone marrow-derived mast cells promotes nuclear localization of SMAD3 and SMAD4 and drives SMAD4-dependent gene transcription.
Mutations in TGFBR1, a gene encoding a component of the TGF-beta signaling pathway, are one of the genetic causes of Loeys-Dietz syndrome.
Mutations in TGFBR2, a gene encoding a component of the TGF-beta signaling pathway, are one of the genetic causes of Loeys-Dietz syndrome.
Mutations in SMAD2, a gene encoding a component of the TGF-beta signaling pathway, are one of the genetic causes of Loeys-Dietz syndrome.
Mutations in SMAD3, a gene encoding a component of the TGF-beta signaling pathway, are one of the genetic causes of Loeys-Dietz syndrome.
Mutations in TGFB2, a gene encoding a component of the TGF-beta signaling pathway, are one of the genetic causes of Loeys-Dietz syndrome.
Mutations in TGFB3, a gene encoding a component of the TGF-beta signaling pathway, are one of the genetic causes of Loeys-Dietz syndrome.
The most typical clinical presentation of Loeys-Dietz syndrome is a triad of hypertelorism, bifid uvula or cleft palate, and aortic aneurysm with arterial tortuosity.
Mutations in SMAD3, a downstream mediator of the TGF-beta signalling pathway, are a genetic cause of Loeys-Dietz syndrome.
Mutations in TGFB2, a ligand of the TGF-beta signalling pathway, are a genetic cause of Loeys-Dietz syndrome.
Mutations in TGFB3, a ligand of the TGF-beta signalling pathway, are a genetic cause of Loeys-Dietz syndrome.
Despite the loss-of-function nature of the causative mutations, aortic tissue from Loeys-Dietz syndrome patients paradoxically shows increased rather than decreased TGF-beta signalling.
The paradoxically increased TGF-beta signalling observed in Loeys-Dietz syndrome tissue offers new potential avenues for therapeutic intervention.
Meester-Loeys syndrome is caused by loss-of-function mutations in the BGN gene, which encodes the small leucine-rich proteoglycan biglycan.
Although the functional consequences of BGN mutations are not fully understood, increased TGF-beta signaling has been observed in Meester-Loeys syndrome.
Aortic dissections in Meester-Loeys syndrome typically occur at young ages and are observed more often in males.
Restraint stress increased plasma corticotropin-releasing factor levels in rats, indicating activation of the stress axis.
Restraint stress increased hippocampal 5-HT levels in the brain of the IBS rat model.
Restraint stress increased cortical 5-HT levels in the brain of the IBS rat model.
Restraint stress increased colonic mast cell inflammatory mediators in the IBS rat model.
Restraint stress increased colonic oxidative stress biomarkers in the IBS rat model.
Restraint stress produced histopathological inflammatory changes in the rat colon.
Restraint stress decreased colonic 5-HT content in the IBS rat model.
Restraint stress induced histopathological inflammatory changes in the colon of rats, consistent with an IBS-like phenotype.
Treatment with the herbal preparation STW 5 normalized the stress-induced alterations in 5-HT levels across the brain-gut axis (hippocampus, cortex, and colon).
STW 5 treatment counteracted the stress-induced increase in oxidative stress biomarkers seen in restraint-stressed rats.
STW 5 treatment reversed the histopathological inflammatory changes and mast cell inflammatory mediator elevations induced by restraint stress in the colon.

A roughly 50% loss of neuronal cell bodies in the myenteric and submucosal ganglia compared to controls appears to represent a critical threshold for the onset of clinical manifestations such as recurrent sub-occlusive episodes, nausea and vomiting.
Aganglionosis can arise as an acquired condition in about 20-30% of patients with Chagas disease, caused by Trypanosoma cruzi infection transmitted by Triatominae insects.
Most Hirschsprung's disease cases carry mutations in RET, affecting coding or non-coding regions of the gene.
Mutations in EDNRB and SOX10 impact RET signaling and thereby contribute to causing Hirschsprung's disease.
A SGOL1 mutation was found to cause chronic atrial and intestinal dysrhythmia (CAID) syndrome, a novel generalized dysrhythmia affecting both cardiac and gut (ICC-generated) rhythmicity.

WES in a large consanguineous family with autosomal recessive CIPO, megaduodenum, long-segment Barrett esophagus and cardiac abnormalities (Mungan syndrome) identified a novel homozygous RAD21 missense variant.
Zebrafish embryos with morpholino-mediated rad21 knockdown showed delayed food transit along the gut compared to controls, assessed via fluorescent bead microgavage.
rad21 morphant zebrafish showed a significant, quantified depletion of enteric neurons (HuC/D-immunolabeled) in the gut compared to controls, providing a neurogenic model of RAD21-related CIPO.

In mouse small intestine, RAD21 immunoreactivity was detected in a subset of myenteric neurons, present in 42.5% of HuC/D-immunoreactive neurons per field, including a subset of ChAT-positive cholinergic neurons.

Preliminary data from a Rad21 conditional knock-in mouse (Ala626Thr) showed an overall reduction of HuC/D myenteric neurons per field versus wild-type controls, approximately 20% in the ileum and 30% in the colon.
Both cholinergic (ChAT+) excitatory and nitrergic (nNOS+) inhibitory myenteric neuron populations were reduced in Rad21KI mice compared to wild-type controls.
TYMP mutations cause thymidine phosphorylase dysfunction leading to accumulation of dThd and dUrd and reduced dCTP in plasma/tissues, disrupting mtDNA replication in MNGIE patients.
POLG mutations cause secondary mtDNA defects (depletion and multiple deletions) leading to a clinical syndrome resembling MNGIE but without brain leukoencephalopathy.
Compound heterozygous RRM2B mutations cause a phenotype with ophthalmoplegia, ptosis, GI dysmotility, cachexia and peripheral neuropathy, clinically indistinguishable from TYMP-mutated MNGIE.
WES in seven CIPO patients with MNGIE-like neurological features from three unrelated families identified compound heterozygous, predicted-damaging LIG3 variants in all patients.
Patient-derived fibroblasts and transfected cells expressing mutant LIG3 showed markedly reduced LIG3 protein levels and a complete lack of mitochondrial ligase activity compared to controls.

LIG3 gene defects altered the mitochondrial network and caused mtDNA depletion (without multiple deletions seen in other mitochondrial disorders), impaired ATP production and increased mitochondrial reactive oxygen species generation.
Disruption of lig3 in zebrafish reproduced key patient features including brain leukoencephalopathy, impaired gut transit, and altered mitochondrial networks.
Histopathology and HuC/D immunoreactivity in gut (colon) biopsies from LIG3 variant patients showed significantly fewer myenteric neuronal cell bodies compared to controls.

Combining human PSC-derived neural crest cells with developing human intestinal organoids recapitulated normal ENS development in vivo, forming neuro-glial structures resembling myenteric/submucosal plexuses with functional ICCs and propagating contractions.

Using the PHOX2B-/- HSCR mouse model, researchers developed a functional intestinal tissue that could be transplanted in vivo, highlighting stem-cell-based therapy potential for severe gut dysmotility.
Molecular profiling identified twelve distinct enteric neuron classes within the myenteric plexus of the mouse small intestine, including motor, sensory and interneurons with class-specific markers.
Genes controlling epigenetic modifications were shown for the first time to coordinate intestinal tract development and influence ENS development.

Single-nucleus RNA-sequencing mapping of enteric neuron subtypes in duodenum, ileum and colon showed overall conservation between humans and mice, but some subtype-specific genes were expressed in morphologically distinct neuron subtypes between species.
TGF-β serum concentrations are elevated in idiopathic PAH patients and implicated in disease pathogenesis via enhanced vascular cell proliferation.
BMPR2 protein levels are reduced in SSc-PAH patients, with increased proteasomal degradation of BMPR2 observed in a relevant mouse model.
A BMPR2 splice variant lacking exon 12 (which encodes the cytoplasmic tail) is associated with increased likelihood of developing PAH.
Loss-of-function mutations in BMPR2 account for over 80% of hereditary PAH cases and approximately 20% of idiopathic PAH cases.
miR-21 is upregulated in pulmonary artery endothelial and smooth muscle cells and regulates target genes including BMPR2, PDCD4/caspase-3, PCNA, cyclin D1, Bcl-xL, and DDAH1 in PAH.
miR-21 suppresses SMAD7, an anti-fibrotic signaling molecule, promoting a pro-fibrotic effect via TGF-β signaling in SSc dermal fibroblasts.

Let-7 family microRNA expression in skin and lung tissue was lower in SSc patients with pulmonary hypertension than in those without, with let-7b and let-7d levels negatively correlating with PH severity.
let-7a expression was downregulated in SSc and localized scleroderma skin, with decreased serum concentration, and miRNA injection improved bleomycin-induced skin fibrosis in mice.

Lower serum miR-29a levels were associated with higher right ventricular systolic pressure in SSc patients, suggesting involvement in pulmonary hypertension pathogenesis, although no significant difference in serum miR-29a was found overall between SSc patients and controls.

miR-29a-3p is decreased in hypoxia-induced pulmonary adventitial fibroblasts, and its overexpression decreases pulmonary artery pressure and right ventricle hypertrophy index while ameliorating pulmonary vascular remodeling in hypoxic PH rats.
Increased miR-155 expression in patients with SSc-associated interstitial lung disease is associated with impaired respiratory function and increased lung fibrosis, and it targets SMAD2 mRNA.

miR-145 was downregulated in SSc fibroblasts while its predicted target Smad3 was upregulated, and in a separate context miR-145 was upregulated in PAH patients and PASMCs where it promoted hypoxia-induced proliferation and migration via ABCA1.

miR-140-5p is downregulated in treatment-naive PAH patients and experimental models; it inhibits HPASMC proliferation/differentiation and promotes apoptosis, preventing PAH development, acting partly by targeting TGF-βR1.
miR-221-3p was elevated in lung tissue and PASMCs of PAH patients and animal models, and together with AXIN2 may regulate PASMC proliferation.
miR-124 expression was reduced in pulmonary vascular and circulating progenitor endothelial cells from PAH patients, contributing to enhanced endothelial cell glycolysis via PTBP1/PKM2.

miR-143 was upregulated in PASMCs, calf models, and lung tissues of PAH patients, and inhibition of miR-143-3p blocked experimental pulmonary hypertension, indicating a protective/essential role in PAH pathobiology.

A missense mutation p.H288Y in KLF2 reduced expression of exosomal miR-181a-5p and miR-324-5p in PAH patients, and these miRNAs reduced proliferative/angiogenic responses and attenuated disease progression in PAH mice.

miR-455-3p-1 was downregulated in PAH patient tissue by microarray analysis; its upregulation was associated with reduced RAS/ERK pathway gene expression and inhibited PASMC proliferation, alleviating PAH in vivo.
miR-223-3p overexpression and ITGB3 knockdown alleviated PAH pathological features in rats, suggesting a role for miR-223-3p in PAH via ITGB3 in the extracellular matrix pathway.

Elevated miR-29 family expression was associated with energy metabolism in heritable PAH patients, with the estrogen metabolite 16α-hydroxyestrone promoting HPAH development via miR-29 upregulation; anti-miR-29 treatment improved HPAH in Bmpr2 mutant mice.
Disturbance of miR-204 expression contributes to activation of STAT3/NFAT signaling, a pathway implicated in PAH-PASMC proliferation and resistance to apoptosis.

The miR-130/301 family shows proliferative and vasoconstrictive actions in pulmonary hypertension, modulating apelin-miR-424/503-FGF2 signaling in endothelial cells and STAT3-miR-204 signaling in smooth muscle cells to promote PH-associated phenotypes, acting via PPARγ.

miR-424(322), secreted by pulmonary arterial endothelial cells, targets SMURF1 and sustains BMPR2 signaling; circulating levels correlate with right ventricle hypertrophy stage and inversely with SMURF1 levels in the monocrotaline rat model.
Persistent STAT3 activation induces miR-17/92 expression, which represses BMPR2 protein expression, implicating this cluster in the pathogenesis of pulmonary hypertension.
AntagomiR-20a treatment restored functional BMPR2 levels in pulmonary arteries in an in vivo PH model, suggesting a potential approach to prevent vascular remodeling.
Rodent models of altered intestinal motility resembling IBS show that CRF receptor 1 (CRF-R1) mediates intestinal hypersensitivity under many conditions.

Translation of preclinical CRF-R1 antagonist studies into successful clinical trials for IBS has not been achieved, likely due to insufficient understanding of CRF-R1 variants and antagonist properties.

Intrauterine NO deficiency induced by maternal L-NAME treatment reduced the total length of adrenergic (sympathetic) nerve fibers in the saphenous artery of two-week-old offspring compared to controls.
The relaxed inner diameter of saphenous arteries was smaller in L-NAME offspring compared to controls.
L-NAME offspring saphenous arteries showed increased sensitivity to moderate concentrations of the α1-adrenoceptor agonist methoxamine but reduced maximum contractile force compared to controls.

Even in the presence of the NOS inhibitor L-NNA (removing endothelial NO influence), saphenous artery sensitivity to methoxamine remained higher in L-NAME offspring than controls, indicating a smooth-muscle-level (denervation-related) hypersensitivity.
Non-muscle β-actin mRNA expression was increased in saphenous arteries from L-NAME offspring, resulting in a decreased α-actin/β-actin expression ratio compared to controls.
Smooth muscle α-actin mRNA expression in the saphenous artery did not differ between L-NAME and control offspring.
Non-smooth-muscle myosin heavy chain (NM-MHC) mRNA expression was slightly increased in saphenous arteries of L-NAME offspring, while SM-MHC and the SM-MHC/NM-MHC ratio were unchanged.
α1A-adrenoceptor mRNA levels in saphenous artery did not differ between L-NAME and control offspring, suggesting adrenergic hypersensitivity is not due to receptor upregulation.
Two-week-old L-NAME offspring had lower baseline mean arterial pressure than control offspring.

Ganglionic blockade with chlorisondamine eliminated the mean arterial pressure difference between L-NAME and control offspring, indicating that the baseline pressure deficit is due to a reduced neurogenic/sympathetic component of vascular tone.

Baseline heart rate and the heart rate response to ganglionic blockade were similar between control and L-NAME offspring, suggesting adrenal catecholamine-driven cardiac chronotropy was less affected by intrauterine NO deficiency than vascular sympathetic tone.

Chronic L-NAME consumption (250 mg/L drinking water, ~37 mg/kg/day) increased systolic blood pressure in pregnant dams at gestation days 15 and 20, with a compensatory decrease in heart rate, modeling preeclampsia-like hypertension.

Blood NO metabolite content was strongly reduced in L-NAME-treated dams and in their offspring at postnatal day 2, confirming the NO deficiency model; NO metabolite levels recovered to control levels in offspring by postnatal day 14.
Offspring born from L-NAME-treated females had reduced body weight at postnatal day 2 but reached control values by postnatal day 14.
About one-fifth of women with endometriosis reported limitations in at least one basic activity of daily living.
Nearly two-fifths of women with endometriosis reported limitations in at least one instrumental activity of daily living such as housework, shopping, or meal preparation.
Women with severe pelvic pain had over three times higher odds of ADL limitations compared with those with less severe pain.
Women with severe pelvic pain had nearly eight times higher odds of IADL limitations compared with those with less severe pain.
Chronic fatigue was positively associated with ADL and IADL limitations and mediated the relationship between pelvic pain and functional limitations.
Pain-catastrophizing thoughts were positively associated with ADL and IADL limitations and mediated the relationship between pelvic pain and functional limitations.

In this UK Biobank cohort, participants with a diagnosis of chronic fatigue syndrome had a significantly higher hazard of developing stomach cancer compared with those without CFS, after adjusting for age, sex, socioeconomic status, BMI, physical activity, alcohol and smoking.
Several HLA class II alleles (HLA-DQA1*01, HLA-DQB1*06, DQB1*0303, HLA-DQ3, HLA-DR4, HLA-DR5) have been reported to associate with increased risk of ME/CFS, though the supporting data are limited.
A statistically significant elevation of anti-EBV-dUTPase antibodies has been reported in a subgroup of ME/CFS patients.
A defective EBV-specific B and T cell response has been reported in a subgroup of ME/CFS patients.
A high rate of active EBV infection has been reported in a subgroup of ME/CFS patients.
Serologic evidence of EBV reactivation with elevated IgM antibodies against late viral capsid antigen (VCA) has been observed in some ME/CFS patients.
EBV-induced gene 2 (EBI2) mRNA was found to be up-regulated in peripheral blood mononuclear cells from a subgroup of ME/CFS patients.
Multiple studies report decreased NK cell cytotoxic activity in ME/CFS patients, though numerous other studies have failed to reproduce this finding.

ME/CFS patients have also been reported to show increased IL-10 levels, augmented Th2 response, Treg expansion, and impaired T cell response to mitogens and other antigens, though replication has been inconsistent.
B-cell depletion using several infusions of rituximab over 12 months was not associated with clinical improvement in patients with ME/CFS.
Results of clinical trials using antiviral agents in ME/CFS have been inconclusive and, in some cases, contradictory.

Anecdotal reports describe resolution of symptoms in some ME/CFS patients with elevated anti-EBV antibodies following treatment with rituximab or antivirals (valaciclovir, valganciclovir), but this has not been confirmed in larger series.

The authors propose that low-dose DNA demethylation agents (e.g., decitabine, 5-azacitidine) followed by EBV-specific T cell immunotherapy and antivirals could be a potential therapeutic strategy for a putative EBV-associated ME/CFS subgroup, based on their demonstrated effect of restoring immunogenic viral antigen expression in EBV-associated lymphoma.
ME/CFS prevalence ranges between 0.1% and 2.5% of the general population depending on the diagnostic criteria applied.
The annual incidence of ME/CFS cases in the United Kingdom is reported as 14.8 per 100,000 people.
A prospective study of college students following infectious mononucleosis found that those who went on to develop ME/CFS had more physical symptoms and immune irregularities at baseline.

The authors hypothesize that HLA-II alleles associated with increased EBV susceptibility may explain the higher prevalence of autoimmune disorders (e.g., rheumatoid arthritis, type 1 diabetes) and cancer observed in first-degree relatives of ME/CFS patients.
Participants described profound biographical disruption and loss of identity as CFS/ME prevented them from sustaining previous roles and activities central to their sense of self.
Participants reported that CFS/ME interrupted anticipated future life trajectories, such as relationships and career, leaving futures uncertain and identities sabotaged.

Participants experienced disbelief and scepticism from healthcare professionals, including being told their illness was psychosomatic, which denied them a legitimate 'sick' identity and compounded distress.
Family and friends' disbelief and refusal to accept the illness were also described as a disabling community that disrupted familial identity and exacerbated the condition.

Participation in closed Facebook peer-support groups functioned as an enabling community, providing normalisation, belonging, and a route from newcomer to expert/advocate identity for people with CFS/ME.
Some participants found renegotiated identity and meaning through new activities (e.g., crochet, college, writing) that allowed continued participation and purpose alongside CFS/ME.
The majority of PASC patients (58%, 24/41) had a peak VO2 below 80% of predicted, consistent with circulatory impairment during cardiopulmonary exercise testing.
Dysfunctional breathing, characterized by erratic ventilation and dissociation between respiratory rate and tidal volume, was observed in 26 of 41 patients (63%) during CPET.

Almost all patients (88%) exhibited abnormal ventilatory findings, including dysfunctional breathing, resting hypocapnia, and/or an excessive ventilatory response to exercise (elevated VE/VCO2 slope).
61% of patients (25/41) had resting end-tidal CO2 below the lower limit of normal (<35 mm Hg), indicating hypocapnia.
PetCO2 significantly increased from rest to anaerobic threshold and then decreased at peak exercise across the cohort.
46% of patients with PASC (19 of 41) met diagnostic criteria for ME/CFS after excluding those with confounding cardiac disease or obesity.
5 of 7 patients undergoing invasive CPET had hemodynamic evidence of preload failure, with blunted right atrial pressure rise during exercise.
All 5 patients with preload failure had symptoms consistent with ME/CFS, though only 3 fully met diagnostic criteria after exclusion for BMI or reduced ejection fraction.
2 of 7 patients undergoing invasive CPET had hemodynamics consistent with exercise-induced pulmonary hypertension and did not meet ME/CFS criteria.
Patients with dysfunctional breathing (n=26) did not differ significantly from those with a normal breathing pattern (n=15) in peak VO2, resting PetCO2, maximum VE, RR, or RER.

Severe hypocapnia (PetCO2 ≤31 mmHg) occurred at similar rates in patients meeting ME/CFS criteria (7/19) and those who did not (6/22), showing no clear association between hypocapnia and ME/CFS status.
Dysfunctional breathing occurred at similar rates in patients meeting ME/CFS criteria (42%) and those who did not (57%).
2 of the 41 PASC patients had a pre-existing diagnosis of postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome as a baseline comorbidity.
22 of 41 patients had a reduced VO2 pulse, indicating impaired stroke volume response during exercise.
23 of 41 patients had an elevated VE/VCO2 slope (>30), indicating ventilatory inefficiency.
27% of patients surviving 4 years after the 2005 SARS epidemic fulfilled criteria for ME/CFS, supporting a post-viral ME/CFS phenomenon analogous to that seen after COVID-19.
CFS/ME patients scored significantly lower on the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) than controls, though both groups remained within the normal range.
A subset of CFS/ME patients (6%, N=5) showed mild cognitive impairment (MoCA score <21), a level not observed in controls.
Women in the CFS/ME group performed significantly better than men on the MoCA test.
The Global Index of Attention and Perception (GIAP), measured by the Toulouse-Piéron sustained attention test, was significantly lower in CFS/ME patients compared to controls.
No statistically significant differences were found in GIAP scores between women and men within the CFS/ME group.
76% (N=64) of CFS/ME patients showed a significant deficit in maintained attention after only 10 minutes of testing, with 6% unable to complete the test due to extreme fatigue.
Pre-test and post-test fatigue (VAS) were highly significantly elevated in CFS/ME patients compared to controls.

CFS/ME patients (both women and men) showed a highly significant increase in fatigue from pre-test to post-test after the Toulouse-Piéron attention test, whereas controls showed no significant change.
Perceived cognitive effort (modified Borg scale) after the attention test was significantly higher in CFS/ME patients than in controls.
Within the CFS/ME group, women reported significantly higher perceived cognitive effort (Borg scale) than men.
There was no significant difference in GIAP scores between CFS/ME patients with a comorbid reactive depression diagnosis and those without.

In one study, better visuospatial learning and poorer letter fluency were associated with higher IL-1β, while better visual attention/processing speed/mental flexibility (Trail Making Test) was associated with higher IL-6, showing mixed-direction relationships between objective executive function and cytokines.
Higher subjective cognitive difficulties (poorer executive function) were associated with higher CD4+ counts and lower CD8+ counts/percentage in two studies.
Poorer objective executive function (visual reproduction) was associated with a lower CD4+ percentage in one study.
Lower perceived ability to enact stress management skills (poorer emotion regulation) was associated with higher IL-2 levels.
No significant association was found between emotion regulation (emotional reactions) and IL-2 receptor levels.
Higher levels of social isolation (poorer interpersonal function) were significantly associated with higher IL-6 levels.
Poorer subjective sleep quality and quantity were significantly associated with higher levels of IL-1β, IL-6, and TNF-α (regression analysis).
Higher levels of sleeplessness were associated with higher levels of IL-6 and IL-2R in another study.
Worse mental health and higher role limitations due to emotional problems were associated with lower CD4+ count/percentage and higher CD8+ percentage in one study.
No significant associations were found between anxiety/phobic anxiety and the cytokines IL-4, IL-6, and TNF-α.
Higher levels of depression were significantly associated with higher IL-6 in one study, but no significant association was found in another.
Higher levels of depressive symptoms were significantly associated with higher composite inflammation (IL-2, IL-6, and TNF-α) using structural equation modeling.
Presence of a personality disorder was associated with lower TNF-α levels, whereas higher global psychiatric symptom intensity was associated with higher TNF-α levels (regression analysis).
More anti-social, sadistic, and passive-aggressive personality styles and higher levels of alcohol and drug dependence were associated with higher CD4+ counts.
No significant associations were found between fatigue/energy level and any of the cytokines examined (IL-1β, IL-2(R), IL-4, IL-6, TNF-α) across studies.
Higher fatigue levels were associated with a higher CD4+ percentage and a lower CD8+ percentage in one study.
No significant associations were found between (bodily) pain and the cytokines IL-2R and IL-6, or between pain and CD4+/CD8+ T cells.

In a placebo-controlled trial of high-dose intravenous immunoglobulin (immunotherapy), percentage decrease in depressive symptoms was significantly associated with percentage increase in CD4+ cell counts following treatment, but not following placebo.

In a randomized controlled trial of cognitive behavior therapy (CBT), despite clinical improvement in fatigue, CBT had no detectable impact on immunological parameters (CD4+/CD8+ counts), and immune status did not predict treatment response.
Of 139 eligible patients, 107 (77.0%) were recruited at baseline and 65 (60.7%) completed the post-treatment measures, an attrition rate of 39.3%.
At 3-month follow-up, 52 of 65 T2 completers (80%) returned questionnaires, giving an overall attrition rate from baseline of 51.4%.
Patients with CFS/ME had markedly higher attrition than those without CFS/ME, with only 50% completing post-treatment measures compared with 62% of non-CFS/ME participants.
Participants with CFS/ME who completed the programme rated their satisfaction with programme length and content very highly (mean 9.0 and 9.2 out of 10).
All five subthemes of the Activity Pacing Questionnaire (APQ-28) improved between baseline and end of the 6-week programme, indicating increased use of activity pacing strategies.
In the CFS/ME subgroup, improvements were observed across all APQ-28 activity pacing subthemes and symptom measures both at end of treatment and at 3-month follow-up.
Physical function (SF-12) improved by a mean of 4.67 points between baseline and end of treatment, exceeding the minimally clinically important change of 3.29.
Avoidance (PASS-20 escape/avoidance subscale) did not show a statistically robust improvement between baseline and 3-month follow-up, as the confidence interval crossed zero.
Physical function (SF-12) improvement from baseline to 3-month follow-up was not statistically robust, with a confidence interval crossing zero.
Mental function (SF-12) improved by a mean of 7.3 points at end of treatment and remained above the minimally clinically important change (3.77) at 3-month follow-up (mean change=5.95).

Health-related quality of life (EQ-5D-5L index) improved by 0.13 between baseline and end of treatment and by 0.07 at 3-month follow-up, both exceeding the minimally important difference of 0.037±0.008.

Pain self-efficacy (PSEQ) improved from a mean of 25.29 at baseline to 36.29 at end of treatment and 34.68 at 3-month follow-up, an improvement exceeding the minimally important change of 5.5, although still below the cut-off of 40.

Depression scores (PHQ-9) fell from the moderate range at baseline (13.7) to mild at end of treatment (7.1) and follow-up (9.1), with a clinically significant reduction (≥5 points) between baseline and end of treatment.
