Mean anxiety scores (GAD-7) reduced from 9.9 at baseline to 5.4 at end of treatment and 6.10 at follow-up, remaining within the mild anxiety classification.
The newly added APQ-28 item on finding a baseline activity level (APQ12) correlated strongly with its allocated Activity Adjustment subtheme, supporting good item-total fit.
The newly added APQ-28 item on having a flexible approach to activities (APQ15) correlated well with its allocated Activity Acceptance subtheme.
Nearly two-thirds of participants (61.3%) reported having two or more coexisting chronic pain/fatigue conditions, illustrating high comorbidity in this population.

Among the 12 participants with CFS/ME, 10 identified it as their main condition, and 11 reported at least one comorbid condition (low back pain, chronic widespread pain, fibromyalgia, or another condition).

The authors note their finding of symptom improvement in CFS/ME patients with the rehabilitative activity pacing framework contrasts with other studies in which pacing (an energy-conservation, symptom-contingent approach) has been reported as ineffective.
In a cited RCT comparing operant pacing with energy conservation for fibromyalgia, only the operant approach (not energy conservation) was associated with reduced avoidance.
The nationwide physician-diagnosed annual incidence rate of CFS in South Korea over 11 years averaged 44.71 per 100,000 individuals.
The nationwide prevalence rate of CFS in South Korea over 11 years averaged 57.70 per 100,000 individuals, equal to about 0.057% of the population.
Females were diagnosed with CFS at a 1.49-fold higher incidence rate than males, a statistically significant difference.
Females showed a 1.49-fold higher CFS prevalence rate than males, consistent with the incidence pattern.
CFS incidence peaked in males over age 80 and in females aged 60-69, both reaching a rate of about 70.7 per 100,000.
CFS prevalence rate peaked in males over 80 years old and in females aged 60-69 years.
Both the incidence and prevalence rates of CFS in South Korea increased substantially over the 11-year study period, more markedly in prevalence.

Among patients newly diagnosed with CFS in 2011, the median duration of continued clinical treatment was approximately 9.13 months, far shorter than the reported natural illness duration of about 7 years.
Follow-up treatment for CFS declined sharply after initial diagnosis, with only 9.97% of 2011-diagnosed patients still receiving CFS treatment the following year, dropping to 1.86% by 2020.

The sex difference in CFS incidence/prevalence is hypothesized to be driven primarily by sex hormones, supported by the onset of the female-predominant pattern coinciding with puberty (around age 13).
Unlike the overall female-predominant pattern, males under age 10 showed a higher CFS incidence rate than females in that age group.
No significant differences were found in CFS occurrence between megacities and other regions, nor in the profile of disorders diagnosed prior to the initial CFS diagnosis.

The physician-diagnosis-based CFS prevalence found in this study (0.057%) was far lower than the ~0.77% pooled prevalence from a prior meta-analysis of five Korean studies using interviews/questionnaires.

South Korea's physician-diagnosed CFS incidence rate (44.71/100,000) was substantially lower than incidence rates reported in US studies (180/100,000 in Wichita; 13.2 vs higher in Olmsted County) and a UK GPRD study (27.0/100,000), reflecting differences in case ascertainment methods.
Among CFS patients who were employed at baseline, 53% remained in employment at follow-up, while 6% who were working at baseline were unable to continue working.
Of the CFS patients who were not working at baseline, 9% had returned to work by follow-up.
Age, fatigue severity, functional impairment, cognitive and behavioural responses, and depressive symptoms were factors that impacted patients' work status at follow-up.
Data from the COVID-19 Symptom Study app (>4 million users, US/UK/Sweden) indicated about 10% of SARS-CoV-2 positive patients remain symptomatic beyond 3 weeks.
Among 3762 participants with confirmed or suspected COVID-19 across 56 countries, 91% took more than 35 weeks to recover, with substantial impact on work capacity.
The risk of developing long COVID increases with age, from 1-2% in patients in their twenties to about 5% in people in their sixties.

In a Bangladesh prospective cohort, 46% of 400 patients developed post-COVID symptoms, of whom 70% had post-viral fatigue; female sex, respiratory distress, longer disease duration, and lethargy predicted susceptibility.

Tansley et al. found 18% of 117 SARS-CoV survivors had a reduced 6-minute walk test due to shortness of breath and fatigue at 1 year, with quality of life reduced at 3 months and improving but not normalizing by 1 year.
Batawi et al. followed 78 MERS-CoV survivors and found reduced quality of life, significantly lower in those with prior critical care admission.
A 3-month follow-up study showed persisting pulmonary radiological abnormalities in 70% of subjects after COVID-19.
A German follow-up study of 100 COVID-19 patients found myocardial inflammation in 60% and cardiac abnormalities in 78% of subjects, independent of initial disease severity.
A cohort of 22 post-SARS-CoV syndrome patients exhibited fatigue, myalgia, depression, and poor sleep resembling ME/CFS.
CFS-like symptoms were described in 48% of MERS-CoV survivors at 1 year follow-up.
A systematic review found that 55.17% of published reports on long-COVID were mainly based on chronic fatigue and pain as main symptoms.
Long/post-COVID syndrome is predominantly seen in females, analogous to other autoimmune disorders, with proposed T- and B-cell dysregulation and possible gut microbiota changes.
Lymphopenia is a typical feature of severe COVID-19, and T- and/or B-cell deficiency correlates with persistent/ongoing virus shedding.

ACE2 receptors, the route of SARS-CoV-2 entry, are expressed in the hypothalamus, pituitary, adrenal gland, thyroid, testes, and pancreatic islets, implicating the endocrine system in COVID-19 and recovery.
Postmortem examination detected SARS-CoV RNA in the pituitary gland, parathyroid, pancreas, and adrenal gland.
In SARS-CoV patients, apoptotic parafollicular and follicular thyroid cells were found, explaining low serum triiodothyronine and thyroxine levels and osteonecrosis of the femoral head.
Evidence of hypocortisolism was found in 39% of 61 SARS survivors prospectively recruited for hormonal derangements 3 months after recovery.
Autopsies of SARS patients showed viral genome, edema, and neuronal degeneration in the hypothalamus.

Hypocortisolism persisted for up to 1 year in most recovered SARS patients along with central hypothyroidism and low DHEAS in some, supporting chronic ACTH deficiency attributed to hypophysitis or direct hypothalamic damage.
Wheatland et al. showed that the SARS virus expresses amino acids mimicking ACTH residues, potentially causing cross-reactive antibody-mediated destruction of ACTH and relative adrenal insufficiency.

In 28 hospitalized COVID-19 patients, 32% had subnormal cortisol levels, and those with more severe disease had both subnormal cortisol and ACTH levels, suggesting a direct association between infection severity and impaired glucocorticoid response.
In CFS patient groups, blunting of the HPA axis has been found, with reduced 24-hour free cortisol excretion, increased sensitivity to ACTH, and attenuated response to CRH.

In a postmortem study by Santana et al., microscopic adrenal lesions were identified in 46% of 28 patients, but cortisol measurement of pre-death stored plasma samples showed no evidence of adrenal insufficiency.

The RECOVERY trial established that dexamethasone use in hospitalized COVID-19 patients resulted in lower 28-day mortality among those receiving invasive mechanical ventilation or oxygen alone at randomization.

Clarke et al. found in a prospective study of 70 COVID-19 patients that adrenal and thyroid function ≥3 months after presentation was preserved, with normal Synacthen response regardless of severity, antibody status, or dexamethasone use, despite persistent fatigue.
Hanley et al. found chronic inflammation with follicular epithelial cell disruption in the thyroid in 2 of 9 (22%) postmortem SARS-CoV-2 patients.
A case report by Knack et al. describes a patient who developed Hashimoto's thyroiditis after remission from SARS-CoV-2, supporting the possibility of virus-triggered autoimmune thyroid disease.
Two cases of autoimmune hyperthyroidism after COVID-19 infection have been reported, one with prior Graves' disease in remission and one with no prior thyroid disease.

Studies found lower total triiodothyronine (TT3) and thyroid stimulating hormone (TSH) levels in COVID-19 patients compared to healthy controls, especially in severe cases, possibly reflecting nonthyroidal illness syndrome.
In adults without prior thyroid disorder followed up for long COVID, most abnormal thyroid function tests from acute COVID-19 resolved, and incident thyroid dysfunction was rare.

In an observational cohort of 334 COVID-19 patients, 86.6% were euthyroid on admission; TSH and free T4 were transiently lower than baseline consistent with nonthyroidal illness, but most patients became euthyroid again by a median follow-up of 79 days.
A prospective study of 70 COVID-19 patients found adrenal and thyroid function preserved at 3 or more months after COVID-19, despite most patients continuing to experience persistent fatigue.
Ding et al. did not detect SARS-CoV viral expression in the thyroid gland on postmortem examination.

Gu et al. found SARS genomic sequence-positive lymphocytes and monocytes within thyroid gland vessels on autopsy, though this may reflect immune cell dissemination rather than direct thyroid infection.

In a postmortem study of nine SARS-CoV-2 patients, Hanley et al. found chronic inflammation with follicular epithelial cell disruption in the thyroid of two patients (22%), of unknown clinical significance.
Knack et al. reported a case of a patient developing Hashimoto's thyroiditis after remission from SARS-CoV-2 infection, supporting a hypothesis of virus-triggered autoimmune thyroid disease.
Two cases of autoimmune hyperthyroidism following COVID-19 infection have been reported, one in a patient with prior Graves' disease in remission and another with no previous thyroid disease.

Studies found that total triiodothyronine (TT3) and thyroid stimulating hormone (TSH) levels were lower in active, severe COVID-19 patients than in healthy controls, possibly reflecting non-thyroidal illness syndrome.
In adults without known thyroid disorder followed up for long COVID, most abnormal thyroid function tests observed during acute COVID-19 resolved, and new-onset thyroid dysfunction was rare.

In an observational cohort of 334 COVID-19 patients, 86.6% were euthyroid on admission; TSH and free T4 were lower than baseline in a subset consistent with non-thyroidal illness, but most patients became euthyroid again by a median follow-up of 79 days, though long COVID symptoms were not assessed.
Both low-dose and high-dose cistanche/ginkgo botanical product significantly improved overall CFS effectiveness (remission plus relief) compared with placebo after 60 days.
Complete remission of CFS symptoms occurred in 15.5% of low-dose and 18.6% of high-dose subjects versus 0% in placebo.
Impaired memory/concentration, muscle pain, unrefreshing sleep, and post-exertional malaise were significantly relieved in both product groups compared to placebo.

Both low-dose and high-dose groups showed significantly lower Chalder physical and mental fatigue scores than placebo after 60 days, though the authors note the effect size (<1 point) may not be clinically meaningful.
The high-dose group showed superior improvement over the low-dose group in total physical fatigue score and drowsiness item, suggesting a dose-response effect.
The product improved quality-of-life scores across physical health, psychological, and social relationship domains but not the environment domain.
Sexual life quality scores improved with the product in all 10 items for male subjects, and in most items for female subjects, correlating with a trend of increased testosterone in men.
Blood ammonia concentration was significantly reduced in both low-dose and high-dose groups compared to placebo after intervention.
Blood lactic acid concentration was significantly lower in both product groups than placebo, with an 8% decrease in the high-dose group.
Testosterone showed a trend of increase after product intervention but did not reach statistical significance.
Changes in blood glucose concentration were significantly associated with CFS symptom effectiveness, with each unit increase in glucose associated with tripled odds of amelioration.
Increases in blood lactic acid concentration were associated with lower odds of CFS symptom amelioration, i.e., higher lactic acid predicted worse outcome.
Change in blood lactic acid concentration was significantly but weakly correlated with total physical fatigue score, problems of tiredness, and need to rest more, on the Chalder questionnaire.
Liver and kidney function biomarkers (ALT, AST, GGT, BUN) remained within normal ranges and showed no significant difference between groups throughout the study, indicating product safety.

Seven mild adverse events (3.68%) occurred across all subjects (upper respiratory infection, diarrhea, elevated BUN, elevated ALT/AST) but none were attributed to the study product, and no severe adverse events occurred.
Nocturia frequency significantly improved in the product group, attributed by the authors to the kidney-yang-tonifying effect of cistanche, and poor sleep quality is linked to nocturia in CFS.
Genetic testing identified a germline variant in COL3A1, encoding type III procollagen, leading to a diagnosis of vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.
Vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome carries a high risk of severe complications, with median life expectancy estimated at 48 years.
The patient developed a recurrent colonic perforation (having had a first perforation requiring Hartmann's operation at age 22), presenting as panperitonitis with abdominal pain.

Despite being generally contraindicated in vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome due to tissue fragility, open abdominal management, transcatheter arterial embolization, and negative-pressure wound therapy were used as life-saving measures and may be useful for patients who develop panperitonitis and massive intra-abdominal bleeding.
In a retrospective case series of 21 EDS patients seen by the senior author, swallowing, voice, and hyolaryngeal skeletal complex problems were the most commonly reported laryngological symptoms.
Among 8 EDS patients with available patient-reported outcome measures, the Reflux Severity Index showed a median of 25.5 with wide variation (range 0-33).
The Eating Assessment Tool (EAT-10) score in the same patient subgroup had a median of 21.5 with a range of 0-35, indicating variable swallowing-related impairment.
The Voice Handicap Index in this patient subgroup showed a median of 21.5 with a very wide range (0-104), reflecting large variability in voice-related handicap.
A literature review identified 12 studies meeting inclusion criteria, collectively describing at least 91 patients with laryngological presentations of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.
The paper reviews cases of spontaneous coronary artery rupture occurring in patients with Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome.
In 95% of patients with preoperative spinopelvic hypermobility, hypermobility (ΔSS stand-sit ≥30°) resolved by one year following total hip arthroplasty.
Mean change in sacral slope from standing to sitting (ΔSS stand-sit) decreased significantly from baseline to one year after THA.
Seated sacral slope increased significantly after THA, corresponding to a clinically significant decrease in seated functional cup anteversion.
Contralateral hip osteoarthritis severity was the only radiological factor found to predict persistence of spinopelvic hypermobility one year after THA.
Two closely spaced missense COL3A1 variants located 20 bases apart were found in cis and cosegregated with vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome across a large four-generation Chinese family.
p.Leu734Phe is a novel, non-glycine substitution missense COL3A1 variant not previously reported in the literature and absent from gnomAD.
p.Gly741Ser is a known pathogenic glycine substitution missense COL3A1 variant previously reported in vEDS patients, found here in cis with a second variant.
In transfected skin fibroblasts, each of the two COL3A1 missense variants alone significantly reduced COL3A1 protein levels compared to wild-type by Western blot.
The two COL3A1 variants in combination produced a synergistic, more profound reduction in COL3A1 protein level than either variant alone, suggesting a combined pathogenic effect.
Both COL3A1 missense variants were predicted to be damaging/harmful by in silico protein function prediction tools SIFT and PolyPhen.

Affected family members presented with severe vascular complications including bilateral internal carotid artery aneurysms, superior mesenteric artery dissection aneurysm, Stanford type B aortic dissection with abdominal aortic aneurysm, and intracranial arterial rupture.

The two COL3A1 variants in cis were found not only in clinically affected family members but also in two clinically healthy carriers (an infant under 1 year and a 16-year-old), indicating incomplete or age-dependent penetrance.
About 65% of COL3A1 mutations in vEDS substitute glycine residues in the triple helix domain and about 25% are splice-site variants causing in-frame exon skipping.
Null mutations causing COL3A1 haploinsufficiency are associated with a two-decade delay in onset of complications and reduced penetrance, with complications largely limited to vascular events.

Individuals with in-frame exon-skipping splice site variants have the lowest median survival, followed by glycine substitutions by bulky residues, while small-residue glycine substitutions produce milder phenotypes.
Substitutions of glutamic acid by lysine in the triple helical domain are associated with a skin phenotype more similar to classical EDS combined with gastrointestinal and vascular fragility.
A few individuals with bi-allelic COL3A1 variants have a severe vEDS phenotype associated with polymicrogyria, a neuronal post-migrational disorder.
As of September 30, 2021, 1904 COL3A1 variants had been submitted to ClinVar, of which 489 were classed pathogenic and 22 likely pathogenic.

gnomAD exome data (125,000 individuals) show COL3A1 is intolerant to loss-of-function variants (only 4 observed vs ~94 expected) and shows missense constraint (516 observed vs 851.7 expected; Z=4.09, observed/expected=0.61).
COL3A1 variants affecting glycine residues and a frameshift mutation have also been reported in sporadic (non-EDS) thoracic aortic aneurysm.
No association was found for common COL3A1 variants in genome-wide association studies for aneurysm formation, supporting a role for rare large-effect coding variants rather than common variants.

Three common COL3A1 variants were associated with stroke recurrence and prognosis in a Chinese cohort, but a large genome-wide meta-analysis covering ~500,000 patients found no association between COL3A1 and stroke risk.
Col3a1−/− mice show skin lesions with open wounds and significant reduction or absence of collagen fibrils in the aortic media, with larger-diameter collagen fibrils in the adventitia.
Col3a1+/− mice have a normal lifespan and no overt phenotype but show reduced collagen III content in aorta and bowel, reduced wall strength, and age-progressive aortic lesions.

CRISPR-generated Col3a1G209S/+ and Col3a1G938D/+ mice exhibit vascular phenotypes seen in vEDS patients, including sudden fatal aortic ruptures, with the more C-terminal mutation (G938D) causing a more severe phenotype and lower survival.

The Tsk2/+ mouse model, harboring a Cys33Ser missense mutation in the N-propeptide of collagen III, develops a systemic sclerosis-like phenotype with tight skin, increased collagen I deposition, fibrosis, thicker collagen fibrils, and autoantibodies.

Dermal fibroblasts from vEDS patients show significantly reduced extracellular collagen III secretion, now accepted as a defining feature of vEDS, also observed in tissues of mouse models with missense mutations.

Fibroblasts harboring glycine mutations and exon-skipping variants at the C-terminal end of the triple helix show almost complete failure to secrete type III collagen, with the non-secreted procollagen sequestered and slowly degraded in a dilated rER.

Patient skin biopsies show C-terminal triple helix COL3A1 mutations associated with smaller collagen fibril diameters (65-80nm vs 93±7.5nm in wild type) versus more variable fibril diameters (85-120nm) for N-terminal mutations.
MMP9 expression is increased in the aorta of Col3a1+/− mice, implicating matrix protease-mediated degradation in vEDS pathology.

vEDS dermal fibroblast analysis showed some signs of ER stress, including expression of CHOP (a marker of chronic UPR) and activation of apoptosis, although a systematic UPR analysis was not reported.

RNA-Seq of dermal fibroblasts from a small allelic series of COL3A1 mutations (two glycine, one splicing mutation) revealed the cell cycle as the most dysregulated pathway, with downregulation of genes involved in cell division, DNA replication and telomere organization, without evidence of classical UPR activation.
COL3A1 mutations reduced mRNA levels of FBN2 (fibrillin 2), which provides elasticity in blood vessels and modulates TGFβ signalling via LTBP binding.
Increased serum TGFβ levels have been observed in vEDS patients, but no evidence of increased TGFβ-mediated signalling was detected in patient fibroblasts.
Transcriptomics of thoracic aorta from Col3a1 glycine-mutant mice identified increased PLC/IP3/PKC/ERK signalling as a key contributor to vascular fragility.

Pharmacological inhibition of the PLC/IP3/PKC/ERK pathway (via ruboxistaurin, cobimetinib, hydralazine) increased survival in Col3a1 glycine-mutant mice, confirming its contribution to vEDS-associated aortic rupture.

Treatment of pregnant Col3a1G209S/+ mice with an oxytocin receptor antagonist combined with immediate pup removal after birth resulted in 95% survival, linking oxytocin signalling, PLC/IP3/PKC/ERK signalling, and pregnancy-associated aortic rupture in vEDS.
Male vEDS patients and mouse models are more severely affected than females; treatment with the androgen receptor antagonist bicalutamide rescued lethality in mouse models.

In a clinical trial, vEDS patients treated with celiprolol (a β1 antagonist/β2 agonist) had vascular complications occur later than untreated patients; a subsequent observational study suggested a survival benefit, but lacked an untreated control arm.
Treatment of two mouse models with the antihypertensive drugs losartan and propranolol reduced blood pressure but did not change incidence of vascular ruptures or survival.

In the only clinical trial conducted in vEDS, celiprolol treatment delayed onset of vascular complications compared to untreated patients, and a follow-up observational study suggested a survival benefit, though this could not be definitively attributed to the drug due to lack of an untreated arm.

Celiprolol produced opposing outcomes in different Col3a1 mouse models, rescuing biomechanical parameters in one model but increasing aortic rupture and death in another, indicating allele-specific treatment responses.
Antihypertensive treatment with losartan and propranolol in two mouse models reduced blood pressure but did not reduce the incidence of vascular rupture or improve survival.

Treatment with the broad-spectrum MMP inhibitor doxycycline reduced aortic lesions in Col3a1+/- mice, supporting MMP inhibition as a potential treatment approach at least for haploinsufficiency mutations.
MMP9 expression was increased in the aorta of Col3a1+/- mice, implicating enhanced matrix degradation in vascular fragility.

Transcriptomics of thoracic aorta from Col3a1G209S/+ and Col3a1G938D/+ mice identified increased signalling of the PLC/IP3/PKC/ERK pathway, and pharmacological inhibition of this pathway increased survival, confirming its causal contribution to disease.

Treatment with an oxytocin receptor antagonist and immediate pup removal after birth resulted in 95% survival of pregnant Col3a1G209S/+ mice, implicating oxytocin-driven PLC/IP3/PKC/ERK signalling in pregnancy/lactation-associated aortic rupture.
Androgen receptor antagonist bicalutamide rescued lethality in vEDS mouse models, consistent with patient data showing males are more severely affected than females.

Modulation of the PLC/IP3/PKC/ERK pathway via ruboxistaurin (PKCβ inhibitor), cobimetinib (MEK inhibitor), and hydralazine (inhibits IP3-mediated ER calcium release and PKCβ activation) demonstrated therapeutic potential in vEDS mouse models, though hydralazine's protective effect was lost around puberty, especially in males, unless combined with spironolactone.

Allele-specific RNA interference knockdown of mutant COL3A1 mRNA in patient fibroblasts improved collagen fibril formation without affecting the wild-type allele, and modestly reduced one ER stress marker.
Serum TGFβ levels were increased in vEDS patients, but no evidence of increased TGFβ-mediated signalling was detected in patient fibroblasts.
COL3A1 mutations reduced mRNA levels of fibrillin 2 (FBN2), a protein important for elasticity and TGFβ modulation in blood vessels, in patient dermal fibroblasts.

Transcriptomic analysis of dermal fibroblasts from a small allelic series of COL3A1 mutations identified the cell cycle as the most dysregulated pathway, with downregulation of genes involved in cell division, DNA replication, and telomere organization.

Electron microscopy of patient skin biopsies showed C-terminal triple helix COL3A1 mutations were associated with smaller collagen fibril diameters (65–80 nm vs 93±7.5 nm in wild type), whereas N-terminal mutations produced more variable diameters (85–120 nm).

Collagen fibrils with a higher collagen III:I ratio tend to be thinner, while fibrils with more collagen I have a larger diameter, indicating that collagen III incorporation limits fibril diameter; altered collagen I:III ratio and increased collagen I have also been observed in sporadic aortic aneurysm.

COL3A1 mutations cause vascular fragility associated with increased circumferential wall stress and reduced intima-media thickness, but do not alter arterial stiffness (pulse wave velocity), elastic modulus, or internal vessel diameter.

The Tsk2/+ mouse, carrying a Cys33Ser missense mutation in the collagen III N-propeptide, develops a systemic-sclerosis-like phenotype with tight/thickened skin, increased collagen I deposition, fibrosis, thicker collagen fibrils, autoantibodies, and increased (not decreased) collagen III levels, contrasting with the vEDS phenotype.

A large genome-wide association meta-analysis of ~500,000 patients found no association between common COL3A1 variants and stroke risk, contrasting with a smaller Chinese cohort study suggesting association with stroke recurrence and prognosis.

Genome-wide association studies found no common variant association between COL3A1 and aneurysm formation, supporting a role for rare large-effect coding variants rather than common non-coding risk variants.
CRISPR/Cas9-generated Chst14 frameshift mutant mice show significantly decreased Chst14 mRNA levels compared with wild-type and heterozygous littermates.
No dermatan sulfate disaccharides were detected in the skeletal muscle of Chst14-/- mice, with a corresponding significant increase in chondroitin sulfate disaccharides.
DS disaccharides were undetectable in urine samples from Chst14-/- mice, mirroring findings in human mcEDS-CHST14 patients.
CS disaccharides were elevated in urine of Chst14 mutant mice compared to wild-type, consistent with compensatory replacement of DS by CS.
Chst14-/- mice showed finer, poorly demarcated collagen fiber bundles in the reticular dermis compared to wild-type mice.
Decorin core protein appeared on thin, filamentous collagen fibers without clear boundaries in Chst14-/- mouse skin, contrasting with thick bundled decorin staining in controls.
Chst14-/- mice had significantly thinner dorsal skin than wild-type and heterozygous mice.
Chst14-/- mice showed markedly weaker skin tensile stress than wild-type mice, indicating reduced tissue strength.
Chst14-/- mice showed significantly lower tensile strain (extensibility measure) of skin than wild-type mice.
Chst14 mutant and gene trap-KO mice showed spreading of the muscle interstitium and cellular infiltration in the tibialis anterior muscle on histology.
Chst14 mutant and gene trap-KO mice showed an increased frequency of smaller-diameter muscle fibers compared to wild-type and heterozygous mice.
Chst14 gene trap-KO mice showed a larger proportion of MHC type I-positive (slow) muscle fibers than wild-type and heterozygous mice.
Decorin immunoreactivity was upregulated in the perimysium and augmented around individual fibers in the endomysium of Chst14 KO mouse muscle compared to wild-type.
Serum CK levels did not differ significantly between wild-type and Chst14 gene trap-KO mice, unlike the mild CK elevation reported in some human mcEDS patients.
Chst14-/- mutant mice showed significantly lower forelimb grip strength than wild-type and heterozygous mice across the experimental period.
Body weight-normalized grip strength was reduced in 2-month-old Chst14-/- mutant mice of both mutant lines compared to wild-type and heterozygous mice.
Chst14 gene trap-KO and Chst14-/- mutant mice showed lower maximum voluntary running speed than wild-type mice.
Chst14-/- mutant mice showed significantly lower voluntary daily running distance than wild-type mice.
Aged Chst14-/- mutant mice showed significantly lower thoracic kyphotic angles (i.e., more pronounced kyphosis) than wild-type and heterozygous mice.
Chst14-/- mutant mice showed a decreased kyphotic index (greater curvature) compared to wild-type and heterozygous mice.
No digital contractures were observed on X-ray imaging of forefoot fingers in Chst14 mutant or gene trap-KO mice, unlike the joint contractures described in some human mcEDS patients.
The birth rate of CRISPR/Cas9-engineered Chst14 homozygous knockout mice declined sharply across successive generations, indicating perinatal lethality.
Chst14-/- mutant mice of both CRISPR lines showed delayed growth and smaller body mass in early life compared to wild-type and heterozygous littermates.
In this retrospective cohort of EDS patients undergoing orthopedic surgery, 91% of surgical cases had post-operative complications, totaling 290 complications.
The most common post-operative complications in EDS patients were persistent pain/discomfort, continued subluxation/dislocation, instability, hardware-related pain, and infection.
Surgical outcomes in individuals with EDS were reported to be worse than in the general population, consistent with findings from other studies.
Aortic surgical procedures were significantly more common among vascular EDS (vEDS) patients compared to non-vascular EDS (nEDS) patients.
Mitral valve procedures were significantly more common among nEDS patients compared to vEDS patients.
Cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB) time was significantly longer in vEDS patients undergoing cardiovascular surgery compared to nEDS patients.
Aortic cross clamp time was significantly longer in vEDS patients undergoing cardiovascular surgery compared to nEDS patients.
Long-term survival following cardiovascular surgery at 5, 10, and 15 years was significantly lower in vEDS patients compared to nEDS patients.
Mortality (early and late deaths combined) after cardiovascular surgery was concentrated among vEDS patients, with 6 of 8 total deaths occurring in the vEDS group.

A 2018 meta-analysis of 37 case-control studies (964 fibromyalgia patients vs 1,025 age-matched controls) found that self-reported cognitive symptoms correlate with objectively reduced performance on cognitive function tests.

A meta-analysis of 23 case-control studies (2,096 participants) found large effect sizes for fibromyalgia-related deficits in learning, memory, attention, and psychomotor speed, and medium effect sizes for executive function and working memory, with anxiety/depression scores partly explaining heterogeneity across studies.

Fibromyalgia cognitive dysfunction has been proposed to arise from hippocampal dysfunction driven by stress-induced glucocorticoid elevation and excessive NMDA receptor-mediated excitatory neurotransmission, leading to hippocampal atrophy.

An EEG study of 18 fibromyalgia patients versus 22 healthy controls during an interference task found increased neural noise (flatter power spectrum slope) and reduced theta/alpha power modulation and midfrontal-posterior theta phase synchronization in fibromyalgia patients.

A case-control EEG study of 19 fibromyalgia patients versus 22 healthy controls found reduced N3 amplitude (conflict detection/ACC-related) and reduced theta activity during executive function tasks, along with smaller P3 amplitude suggesting longer reaction times in fibromyalgia patients.

In an emotional Go/No-Go EEG study of 31 fibromyalgia patients versus 28 healthy controls, pain-related facial expressions were associated with longer reaction times, more errors, and higher theta/delta/P3 amplitude to No-Go stimuli, with impaired N3 modulation to pain faces in fibromyalgia patients compared to controls.

A stop-signal EEG study of 27 fibromyalgia patients versus 27 healthy controls found preserved motor inhibition (similar N2, P3, and behavioral results) but reduced modulation of posterior alpha power after go/stop stimuli in fibromyalgia patients, suggesting difficulty mobilizing visual attentional resources.

Near-infrared spectroscopy during a verbal fluency test in 11 fibromyalgia patients versus 13 healthy controls showed reduced frontal (inferior frontal gyrus/temporal) brain activity in fibromyalgia patients.

A structured review of neuroimaging studies found increased activity in pain-processing cortical regions (medial frontal, insular, sensory/motor cortex, cerebellum) but decreased activity in inhibitory-control regions (rostral anterior cingulate cortex) in fibromyalgia, along with default mode network abnormalities affecting the executive control network.
Somatosensory temporal discrimination threshold was higher in 15 fibromyalgia patients compared to 15 healthy controls and strongly correlated with pain intensity and symptom severity scores.

In 44 fibromyalgia patients versus 48 healthy controls, salivary cortisol was significantly lower in FM at 30 minutes post-awakening (large effect) and at bedtime (medium effect), but not significantly different at awakening or 3pm, supporting a link between stress maladaptation and dyscognition.

In 30 fibromyalgia patients versus 30 healthy controls, no significant difference in cortisol levels was found between groups despite FM patients scoring lower on neuropsychological measures, and stress exposure was associated with reduced memory and cognitive flexibility performance in both groups.

Among fibromyalgia, neuropathic pain, chronic pain, and healthy control groups, cognitive performance was lowest in the fibromyalgia group, with pain intensity and depression—but not anxiety or sleep quality—associated with reduced cognitive function, and depression acting as a confounding factor between pain and cognition.
In 42 women with fibromyalgia versus 30 healthy women, higher pain intensity ratings during pressure stimulation were inversely associated with performance across all tested cognitive domains.

Among 17 low-depression FM patients, 18 high-depression FM patients, and 18 healthy controls, higher depression was associated with slower reaction time and poorer inhibitory task performance, indicating an inverse relationship between depression and cognitive performance.

In a survey of 66 fibromyalgia patients, current smoking was associated with worse cognitive performance, worse quality of life, greater sleep disturbance, and increased anxiety compared to non-smoking FM patients.

In 52 fibromyalgia syndrome patients versus 32 healthy controls, pain intensity and higher BMI were associated with the greatest reduction in executive/cognitive performance; mean BMI was higher in FMS patients (28.9 ± 4.49) than controls (26.49 ± 4.36).

Transcranial direct-current stimulation of the primary motor cortex (M1) reduces pain, while tDCS of the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex improves anxiety, depression, attention, memory, and cognitive impairment in fibromyalgia patients.

In a randomized controlled trial of 20 fibromyalgia females, active transcranial random noise stimulation (tRNS) of M1 significantly improved pain, depression, anxiety, verbal fluency, Trail Making Test performance, Fibromyalgia Impact Questionnaire scores, and Rey Auditory Verbal Learning Test performance versus placebo.

A randomized controlled trial found that anodal tDCS over the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex combined with working memory training significantly improved immediate memory, verbal fluency, and short-term memory compared to sham stimulation in fibromyalgia patients.
A 2019 review found that tDCS targeting the motor cortex (M1) shows great efficacy in reducing pain in fibromyalgia patients.

The same 2019 review found that tDCS stimulation of the DLPFC has less efficacy for pain reduction and only a limited effect on cognitive and affective symptoms, contrasting with an earlier claim that DLPFC tDCS improves anxiety, depression, attention, memory, and cognitive impairment.
A case-control study by Estévez-López et al. found that cognitive dysfunction in fibromyalgia patients is associated with reduced physical performance and increased pain catastrophizing.
Event-related potentials (ERP) and EEG are proposed as potential diagnostic tools to detect cognitive dysfunction in chronic pain syndromes including fibromyalgia.
Magnetic resonance spectroscopy is suggested as a neuroimaging tool useful for monitoring response to pharmacological treatment in fibromyalgia.

An RCT by Pérez-Aranda et al. found mindfulness-based stress reduction superior to usual fibromyalgia treatment modalities in reducing functional impairment both immediately post-treatment and at 12-month follow-up, though the effect on cognitive dysfunction specifically was not assessed.

A case-control study by Blanco et al. of 146 fibromyalgia patients and 122 healthy controls found olfactory nerve dysfunction to be correlated with cognitive decline, suggesting it as a potential early marker of dyscognition in fibromyalgia.

Transfer of serum IgG from FMS patients into rodents reproduced clinical FMS features (pressure and cold hypersensitivity, reduced grip strength and movement, small fiber pathology) compared to transfer of healthy volunteer IgG.
FMS patient-derived IgG antibodies were shown to specifically bind to structures within mouse and human dorsal root ganglia.

In the FMS IgG-transfer rodent model, dermal nerve fibre density in hind paw skin was reduced by 4 days after transfer, while behavioral abnormalities appeared as early as 1 day after human IgG administration.
Small fiber pathology is often found in FMS patients and correlates with disease severity in some subgroups, as established by several research groups.
Nociceptor excitability measured by microneurography is frequently abnormal in FMS patients.
Efficacy of IVIG treatment in a subgroup of non-comorbid FMS patients has previously been cited as indirect evidence for immune involvement in FMS.
Abnormal IgG deposits have been demonstrated in the skin of FMS patients, supporting an immune contribution to pathogenesis.

Antibody profiles and functional effects in FMS appear distinct from those previously described in Complex Regional Pain Syndrome and non-inflammatory RA joint pain, suggesting condition-specific autoantibody-driven pain phenotypes.
Longer FMS illness duration has been noted to be associated with lower placebo responses in trials.

Expert stakeholders recommended (with agreement, though not among the highest-consensus items) a three-arm trial comparing IgG immunoadsorption versus plasma exchange to clarify the clinical relevance of pain-sensitizing autoantibodies in FMS.

Stakeholders reached high consensus that FMS patient populations differ markedly depending on which diagnostic criteria (e.g., ACR 2010 vs ACR 2016) are applied, warranting clearer phenotyping in future research.
No evidence for central nervous system binding of FMS-derived autoantibodies has yet been identified, although this does not exclude low-intensity or spatially restricted binding.
Total thalamic volume did not significantly differ between FM and HC groups despite a numerically lower volume in FM.
Vertex-wise shape analysis revealed inward deformation (regional atrophy) of the left posterior thalamus, encompassing the pulvinar and VPL nuclei, in individuals with FM compared to HC.
Individuals with FM had thinner cortical thickness in the left superior frontal cortex compared to healthy controls.
In FM patients, thinner left superior frontal cortical thickness correlated with lower pressure pain threshold (PPT) at the thenar muscle, a relationship not seen in HC subjects.

Whereas healthy controls showed positive structural covariance between the posterior thalamus and left inferior parietal lobule/right cuneus, this covariance pattern was largely absent or inverted in the FM group.

Seed-based functional connectivity analysis showed increased connectivity between the left posterior thalamus (pulvinar) and bilateral IPL (including angular gyrus) and left middle/inferior temporal gyrus in FM compared to HC.

In FM patients, increased posterior thalamus functional connectivity with IPL, precuneus, and middle cingulate cortex was negatively correlated with electrical pain threshold, indicating that greater thalamo-cortical connectivity was associated with greater electrical pain sensitivity.
ROI-to-ROI analysis showed significantly reduced functional connectivity between the thalamus and periaqueductal gray (PAG) in FM compared to HC, suggesting impaired descending pain modulation.
Thalamus-rACC functional connectivity was marginally reduced in FM compared to HC but did not survive strict multiple comparisons correction.
There was no significant difference between FM and HC groups in thalamus connectivity with medial or lateral hypothalamus.
No significant correlation was found between depressive symptoms (BDI) and any of the brain structural or functional measures examined.
Quantitative sensory testing (previously published) showed the FM group had significantly lower pressure pain threshold (PPT) and electrical pain threshold (EPT) than controls.

In severe asthma, gene signatures reflecting FcεRI activation, LPS activation, IL-33 activation, and a mild-asthma single-cell mast cell signature were all enriched in sputum compared with healthy controls.

Mast cell activation signatures were enriched in the eosinophilic subset of severe asthma, while LPS- and IL-33-dependent signatures were further enriched in neutrophilic or mixed granulocytic severe asthma.

FcεRI-related mast cell signatures were enriched predominantly in the Th2 eosinophilic TAC1 molecular phenotype, whereas LPS- and IL-33-dependent signatures were enriched in the TAC2 neutrophil inflammasome-associated phenotype.
Mast cell activation signatures were similarly enriched in individuals with asthma who had airflow obstruction compared with those without.
Mast cell activation gene signatures correlated poorly with tissue mast cell numbers, supporting the idea that mast cell activation and localization matter more than absolute mast cell counts.

Human peripheral blood progenitor-derived mast cells show core gene expression changes common to FcεRI, LPS, and IFN-γ activation, but also many stimulus-specific changes that are further modified by combined stimulation.
A treatment targeting Kit signaling with masitinib to reduce mast cell survival showed promising results in both eosinophilic and noneosinophilic asthma.
Omalizumab shows only partial efficacy in severe atopic asthma, illustrating that a treatment effective against one mast cell activation pathway may be ineffective for another.
MRGPRX2 activation is proposed to explain roughly 30% of drug-induced anaphylaxis events previously classified as mechanistically uncertain.
Mouse studies support involvement of MrgprB2 (murine MRGPRX2 homologue) in drug-induced anaphylaxis to polybasic compounds such as neuromuscular blocking agents (NMBAs).
Pre-clinical screening of a drug library found around 20% of compounds activated MRGPRX2.
Recent work suggests serum tryptase changes cannot reliably discriminate IgE-dependent from MRGPRX2-dependent anaphylaxis, consistent with in vitro evidence of non-IgE-dependent tryptase secretion.
A recent study suggested functional expression of MRGPRX2 on basophils, complicating the use of basophil activation tests as a discriminatory assay for IgE vs MRGPRX2-dependent anaphylaxis.
Btk inhibitors, used clinically to treat leukemia, potently inhibit IgE-dependent human mast cell activation and are predicted not to affect the MRGPRX2 pathway.
MRGPRX2 expression is particularly high and consistent in skin and fat mast cells, with more variable expression in gut and lung mast cells.
Studies show MRGPRX2 mRNA levels are a poor proxy for the receptor's surface expression, implying non-transcriptional regulation of surface levels.
Chronic IL-6 treatment during generation of blood-derived mast cells only modestly enhanced MRGPRX2 surface levels and function.
TSLP selectively enhances MRGPRX2-mediated degranulation of skin mast cells.
Culturing normally unresponsive mast cells in fibronectin or with fibroblasts induces sensitivity to polybasic MRGPRX2 stimuli.
MRGPRX2 levels on mast cells are elevated in chronic spontaneous urticaria (CSU) and asthma.
A study found enhanced functional MRGPRX2 activation in lesional biopsies from ulcerative colitis patients compared to matched non-lesional controls.
A systematic review found patients with mastocytosis have an increased but lower-than-expected rate (1-5%) of reaction to drug exposure during invasive procedures compared to the general population.
Enhanced MRGPRX2 expression was demonstrated in patients with maculopapular cutaneous mastocytosis.
A lower burden of skin mast cells was identified as a risk factor for anaphylaxis in systemic mastocytosis, contrasting with expectations based on MRGPRX2 expression.

A small study comparing blood-derived mast cells from patients with likely IgE-dependent versus possible MRGPRX2-dependent drug-induced anaphylaxis found no difference in reactivity to MRGPRX2 agonists between the two cohorts.
Mast cells derived from human induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) show responsiveness to MRGPRX2 agonists, a novel model for studying MRGPRX2-dependent anaphylaxis.
Examination of the most common MRGPRX2 variants found they were either functionally neutral or showed loss of function to agonists.
Some gain-of-function polymorphisms in the MRGPRX2 C-terminal region were identified with modest enhancement of degranulation.
A rare PLCG2 variant is associated with cold-induced mast cell activation and urticaria, suggested as a precedent for gene variants underlying heightened MRGPRX2-related sensitivity.
Diminished levels of PGE2 were identified as a contributing factor to anaphylaxis in patients with Hymenoptera sting-induced (likely IgE-dependent) reactions.
Sugammadex showed inhibitory activity on some, but not all, endogenous activators of MRGPRX2, suggesting a possible use beyond rocuronium reversal to modulate MRGPRX2 activation.
An anti-MRGPRX2 antibody conjugated to IR700DX and activated by near-infrared light selectively depleted dermal mast cells in a human skin explant model.

Skin injection site reactions are commonly observed with known MRGPRX2 activators like icatibant, consistent with high skin MRGPRX2 expression, but systemic anaphylaxis to these compounds has not been reported.
CIBERSORT-inferred resting mast cell proportion was nearly eliminated in psoriatic lesional skin compared with non-lesional and healthy skin.
Activated mast cells were enriched in psoriatic lesional skin compared with non-lesional and healthy skin, suggesting a role for mast cell activation in psoriasis pathogenesis.
The proportion of resting mast cells gradually returned toward normal levels in psoriatic lesional skin during etanercept treatment.

Hierarchical clustering of CIBERSORT-inferred immune cell fractions showed enrichment of activated dendritic cells, activated CD4+ memory T cells, macrophage M0, macrophage M1 and neutrophils in psoriatic lesional skin compared with non-lesional and healthy skin.
Activated NK cell proportion was decreased while resting NK cell proportion was increased in psoriatic lesional skin compared with non-lesional and healthy skin.
T follicular helper cells, neutrophils, macrophage M0 and macrophage M1 fractions were significantly enriched in psoriatic lesional skin compared with non-lesional and healthy skin.
Activated mast cells present in lesional psoriatic skin were quickly depleted upon etanercept treatment, supporting their pro-inflammatory role.
The proportion of resting mast cells gradually increased during etanercept treatment, suggesting a role in restoring skin homeostasis.
T follicular helper cell proportion gradually decreased during etanercept treatment, reaching a level similar to non-lesional skin by 12 weeks.
The mast cell marker gene IL1B was significantly up-regulated in psoriatic lesional skin, while FAM124B and FAM174B were down-regulated, consistent with mast cell activation.

Activation markers of dendritic cells (CD1A, NR4A3, IL12B) and activated CD4+ memory T cells (IL17A, IL26, ORC1) were up-regulated in psoriatic lesional skin compared with non-lesional and healthy skin.
Marker genes for follicular T helper cells, neutrophils, macrophage M0 and macrophage M1 were significantly up-regulated in psoriatic lesional skin compared with non-lesional and healthy skin.
Universal mast cell marker genes (KIT, ENPP3, CMA1, CTSG, TPSAB1, TPSG1) mRNA levels were decreased in psoriatic lesional skin, indicating a reduced total mast cell fraction.
The MCTC (tryptase/chymase double-positive) mast cell marker gene CMA1 was significantly down-regulated in psoriatic lesional skin.
Toluidine blue staining of skin biopsies confirmed that total mast cell population is decreased in psoriatic skin compared with healthy controls.
Immunofluorescence double staining for c-Kit and tryptase with spindle-shaped morphology showed a significantly higher proportion of activated mast cells in psoriatic skin than in healthy skin.

Up-regulated genes in psoriatic lesional skin were enriched for inflammatory response, immune response, defense response to virus, and type I interferon signaling, while down-regulated genes were enriched for extracellular matrix and metabolism pathways.
GSEA showed significant enrichment of interferon-alpha and interferon-gamma response gene sets in psoriatic lesional skin, confirming heightened immune response.
The KIT D816V mutation is the disease-driving mutation found in around 90% of adult patients with non-advanced systemic mastocytosis.

Hereditary alpha-tryptasemia, caused by increased TPSAB1 copy number, is associated with elevated basal serum tryptase and may increase risk of severe anaphylaxis in SM patients, especially with concomitant allergy.

CD30 expression on mast cells is strongly associated with systemic mastocytosis and detectable in the majority of ISM and advanced SM patients by flow cytometry and immunohistochemistry, but is not found in other myeloid neoplasms.
Initial data suggesting a correlation between strong cytoplasmic CD30 expression and advanced SM was not confirmed in subsequent validation studies, so CD30 does not qualify as a grading marker.
Basal serum tryptase is elevated in most SM patients and a level above 20 ng/mL is proposed as a minor diagnostic criterion for SM.

In patients with hereditary alpha-tryptasemia, the basal tryptase level should be mathematically corrected (divided by 1 plus extra alpha-tryptase gene copies) before being applied as an SM diagnostic criterion.
A high variant allele frequency of KIT D816V (>10%) in bone marrow or peripheral blood leukocytes is proposed as a new B-finding indicating high mast cell burden or multilineage involvement in SM.

Neoplastic cells in patients with SM-associated hematologic neoplasms (AHN) may display additional somatic mutations in genes such as ASXL1, SRSF2, TET2, JAK2, RUNX1, or RAS, associated with unfavorable prognosis.
Bone marrow mastocytosis (BMM) with low disease burden (no B-findings, tryptase <125 ng/mL) has a better prognosis than typical ISM, SSM, and high-risk BMM.

BMM is typically characterized by a relatively high prevalence of severe IgE-mediated allergies to bee/wasp venom (often with MCAS) and osteoporosis, with favorable prognosis regarding progression to advanced SM.

MCAS can be classified as primary (monoclonal, MMAS with clonal MC/SM/CM), secondary (allergic/reactive underlying condition), idiopathic (no clonal MC or other underlying condition), or mixed (clonal plus secondary), with mixed-form patients at highest risk of fatal anaphylactic episodes.

Novel treatments including KIT D816V-targeting tyrosine kinase inhibitors, allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation, immunotherapies, and IgE-targeting approaches have greatly improved prognosis, survival, and quality of life in mastocytosis patients over the past two decades.
Well-differentiated systemic mastocytosis (WDSM) typically lacks KIT codon 816 mutations but may carry other KIT mutations such as K509I or F522C, some of which are sensitive to imatinib therapy.

In mice fed a high fat/high cholesterol diet, suppression of hepatic FXR signaling by muricholic acids protects against a pro-atherogenic lipid profile by enhancing cholesterol disposal via bile acids.
Muricholic acids, unlike chenodeoxycholic acid, act as FXR antagonists and promote CYP7A1-dependent increases in bile acid synthesis.

Treatment of HFD-fed mice with obeticholic acid, an FXR agonist, failed to improve liver histopathology and instead reduced Cyp7a1 and Cyp8b1 gene expression along with bile acid synthesis and excretion.
Atorvastatin treatment mitigated liver and vascular injury caused by the high fat diet while increasing bile acid synthesis and excretion.
Atorvastatin increased the percentage of intestinal bacteria expressing 7α-dehydroxylase, promoting formation of the GPBAR1 agonists deoxycholic acid and lithocholic acid.
Atorvastatin increased the expression of GPBAR1-regulated genes in white adipose tissue and colon.
Fluvastatin enhanced IL-33-induced TNF and IL-6 production by mast cells, in contrast to its suppressive effect on IgE-mediated mast cell activation.
The fluvastatin-mediated enhancement of IL-33-induced mast cell cytokine production required stem cell factor (SCF), a key mast cell growth factor.
Treatment of IL-33-activated mast cells with mevalonic acid or isoprenoids reduced the fluvastatin-mediated enhancement, indicating fluvastatin acts partly through reducing isoprenoid production.
Fluvastatin enhanced IL-33-induced NF-κB transcriptional activity in mast cells.
Fluvastatin promoted neutrophilic peritonitis in vivo through a mechanism requiring mast cell activation.
Other statins tested did not enhance IL-33 responsiveness in mast cells, unlike fluvastatin.
Anesthetized rats given NaV1.7 inhibitor peptides showed treatment-related increases in plasma histamine concentrations.

Anesthetized rats given NaV1.7 inhibitor peptides showed treatment-related decreases in blood pressure that were reversible with a mast cell stabilizer, supporting a mast cell degranulation mechanism.
In vitro exposure of rat mast cells to NaV1.7 peptides produced a concentration-dependent increase in histamine release.
Pharmacodynamic modeling established an in vitro to in vivo correlation using histamine as a biomarker predicting blood pressure decline via the mast cell degranulation mechanism.
Structure-activity relationship analysis identified that peptides with hydrophobic and cationic characteristics carry elevated risk for mast cell degranulation toxicity.
Incorporating anionic residues into the protoxin II peptide scaffold reduced or avoided the risk of mast cell degranulation-related toxicity.
In 14 healthy adults sampled weekly over 10 weeks, the mean serum tryptase concentration was 3.1 µg/L with a range of 1.2-5.4 µg/L.
The between-subject biological variation (CVG) of tryptase was considerably higher than the within-subject (CVI) and analytical (CVA) variation.

The index of individuality for tryptase was calculated as 0.18, which by convention (<0.6) indicates marked individuality, favoring use of individual reference/change values over population-based reference intervals.

Using the mean tryptase value of 3.1 µg/L, the reference change value (RCV) based on untransformed data corresponded to a change of 0.73 µg/L, suggesting significant changes may be detected with smaller increases than the currently used 2 µg/L + 20% consensus threshold.
For log-transformed tryptase data, the RCV corresponded to changes of 0.65 µg/L downward and 0.82 µg/L upward.
No significant difference in tryptase values was found between males and females.
No significant relationship between tryptase levels and age was found in this young adult cohort.
No evidence of a time trend in tryptase levels was found across the 10-week sampling period.

The analytical coefficient of variation (CVA) of the tryptase assay exceeded the minimum analytical performance specification (0.25 × CVI), potentially causing increased (>25%) variability between test results and posing diagnostic limitations.

The maximum within-subject difference in tryptase over the 10-week study (1.4 µg/L) was broadly consistent with the 2 µg/L maximum difference reported over 14 weeks in a prior insect-venom challenge study of asymptomatic individuals.

Outlier analysis using the Fraser and Harris procedure and Reed's criterion identified only one potential duplicate outlier per model (tryptase and log-transformed tryptase), but statistical testing (Cochran c test) found no true outliers, and sensitivity analyses excluding these observations showed small differences from the original results.
Treatment of mouse bone marrow-derived mast cells (BMDMCs) with the lysosomotropic agent LLME rapidly induced cell death, replicating prior reports.
Serine protease inhibition with Pefabloc (AEBSF) reduced LLME-induced mast cell death in a dose-dependent manner, with optimal effect at 10-40 μM, though it was toxic at higher concentrations.
Caspase inhibition with Q-VD-OPh also reduced LLME-induced BMDMC death, alone or combined with Pefabloc, and showed synergistic pro-survival effects with Pefabloc in the human mast cell line HMC-1.2.

LLME treatment induced strong activation (cleavage) of caspase-3, which was blocked by both Q-VD-OPh and Pefabloc, suggesting granule serine proteases contribute to caspase-3 activation leading to apoptosis.

mRNA expression profiling of BMDMCs during in vitro differentiation revealed relatively high expression of mast cell-restricted chymases mMCP-2 and mMCP-5, and tryptase mMCP-6, while mMCP-4, -7, -9, and -10 were weak or undetected.

Cathepsin G (CatG), granzyme B (GzmB), and granzyme A (GzmA), proteases not restricted to mast cells, are expressed in BMDMCs at levels similar to mMCP-2, independent of maturation state, whereas perforin was undetected.

Despite mRNA expression, GzmA protein was not detected in peritoneal mast cells or BMDMCs by intracellular staining, unlike in NK cells, suggesting post-transcriptional regulation of GzmA in mast cells.
The cytosolic CatG inhibitors Serpinb1a and Serpinb6a had the highest expression levels among clade B serpins in BMDMCs, while Serpinb1b was undetectable.

Deletion of Serpinb1a, Serpinb6a, Serpinb9a, or double Serpinb1a/Serpinb6a did not alter peritoneal mast cell frequency compared to WT mice, indicating these serpins are not required for steady-state mast cell development.

Serpinb9a-deficient BMDMCs showed significantly reduced survival compared to WT BMDMCs after LLME treatment for 2 and 4 hours, with or without caspase inhibition, indicating Serpinb9a is important for survival following granule protease leakage.
GzmB-deficient BMDMCs were highly resistant to LLME-induced cell death compared to WT BMDMCs, identifying GzmB as a principal mediator of mast cell apoptosis following granule leakage.

GzmB.Sb9a double-deficient BMDMCs showed similar resistance to LLME as GzmB-deficient BMDMCs, demonstrating that susceptibility of Sb9a-deficient BMDMCs to granule protease-mediated suicide is principally due to unleashed GzmB activity.

CatG-deficient BMDMCs showed no survival benefit compared to WT BMDMCs after LLME treatment, and triple CatG.Sb1a.Sb6a-deficient BMDMCs were also similar to WT, indicating CatG plays only a minor role in mast cell death.

Serpin- and protease-deficient BMDMCs (Sb1a, Sb6a, Sb9a, GzmB, CatG-deficient) showed no significant difference in apoptosis kinetics compared to WT following IL-3 withdrawal, indicating this growth-factor deprivation apoptosis pathway does not require granule proteases GzmB/CatG or their serpins.

Absence of GzmB in GzmB-/- and GzmB.Sb9a-/- BMDMCs prevented cleavage of pro-caspase-3 into active fragments after LLME treatment, whereas caspase-3 processing was accelerated in Sb9a-/- BMDMCs, showing complete conversion to active p17 fragment even at low LLME concentrations.

The authors note, consistent with prior work, that serglycin is required for granular localization of GzmB (but not CatG) and that Serglycin-deficient mast cells are protected against LLME-induced apoptosis, supporting a serglycin-dependent GzmB pathway.

Diabetes patients, both with and without painful neuropathy, showed increased nociceptive detection thresholds compared to healthy controls, with the largest increase in those with painful neuropathy.
Current EEG-based evoked potential data did not show significant differences between diabetic patients and healthy controls.
Duodenal mucosal mast cell infiltration was significantly higher in IBS patients compared to control subjects.
Intraepithelial lymphocyte infiltration was significantly higher in both the duodenum and terminal ileum of IBS patients compared to controls.
The numbers of duodenal and ileal intraepithelial lymphocytes were significantly correlated with each other across the study population.
Duodenal and terminal ileal IEL numbers, but not mast cell numbers, were significantly correlated with diarrhea frequency in both control subjects and IBS patients.
Duodenal and terminal ileal mast cell numbers were not significantly correlated with diarrhea frequency, in contrast to IEL numbers.
Duodenal mRNA expression of the chemokine CXCL11 was significantly higher in IBS patients than in controls.
Ang II treatment of HL-1 cardiomyocytes increased expression of the fibrosis markers TGF-β, TIMP1, MMP-2, CTGF, and galectin-3 at both mRNA and protein levels.
Addition of Ang-(1-7) or the c-Src inhibitor SU6656 reduced Ang II-induced increases in fibrosis-related genes/proteins and MAPK/Akt phosphorylation, an effect reversed by the SHP-1 inhibitor SSG.
Ang II treatment markedly increased phosphorylation of ERK1/2, Akt, and p38MAPK in HL-1 cells, indicating activation of the downstream MAPK/Akt signaling pathway.
Continuous subcutaneous Ang II infusion for 28 days markedly increased tail artery systolic blood pressure in rats, while Ang-(1-7) infusion alone had little effect on blood pressure.

Despite reversing atrial fibrosis, Ang-(1-7) did not significantly lower Ang II-induced systolic blood pressure, and blood pressure remained elevated similarly across Ang II, Ang II+Ang-(1-7), Ang II+SU6656, and Ang II+Ang-(1-7)+SSG groups.

Picrosirius red and Masson's trichrome staining showed that Ang II induced marked atrial fibrosis and collagen deposition in rats, which was reduced by Ang-(1-7) and SU6656 and this protective effect was blocked by SSG.

Collagen I protein expression was markedly elevated by Ang II and reversed by Ang-(1-7) or SU6656, with SSG attenuating the Ang-(1-7) protective effect, while collagen III showed no significant difference between groups.
Co-immunoprecipitation demonstrated that c-Src directly binds to SHP-1 in cells, indicating a physical protein-protein interaction between the two regulators.
Ang II promoted phosphorylation (activation) of c-Src while reducing phosphorylation of SHP-1; Ang-(1-7) antagonized Ang II-induced c-Src activation by promoting SHP-1 phosphorylation.

The SHP-1 inhibitor SSG antagonized the protective effects of Ang-(1-7) on ERK1/2, p38, and Akt phosphorylation induced by Ang II, confirming SHP-1 as necessary for the Ang-(1-7) protective mechanism.

Only 28.9% of Veterans meeting Kansas criteria for Gulf War Illness had a documented clinical diagnosis of any MUS condition, significantly lower than the 38.2% who were service-connected (received disability benefits) for a MUS condition.

Among Veterans meeting Gulf War Illness criteria, 15.7% had a clinical diagnosis of irritable colon/IBS while a significantly higher 25% were service-connected for it, with moderate diagnosis-service-connection concordance.
Fibromyalgia was diagnosed in 11.3% of Veterans but service-connection was granted to 18.6%, a significant difference, with moderate concordance between diagnosis and service-connection.
Chronic fatigue syndrome diagnosis (8.3%) and service-connection (7.8%) rates did not differ significantly, with moderate concordance between the two.
Migraine diagnosis (17.2%) and service-connection (18.1%) rates were similar, with moderate concordance between diagnosis and service-connection status.
Mental health diagnosis (76.5%) and service-connection (74.0%) rates were similar and much higher than rates seen for MUS conditions, with moderate diagnosis-service-connection concordance.
Musculoskeletal condition diagnosis (86.3%) and service-connection (79.4%) rates were not significantly different, but concordance between the two was low.
Illness-related (medically explained) conditions were diagnosed in 97.5% of Veterans but only 49% were service-connected for them, a large and significant discrepancy with very low concordance.
Carriers of the CC/TT genotype of the HTR2A rs6311 and rs6313 polymorphisms had higher pressure pain thresholds (i.e., lower pain) than CT carriers, under the overdominant model.

An interaction between COMT rs4818 and OPRM1 rs1799971 genotypes was significantly associated with pain catastrophizing under the codominant model, with the direction of effect reversing depending on the combined genotype.
An interaction of ADRA1A rs573542 genotype and physical activity was nominally significant for pain self-efficacy, but was based on only seven participants and considered underpowered.

Genotype-bodily pain (SF-36) associations for COMT (rs4680, rs165599), CHMP1A (rs6860) and ADRA1A (rs1383914) polymorphisms differed by sedentary behaviour level, with low sedentary behaviour linked to lower pain only in specific genotype carriers (AA/GG for rs4680, rs6860, rs165599; AG for rs1383914), while high sedentary behaviour groups showed similar pain regardless of genotype.
Participants carrying the CC/TT genotype of SCN9A rs12994338 who also had high sedentary behaviour showed the worst bodily pain scores on the SF-36.

An interaction of SLC6A4 rs25531 genotype and sedentary behaviour was statistically significant for acute pain (VAS) but was based on a very small subgroup (18 participants total, 9 per sedentary level) and considered underpowered.

Two apparent gene-gene interactions (ADRA1A rs1383914 x GCH1 rs752688, and ADRB2 rs1042713 x APOE rs429358) reached statistical significance but were judged false positives due to near-empty genotype cells (none or one participant).
The COMT rs4680 polymorphism is a missense variant causing a Val158Met amino acid change associated with altered drug response to substances including nicotine, tramadol, methadone and morphine.

Bioinformatic (STRING/DAVID) functional analysis of COMT and 10 interacting genes showed enrichment for alcohol consumption, drug-related pathways, oxidoreductase activity, and most strongly tyrosine metabolism.
A meta-analysis of 12 studies confirmed a significant association between the COMT rs4680 polymorphism and pain in fibromyalgia under both codominant and dominant genetic models.
Losartan reduced left ventricular hypertrophy severity as measured by echocardiography and histology at week 15 in irradiated rat hearts.
Losartan reduced left ventricular fibrosis (collagen content, Col1a1, Ctgf overexpression) in irradiated rat hearts at week 15.
SMAD2/3 protein levels were significantly increased in irradiated hearts at weeks 3 and 15, and losartan significantly reduced SMAD2/3 at week 3.
Mast cell chymase was significantly overexpressed in irradiated hearts at weeks 3 and 15, and this overexpression was markedly reduced by losartan treatment.
The β-MHC to α-MHC ratio, a molecular marker of LVH via fetal gene reprogramming, was significantly increased in irradiated hearts at weeks 1, 3, and 15.
pERK1,2/tERK1,2 ratios were significantly increased in irradiated hearts at week 15 and further increased by losartan treatment, opposite to effects reported in other heart failure models.

AT1 receptor protein levels were significantly decreased in irradiated hearts at week 15, likely due to receptor downregulation in response to elevated AngII, consistent with human heart failure data.
Il6 expression was significantly overexpressed in irradiated hearts across all timepoints (weeks 1, 3, 15), and losartan significantly reduced this overexpression at week 3.

Septal mitral annulus velocity (e'), a sensitive diastolic function parameter, was significantly decreased in irradiated hearts at all timepoints, indicating diastolic dysfunction that was not fully reversed by losartan at week 15.
Cardiomyocyte cross-sectional area was significantly increased in irradiated hearts at week 15 (compensatory hypertrophy despite smaller heart size), and losartan prevented this increase.
Left ventricular weight was significantly reduced in irradiated groups (with or without losartan) compared to controls at all timepoints (1, 3, and 15 weeks).
Prior preclinical evidence indicates irradiation can upregulate AngII expression in the rat heart and lungs in a dose-dependent manner, motivating investigation of AT1 receptor blockade as therapy.

In the PRADA clinical trial cited, candesartan improved reduced ejection fraction in early breast cancer patients treated with anthracycline-based regimens and radiotherapy, contrasting with a retrospective study showing ACE inhibitors/ARBs plus higher RT doses were associated with lower overall survival in cancer patients who underwent PCI.
ME/CFS patients show increased intestinal permeability (leaky gut) and gut inflammation compared with the general expectation of a healthy gut barrier.
Serum antibodies (IgM and IgA) against LPS are increased in a substantial proportion of ME/CFS patients, indicating gut-derived endotoxin exposure.
In animal experiments, administration of LPS was sufficient to induce fatigue in mice, supporting a causal role for endotoxin in fatigue pathophysiology.
Administration of natural anti-inflammatory and antioxidative substances that normalized leaky gut was accompanied by clinical improvement in ME/CFS patients.
POTS is described as a common comorbidity of ME/CFS, itself a vascular disorder associated with gastrointestinal dysfunction.
Impaired blood pressure variability and arrhythmia have been observed in ME/CFS patients, indicating autonomic dysfunction.
Chronic inflammation, including inflammation of the brain, underlies ME/CFS, consistent with the disease name myalgic encephalomyelitis.
Oxidative and nitrosative stress (O&NS) has been documented in ME/CFS, and patients' cytokine profiles differ from those of healthy controls.
NLRP3 inflammasomes have been linked to inflammation in ME/CFS.
Brain imaging studies in ME/CFS revealed significant neuroinflammation and white matter abnormalities, confirmed by autopsy studies.
Tilt-table studies have shown reduced cerebral blood flow in ME/CFS patients.
Some ME/CFS patients present signs of increased intracranial pressure, consistent with altered cerebral blood flow.
Hyper-coagulation has been proposed as a contributing factor in ME/CFS, but findings across studies have not been consistent.
Endothelial function is impaired in ME/CFS patients, both in large vessels and in microcirculation.
Altered expression of miRNAs relevant to endothelial function has been found in ME/CFS, paralleling findings in heat stroke.
Impaired energy production and reduced mitochondrial activity are considered central to ME/CFS pathology.
Mitochondrial fragmentation, impaired pyruvate dehydrogenase function, and lactate degradation deficiencies have been observed in ME/CFS.
Metabolite irregularities in ME/CFS patients are proposed to reflect a hypometabolic or 'dauer'-like protective cellular state.
Transcriptome studies show altered gene expression in peripheral immune cells of ME/CFS patients related to inflammation, mitochondrial function, oxidative stress, and immune function.
Specific microRNA expression patterns have been found to associate with specific symptom severities in ME/CFS.
ME/CFS shows a strong female predominance, with a female-to-male ratio ranging from 2:1 to 6:1.

ME/CFS is characterized by impaired heat shock protein production, which combined with oxidative/nitrosative stress and low-grade inflammation could explain muscle dysfunction and exercise intolerance.

Genetic polymorphisms in genes related to immunomodulatory response, hormone action, and kynurenine metabolic pathways have been proposed as ME/CFS risk factors, but genetic associations are inconsistent and affected by quality-control issues.
Reactivation of latent EBV and CMV in the context of a suppressed immune system has long been hypothesized as a predisposing/triggering factor for ME/CFS.
Cumulative life stress is considered a predisposing factor for ME/CFS and is thought to alter gut permeability and immune function.
Microbiome disturbances and dysbiosis have been associated with ME/CFS pathology, mirroring the gut findings in heat stroke.
ME/CFS patients and COVID-19 recovery patients share molecular signatures suggestive of overlapping immune and metabolic dysregulation.
ME/CFS patients reported significantly higher fatigue scores than controls on Day One, with a further disproportionate increase in fatigue scores after the second day of maximal exercise testing.
Heart rate at ventilatory threshold was significantly lower on Day Two compared with Day One, interpreted as a physiological marker of increased post-exertional fatigue.
ME/CFS patients showed significantly lower heart rate recovery in the first minute post-exercise (HRR Δ1) compared with controls, most pronounced on Day One.

SFN patients carrying the G1662S mutation showed abnormal quantitative sensory testing thresholds for warmth and cold sensation.
Autonomic symptoms were commonly reported in patients with DYT/PARK-TH, a genetic subtype of dopa-responsive dystonia caused by TH mutations.
Autonomic symptoms, along with seizures and microcephaly, were commonly reported in patients with DYT/PARK-PTS, a genetic subtype of dopa-responsive dystonia caused by PTS mutations.

RNA sequencing of dermal fibroblasts from twins discordant for systemic sclerosis identified 742 differentially expressed genes, with MCHR1 emerging as a significantly upregulated hub gene in network analysis.
qPCR confirmed that MCHR1 mRNA expression was significantly higher in dermal fibroblasts from SSc patients with early disease compared to healthy subjects.
PDGF-BB and bleomycin significantly increased MCHR1 expression in normal human dermal fibroblasts (NHDF), whereas TGFβ1 caused a non-significant decrease.

PDGF-BB induced a time-dependent increase in MCHR1 mRNA beginning at 2 hours, reaching significance by 24 hours and returning to baseline by 96 hours; MCHR1 protein was similarly elevated at 48 and 72 hours.

Pharmacologic inhibition of PI3K (LY294002) and MEK (U0126), but presumably not STAT3, significantly reduced PDGF-BB-induced MCHR1 mRNA and protein levels, indicating PI3K and MEK pathways mediate PDGF-BB induction of MCHR1.
PDGF-BB significantly increased mRNA expression of Col1α1 (6, 24 hrs), CTGF (4, 6 hrs), and TGFβ1 (6, 24 hrs) in NHDF.
48-hour PDGF-BB stimulation significantly increased protein abundance of Col1A1, FN1, CTGF, and TGFβ1 in NHDF, while the increase in myofibroblast marker αSMA/ACTA2 was not statistically significant.
Inhibition of PDGF receptor with CP-673451 significantly attenuated PDGF-BB-induced increases in MCHR1 and TGFβ1 protein, and reduced (non-significantly) FN1 and CTGF.

ALK5 (TGFβ receptor) inhibitor SB431542 significantly decreased PDGF-BB-induced Col1A1 and FN1 protein but did not significantly affect CTGF or TGFβ1, indicating PDGF-BB induces CTGF/TGFβ1 independently of TGFβ receptor signaling while Col1A1/FN1 induction is TGFβ-receptor dependent.
MCHR1 silencing in NHDF significantly decreased PDGF-BB-induced CTGF and TGFβ1 gene expression and protein secretion into conditioned media, without affecting basal profibrotic gene levels.
In SSc dermal fibroblasts, MCHR1 silencing reduced PDGF-BB induction of TGFβ1 but CTGF was not induced by PDGF-BB in SSc fibroblasts at the timepoint examined, unlike in NHDF.
Unlike PDGF-BB, treatment of NHDF with the endogenous MCHR1 ligand MCH did not increase profibrotic factor expression, suggesting the profibrotic effect is specific to MCHR1 activation by PDGF-BB.

PDGF-BB directly binds MCHR1, demonstrated by western ligand blot using biotinylated PDGF-BB on NHDF membrane fractions and recombinant MCHR1, and confirmed by surface plasmon resonance showing an average KD of 46.6 nM.

PDGF-BB and MCH both reduced intracellular cAMP levels in NHDF, and this reduction was prevented by pre-incubation with the selective MCHR1 inhibitor ATC0065, indicating PDGF-BB reduces cAMP through MCHR1.
PDGF-BB induced NHDF cell proliferation, with a significant increase observed 72 hours after stimulation.

Neither MCHR1 silencing nor chemical inhibition with ATC0065 affected PDGF-BB-induced NHDF cell proliferation, and MCH alone had no effect on proliferation, indicating PDGF-BB-driven proliferation is MCHR1-independent.
Caspase-3 protein abundance significantly increased in PDGF-BB treated NHDF, consistent with the observed proliferation assay results.

RNAseq meta-analysis comparing PDGF-BB effects in control vs MCHR1-silenced NHDF identified 1,473 genes uniquely regulated by PDGF-BB through MCHR1, including GRPR (upregulated), ITGB4 (downregulated), and VTN (downregulated), all linked to fibrosis or inflammation.
