RNAseq comparing PDGF-BB-treated MCHR1-silenced NHDF to PDGF-BB-treated control NHDF showed 1,095 DE genes, with TGFβ1, Col1α1, Col2α1, Col3α1 and FN1 all downregulated when MCHR1 was silenced, consistent with qPCR data.

Upstream regulator analysis identified JAK1 and PDGFRA among 34 regulators unique to MCHR1-dependent PDGF-BB-driven differential gene expression, suggesting MCHR1 may modulate canonical PDGF signaling components.
Mast cell numbers in labial salivary glands were significantly higher in patients with primary Sjögren's syndrome than in sicca control individuals.
Mast cell numbers in pSS salivary glands were significantly correlated with the extent of fibrosis present in the tissue.
Mast cells located near fibrous tissue in pSS salivary glands were shown to express TGFβ1 by immunofluorescence.
In coculture experiments, collagen Type I mRNA was upregulated in fibroblasts and TGFβ1 mRNA was upregulated in HMC-1 mast cells.

Fibroblasts cultured in HMC-1 mast cell conditioned medium showed upregulated Col1a mRNA, an effect that was abrogated by TGFβ1 neutralizing antibodies, indicating TGFβ1 drives collagen synthesis induced by mast cells.
Among individuals reporting always hearing tinnitus, absence of irritable bowel syndrome was associated with better self-rated health.
Among individuals reporting always hearing tinnitus, absence of fibromyalgia was associated with better self-rated health.
In the total study population, tinnitus was negatively associated with self-rated health even after adjusting for demographics, physical and mental health history, lifestyle, and personality.
In the general population, 6.4% reported always hearing tinnitus, and among these, 83.7% still reported good to excellent self-rated health.
Within the tinnitus group, younger age, higher education, good sleep quality, more social contacts, high competence, and low impulsivity were the strongest positive correlates of self-rated health.

The review proposes that the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) is a primary and especially sensitive neural target of neuroinflammation arising from gastrointestinal diseases and disorders, accounting for altered mood and cognition seen in these conditions.

Chronic peripheral inflammation is proposed to over-drive ACC threat-signaling processes, causing long-term structural remodeling of the ACC and excessive threat signaling that produces anxiodepressive phenotypes even in the absence of direct threats.

The review proposes a bidirectional feedback loop in which ACC-driven threat signaling activates the autonomic nervous system, exacerbates immune dysfunction, and promotes further gut pathology, linking gastrointestinal, immunological, and neural systems in GIDD.
Acute mental stress was found to increase IBS-specific gastrointestinal symptomatology compared to non-stress conditions across included case-control studies.
Acute mental stress altered gastrointestinal motility in patients with IBS relative to healthy individuals across studies examining objective motility parameters.
Some patients with IBS exhibited emotional hyperresponsivity to acute psychological stressors compared with healthy controls.
Functional brain activity studies showed different patterns of neural activation in response to stress in patients with IBS compared with healthy individuals.
Autonomic nervous system stress responses in IBS patients depended on stressor type and showed no clear evidence of differential reactivity versus healthy controls, partly due to confounding factors.
Hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis stress responses in IBS patients depended on stressor type and showed no clear evidence of differential reactivity compared to healthy individuals.
Data on acute immunological changes in response to stress in IBS patients remain sparse (only 3 studies) and require further investigation.

Overall, current evidence suggests altered stress reactivity in patients with IBS, but it remains unclear whether this reflects the syndrome itself or the high prevalence of comorbid psychiatric conditions.
Acute porphyric attacks feature prominent autonomic nervous system involvement in the splanchnic and cardiovascular districts, including gastrointestinal, cardiac, and sphincter disturbances.

AHP-associated peripheral neuropathy typically manifests as an acute axonal motor neuropathy starting proximally and in the upper limbs, often with sensory involvement and risk of respiratory/bulbar paralysis.
Phenotypic penetrance of AIP-causing HMBS mutations is very low in the general population, despite a mutation carrier rate of about 1 in 1675 and estimated clinical penetrance around 1%.

PEPT2-deficient mice showed markedly lower ALA concentrations in most tissues but a five-fold higher CSF ALA concentration and eight-fold higher CSF/blood ratio, and displayed greater susceptibility to ALA neurotoxicity.
In AIP patients, homozygous carriers of the higher-ALA-affinity PEPT2*1*1 variant showed worse renal function and faster annual eGFR decline than carriers of lower-affinity variants.
Children carrying the lower-affinity PEPT2*2*2 variant showed poorer motor dexterity and working memory in the context of low-level lead exposure.
ALA induces oxidative mitochondrial damage in vitro, causing mitochondrial swelling and loss of transmembrane potential, likely via ROS-driven thiol cross-linking.

ALA-treated Schwann cells show dose-dependent reductions in myelin-formation and myelin-maintenance proteins, decreased sphingomyelins/phosphatidylcholines, and increased carbonylated proteins and peroxidated lipids indicating oxidative damage to myelin.
ALA acts as a GABA-mimetic agonist at presynaptic GABAA autoreceptors, displacing GABA release, and chronic ALA exposure reduces GABAA receptor binding/density in brain tissue.

Succinylacetone-induced heme deficiency impairs NGF-induced neuronal differentiation in PC12 cells via caspase-dependent apoptosis, JNK activation, Ras-ERK1/2 inhibition, and downregulation of the NMDA receptor.
AIP patients are known to have decreased plasma melatonin levels, a finding also confirmed in ALA-treated animal models and pinealocyte cultures.

A cohort of 21 AIP patients had significantly lower plasma pyridoxal phosphate and higher xanthurenic acid excretion compared to age-matched healthy controls, supporting a functional vitamin B6 deficiency in AIP.

In a cohort of 50 patients with HMBS mutations, plasma pyridoxal phosphate levels were normal but urinary 3-hydroxykynurenine/xanthurenic acid ratio, homocysteine, and methionine were significantly higher than controls, suggesting a functional (rather than absolute) vitamin B6 deficiency.

A pilot study found that AHP patients with moderate-to-severe symptoms had significantly lower basal and maximal oxygen consumption rates (mitochondrial bioenergetic profile) compared to controls and to AHP patients with mild or no symptoms.

NOS dysfunction in myenteric plexus neurons is proposed to underlie dysautonomic gastrointestinal symptoms, and impaired NOS activity following heme depletion has been proposed as an explanation for the neurovisceral manifestations of AHP.

Trypanosoma cruzi epimastigotes produce and excrete ALA into culture medium; T. cruzi causes Chagas disease, which manifests with neuropathy and autonomic dysfunction, suggesting a possible ALA-mediated link between the parasite and autonomic/neurologic damage.
Griseofulvin-induced heme depletion in mice caused a shorter circadian period and phase advances in diurnal core body temperature rhythm, both reversible upon heme supplementation.

Givosiran, a small interfering RNA targeting hepatic ALAS1 mRNA, reduces biochemical disease markers, lowers the annualized rate of porphyric attacks, and improves quality of life in AHP patients, though it can cause partly reversible adverse events linked to induced relative heme deficiency.
Endothelial-specific markers CD31, vWF, and VE-cadherin mRNA were expressed at lower levels in varicose vein tissue compared with healthy saphenous veins.
Mesenchymal marker transcripts (α-SMA, SM22α, calponin1, fibronectin, vimentin, N-cadherin) were significantly increased in varicose vein tissue relative to control veins.
Immunohistochemistry showed VE-cadherin protein was reduced 5.5-fold in varicose veins compared with control veins.
Immunohistochemistry quantification showed α-SMA, transgelin, fibronectin, and calponin1 overexpressed in varicose veins by 3.42-, 3.3-, 5.25-, and 6.92-fold respectively compared with control veins.
SNAI1, SNAI2, and TWIST1 mRNA were higher in varicose veins than in healthy veins, by 4.27-, 4.20-, and 4.18-fold respectively.
TWIST2 mRNA was significantly elevated (2.96-fold) in varicose veins versus control veins, though less than TWIST1.
TGFβ1 mRNA was upregulated 3.63-fold in varicose veins, higher than TGFβ2 (0.93-fold) and TGFβ3 (2.04-fold) isoforms compared to control veins.
BMP4 mRNA expression was 5.5-fold higher in varicose veins than in control veins.
All SMADs were significantly upregulated in varicose veins, particularly SMAD2 (TGFβ pathway), SMAD5 and SMAD9 (BMP pathway), and co-SMAD4.

IHC showed BMP4 and pSMAD5 were intensely expressed in 25/27 (92.59%) varicose veins, more prominently than TGFβ1 and pSMAD2, which were overexpressed in 15/27 (55.56%) samples, indicating BMP4/pSMAD5 as the dominant EndMT pathway in varicose veins.
In HUVECs exposed to disturbed (non-uniform) flow for 24-48h, endothelial markers CD31, vWF, and VE-cadherin mRNA were decreased compared to static and parallel laminar flow.

Mesenchymal marker mRNA increased in HUVECs exposed to disturbed flow for 24h compared to static culture: α-SMA 6.26-fold, transgelin 5.17-fold, N-cadherin 5.26-fold, fibronectin 4.72-fold, calponin1 5.24-fold, and vimentin 4.32-fold.

SNAI1 was induced ~5.995-fold in HUVECs exposed to disturbed flow compared with 1.046-fold in static culture and 1.203-fold under parallel uniform flow, indicating flow-pattern-specific induction rather than shear magnitude alone.
TGFβ1 mRNA was significantly higher in HUVECs exposed to disturbed flow (4.67-fold vs static) compared to parallel uniform flow (1.13-fold vs static).

BMP4 mRNA was significantly more elevated (mean 6.443-fold) than TGFβ1 (4.669-fold) in HUVECs exposed to disturbed flow at 24h, with SMAD1/5/9 also elevated, unlike TGFβ2/3 which required longer exposure.

Immunofluorescence showed higher cytoplasmic BMP4 and nuclear translocation of pSMAD5 in HUVECs exposed to disturbed flow compared to static and parallel flow conditions, with minimal expression under uniform venous shear stress.

The BMP4 pathway inhibitor LDN193189 effectively blocked pSMAD5 (p < 0.001) and pSMAD2 (p < 0.05) and reduced nuclear translocation of SNAI1/2 in HUVECs under disturbed flow, and was more effective than the TGFβ inhibitor SB505124 at reducing SNAI1/2 expression.
The TGFβ type 1 receptor inhibitor SB505124 inhibited pSMAD2 signaling in HUVECs exposed to disturbed flow.
Both SB505124 and LDN193189 reduced TGFβ1 and BMP4 ligand expression in HUVECs exposed to disturbed flow, suggesting feedback regulation of ligand expression by ALK-SMAD inhibition.

Histological analysis showed varicose veins had thickened walls with neointima formation and clustered circular/longitudinal smooth-muscle-cell stacks in the tunica media compared to the simple longitudinal SMC arrangement in control veins.
Plasma CRP levels were significantly higher in post-COVID-19 patients than in healthy subjects.
Vaccinated subjects had significantly lower CRP than both healthy subjects and PC patients, suggesting vaccination does not induce systemic inflammation.
Circulating LDH levels were significantly higher in both moderate and severe PC patients compared to healthy subjects.
Plasma complement complex C5b-9 was significantly higher in PC patients than in healthy and vaccinated subjects, with no difference between moderate and severe PC patients.
No difference in circulating C3a levels was observed between healthy, vaccinated, and PC groups.
Circulating IL-6 levels were significantly reduced in all PC blood samples compared to healthy and vaccinated subjects, with no difference by severity or fibrosis status.
PC patients had higher circulating IFN-β levels than healthy subjects, and vaccinated subjects had even higher IFN-β levels than both PC patients and healthy subjects.
Moderate COVID-19 patients showed a non-significant tendency toward higher IFN-β than severe patients.
PC patients who developed pulmonary fibrosis-like changes had lower circulating IFN-β than PC patients without fibrosis, regardless of severity grade.
CXCL10 levels were significantly higher in PC patients than in healthy and vaccinated subjects.
Severe grade COVID-19 induced higher CXCL10 compared to healthy and vaccinated subjects, contrasting with the IFN-β pattern.
Severe and moderate PC patients with lung fibrosis-like changes had higher CXCL10 than healthy subjects.
Overall plasma IL-1α levels in PC patients were not statistically different from healthy subjects, though vaccinated subjects had higher IL-1α.
When stratified by fibrosis status, both moderate and severe PC patients with lung fibrosis-like changes had higher (though not statistically significant) IL-1α than healthy subjects.
IL-2, IL-18, IL-33, and CXCL8 were not increased in PC patients compared to healthy subjects.
Vaccinated subjects had significantly higher IL-18 levels than PC patients, attributed to vaccine effectiveness.
PC patients had higher plasma TGF-β compared to healthy subjects, with vaccinated subjects showing even higher levels.

Severe PC patients with lung fibrosis-like changes had higher TGF-β than both healthy subjects and severe PC patients without fibrosis; moderate patients with fibrosis showed only a slight increase versus healthy.
Severe COVID-19 grade was significantly associated with development of post-COVID lung fibrosis-like changes (82.6% of severe cases vs. 72.4% of moderate cases without fibrosis).

A plasma IFN-β cut-off of 194.3 pg/mL, derived by ROC analysis, discriminated PC patients with versus without lung fibrosis-like changes, with severe patients with fibrosis showing lower IFN-β and moderate patients with higher IFN-β showing no fibrosis.
The authors estimated an approximately 2.8-fold increased relative risk of lung fibrosis-like changes in PC patients associated with the combination of higher IL-1α and TGF-β but lower IFN-β.

Combined prophylactic-plus-therapeutic rhANP treatment (before and after LPS) reversed LPS-induced body weight loss and increased spleen weight/spleen-to-body-weight ratio, and reduced plasma IL-6, IL-17A, IFN-γ and TNF-α levels compared to saline-treated LPS mice.

Single-dose administration of rhANP given only 24h before or only 10min after LPS had no significant effect on spleen weight, spleen/body weight ratio, plasma cytokines, or cognitive test latency, in contrast to the combined dosing regimen.
Spleen weight was significantly positively correlated with plasma levels of IL-6, IL-17A, IFN-γ and TNF-α across LPS-challenged mice.
Combined rhANP treatment reversed LPS-induced increases in hippocampal iba-1, IL-6, IL-17A, IFN-γ, TNF-α and iNOS protein expression, while no significant effect was seen in the prefrontal cortex.

rhANP treatment significantly alleviated LPS-induced deficits in Y maze novel arm entries/duration and reduced latency to eat food in the buried food test, indicating improved spatial recognition memory and olfactory-dependent cognitive function.

Subdiaphragmatic vagotomy (SDV) itself significantly attenuated LPS-induced body weight loss, plasma inflammatory cytokines (IL-6, IL-17A, IFN-γ, TNF-α) and hippocampal inflammatory mediator expression, independent of rhANP treatment.

In LPS-challenged mice pre-subjected to SDV, combined rhANP treatment could not further reduce body weight loss, plasma cytokines, or hippocampal inflammatory mediator expression beyond the effect of SDV alone, suggesting rhANP's anti-inflammatory effect requires an intact subdiaphragmatic vagus nerve.
Combined rhANP treatment significantly increased hippocampal (but not prefrontal cortex) p-TrkB and BDNF expression in LPS-challenged mice compared to saline-treated LPS mice.

SDV alone significantly increased hippocampal p-TrkB and BDNF expression compared to sham operation in LPS-challenged mice, and combined rhANP treatment could not further increase these levels after SDV.

Pseudo germ-free mice transplanted with fecal microbiota from LPS-challenged donor mice showed decreased hippocampal BDNF expression and worse Y maze/buried food test performance compared to PGF mice given microbiota from saline-treated or rhANP-treated LPS donors.

In PGF mice that had received SDV, fecal transplant from LPS-challenged donors (with or without rhANP treatment) no longer significantly altered hippocampal BDNF expression or Y maze/buried food test performance, indicating the subdiaphragmatic vagus nerve is required for gut microbiota to affect cognition.

Pharmacological blockade of TrkB/BDNF signaling with ANA-12 significantly weakened the cognitive-improving effects of rhANP in LPS-challenged mice (Y maze entries/duration and buried food latency), confirming TrkB/BDNF signaling as necessary for rhANP's benefit.
Exome sequencing of 302 AIS patients identified nine pathogenic variants in FBN1, COL11A1, COL11A2 and TGFBR2 under a monogenic inheritance model.
Three AIS patients carried co-occurring variant pairs in ADAMTSL2 and LTBP4, whereas no such pairs were found in controls.
Variant pairs in ADAMTSL2 and LTBP4 disrupted the interaction between the two proteins and led to upregulation of the TGF-beta signaling pathway in human fibroblasts.
After O2-O3-AHT, female ME/CFS patients showed significantly higher Fatigue Severity Scale improvement scores than male patients.
In the youngest age subgroup (14–29 years), females showed markedly better response to O2-O3-AHT than males, with a 28.3% difference in FSS scores.
When patients were grouped into three age clusters (14–29, 30–49, ≥50 years), FSS response to O2-O3-AHT did not differ significantly within either sex.
Among male patients specifically, FSS response across age clusters showed high heterogeneity and did not reach statistical significance.
O2-O3-AHT relieved fatigue in approximately half of the overall ME/CFS patient cohort.
Effect size analyses (Cohen's d/Hedges' g and Glass's delta) confirmed a statistically significant pre- versus post-treatment change in FSS scores with O2-O3-AHT.
The paper's discussion notes that mitochondrial activity, including ROS signaling, is greatly disturbed in ME/CFS, contributing to inflammatory disorders.
The paper cites that ME/CFS is associated with an increase in CD4+CD25+Foxp3+ regulatory T cells, which may be modulated by ozone therapy.
CCR6+ Th17 cells in ME/CFS patients secrete less IL-17 and have lower blood frequency compared to healthy subjects, a deficit reported to be restorable by ozone.
The discussion notes that 4-hydroxynonenal (4-HNE) induces thioredoxin reductase 1 via Nrf2 signaling and subsequently increases Treg levels, a possible mechanism relevant to ozone's effects.
ME/CFS patients reportedly show normal levels of nitric oxide (NO) and IL-6 both before and after physical exercise, despite fatigue symptoms.
ME/CFS patients reportedly show elevated F2-isoprostanes, an oxidative stress biomarker, which may be quenched by ozone's action on the Nrf2/Keap1/ARE system.
The authors hypothesize that the greater female response to O2-O3-AHT may involve ER-beta signaling effects on Treg biology, a mechanism proposed for future investigation.
Prior to exercise, ME/CFS subjects showed lower overall BOLD activation across ascending arousal network seed regions during the 2-back>0-back task than both healthy controls and GWI subjects.
Before exercise, healthy controls had significantly greater BOLD activation than ME/CFS subjects in bilateral PTN, left parabrachial complex, and VTA.
Before exercise, GWI subjects had significantly higher BOLD activation than ME/CFS subjects in left PTN and left pontis oralis.
After the second exercise session, both control and ME/CFS groups had significantly greater overall BOLD activation than GWI subjects.

After exercise, controls showed greater activation than GWI in bilateral MRF, VTA and right PTN, while ME/CFS subjects showed greater activation than GWI in midline PAG, DR, MR and right MRF, LC and PBC.

Exercise induced an increase in BOLD activation in ME/CFS subjects but a decrease in GWI subjects across most midbrain seed regions, indicating opposite exercise-induced pathophysiology in the two conditions.
Prior to exercise, males showed significantly higher overall BOLD activation than females across all nodes, with a significant sex difference specifically in left pontis oralis.
Multivariable general linear modeling confirmed that left PTN activation was significantly lower in ME/CFS than in both controls and GWI subjects before exercise.
Orthostatic status significantly affected pre-exercise BOLD, with left parabrachial complex activation lower in STOPP (normal orthostatic response) subjects than in POTS and START phenotypes.

After exercise, gender was a significant covariate for right locus coeruleus and right parabrachial complex, with males showing greater BOLD activation than females after adjustment for other variables.

Exercise induced a significant negative incremental BOLD change in the START (exercise-induced postural tachycardia) group in right locus coeruleus and bilateral parabrachial complex, whereas STOPP subjects showed no change, implicating exercise-induced autonomic dysfunction in START.

Exercise significantly worsened light sensitivity in both ME/CFS and GWI subjects, and worsened sound sensitivity in ME/CFS subjects, with the incremental change being significantly larger in ME/CFS than in GWI and controls.
Baseline light sensitivity was far more prevalent in ME/CFS and GWI subjects than controls, with only 30.8% of ME/CFS and 21.1% of GWI subjects reporting no discomfort compared to 83.3% of controls.
ME/CFS and GWI groups had comparable, worse-than-control symptom scores overall, except that pain and SF-36 Role Emotional and Mental Health scores indicated greater impairment in GWI than ME/CFS.
No significant correlations were found between subjective symptom/quality-of-life questionnaire scores and objective pre- or postexercise midbrain BOLD outcomes.

Effect sizes for the significant group differences in BOLD activation were moderate-to-high (Hedges' g 0.50-0.81), suggesting these findings should be replicable with adequately powered future studies.

The cholinergic pedunculotegmental nucleus, which maintains wakefulness and sustains attention via cerebral acetylcholine release, showed reduced activation in ME/CFS, potentially impairing updating of rapidly changing information required for working memory tasks.

Reduced cerebral blood flow in ME/CFS during head-up tilt and exercise may compromise oxygen supply to the metabolically active and vulnerable inferior colliculus, contributing to dorsal midbrain dysfunction.

After exercise, right locus coeruleus activation was significantly lower in GWI subjects than in ME/CFS subjects, consistent with the locus coeruleus's role in noradrenergic arousal and its known atrophy in PTSD.

Nearly half of ME/CFS patients treated with oxygen-ozone autohemotherapy (O2-O3-AHT) showed the maximal improvement in fatigue, moving from the worst FSS score (7) to the best (1), with over 75% of these responders being female.

Male patients responded to therapy at a rate 1.5-fold higher in overall population proportion (59.48%) compared to females (74.58%), though females showed a higher absolute response rate with more variability.
Patient age did not significantly affect treatment response to O2-O3-AHT for fatigue.
No adverse events were reported in ME/CFS patients treated with O2-O3-AHT during treatment or in the 3 months following treatment.
The paper cites prior literature indicating ME/CFS is characterized by an increase in CD4+CD25+Foxp3+ regulatory T (Treg) cells, which ozone may modulate and lower.

The paper cites prior literature reporting that CCR6+ Th17 cells in ME/CFS secrete less IL-17 and have significantly lower circulating frequency compared to healthy subjects, and that ozone can restore their amount.

The paper cites prior literature indicating ME/CFS patients have normal nitric oxide (NO) and IL-6 levels before and after physical exercise, but exhibit high levels of F2-isoprostanes, an oxidative stress biomarker.

The paper proposes that the major ozone-induced blood byproduct 4-HNE induces thioredoxin reductase 1 via the Nrf2 pathway, thereby increasing Treg levels, as a candidate mechanism for the fatigue-relieving effect of O2-O3-AHT.
In a sample of 25 ME/CFS patients and 25 healthy controls, midbrain white matter volume was negatively correlated with duration of fatigue, interpreted as glial cell loss/shrinkage.
Absolute gray matter volume of the brainstem was positively correlated with seated pulse pressure in ME/CFS patients but not in healthy controls.
No overall group mean differences were found in T1W or T2W signal levels, or WM/GM volumes, between ME/CFS and controls in this early study.

In a follow-up analysis of the same cohort, T1W signal level (suggestive of increased myelination) in the ventrolateral thalamus, internal capsule, and prefrontal white matter increased with greater ME/CFS disease severity.
Increased T2W signal level, suggestive of decreased regional blood volume, was found in the right middle temporal white matter in ME/CFS compared to HC.

Abnormal correlations between MRI measures in focal brainstem vasomotor structures and physiological measures (blood pressure, heart rate) were found in ME/CFS compared to HC, though no group mean differences in these structures' signal or volume were detected.
Finkelmeyer et al. reported reduced white matter volume in the midbrain and pons in ME/CFS compared to HC.
Finkelmeyer et al. reported higher adjusted gray matter volumes in the temporal, frontal, and occipital lobes in ME/CFS patients compared to HC, with no clear explanation identified.
Negative associations were found between symptom severity and total intracranial volume, unadjusted gray matter volume, and cerebrospinal fluid volume in ME/CFS.

In a larger sample of 43 ME/CFS and 27 HC, decreased T1W signal levels (suggestive of decreased myelination) were found in brainstem regions (ventral tegmental, pontine nuclei, medulla) alongside increased T1W signal in cortical WM regions (premotor, sensorimotor cortices) in ME/CFS vs HC.

Thapaliya et al. found an increased T1W/T2W ratio (indicative of higher myelin and/or iron levels) in 16 white matter regions including brainstem ROIs (corticospinal, medial lemniscus tracts) and projection tracts in 45 ME/CFS vs 27 HC, correlated with clinical and functional measures.
Increased T1W/T2W ratio was found in all four subcortical gray matter regions studied (left and right putamen and pallidum) in ME/CFS compared to HC, with no region showing a lower ratio.

Addiego et al. found decreased volume of the putamen, caudate, and cerebellum white matter in 38 ME/CFS patients compared to 34 HC (also compared to 90 Gulf War Illness participants), adjusted for intracranial volume and age; brainstem volume correlated with ventral diencephalon, pallidum, and cerebellum WM volumes in ME/CFS, with different correlation patterns than HC.

The only DTI study in this review found decreased transverse diffusivity and fractional anisotropy in the midbrain/pons and superior longitudinal fasciculus in ME/CFS patients meeting International Consensus Criteria (n=18) compared to HC (n=26), correlated with clinical measures.
No group differences in DTI parameters were seen in any brain region between the ME/CFS-Fukuda subgroup and HC, in contrast to the ICC subgroup.

During a fatiguing cognitive task (PASAT), functional connectivity between the inferior frontal gyrus and the brainstem and other regions (lingual gyrus, cerebellar vermis, cerebellum, parahippocampal gyrus) progressively increased in ME/CFS patients (n=19) versus a decrease in HC (n=15), with the increase associated with higher end-task fatigue.

During a Stroop task, connectivity deficits between the cuneiform nucleus and medulla, and from the brainstem to the hippocampus and intralaminar thalamus, were found in 45 ME/CFS patients compared to 27 HC, with reduced connectivity associated with greater symptom severity.

In 6 ME/CFS and 10 HC participants, baseline functional connectivity differed between groups, including greater connectivity between right inferior parietal lobule and posterior cingulate cortex/right superior frontal gyrus, lower connectivity between posterior cingulate cortex and left superior frontal gyrus/precentral gyrus, and greater salience network connectivity to the left superior temporal gyrus and to the medulla/cerebellar tonsil in ME/CFS.

At a second scan (timed to onset of post-exertional malaise), increased functional connectivity between right insula and orbitofrontal cortex/thalamus/hypothalamus/basal ganglia, and decreased connectivity between right insula and right inferior temporo-occipital cortex, were found in ME/CFS, accompanied by increased fatigue and pain.

The review cites prior evidence that methylphenidate, a dopamine reuptake inhibitor, decreases fatigue and disrupted concentration in adults with ME/CFS, supporting a hypothesized dopaminergic/midbrain dysfunction.
CFS patients reported significantly greater symptom severity than controls for fatigue, exertional exhaustion, unrefreshing sleep, and muscle pain.
Chalder fatigue total score and subscores were significantly higher in ME/CFS than controls.
Depression scores (CESD) did not differ significantly between ME/CFS and control groups.
Orthostatic status (STOPP/START/POTS classification) was not a significant covariate in models predicting resting-state BOLD amplitude before or after exercise.
Before exercise, controls had significantly higher BOLD amplitude than ME/CFS in salience (SAL_SMA), sensorimotor (SM_RS2, SM_LS2), subcortical (SUB_vDien), and visual (VIS0063) nodes.

After exercise, controls had greater BOLD activation than ME/CFS across salience (SAL_dACC, SAL_SMA, SAL_mIns), sensorimotor (SM_LS2), subcortical (SUB_Thal, SUB_Midbrain, SUB16vDien, SUB_Pons) and visual (VIS0017, VIS0041, VIS0053, VIS0063) nodes.
After exercise, ME/CFS showed significantly higher DMN_mPFC BOLD activation than controls after adjusting for orthostatic status, gender, age, and BMI.
After accounting for significant age effects on multiple nodes, DMN_mPFC remained the only node significantly associated with ME/CFS status postexercise.
The exercise-induced change (post minus pre) in DMN_mPFC was larger in ME/CFS than controls, while the exercise-induced change in VIS0017 was larger in controls than ME/CFS.
Overall average resting-state BOLD amplitude across all brain regions was significantly lower in ME/CFS than controls both before and after exercise.
Both control and ME/CFS groups showed significantly lower overall BOLD activation on the postexercise day compared to preexercise.

Submaximal exercise produced reciprocal effects on DMN_mPFC activation: a significant decrease in controls but a significant increase in ME/CFS, resulting in significantly higher DMN_mPFC signal in ME/CFS than controls postexercise, proposed as a biomarker of post-exertional malaise.
Four brain regions (anterior insula, midbrain, pons, and a visual node) showed persistently lower BOLD in ME/CFS than controls both before and after exercise, unaffected by provocation.

Exercise induced a relative deficit in visual network BOLD (VIS0017, VIS0057, VIS0041, VIS0053) in ME/CFS compared to controls, driven by a slight postexercise increase in controls with no change in ME/CFS.

Before exercise, ME/CFS showed markedly reduced inter-nodal functional connectivity compared to controls, with significant correlations (R>0.8) confined to sensorimotor and visual networks; DMN_mPFC was correlated only with the cerebellar vermis (SUB_Vermis).

Despite increased activation postexercise, DMN_mPFC showed loss of functional connectivity with other nodes after exercise in both controls (no correlations >0.5) and ME/CFS (no correlations >0.3), suggesting decoupling of the anterior DMN hub.
Age- and gender-regressed BOLD amplitudes showed no significant correlation with subjective measures of fatigue, pain, tenderness, or depression.

A similar pattern of elevated anterior DMN (mPFC) activation following exercise, during a low cognitive load task, has been reported in Gulf War Illness, suggesting a shared post-exertional pathophysiology across conditions.
Researchers correctly classified 83% of ME/CFS patients versus controls based on gut dysbiosis combined with elevated blood inflammatory markers indicating microbial translocation.
Multiple research teams reported reduced abundance of SCFA-producing bacteria, especially butyrate producers, in ME/CFS patients.
Increased fecal short-chain fatty acid (SCFA) levels, including butyrate, isovalerate and valerate, were found in ME/CFS patients in one study, contradicting the butyrate-deficiency hypothesis.
Increased fecal colonization by D-lactic acid producing Gram-positive bacteria was found alongside decreased absolute fecal lactate levels in ME/CFS patients.
Targeting D-lactic acid producing bacteria with antibiotics and probiotics did not improve fatigue in ME/CFS patients, raising doubt about the D-lactate theory.
Significantly elevated IgA and IgM antibodies against the bacterial translocation marker LPS were found in ME/CFS patient blood and correlated with illness severity.
Increased bacterial abundance was found in the blood of ME/CFS patients following an exercise test, suggesting exercise-induced bacterial translocation.

In a large cytokine study, 17 cytokines were significantly abnormal and correlated with severity in ME/CFS patients, including elevated anti-inflammatory TGF-β amid a predominantly pro-inflammatory profile.
A subset (29%) of 268 ME/CFS patients had elevated autoantibodies against neurotransmitter receptors, supporting an autoimmune hypothesis.
Removing autoantibodies via immunoadsorption led to rapid symptom improvement in 7 of 10 ME/CFS patients.

Post-infectious ME/CFS showed higher prevalence of PTPN22 rs2476601 and CTLA4 rs3087243 autoimmunity-risk alleles, while non-infection-triggered ME/CFS showed lower frequency of IRF5 rs3807306 and TNF rs1799724 risk alleles.
A monozygotic twin study found 55% concordance for ME/CFS symptoms in both twins, supporting a genetic component in at least a subgroup of disease.
Naviaux and co-workers found strong evidence for a hypometabolic state, with significant variation in 20 metabolites in ME/CFS patients, of which 80% were reduced.
Elevated plasma ceramide levels correlated with increased physical fatigue in ME/CFS patients and were hypothesized to result from LPS hydrolysis contributing to epithelial barrier dysfunction.

A 24-hour repeat cardiopulmonary exercise test showed normal oxygen consumption initially but significantly reduced VO2 on the second test, distinguishing ME/CFS patients from controls with 95% accuracy.
Risk of developing ME/CFS is significantly higher in patients with inflammatory bowel disease, particularly Crohn's disease, compared to individuals without IBD.
Women who developed Helicobacter pylori-associated peptic ulcer disease showed significantly increased risk of subsequently developing ME/CFS in a retrospective cohort study.

ME/CFS patients showed increased Firmicutes and Actinobacteria and reduced Bacteroidetes compared to healthy controls, with a microbial signature similar to Q-fever fatigue syndrome patients and distinct from healthy controls.

Metagenomic analysis associated ME/CFS with increased Alistipes and decreased butyrate-producer Faecalibacterium, proposed as top diagnostic biomarker candidates, though findings on Clostridium abundance conflicted with another study.

The 'metabolic trap hypothesis' proposes that ME/CFS patients carry more mutations in the IDO2 isoform, correlating with symptom severity, leading to insufficient kynurenine production, elevated tryptophan, and disrupted serotonin/melatonin/NAD+ pathways.

An interventional study found no direct alteration of the kynurenine/tryptophan (KYN/TRP) ratio in diagnosed ME/CFS patients, suggesting abnormal kynurenine metabolism may matter more at disease initiation than during the established syndrome.

Transcolonoscopic infusion of a Bacteroidetes/Clostridia/E. coli combination produced a beneficial transient response in 70% and a lasting response in 58% of ME/CFS patients with gastrointestinal symptoms, though the cohort was restricted to those with comorbid IBS.

Fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) produced massive improvement (65-95%) in energy levels for 17 of 21 ME/CFS patients, significantly greater than oral pre-/probiotic treatment, with some long-term ME/CFS patients reportedly cured.
In one of the few RCTs in this field, oral Bifidobacterium infantis reduced systemic inflammatory markers including CRP and TNF-α in ME/CFS patients compared to placebo.
Probiotic intervention with Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium significantly ameliorated anxiety in a small ME/CFS cohort, though anxiety is not a core disease symptom.

A double-blind randomized-controlled cross-over trial of 20-day high-dose thiamine supplementation in 40 IBD patients with severe fatigue showed a significant treatment effect on fatigue, relevant given reduced thiamine-producing gut bacteria observed in ME/CFS.
Oral ginseng administration has shown anti-fatigue properties in ME/CFS, MS-related fatigue and cancer-related fatigue across several blinded RCTs.
A meta-analysis found post-exertional malaise (PEM) to be 10.4 times more common in ME/CFS diagnoses than in healthy controls, supporting its use as the cardinal differentiating symptom.
Women who had been pregnant showed a 31-fold higher risk of developing ME/CFS, implicating reproductive/hormonal events in disease onset.
The autoimmunity-risk allele PTPN22 rs2476601 was found at significantly higher prevalence in post-infectious ME/CFS patients but not in those without an infection-triggered onset.
The CTLA4 rs3087243 autoimmunity-risk allele was more prevalent in post-infectious ME/CFS compared to non-infection-triggered ME/CFS.

The IRF5 rs3807306 and TNF rs1799724 risk alleles showed significantly lower allele frequency in ME/CFS patients without infection-triggered onset, suggesting reduced TNF-α/IFN-α production may predispose to infection-triggered disease.
A monozygotic twin study found that 55% of both identical twin pairs showed ME/CFS symptoms in both twins, supporting a genetic contribution in a subgroup of patients.
In a cohort of 268 ME/CFS patients, 29% had elevated autoantibodies against neurotransmitter receptors, supporting an autoimmune hypothesis for a subset of the disease.
Removing autoantibodies via immunoadsorption produced rapid symptom improvement in 7 of 10 ME/CFS patients.

In a study of 192 ME/CFS patients and 392 controls, 17 cytokines were significantly abnormal and correlated with disease severity, with 13 pro-inflammatory and the anti-inflammatory cytokine TGF-β significantly elevated.
Reduced mitochondrial function was found in ME/CFS cohorts regardless of disease severity.

Shungu and colleagues found significantly higher lactate in the brain ventricles of ME/CFS patients, proposing that infection-induced cytokines raise ROS/NO leading to cerebral hypoperfusion and anaerobic metabolism.

Armstrong and colleagues found higher ROS levels, inhibited glycolysis, and lower amino acid levels in blood and urine of 34 ME/CFS patients, suggesting inefficient energy production underlies fatigue.
Naviaux and colleagues found significant variations in 20 different metabolites in ME/CFS patients, 80% of which were reduced, indicating a hypometabolic state.
Germain and colleagues reported a broad redox imbalance in ME/CFS patients, but a subsequent study could not reproduce these findings.
Elevated plasma ceramide levels (a sphingolipid) were found in ME/CFS patients and correlated with increased physical fatigue.

A two-day cardiopulmonary exercise test found normal oxygen consumption on day one but significantly reduced consumption on a second test 24 hours later, distinguishing ME/CFS patients from controls with 95% accuracy.
MRI studies found decreased reticular activation system connectivity in the brainstem and hippocampus of ME/CFS patients, correlating with symptom severity.
A study of 50 ME/CFS patients found EEG abnormalities showing global hypoactivation of the central nervous system.
Clinical trials of autoimmunity-targeting treatments including rituximab, cyclophosphamide, and IgG showed some evidence of efficacy in a subset of ME/CFS patients.
Risk of developing ME/CFS in IBD patients, especially Crohn's disease, is significantly higher compared to individuals without IBD (3.7% vs 0.2%).
A retrospective cohort study showed a significantly increased risk of women developing ME/CFS following Helicobacter pylori-associated peptic ulcer disease.

Following a maximal exercise test, Shukla and colleagues observed differential changes in blood microbiota, with Clostridium increased 15 minutes post-exercise and Bacilli increased at 48 hours, suggesting post-exertional bacterial translocation.

A study comparing ME/CFS (n=50) to Q-fever fatigue syndrome patients and healthy controls (n=72) found similar microbial signatures between ME/CFS and Q-fever, with increased Firmicutes and Actinobacteria and reduced Bacteroidetes in ME/CFS versus controls.
One treatment with antibiotics increases the risk of developing IBD by 84%, with each subsequent treatment adding a further 6% risk, and earlier/more frequent antibiotic use increasing risk further.

Women have 27% higher antibiotic exposure than men generally, rising to 40% more prescriptions in the 16-54 age group, which the authors link to the female predominance of ME/CFS via antibiotic-driven microbiome changes.
In an RCT, oral Bifidobacterium infantis reduced systemic inflammatory markers such as CRP and TNF-α in ME/CFS patients (71% vs 11% in comparator).
A probiotic intervention with Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium significantly reduced anxiety in ME/CFS patients in a small trial of 15 subjects, though anxiety is not a core ME/CFS symptom.

A rectal transcolonoscopic infusion of Bacteroidetes, Clostridia and E. coli produced a beneficial transient response in 70% (42/60) and a lasting response in 58% (35/60) of ME/CFS patients with concurrent gastrointestinal symptoms, though most were also IBS comorbid.
In a retrospective observational study, 17 of 21 ME/CFS patients with IBS undergoing FMT showed massive improvement (65-95%) versus oral nutritional remedies, with seven patients reportedly cured.

In IBS patients, FMT increased fecal SCFA levels and this increase inversely correlated with fatigue symptoms across two double-blind RCTs, suggesting SCFAs play a role in fatigue pathophysiology relevant to ME/CFS.

A double-blind randomized-controlled cross-over study of 40 IBD patients with severe fatigue found that 20-day high-dose thiamine supplementation significantly improved fatigue as measured by the IBD-fatigue questionnaire.
A randomized controlled trial of acupuncture/moxibustion showed improved fatigue in ME/CFS patients, associated with alterations in the intestinal microbiome.

Oral ginseng administration has shown anti-fatigue properties in ME/CFS, MS-related fatigue, and cancer-related fatigue across several blinded RCTs, with effects possibly mediated by the gut microbiome.

A recent interventional clinical study found no direct alteration of the kynurenine/tryptophan (KYN/TRP) ratio in established ME/CFS patients, suggesting abnormal kynurenine metabolism may matter more at disease initiation than in established illness.
A systematic review found no evidence for a benefit of elimination or modified diets in ME/CFS patients.
Mitochondrial DNA genome variation does not appear to influence susceptibility or resistance to ME/CFS but might affect the type and severity of symptoms.
Mitral valve prolapse was identified in 7.5% of patients with hEDS or HSD referred for joint hypermobility evaluation.
Thoracic aortic dilatation was found in 15.2% of the overall hEDS/HSD cohort.
Aortic dilatation was more common in patients diagnosed with hEDS (20.7%) than in those with a hypermobility spectrum disorder (7.7%).
Aortic dilatation was similarly prevalent between males and females, but severity differed, being mild in over 90% of affected females versus moderate-to-severe in 50% of affected males.
Five individuals (1.9%) with hEDS/HSD had extra-aortic arterial involvement including cervical artery dissection, spontaneous coronary artery dissection, and SCAD with celiac artery pseudoaneurysm.
This is described as the first case series to report the prevalence of cervical artery dissection and spontaneous coronary artery dissection specifically in hEDS/HSD patients.
Hypermobile EDS patients frequently present with multidirectional shoulder instability, often first diagnosed after an atraumatic shoulder dislocation in a young girl with generalized hyperlaxity.

Conservative management (specific physiotherapy, pain management, multidisciplinary clinics) is recommended as first-line treatment before surgery is considered in h-EDS patients with shoulder instability, given a high failure rate of standard surgical procedures.

The described arthroscopic capsular plication technique purse-strings the anterior, inferior, and posterior glenohumeral capsule to reduce capsular volume and stabilize the shoulder, with pain reduction being the main clinical outcome rather than perfect stabilization.
Nonabsorbable rather than absorbable suture threads are recommended for capsular plication in h-EDS patients because tissue fragility increases the risk of recurrence with absorbable sutures.

Vavken et al. found that open capsular shift improved both objective and subjective shoulder function and stability in EDS/generalized ligamentous hyperlaxity patients after failed conservative treatment.

Witney-Lagen et al. reported that in 50 consecutive patients with symptomatic MDSI unresponsive to at least 6 months of physiotherapy, arthroscopic capsular plication achieved satisfaction in 47 patients and return to prior sport level in 45, with only 2 complications (stiffness and wound infection).
Sekiya et al.'s cadaveric study found that arthroscopic capsular plication reduced glenohumeral joint volume at least as effectively as the standard open technique.
Alberta et al. concluded that arthroscopic plication using a 10-mm anteroinferior arthroscopic suture plication was effective in reducing both anterior translation and external rotation.
Thermal shrinkage and laser-assisted capsulorraphy techniques are no longer recommended for MDSI due to poor outcomes and high complication rates.
The authors report that the failure rate of arthroscopic capsular plication is higher in h-EDS patients than in non-h-EDS patients with MDSI, based on their clinical experience.

After diagnosis of EDS-HT, healthcare utilization patterns shifted from diagnostic visits (genetics, rheumatology, orthopedics) toward treatment-oriented visits (physical therapy, pain management, cardiology, neurology).
Frequency of testing and hospital encounters/procedures did not significantly change between the pre- and post-diagnosis periods.

The authors hypothesize that Ehlers-Danlos syndrome hypermobility type (EDS-HT), through collagen synthesis deficits causing temporal bone fragility, may predispose patients to development of superior semicircular canal dehiscence (SSCD).
A prior study (Dolan et al.) found that EDS patients experienced bone formation abnormalities more frequently than age-matched controls.

The index patient had a documented history of Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome, postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (POTS), and chronic migraines, later found to have bilateral SSCD after a traumatic fall.
Vestibular-evoked myogenic potential (VEMP) testing showed reduced/abnormal thresholds and amplitudes bilaterally, consistent with SSCD.
High-resolution CT imaging revealed bilateral semicircular canal osseous roof thinning with possible dehiscence, larger on the left side.
In a previously reported case from the same lab, CT imaging showed 5 mm and 4 mm dehiscence of the right and left superior semicircular canal apices, respectively.

Left-sided middle cranial fossa craniotomy repair of SSCD led to drastic improvement in dizziness, nausea, and left-sided sound/motion sensitivity, with complete resolution of transient eyebrow movement impairment by 6-9 week follow-up.

Right-sided SSCD repair performed six weeks after the left repair resulted in significant bilateral improvement in hyperacusis and improved hearing/noise sensitivity on the right side by six-week follow-up.
Across all three reported EDS-HT patients with SSCD (this case plus two prior), surgical repair resulted in symptomatic improvement on the ipsilateral side.
Unlike SSCD, otological symptomology is described as rare in EDS-HT itself, although headache and dizziness can occur in both conditions, creating diagnostic overlap.
Audiometric air-bone gap findings were inconsistent across the three reported EDS-HT/SSCD cases: present in the first case but absent in the second and in the current case.

Because type 1 collagen is the main organic component of bone, the authors propose that EDS-HT-related collagen deficits may cause temporal bone fragility, increasing susceptibility to dehiscence via trauma, osteopenia, or elevated intracranial pressure.
The patient's SSCD symptoms began after a traumatic ice-skating fall, presented as an anecdotal example linking trauma to symptom onset in an EDS-HT patient.
Using newer estimation models, EDS prevalence may be as high as 194 per 100,000 as of 2016/2017, higher than historically believed.
Hypermobility EDS remains genetically unlinked and cannot currently be diagnosed with genetic testing, unlike most other EDS subtypes.

Relaxin, a pleiotropic hormone that surges during pregnancy, promotes connective tissue remodeling via increased collagen turnover, contributing to ligamentous laxity that can persist into the postpartum period and compound EDS symptoms.

Pregnancy in EDS mothers is associated with complications including uterine rupture, precipitous delivery (<4 hours), arterial dissection/rupture, and miscarriage, which can create impediments to lactation.
Many women with EDS experience neuropathic pain and/or small fiber neuropathy, which can contribute to breast/nipple pain during lactation, particularly with poor latch.
Raynaud's syndrome is very common among EDS patients and can contribute to nipple and breast pain during lactation.

Many patients with EDS have associated dysautonomia diagnoses such as POTS, causing dizziness, palpitations, and near-fainting that can be misdiagnosed as postpartum anxiety and complicate infant handling.
EDS patients commonly experience gastrointestinal symptoms such as constipation, diarrhea, reflux, nausea and abdominal pain, which can challenge adequate maternal nutrient intake during lactation.
Nifedipine has been reported to successfully manage nipple vasospasms in mothers with EDS.
Magnesium supplementation has been reported to be helpful for alleviating breast/pain symptoms in EDS mothers.
Warm compresses have been reported to help alleviate pain symptoms in EDS mothers, along with other techniques such as rhythmic sensory stimulation, TENS, lidocaine patches, and joint injections.

Rehabilitative (kinesiology) tape can be used to create external splinting tension for joint stabilization in EDS mothers, but should be used cautiously in those with moderate to severe dermal manifestations.

Mothers with EDS may experience extreme engorgement due to hyperplastic breast tissue, and some exhibit a strong let-down with high-pressure milk flow, attributed to dysfunctional collagen affecting smooth muscle coordination of mammary tissue.

Increased laxity of Cooper's ligaments, which suspend breast tissue, combined with the weight of lactating breast tissue, can cause pain that makes positioning and feeding ergonomics challenging and may interfere with or inhibit milk production or flow.

EDS patients can experience shearing injuries to circummammary ligaments from routine breast-related movements (e.g., hair washing, bra adjustment, latching), risking shoulder or ligament injury during the postpartum period.

Trio exome sequencing with CNV analysis identified a de novo in-frame heterozygous deletion spanning exons 45 to 54 of COL12A1 in a boy with fetal hypokinesia, severe neonatal weakness, hyperlaxity, and skeletal anomalies consistent with Ehlers-Danlos/myopathy overlap syndrome.
Immunostaining of cultured skin fibroblasts from the patient showed intracellular retention of collagen XII, supporting the pathogenicity of the COL12A1 deletion.
The patient's phenotype, including fetal hypokinesia, was noted to be slightly more severe than previously reported cases with dominantly acting COL12A1 mutations.
Across the EDS cohort as a whole, mean changes in pain, sleep, fatigue, and health survey scores were small over a median 11.6-year follow-up interval.
Individual EDS participants showed highly heterogeneous longitudinal symptom trajectories, with some markedly improving and others dramatically worsening over the follow-up period.
Men with EDS experienced a greater increase in mean pain severity over the follow-up period compared to women with EDS.
Loss-of-function of COL1A2 is stated to cause osteogenesis imperfecta types I-IV and the cardiac valvular and arthrochalasia types of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.

A homozygous COL1A2 knockout human embryonic stem cell line (WAe009-A-72) generated via CRISPR/Cas9 retained normal colony morphology, a normal karyotype, robust pluripotency marker expression, and the ability to differentiate into all three germ layers.
High-frequency rTMS applied to the left primary motor cortex significantly reduced pain immediately and at 1-4 weeks post-treatment, but this effect was not sustained at 5-12 weeks follow-up.
Quality of life in fibromyalgia patients improved after high-frequency rTMS on the left primary motor cortex, but this benefit only appeared later, at 5-12 weeks of follow-up.
High-frequency rTMS applied to the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex did not reduce pain in fibromyalgia patients.
rTMS treatment at either the left primary motor cortex or the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex did not significantly improve affective (mood-related) problems in fibromyalgia patients.
Skin biopsy studies have identified small fiber neuropathy in a large proportion of fibromyalgia patients, supporting a peripheral nervous system contribution to the condition.
A dysfunction in central processing of nociceptive inputs has been proposed as the primary cause of fibromyalgia, based on neuroimaging, electrophysiological, and morphological evidence.
A genome-wide linkage study cited in this review found a 13.6-fold increased risk of developing fibromyalgia among first-degree relatives, supporting a genetic/familial component.
Polymorphisms of the serotonin transporter gene (referred to as SLC64A4, likely SLC6A4) have been linked to altered endogenous pain modulation in fibromyalgia.
Polymorphism of the transient receptor potential vanilloid channel 2 gene (TRPV2) has been linked to endogenous pain modulation in fibromyalgia patients.

Two additional candidate genes, MYT1L (neuronal differentiation/cognition) and NRXN3 (neuronal receptor/cell adhesion molecule), have been proposed as susceptibility genes in fibromyalgia, though no SNP reached genome-wide significance.

Brain imaging studies cited show elevated glutamate levels in pain-related brain regions (posterior cingulate gyrus, posterior insula, ventrolateral prefrontal cortex, amygdala) in patients with fibromyalgia.
Patients with fibromyalgia show increased glutamate and glycine concentrations in cerebrospinal fluid.

Treatment with pregabalin decreases elevated insular glutamate levels and reduces functional connectivity between the default mode network and insula, correlating with reduced clinical and experimental pain.

In a double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover trial, a single IV ketamine infusion (0.3 mg/kg) produced a >50% reduction in pain intensity (VAS) at end of infusion and 20-80 minutes later versus placebo in 11 female fibromyalgia patients.

Ketamine-treated fibromyalgia patients showed significant decreases in tenderness and pain threshold, along with increased muscle endurance and pain tolerance at tender/control points compared to placebo.

In a second Sörensen et al crossover trial of 18 fibromyalgia patients, ketamine responders showed sustained improvements in pain threshold and tolerance up to 120 minutes and significantly improved Fibromyalgia Impact Questionnaire (FIQ) scores relative to placebo.

In a crossover trial of 29 fibromyalgia patients (Graven-Nielsen et al), IV ketamine (0.3 mg/kg) reduced muscular hyperalgesia and hypertonic-saline-induced muscle pain, and decreased temporal summation to cutaneous and muscular electrical stimulation compared to placebo.

Noppers et al found a single S-ketamine infusion (0.5 mg/kg) produced a significant initial pain reduction versus baseline and a higher number of responders than active placebo (midazolam) in 24 fibromyalgia patients.

In the same Noppers et al trial, no significant difference in treatment effect on fibromyalgia pain or experimental heat pain was found between S-ketamine and midazolam at 2.5 hours post-infusion or during 8-week follow-up.

Cohen et al found that low-dose ketamine infusion (0.1 mg/kg) followed by oral dextromethorphan produced a >50% VAS pain reduction in 18 of 34 fibromyalgia patients, with pain relief significantly correlated between the two agents.
Cohen et al observed no long-term benefit from a single low-dose ketamine infusion in fibromyalgia patients.

A case study (Hanna and Smith) of a fibromyalgia patient given escalating high-dose IV ketamine (200-800 mg over 4 hours daily for 5 days, with an 800 mg booster 2 weeks later) resulted in long-lasting remission from chronic pain and improved quality of life.

In a second case study, a patient with fibromyalgia and rheumatoid arthritis who received 10 consecutive escalating-dose ketamine infusions (428-1,063 mg) achieved gradual pain reduction sustained at 80% improvement, maintained with booster infusions roughly every 3 months.

Low total doses of IV ketamine in the reviewed RCTs produced mild to moderate, short-lasting psychomimetic side effects including nausea, dizziness, confusion, and drowsiness that resolved within about 30 minutes.
In the two high-dose case studies, higher ketamine doses administered more frequently were well tolerated with no unexpected adverse effects, including no hepatotoxicity.
Vitexin treatment suppressed mast cell activation and degranulation along with inflammatory cell infiltration in OVA-LPS induced allergic asthma mice.
Vitexin decreased phosphorylated connexin 43 and p-c-Fos expression, indicating reversal of lung vascular permeability and mast cell degranulation-related signaling.
Vitexin reduced TGF-β and Smad2/3/4 expression, indicating reversal of fibrosis in the allergic asthma lung model.
Vitexin decreased Caspase9/3 and increased Bcl2/Bax ratio, indicating reduced apoptosis in allergic asthma lung tissue.
Vitexin decreased LC3A/B and increased beclin-1 and p62 co-localization, suggesting amelioration of autophagosome impairment in allergic asthma.
Sensitized allergic asthma mice showed upregulation of p-NF-κB, p-PI3K, p-Akt, p-p38, p-Stat3 and GATA3, which vitexin treatment decisively counteracted.
Vitexin treatment decreased TGF-β and Smad2/3/4 expression in OVA-LPS sensitized mouse lungs, indicating reversal of fibrosis.
Vitexin decreased Caspase9/3 expression while increasing the Bcl2/Bax ratio, indicating suppression of apoptosis in sensitized lung tissue.
Vitexin reduced LC3A/B expression and increased beclin-1/p62 co-localization, indicating restoration of impaired autophagosome function.
Vitexin decreased phosphorylated connexin 43 and c-Fos levels, indicating reversal of lung vascular permeability and mast cell degranulation.
Sensitized mice exhibited upregulation of p-NF-κB, p-PI3K, p-Akt, p-p38, p-Stat3 and GATA3, which were decisively counteracted by vitexin treatment.
Sensitized mice showed downregulation of phosphorylated PTEN, which was reversed by vitexin treatment.
In silico modeling demonstrated target specificity of vitexin for NF-κB, PI3K, Akt, p38, Stat3, GATA3 and PTEN proteins.
Sensitized mice showed upregulation of phosphorylated NF-κB, PI3K, Akt, p38 and Stat3 along with GATA3, and this activation was decisively counteracted by vitexin treatment.
Phosphorylated PTEN was downregulated in sensitized mice, and this reduction was reversed by vitexin treatment.
In silico docking studies indicated that vitexin has target specificity for the signaling proteins identified (e.g., NF-κB, PI3K, Akt, p38, Stat3, PTEN) implicated in allergic asthma pathology.
Vitexin treatment suppressed myeloid cell activation while enhancing regulatory T cell (Treg) populations, demonstrating an immunomodulatory effect in allergic airways.
Corneal nerve fiber length in the peripheral cornea was significantly lower in ALS patients than in healthy controls.
Corneal nerve fiber density in the peripheral cornea was significantly lower in ALS patients than in controls.
Corneal nerve branch density in the peripheral cornea was significantly higher in ALS patients, suggesting a more complex/regenerative nerve pattern.
Dendritic cell density in the peripheral cornea was significantly higher in ALS patients than controls, indicating a secondary immune response.
Nerve fiber length in the inferior whorl area of the cornea was significantly lower in ALS patients than in healthy controls.
Dendritic cell density in the inferior whorl area was significantly higher in ALS patients than in controls.
IWL correlated positively with ALSFRS-R disease severity score, indicating greater nerve length with milder disease.
IWL correlated positively with the bulbar sub-scores of the ALSFRS-R.
IWL correlated negatively with disease progression rate (ΔFS), so lower IWL was associated with faster disease progression.
IWDC was not significantly correlated with ALS disease severity or progression scores.
CNFL showed a relatively weak positive correlation with ALSFRS-R disease severity score.
Aside from the weak CNFL correlation, no other peripheral CCM parameters showed significant correlations with ALS disease severity or progression scores.
ALS patients with bulbar involvement had significantly lower IWL than those without bulbar involvement.
ALS patients with bulbar involvement had significantly higher IWDC than those without bulbar involvement.

There were no significant differences in peripheral area CCM parameters between ALS patients with and without bulbar involvement, although a similar trend of lower nerve length and higher dendritic cell density was observed.
CCM was safely and well tolerated in ambulatory ALS patients with no adverse events reported.
Corneal nerve fiber length (NFL) was significantly decreased in ALS patients compared with controls.
Corneal nerve fiber density (NFD) was significantly decreased in ALS patients compared with controls.
Corneal nerve fiber tortuosity (NFT) was significantly increased in ALS patients compared with controls.
Corneal nerve branch density (NBD) did not differ significantly between ALS patients and controls.
The duration of ALS disease course correlated with corneal nerve fiber tortuosity (NFT).

Five asymptomatic carriers of the TTR p.Val50Met (Val30Met) mutation from a single family, causative of hereditary ATTR amyloidosis with polyneuropathy, were followed prospectively with multiple diagnostic tests over three years.
Intraepidermal nerve fiber density on skin biopsy was already low at baseline in three of five carriers and declined below normative values in all carriers over the follow-up period.

Corneal sub-basal nerve density, measured by in vivo corneal confocal microscopy, was reduced in all carriers compared with controls throughout the entire three-year follow-up, even before other tests became abnormal.

Standard autonomic and large-fiber tests (nerve conduction studies, sympathetic skin response, heart rate variability) remained normal in all carriers throughout the three-year follow-up, unlike small fiber measures.

Quantitative sensory testing (QST) and the SFN-SIQ questionnaire were normal at baseline but became abnormal during follow-up in two carriers who developed small fiber neuropathy symptoms, indicating these tools can detect transition from asymptomatic to symptomatic ATTRv-polyneuropathy.

SFN-SIQ questionnaire and quantitative sensory testing were identified as useful clinical tools for detecting the transition from asymptomatic carrier status to symptomatic small fiber involvement in ATTRv-polyneuropathy.
Cutaneous interleukin levels were implicated as an inflammatory biomarker process in CRPS Type I skin.
Cutaneous TNF-alpha expression was identified as an inflammatory biomarker in CRPS Type I skin.
ET-1 disturbances in skin were identified as evidence of vascular dysregulation in CRPS Type I.
Nitric oxide (NOx) disturbances in skin were identified as evidence of vascular dysregulation in CRPS Type I.
Cutaneous hypoxia with elevated lactate was identified as evidence of vascular dysregulation in CRPS Type I skin.
Skin biopsies showed neurite loss consistent with small fiber neuropathy in CRPS Type I patients.
Skin biopsies revealed increased expression and disturbed migration of mast cells in CRPS Type I patients.
Keratinocytes in CRPS Type I skin showed increased expression of alpha1-adrenoceptors.
Evidence for cutaneous hypersensitivity as a biomarker in CRPS Type I was identified but judged to carry a high risk of bias in the quality assessment.

Stimulation with the regular patch electrode was perceived as dull, whereas the novel planar concentric array electrode produced a sharp sensation that increased in sharpness with higher stimulation intensity.
Numerical rating scale pain scores were higher with the planar concentric array electrode than with the patch electrode and increased further with rising stimulation current intensity.

Reaction times and event-related potential latencies were longer for the planar concentric array electrode compared to the patch electrode, consistent with preferential activation of slower-conducting small fibers.
Patients with SFN had lower intraepidermal nerve fiber density than healthy controls.
The number of subepidermal Schwann cells per millimeter was lower in SFN patients than in healthy controls.
The number of Schwann cell clusters per millimeter was lower in SFN patients compared with healthy controls.
Among SFN patients, those with reduced distal IENFD had fewer solitary Schwann cells per millimeter than those with normal distal IENFD.
SFN patients with reduced distal IENFD had fewer subepidermal nerve fibers associated with Schwann cell branches than those with normal distal IENFD.
Schwann cell counts, clusters, and associated fibers all correlated positively with distal intraepidermal nerve fiber density.
No correlation was found between Schwann cell counts and clinical pain characteristics in SFN patients.

Classic GCH1-associated dopa-responsive dystonia presents as early-onset asymmetrical lower limb dystonia with sleep benefit, diurnal variation, and an excellent, sustained response to low doses of levodopa.

A described case of GCH1-associated late-onset dopa-responsive dystonia, with a family history of parkinsonism and cervical dystonia, showed a poor response to levodopa complicated by dyskinesia, blepharospasm, and severe nonmotor symptoms.

GCH1-related dystonia can show wide intrafamilial phenotypic variability with no diurnal fluctuation, poor levodopa response, and complications including dyskinesia, epilepsy, sleep disorders, autonomic dysfunction, oculogyric crisis, myoclonus, or tics.
Rare GCH1 variants have more recently been found to be associated with Parkinson disease.
Esomeprazole treatment suppressed the migration of dermal fibroblasts derived from systemic sclerosis patients.
Esomeprazole downregulated the profibrotic markers COL1A1, alpha-SMA, CTGF and MMP1 in SSc dermal fibroblasts.
Esomeprazole acts as an exogenous agonist of AhR signaling, which limits collagen production in SSc fibroblasts.
Esomeprazole blocked Smad2/3 phosphorylation concurrently with reduced collagen production via AhR signaling.
In a bleomycin-induced systemic sclerosis mouse model, esomeprazole ameliorated fibrosis in both skin and lung, consistent with in vitro findings.
Homozygous QDPR mutations were the most common genetic cause identified, found in 6 of 9 patients with tetrahydrobiopterin metabolism disorders.
Homozygous GCH1 mutations (GTP cyclohydrolase I deficiency) were identified in 2 of 9 patients.
A homozygous PTS gene mutation (6-pyruvoyltetrahydropterin synthase deficiency) was identified in 1 of 9 patients.
Tetrahydrobiopterin metabolism disorders manifest mainly in infancy or childhood with developmental delay, neuroregression, epilepsy, movement disorders, and autonomic symptoms.
Neuroregression was the most common clinical manifestation, seen in 89% of patients.
Developmental delay was present in 78% of patients.
Dystonia was present in 78% of patients.
Diagnosis was delayed by a median of 9 months after symptom onset, with median age at onset of 6 months versus median age at diagnosis of 15 months.
Management strategies for patients included a phenylalanine restricted diet.
Patients were managed with levodopa/carbidopa as neurotransmitter replacement therapy.
5-Hydroxytryptophan was used as a serotonin precursor replacement therapy in management.
Folinic acid was administered as part of management, likely for patients with folate metabolism involvement such as QDPR deficiency.
Only one patient (Patient-2) could afford and received BH4 (sapropterin) supplementation, and this was at a sub-optimal dose and started later in the disease course.

Over a median follow-up of 15 months, biochemical response to treatment was marked overall, but clinical improvement in developmental milestones, seizures, and dystonia was only mild, except in patients with GTPCH (GCH1) deficiency who had better outcomes.

The meta-analysis found that current evidence is insufficient to determine whether gastrointestinal disorders (including IBS) are genuinely associated with oral lichen planus, warranting higher-quality studies before any conclusion can be drawn.

The meta-analysis found that current evidence is insufficient to determine whether fibromyalgia is genuinely associated with oral lichen planus, warranting higher-quality studies before any conclusion can be drawn.
Genetic testing identified a heterozygous variant of uncertain significance in TGFBR1 (c.1445G>A, p.Arg482Lys) in a patient with clinical and radiologic features of Loeys-Dietz syndrome.
The patient presented with a severely dilated aortic root and ascending thoracic aorta (6.8 cm), an acute type A aortic dissection, and large hemopericardium with tamponade physiology.
Physical exam and imaging demonstrated a bifid uvula and hypertelorism, classic craniofacial features supporting a diagnosis of Loeys-Dietz syndrome.

CTA of the head and neck showed marked arterial tortuosity involving the vertebrobasilar system, proximal anterior cerebral arteries, mid/upper cervical internal carotid arteries, and lower cervical vertebral arteries.
CTA of the abdomen and pelvis revealed aneurysmal dilation of the proximal superior mesenteric artery to 1.4 cm.
Prior literature reports hypertelorism in 93% of LDS patients and cleft palate or bifid uvula in 100% of LDS patients, distinguishing LDS from Marfan syndrome.
Ectopia lentis is not associated with LDS but occurs in Marfan syndrome and Shprintzen-Goldberg syndrome, making its presence a clue toward an alternative diagnosis.
Intracranial aneurysms are a recognized neurovascular manifestation of LDS, reported in up to 28% of patients.
Intracerebral bleeding has been reported as the cause of death in up to 7% of patients with LDS.
The average age of death in LDS has been reported as young as 26 years, with thoracic aortic dissection as the leading cause of death.
A prior study found arterial tortuosity of the head or neck in all 25 reviewed LDS patients.
Quantitative carotid bifurcation widening, recently termed the 'chalice sign,' has been proposed as a distinguishing radiologic feature for diagnosing LDS.

Increased vertebral artery tortuosity in connective tissue disease patients may predict major adverse cardiovascular outcomes, including severe aortic root dilation, younger age of aortic dissection, and death.
Surgical management for aortic aneurysm in LDS is often considered once thoracic aortic diameter reaches 4.0 cm.

The paper describes creation of a multidisciplinary complex care coordination (C3) clinic specifically for patients with concomitant fibromyalgia and chronic abdominal pain/irritable bowel syndrome, framed as central sensitization-based conditions.

Fibromyalgia is estimated to affect 2%-8% of the US population, with the National Fibromyalgia Association estimating approximately 10 million affected Americans and total related health care costs of $10 billion annually.
IBS/chronic abdominal pain is cited as a central-sensitization-based condition with a global prevalence of about 11% and health care costs exceeding $20 billion annually.
Chronic fatigue syndrome/myalgic encephalomyelitis is cited as a central-sensitization-based condition affecting up to 2.5 million Americans with an economic cost of $17-24 billion annually.
Postural tachycardia syndrome (POTS) is listed among central-sensitization-based conditions with an estimated prevalence of 0.2%.
An estimated 25% of patients seeking Division of General Internal Medicine consultative service at the Mayo Clinic have a central-sensitization-related condition.
Median age was numerically lower in the C3 clinic pilot cohort compared with the contemporary comparison cohort, but the difference did not reach statistical significance.
The C3 clinic pilot cohort had a significantly higher proportion of female patients than the contemporary comparison cohort.
Patients seen through the C3 clinic spent significantly more total days on-campus (from first face-to-face consultation through 31 days follow-up) than the comparison cohort.

There were no significant differences between the C3 clinic cohort and comparison cohort in the number of added appointments/imaging/procedures or total added and cancelled appointments/imaging/procedures.
Post-visit patient portal messaging (medical advice requests and schedule requests) did not differ significantly between the C3 clinic cohort and the comparison cohort.

General internal medicine physicians reported spending an average of 14 minutes preparing, 25 minutes on the virtual previsit call, and 12 minutes on post-visit documentation per C3 clinic patient, rating the visits' value at 6/10 on average.

Gastroenterology specialists reported spending an average of 22 minutes preparing, 17 minutes on the video call, and 10 minutes on documentation per C3 clinic patient, rating the visits' value highly at 9/10 on average.
General internal medicine and gastroenterology physicians showed a high degree of agreement in rating patient fit for the C3 clinic intent, both averaging a score of 6 on a 10-point scale.

The paper cites prior evidence that patient education for fibromyalgia is associated with substantial improvement in disease perceptions and reductions in catastrophizing, pain intensity, and anxiety.
The paper cites prior evidence that guided self-help (GSH) interventions for IBS are associated with decreased symptom severity and increased quality of life.
Recombinant CCN2(IV) treatment significantly increased TβRII protein levels in cultured vascular smooth muscle cells at both 50 and 100 ng/mL doses after 48 hours compared with untreated basal cells.
In contrast to CCN2(IV), treatment with TGF-β (10 ng/mL) significantly decreased TβRII protein levels in VSMCs after 48 hours.
Neither CCN2(IV) nor TGF-β altered TβRI protein levels in VSMCs, indicating a selective effect on TβRII.
CCN2(IV) increased TβRII mRNA levels in VSMCs at 50 and 100 ng/mL after 48 hours, whereas TGF-β dramatically decreased TβRII mRNA levels.
CCN2(IV) treatment did not alter TβRI or TGF-β mRNA levels in VSMCs at any dose tested after 48 hours.
CCN2(IV) directly activated the SMAD pathway in VSMCs, significantly increasing phosphorylated SMAD3 and SMAD2 levels after 10, 15 and 20 minutes of treatment.
SMAD pathway activation by CCN2(IV) was confirmed by nuclear translocation of phosphorylated SMAD2 and SMAD4 in VSMCs after 10 and 20 minutes.
Intraperitoneal CCN2(IV) administration in mice increased p-SMAD3 and p-SMAD2 levels in aortic VSMCs in vivo after 24 hours, confirming the in vitro findings.
Preincubation of VSMCs with the SMAD3 phosphorylation inhibitor SIS3 blocked CCN2(IV)-induced TβRII upregulation, demonstrating that SMAD3 activation is required for this effect.
Preincubation with galunisertib, a TβRI inhibitor, did not block CCN2(IV)-induced TβRII upregulation, indicating this effect is independent of TGF-β receptor signaling.
Preincubation of VSMCs with the EGFR inhibitor erlotinib prior to CCN2(IV) administration prevented TβRII upregulation, indicating EGFR is required for CCN2-induced TβRII overexpression.

eNOS protein expression (immunohistochemistry) and mRNA were significantly decreased in the carotid artery of reserpine-induced fibromyalgia rats compared to controls, indicating endothelial dysfunction.
eNOS expression (immunohistochemical and mRNA) in the cerebral cortex was significantly decreased in the reserpine-induced fibromyalgia group compared to controls.
Fisetin treatment significantly restored eNOS mRNA and protein expression in both carotid artery and cerebral cortex compared to the untreated reserpine group.
Reserpine-induced fibromyalgia was associated with increased caspase-3 mRNA and decreased Bcl-2 mRNA in both the carotid artery and cerebral cortex, indicating stimulated apoptosis.
Fisetin treatment significantly reduced apoptosis induction (decreased caspase-3, increased Bcl-2) in reserpine-treated rats (p < 0.001).
TNF-α mRNA expression was increased in both carotid and cerebral tissues of reserpine-induced fibromyalgia rats, indicating an inflammatory reaction.
CHOP gene expression, an ER stress marker, was elevated in reserpine-induced fibromyalgia rats and was more pronounced in cerebral cortical tissue than in carotid vessels.
Autophagy markers LC-3 and BECN-1 mRNA were significantly increased in the reserpine-induced fibromyalgia group, indicating induction of excessive autophagy.

Fisetin decreased LC3 and BECN-1 gene expression relative to the untreated reserpine group, though levels remained significantly higher than in controls, suggesting a modulating rather than fully suppressive autophagy effect.
