Serum MDA (lipid peroxidation marker) was significantly increased in reserpine-induced fibromyalgia rats compared to controls.

Serum NO levels were significantly increased in the reserpine-induced fibromyalgia group compared to controls, alongside decreased eNOS-derived vascular/cerebral NO signaling, suggesting a nitrosative-stress-related elevation distinct from eNOS-mediated NO.
Serum total antioxidant capacity was significantly decreased in reserpine-induced fibromyalgia rats compared to controls.
Fisetin treatment significantly reversed the oxidative stress markers (MDA, NO, TAC) toward control levels, though not fully normalizing them.

Carotid artery intima-media thickness (IMT) was significantly increased in the reserpine-treated fibromyalgia group compared to controls, and was non-significantly different from controls in the fisetin co-treated group.

Area percentage of collagen deposition in the carotid artery tunica media and adventitia was significantly increased in the reserpine-treated group, and was not significantly different from controls after fisetin co-treatment.
Ultrastructural mitochondrial number in the carotid artery was significantly increased in the reserpine-treated group compared to controls and significantly decreased after fisetin co-treatment.
Ultrastructural mitochondrial number in the cerebral cortex was significantly increased in the reserpine-treated group compared to controls and significantly decreased after fisetin co-treatment.

Reserpine-induced fibromyalgia rats showed histological carotid artery damage including endothelial cell loss/exfoliation, foam cells, vacuolated smooth muscle cells with pyknotic nuclei, and adventitial inflammatory infiltrate with mast cells, largely improved by fisetin.

Reserpine-induced fibromyalgia rats showed cerebral cortex histological damage including apoptotic pyramidal cells, perineuronal empty spaces, neuropil vacuolation, inflammatory infiltration, and dilated congested blood vessels, notably improved by fisetin.

Ultrastructural examination of the cerebral cortex in the reserpine group showed markedly dilated rough endoplasmic reticulum cisternae in pyramidal and granular cells, consistent with ER stress, correlating with increased CHOP gene expression.

Fisetin (25 mg/kg oral for 3 weeks) significantly improved behavioral measures of mechano-hyperalgesia (Randall-Selitto), thermal pain sensation (Hargreaves test), and agitation/immobility (tail suspension test) in the reserpine-induced fibromyalgia rat model.
Patients with irritable bowel syndrome did not consistently show higher levels of perceived stigma compared to patients with a comparable explained condition.
Patients with chronic fatigue syndrome experienced higher levels of perceived stigma than patients with a comparable explained condition.
Patients with fibromyalgia experienced higher levels of perceived stigma than patients with a comparable explained condition.
All included studies found a correlation between perceived stigma and negative physical or mental health outcomes in patients with functional somatic syndromes.
HMB supplementation increased cross-sectional area (CSA) of muscle fibers in non-injured muscle compared to all other groups.
Injured sedentary muscle without HMB (SED) showed lower CSA and higher connective tissue percentage than the other groups, indicating impaired regeneration and greater fibrosis.
Injured sedentary muscle without HMB (SED) showed significantly increased myogenin protein levels compared to the other sedentary groups.
Injured sedentary muscle without HMB (SED) showed significantly increased TGF-β1 protein levels compared to the other sedentary groups, consistent with a fibrogenic response.
Both injured groups (SED and SED-HMB) showed significantly increased IGF-1 protein levels compared to non-injured control groups.
Both injured groups (SED and SED-HMB) showed significantly increased phospho-Akt (Ser473) levels compared to non-injured control groups.
HMB supplementation in non-injured muscle significantly increased the phospho-mTOR/total mTOR ratio compared to non-supplemented non-injured controls.
p70S6K protein level was elevated only in the injured sedentary non-supplemented (SED) group among sedentary groups.
Injured sedentary muscles (SED and SED-HMB) showed significantly increased GDF8/myostatin protein levels compared to non-injured muscles.
No significant differences were observed in FoxO3a, MAFbx, and MuRF1 protein levels among sedentary groups, indicating atrophy pathway markers were not altered by injury or HMB in sedentary animals.
Higher-intensity/higher-frequency training with load (HT3L, HT5) resulted in significantly lower muscle fiber CSA compared to low-frequency no-load training (HT3).
High-frequency loaded training (HT5L) significantly increased connective tissue (fibrosis) compared to the other three training groups (HT3, HT3L, HT5).

Low-frequency no-load training with HMB (HT3) had increased myogenin levels compared to high-frequency no-load training (HT5) and decreased TGF-β levels compared to loaded training groups (HT3L, HT5L).
HT3 (low-intensity, low-frequency training with HMB) had significantly higher IGF-1 and phospho-Akt levels than HT5 and HT5L groups.
HT3 (low-intensity, low-frequency training with HMB) showed significantly higher phospho-Akt levels than HT5 and HT5L groups.
There were no statistical differences in p70S6K protein levels among the different training-intensity/frequency groups.
No differences in FoxO3a and MAFbx expression were observed among the different training groups.
Normalized MuRF1 protein level was significantly decreased in all training groups compared to the HT3 group.
GDF8 (myostatin) protein level was significantly increased in the HT3 (low-intensity, low-frequency) training group compared to the HT5 group.

The combination of HMB supplementation with low-intensity (no-load), low-frequency (3x/week) aerobic exercise training appeared to be the most effective protocol for improving skeletal muscle regeneration after cryoinjury.
CAV1 expression was reduced in fibrosis-activated (stenotic) intestinal areas compared with nonstenotic areas in patients with Crohn's disease and in a DSS-induced mouse model of intestinal fibrosis.
Knockdown of CAV1 in human primary colonic fibroblasts and CCD-18Co cells promoted fibroblast activation (increased expression of fibrosis markers) in vitro.
Overexpression of CAV1 in fibroblasts inhibited TGF-β-induced fibroblast activation in vitro.
SQSTM1/p62 expression positively correlated with CAV1 expression levels in patients with Crohn's disease, suggesting indirect modulation of SQSTM1/p62 by CAV1.

Rescue experiments showed that CAV1 decreases primary human intestinal fibroblast activation by inhibiting fibroblast autophagy through modulation of SQSTM1/p62, indicating SQSTM1/p62 mediates CAV1's anti-fibrotic effect.
Women with one preexisting chronic pain diagnosis had a 54% higher cumulative risk of midurethral sling revision/removal compared with women without such diagnoses.
Risk of sling revision/removal increased with the number of chronic pain diagnoses, with those having 4 or more diagnoses having over three times the risk of controls.
A preoperative diagnosis of dyspareunia was associated with the greatest adjusted odds of subsequent mesh sling revision/removal among the pelvic pain conditions studied.
A preoperative diagnosis of interstitial cystitis was associated with increased adjusted odds of mesh sling revision/removal.
Women with a preoperative diagnosis of pelvic/perineal pain had increased adjusted odds of midurethral sling revision/removal compared with those without this diagnosis.

Women with co-occurring dyspareunia and either interstitial cystitis or pelvic/perineal pain had a 12.7% cumulative incidence of mesh sling revision/removal, higher than in those without such overlapping diagnoses.
Cox proportional hazards analysis found that women with pelvic pain conditions had the greatest hazard of undergoing sling revision/removal over time compared with those without pain diagnoses.
Plasma acetaminophen levels were significantly elevated in ME/CFS cases compared to controls in the biogenic amines panel.
Plasmalogen levels were significantly decreased in ME/CFS cases compared to controls, consistent with peroxisomal dysfunction.
Unsaturated phospholipid ether levels were significantly decreased in ME/CFS cases compared to controls.
Unsaturated phosphatidylcholine (PC) levels were significantly decreased in ME/CFS cases compared to controls, suggesting dysregulation of the CDP-choline pathway.
An unsaturated sphingomyelin was significantly decreased in ME/CFS cases compared to controls.
An unsaturated lysophosphatidylcholine (LPC) was significantly decreased in ME/CFS cases compared to controls.
Resolvin D1, a pro-resolving lipid mediator derived from DHA, was significantly decreased in ME/CFS cases compared to controls.
Choline levels within the food exposome metabolite cluster were significantly reduced in ME/CFS cases compared to controls.
Succinic acid, a TCA cycle intermediate, was significantly elevated in ME/CFS cases compared to controls.
Alpha-ketoglutarate, a TCA cycle intermediate, was significantly elevated in ME/CFS cases compared to controls.
In female ME/CFS patients, PC, phosphatidylethanolamine (PE), and SM levels were decreased compared to female controls.
Plasma alprazolam levels were up-regulated in female ME/CFS patients compared to female controls.
Plasma acyclovir levels were up-regulated in female ME/CFS patients compared to female controls.
No plasma metabolites were significantly associated with ME/CFS status in male subjects, likely reflecting limited sample size.
Among subjects without self-reported IBS, PC and PE levels were decreased in ME/CFS cases compared to controls without sr-IBS.
Self-reported IBS was substantially more prevalent among ME/CFS cases (33.0%) than among controls (3.3%).
A Lasso classifier using metabolites with Bayes factor >1 distinguished female ME/CFS patients from female controls with an AUROC of 0.794.
A Lasso classifier using metabolites with Bayes factor >3 distinguished ME/CFS patients without sr-IBS from controls without sr-IBS with an AUROC of 0.873.
Machine learning classifiers were unable to differentiate the full ME/CFS cohort from all controls using plasma metabolomic profiles.
Plasma carnitine levels were significantly reduced in ME/CFS subjects, consistent with impaired mitochondrial fatty acid transport and possible peroxisomal compensation.
Unsaturated long-chain triglyceride (TG) levels were increased in ME/CFS subjects compared to controls, potentially due to carnitine depletion promoting lipid peroxidation.
In male ME/CFS patients, triglyceride TG(56:6) levels were positively correlated with MFI general fatigue scores.
In male ME/CFS patients, triglyceride TG(54:7)B levels were positively correlated with MFI physical fatigue scores.
Overall plasma choline levels showed a trend toward depletion in ME/CFS but did not meet the pre-specified significance criteria.
Hydroxy-eicosapentaenoic acid (HEPE) levels were increased in ME/CFS cases compared to controls in enrichment analysis.
Downstream prostaglandins PGD2 and PGF2α, products of PC metabolism, were decreased in ME/CFS patients.
Serum IgE levels were significantly higher in hypertensive patients compared to non-hypertensive individuals.
IgE levels were significantly increased in mice with Ang II-induced hypertension.
Genetic knockout of FcεR1 significantly alleviated Ang II-induced vascular remodelling and hypertension in mice.
Treatment with an anti-IgE monoclonal antibody significantly alleviated Ang II-induced vascular remodelling and hypertension in mice.
Omalizumab, a clinical IgE antagonist, markedly inhibited Ang II-induced hypertension in mice.
Using cell-type-specific conditional knockouts, IgE-mediated hypertension was found to be largely dependent on FcεR1 expression in mast cells but not in smooth muscle cells or endothelial cells.
RNA-seq and signalling pathway analyses of mouse bone marrow-derived mast cells identified IL-6 as a critical mediator of IgE-mediated hypertension.

IL-6 derived from IgE-stimulated mast cells promoted reactive oxygen species production and decreased phosphorylated endothelial nitric oxide synthase levels in endothelial cells, leading to endothelial dysfunction.
RNA-seq and signalling pathway analysis of mouse bone marrow-derived mast cells identified IL-6 as a key mediator downstream of IgE-FcεR1 signalling in mast cells during hypertension.
IL-6 secreted by IgE-stimulated mast cells promoted reactive oxygen species (ROS) production in endothelial cells.
IL-6 from IgE-stimulated mast cells decreased levels of phosphorylated eNOS in endothelial cells, contributing to endothelial dysfunction.
The patient had mildly elevated α3 nicotinic ganglionic acetylcholine receptor antibodies, supporting an autoimmune mechanism for her post-COVID gastrointestinal dysmotility.
Anti-striational antibodies were also mildly elevated, consistent with an autoimmune process affecting neuromuscular/autonomic function after SARS-CoV-2 infection.
Gastrointestinal transit scintigraphy demonstrated delayed gastric emptying and slowed small bowel transit consistent with gastroparesis and generalized gut dysmotility.
Thermoregulatory sweat testing revealed areas of anhidrosis, indicating autonomic sudomotor impairment as part of the post-COVID dysautonomia presentation.
Treatment with IVIG led to dramatic clinical improvement, allowing the patient to tolerate a full oral diet after ten months of enteral/parenteral nutrition dependence.
Following IVIG, repeat transit studies and thermoregulatory sweat testing showed objective improvement, corroborating the clinical response.

The author hypothesizes that endothelial and lymphatic vascular dysfunction in ME/CFS causes leaked interstitial fluid to accumulate, generating hypoxia and fibrosis similar to mechanisms described in lipedema, contributing to widespread pain and inflammation.

In the author's daughter, manual lymphatic drainage, tissue squeezing, and manual break-up of fibrotic adipose tissue reportedly ameliorated pain from fibrotic tissue and apparent nerve compression from accumulated interstitial/lymphatic fluid.

Manual lymphatic drainage and squeezing of affected tissue reportedly accelerated recovery from post-exertional malaise, with a dose-response relationship observed such that more exercise produced more tissue fluid and required more manual drainage.

The author hypothesizes that increases in cortisol during physical or cognitive exertion increase fluid and blood volume, contributing to excess interstitial fluid and post-exertional malaise, and may also explain worsening symptoms with stress or anxiety.
The author hypothesizes that elevated estrogen levels, when present, may exacerbate vascular fluid leakage by increasing fluid volume, potentially worsening ME/CFS symptoms.

The author observed impaired drainage of fluid from the glymphatic system in his daughter, both at the cribriform plate and along the spine, and hypothesizes this may relate to damaged lymphatic vessels or blockages from fibrotic adipose tissue.
Valaciclovir treatment for 3 months achieved PCR negativity for HHV-6 in 37% of cases, up from 26% at 1 month and 34% at 2 months.
Valaciclovir treatment for 3 months achieved PCR negativity for HHV-7 in 34% of cases, up from 23% at 1 month and 28% at 2 months.
Valganciclovir treatment for 3 months achieved PCR negativity for HHV-6 in 48% of cases, up from 35% at 1 month and 44% at 2 months.
Valganciclovir treatment for 3 months achieved PCR negativity for HHV-7 in 45% of cases, up from 33% at 1 month and 39% at 2 months.
Artesunate treatment for 3 months achieved PCR negativity for HHV-6 in 68% of cases, up from 44% at 1 month and 57% at 2 months, the highest clearance rate among the three drugs.
Artesunate treatment for 3 months achieved PCR negativity for HHV-7 in 63% of cases, up from 41% at 1 month and 53% at 2 months, the highest clearance rate among the three drugs.
Across the three-month treatment course, artesunate produced higher rates of PCR negativity for both HHV-6 and HHV-7 than valganciclovir and valaciclovir, indicating superior antiviral efficacy.
Wearing 20–25 mmHg (class II) compression stockings significantly reduced the percentage drop in cardiac output during head-up tilt compared to without stockings.
Compression stockings significantly reduced the percentage drop in cerebral blood flow during head-up tilt compared to without stockings.
Supine cardiac output and cerebral blood flow measurements did not differ significantly between the stockings-on and stockings-off test sessions, indicating good measurement reproducibility.
Supine and end-tilt CBF measurements in a subset of patients were consistent with a previous tilt test performed up to 7 months earlier, indicating longer-term measurement reproducibility.
No carry-over effect was found between the first and second tilt tests, as supine CBF and CO did not differ significantly between the two periods regardless of stocking order.

Percent reduction in cardiac output during tilt was significantly and positively correlated with percent reduction in cerebral blood flow, with a similar relationship (slope) whether or not compression stockings were worn.

Even with compression stockings on, the percentage reductions in CO and CBF during tilt in ME/CFS patients remained greater than those previously reported in healthy controls without stockings, indicating incomplete normalization of hemodynamics.

ME/CFS patients with orthostatic intolerance but normal heart rate and blood pressure responses (no POTS, no orthostatic hypotension) showed significant reductions in cardiac output and cerebral blood flow during tilt testing.
HUVECs cultured with plasma from ME/CFS patients produced less basal nitric oxide than HUVECs cultured with plasma from healthy controls.
NO production stimulated by eNOS activators (tyrosine kinase and G protein-coupled receptor agonists) was reduced in HUVECs exposed to ME/CFS plasma compared to healthy control plasma.

GPCR agonists (bradykinin, histamine, acetylcholine) elicited NO production that was more impaired by ME/CFS plasma than the TKR agonist insulin, suggesting receptor-specific effects on eNOS activation.
Inhibitory phosphorylation of eNOS at Thr495 was higher in HUVECs treated with ME/CFS plasma than with healthy control plasma, consistent with reduced eNOS activity.
The study proposes an unreported role of eNOS dysfunction, driven by circulating factors in ME/CFS plasma, in the pathophysiology of ME/CFS-associated endothelial dysfunction.
In a cohort of 100 Chernobyl liquidators exposed to less than 300 mSv of radiation, 26 met diagnostic criteria for CFS/ME with persistent fatigue, malaise, and immune dysfunction.
The prevalence of CFS/ME among Chernobyl liquidators declined significantly a decade after radiation exposure.
Extent of neurodegeneration in Chernobyl liquidators correlated with estimated radiation dose and time spent in high-radiation areas, suggesting a dose-related link to CFS/ME symptoms.
CFS/ME patients showed a lower mean age of death for cancer (66.3 years) compared to the general US population (71.1 years), indicating poorer outcomes among CFS/ME patients who develop cancer.
One study reported an increased incidence of brain tumors and non-Hodgkin lymphoma among people with CFS/ME, based on analyses of two fatigue-illness outbreaks.
Another study found an increased incidence of brain tumors in CFS/ME patients but no increase in non-Hodgkin lymphoma, contradicting the prior study's finding on NHL.

A recent study found CFS/ME associated with an increased risk of various non-Hodgkin lymphoma subtypes, and nominal associations with pancreatic, breast, oral cavity, and pharyngeal cancers that did not survive multiple comparison correction.
Expression of the metabolite-sensing receptor P2RX7 was modulated in both prostate cancer patients and CFS/ME patients relative to controls.
Expression of the heat shock protein HSPA2 was modulated in both prostate cancer patients and CFS/ME patients relative to controls.
Expression of DBI, a GABA-A receptor modulator, correlated with fatigue severity in both prostate-cancer-fatigue and CFS/ME patients.
Compared with a cancer-related-fatigue group, CFS/ME patients showed lower hs-CRP levels and higher HRV-index scores, and could be distinguished by EEG; the study had no healthy control group.
HPA axis dysfunction with detectable adrenal/cortisol abnormalities was reported in CFS/ME patients, leading to a proposal that physiologic-dose cortisol administration be tried as therapy.
Low cortisol levels in CFS/ME were reported to be more common in women than in men, supporting a multidimensional etiology and possible benefit of cognitive-behavioral therapy.
One study found increased free tryptophan in the blood of CFS/ME patients, implicating serotonin metabolism in the disease.
A systematic review found that reduced serotonin transporters were reported across several studies examining CNS abnormalities in CFS/ME patients.
A study of eight CFS/ME patients found lower daytime activity and less regular activity-rest cycles, suggesting overlap between CFS/ME symptoms and disrupted circadian rhythm.
An early-1990s study reported retroviral sequences related to HTLV-2 in CFS/ME patients, but this finding could not be replicated by several later groups and is no longer supported.
Decreased natural killer cell activity was found to positively correlate with the severity of CFS/ME.
The plasma cytokine profile of female CFS/ME patients was reported to be consistent with processes active in latent viral infection.
Broderick et al. found significant differences in IL-8 and IL-23 concentrations in adolescents with post-infection CFS/ME.

Broad-spectrum plasma metabolomics of 84 CFS/ME patients across 612 metabolites and 63 biochemical pathways found significant abnormalities in roughly one-third of metabolites, described as a homogenous hypometabolic response tracing to mitochondria.
Analysis of blood samples from 74 CFS/ME patients found significant evidence of mitochondrial dysfunction and deficiencies in ATP production.

Metabolic profiling of blood and urine in CFS/ME patients showed elevated blood glucose and reduced blood lactate, urine pyruvate, and urine alanine, suggesting glycolytic dysfunction and oxidative stress.
In contrast to other metabolic reports, one study found normal lactate metabolism and oxygen uptake in CFS/ME patients.
Regional hypometabolism has been observed by several research groups in CFS/ME patients according to a systematic review.

In vitro work found serotonin is required for radiation-induced bystander effects, with variability in commercial serum serotonin content proposed to explain inter-laboratory variation in bystander responses; a p53-dependent interaction with serotonin levels was also found.
In an RCT, adding the Lightning Process intervention to specialist medical care significantly reduced depressive symptoms at 12 months compared with specialist medical care alone.
In the same RCT, the Lightning Process intervention produced an even larger reduction in anxiety symptoms than in depressive symptoms at 12 months compared with specialist medical care alone.
In a 20-year retrospective observational cohort, baseline depression and anxiety scores did not differ between children with CFS/ME who later self-reported recovery and those who did not.
Children with CFS/ME have a substantially higher prevalence of comorbid depression compared with adolescents without CFS/ME.
Children with CFS/ME have a substantially higher prevalence of comorbid anxiety compared with adolescents without CFS/ME.
Among children with CFS/ME attending a specialist service who meet diagnostic criteria for depression, the majority also have a comorbid anxiety disorder.
Comorbid depression in paediatric CFS/ME is associated with greater functional disability, worse fatigue, and more pain compared with those without depression.
Three observational studies found that face-to-face and telephone-delivered CBT improved depression, anxiety, functioning and social adjustment in paediatric CFS/ME.
An RCT found that internet-delivered CBT improved fatigue and school attendance at 6 months compared with usual care, but anxiety was not measured at follow-up.
An RCT of the STAIRway to Health incremental rehabilitation intervention showed greater improvement in anxiety levels compared with a pacing intervention.
An RCT of intravenous gammaglobulin infusions found insufficient evidence that this pharmacological treatment improved anxiety symptoms in paediatric CFS/ME.
An observational study of antiviral treatment (vancyclovir) found insufficient evidence for improving depressive symptoms in paediatric CFS/ME.

Three studies including one RCT found that a 4-week inpatient behavioural programme focused on graded exercise (physiotherapy, aerobic exercise, resistance training) improved mood post-treatment, maintained at 6-month follow-up in one study.
In the inpatient graded exercise programme studies, internalising problems (which include anxiety/depression-related symptoms) had returned to pre-admission levels by 6 months.
The majority of long COVID participants reported clinically significant chronic fatigue, with a mean FACIT-Fatigue score of 18 (SD=10) out of 52, where lower scores indicate more severe fatigue.
Postexertional malaise affected most long COVID participants, with 58.7% meeting the PEM scoring thresholds used for myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome.

The authors suggest that beneficial interventions for long COVID should first ensure symptom stabilization via pacing, a self-management strategy for activity intended to minimize postexertional malaise.
Easy fatigability was the most commonly reported long-COVID symptom, occurring in about half of the follow-up cohort.
Ninety percent of followed patients reported at least one long-COVID symptom at 9-month follow-up.

Constitutional neuropsychiatric symptoms (palpitation, dizziness, anxiety, mood swings, irritability, suicidal ideation, paresthesia, depression) formed the most commonly reported long-COVID symptom cluster.
Female sex was a significant predictor of developing chronic fatigue syndrome as a long-COVID symptom, with CFS more common in women than men.
Age was not a significant predictor of chronic fatigue syndrome at follow-up.
Constitutional neuropsychiatric symptoms during the acute COVID-19 phase predicted the later development of chronic fatigue syndrome.
Specific neuropsychiatric symptoms in the acute phase were associated with gastrointestinal symptoms during long-COVID follow-up.
Specific neuropsychiatric symptoms during the acute phase predicted later dermatologic disturbances as long-COVID.
Specific neuropsychiatric symptoms during the acute phase predicted respiratory symptoms as long-COVID.
Constitutional and olfactory symptom clusters in the acute phase predicted ear-nose-throat symptoms as long-COVID.
Acute-phase COVID-19 severity was not significantly associated with the number of long-COVID symptoms reported at follow-up.
Acute-phase COVID-19 severity was not significantly associated with development of chronic fatigue syndrome at follow-up.
A greater number of symptoms during the acute phase of COVID-19 predicted the development of chronic fatigue syndrome as a long-COVID symptom.
MoCA cognitive score at follow-up did not correlate with acute-phase COVID-19 severity (admission status).
Longer duration of acute COVID-19 symptoms was associated with lower MoCA cognitive scores at follow-up, though this was confounded by patient age.
The total number of symptoms during the acute phase did not predict later MoCA cognitive scores.
Patients with constitutional neuropsychiatric symptoms in the acute phase had lower MoCA cognitive scores and poorer delayed recall performance at follow-up.
Treatment with HRG80 Red Ginseng produced a significant mean increase in VAS composite and all VAS subscale scores from pre- to post-treatment, with predominately large effect sizes.

Among the subset of subjects who self-reported feeling better or much better (improvers, n=113), the same pattern of VAS score improvement was seen but with notably larger effect sizes than the full sample.
There was no significant group-by-treatment interaction between subjects whose illness onset was viral versus non-viral, indicating similar treatment response regardless of viral trigger.
No significant group-by-treatment interaction was found between capsule and tablet supplement forms, indicating similar treatment effects across both formulations.

Exploratory analysis of four dose/form subgroups (1 tablet, 1 capsule, 2 tablets, 2 capsules daily) showed no statistically significant difference in VAS score change, suggesting 100 mg tablet with gamma-cyclodextrin was as effective as higher doses.
Overall, 60.1% of study subjects reported improvement in their clinical status following one month of HRG80 Red Ginseng treatment.
Among improvers, average self-reported increases were 67% in energy, 72% in stamina, and 48% in mental clarity.

A subset of participants experienced adverse effects including overstimulation, nausea, headaches, chest heaviness (in a subject with mitral valve prolapse), and one case of hypoglycemia with blood glucose dropping to 61 mg/dL, leading to study discontinuation in six subjects.
Preference for daily dosing frequency (once vs twice daily) differed significantly between subjects using capsules versus tablets.
Batch analysis of HRG80 Red Ginseng showed acceptable consistency of total ginsenoside (~12%) and rare ginsenoside (~10%) content across three randomly selected recent batches.

A prior study found the effective total daily dose of HRG80 Red Ginseng for treating day-to-day fatigue (in a non-CFS population) was 418 mg, higher than the 100 mg dose found effective in this CFS/FMS sample when combined with gamma-cyclodextrin.
The hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis is described as significantly impaired in CFS, with a decreased adrenal gland response to CRH stimulation.
In vitro studies of HRG80 reported positive effects on neuroinflammation, cellular senescence, apoptosis, and immune responses, observed even at a wide range of low concentrations.
Targeted exome sequencing detected no pathogenic variants in COL3A1, allowing vascular EDS to be excluded in this patient.
A low-frequency FBN2 missense variant (c.6833C>T), present in 0.6% of the Japanese population, was detected but deemed to have no pathological significance.
The patient was ultimately diagnosed with hypermobile EDS (hEDS) based on clinical criteria after vEDS was excluded by genetic testing.
The authors note that hEDS often leads to postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (POTS) and a tendency toward anxiety and depression during pregnancy and the postpartum period.
Total maternal mortality in pregnancy complicated by vascular EDS is estimated at 5%-6%, underscoring the seriousness of ruling out vEDS in this patient.
The patient's mother died of sudden cardiovascular rupture at age 47 during cardiac catheterization, with autopsy revealing suspected EDS of unknown type.
The patient developed worsening hip, back, and pelvic pain during pregnancy that required inpatient bed rest from 29 weeks of gestation and ultimately made continuing the pregnancy untenable.
After delivery via elective caesarean section at 34 weeks, the patient's arthralgia improved but she developed postpartum depression requiring psychiatric referral.
Both twin infants were healthy at birth but were followed up by a paediatrician due to suspicion of joint hypermobility.
The authors note that even in singleton pregnancies, caesarean section in EDS patients has been reported to be associated with recurrent joint dislocation and pain.

A case of spondylodysplastic EDS was found to have B4GALT7 gene variants identified via whole-genome low-coverage sequencing and medical exome sequencing, presenting with short stature, hypotonia, and mild intellectual disability.
Children with hypermobile EDS show a high rate of developmental coordination disorder along with learning disability and ADHD.

A high prevalence of ADHD and autism spectrum disorder has been found in patients with hEDS, though the study lacked a matched control group so it is inconclusive whether prevalence is higher than the general population.
One study reported that ADHD was significantly enriched in hypermobility spectrum disorders but not in the EDS group compared to the general population.
Casanova et al. suggested comorbidity and familial co-occurrence between EDS and autism, and Baeza-Velasco et al. reported overrepresentation of ASD in EDS patients.
Elevated serum tyrosine and hydroxyproline levels in patients with ASD were proposed as biological evidence linking ASD and EDS, given the association of hydroxyproline with collagen damage.
Opioid use was approximately double in EDS patients compared to controls in both children (27.5% vs 13.5%) and adults (62% vs 34.1%).
Increases in tobacco and alcohol use were found in hEDS patients, thought to be used to cope with distress and anxiety.
A high prevalence of anxiety, and panic disorder in particular, was found in patients with EDS/hEDS as reported by recent research and meta-analyses, although some studies reported different results.
Pasquini et al. found higher Hamilton Anxiety Rating Scale (HAM-A) and Hamilton Depression Rating Scale (HAM-D) scores in an hEDS patient group compared to healthy controls.

Using the Symptom Check List-90-Revised, a high percentage of EDS patients reported somatization and obsessive-compulsivity, with these symptoms more severe than depressiveness, general anxiety, hostility, and phobic anxiety.
A patient with classical-like EDS due to a homozygous null mutation in TNXB presented with generalized pain enhanced by anxiety, without atrophic scarring typical of classical EDS.
Overall psychotropic drug use was 41.4% in patients with EDS compared with 13.9% in controls.
A large-scale Swedish population study found that patients with EDS have a higher risk of mood and developmental disorders than the general population.

A single nucleotide polymorphism in the TNX gene was initially reported by Tochigi to be associated with schizophrenia, but replication studies from other researchers could not confirm the association.
Patients with hEDS had obsessive-compulsive personality disorder (OCPD) with an observed prevalence rate of over 10%.
Risperidone was reported effective for managing anxiety symptoms in patients with EDS.
A patient with borderline personality disorder and EDS reported reduced suicidal ideation after treatment with an SSRI and lithium augmentation.

A patient with emotionally unstable personality disorder and EDS treated with duloxetine, quetiapine, lamotrigine, and Dialectical Behavioral Therapy achieved self-harm-free status and stable emotion.

In the authors' own clEDS patient with general body pain, duloxetine was dramatically effective for both pain relief and anxiety/depressiveness, consistent with its known analgesic effect in fibromyalgia and other chronic pain conditions.

A case report describes a Japanese woman with classical EDS who developed anorexia nervosa, dissociative identity disorder, gender dysphoria, and dysthymia, hypothesized to be linked to bullying over facial scars and maternal overprotectiveness, while her monozygotic twin sister with EDS had no psychiatric symptoms.

hEDS presents with gastrointestinal problems, temporomandibular disorders, and smell/taste abnormalities that can produce significant implications for eating and contribute to development of eating disorders such as anorexia nervosa, as illustrated by two reported cases.
WES identified a novel de novo heterozygous splicing-site variant in COL5A1 (c.4609-2A>C) in Patient 1, consistent with a diagnosis of classic EDS.
The COL5A1 splicing variant found in Patient 1 was classified as 'Pathogenic' per ACMG criteria with evidence levels PVS1+PM2+PP4.
WES identified a de novo heterozygous missense variant COL3A1 c.3554G>T (p.Gly1185Val) in Patient 2, located in the Gly-Xaa-Yaa triplet repeat domain, consistent with vascular EDS diagnosis.

Patient 2 with vEDS developed severe, ultimately fatal vascular and gastrointestinal complications including superior mesenteric dissecting aneurysm, spontaneous celiac hemorrhage, small intestine necrosis, coagulation dysfunction, and splenic infarction, dying from celiac hemorrhage within 24 hours.
Patient 2 exhibited unexplained hypertension, insulin resistance, and hyperlipidemia concurrently with vEDS, an uncommon symptom combination also described in another patient in prior literature.

WES identified a novel de novo heterozygous missense variant COL1A1 c.545G>T (p.Gly182Val) in Patient 3, classified as a variant of uncertain significance (VUS), potentially underlying an atypical cEDS/vEDS overlapping phenotype.
The amino acid residues altered by the two missense variants, COL3A1 Gly1185 and COL1A1 Gly182, were found to be highly conserved across species, supporting a pathogenic effect.
In-silico Revel prediction scores for both missense variants exceeded 0.9 (cutoff ≥0.7), supporting a deleterious effect on protein function.
Whole-exome sequencing enabled definitive molecular diagnosis in patients with clinically overlapping EDS phenotypes, demonstrating its value for differential diagnosis among EDS subtypes.
Patient 1 presented with classic EDS clinical features including fragile skin with atrophic scarring at trauma-prone sites, hyperextensible skin, and hypermobile wrist and finger joints.

Patient 3 exhibited milder EDS features than Patient 1, with atrophic scars, mild skin translucency, and hypermobile finger joints but no history of joint dislocation, not fully matching classic or arthrochalasia EDS criteria.
41.5% of eating disorder patients scored positive for joint hypermobility (Beighton score ≥4), a higher prevalence than reported in the general population (10-20%).
Compared to the 63% JHM prevalence reported by Goh et al. in anorexia nervosa patients, this study found a lower JHM frequency of 47.2% among AN patients.
No relationship was found between bulimia nervosa and joint hypermobility in this sample.
Hypermobile eating disorder patients were significantly younger than non-hypermobile eating disorder patients.
Non-hypermobile eating disorder patients had a significantly longer duration of illness than hypermobile patients.
Anorexia nervosa patients with the restricting subtype were significantly more common in the non-hypermobile group compared to the hypermobile group.
Non-hypermobile eating disorder patients scored significantly higher on cognitive rigidity (DFlex) than hypermobile patients.
Hypermobile eating disorder patients had a significantly greater proportion presenting with easy bruising compared to non-hypermobile patients.
Hypermobile eating disorder patients had a significantly greater proportion presenting with joint pain compared to non-hypermobile patients.
Binary logistic regression showed that cognitive rigidity and duration of eating disorder distinguished hypermobile from non-hypermobile ED patients.
A second logistic regression model found that age and cognitive rigidity could predict joint hypermobility status among eating disorder patients.
Hypermobile ED patients tended to have their first ED consultation earlier (during adolescence) than non-hypermobile patients, though this difference did not reach statistical significance.
A higher proportion of hypermobile ED patients had consulted a physiotherapist compared to non-hypermobile ED patients.

A 32-year-old man with Ehlers-Danlos syndrome sustained a divergent (posterior elbow plus proximal radioulnar joint) dislocation of the elbow after a snowboarding fall, treated successfully with open reduction and ligament/capsule repair.

Aneurysmosis of visceral arteries, including intercostal arteries, is described as occurring in connective tissue disorders such as Ehlers-Danlos syndrome due to mesodermal dysplasia of small arteries causing weakened vessel walls.

A 42-year-old man with cocaine-induced non-ischemic cardiomyopathy and no other identifiable connective tissue or infectious etiology was found to have at least 12 bilateral intercostal artery aneurysms (0.4-1.7 cm) from T5-T10, presumed secondary to chronic long-term cocaine abuse.

A cited study (Satran et al.) found coronary artery aneurysms occurred in 30.4% of cocaine users compared with 7.6% of non-users, indicating a strong association between cocaine use and aneurysm formation.

Cocaine-induced vascular complications, including arterial dissection and predisposition to aneurysm formation, are attributed to a multifactorial mechanism involving stimulation of adrenergic receptors, increased prothrombotic factors, endothelial cell dysfunction, and significant increases in systemic arterial pressure.

Among 7568 individuals enrolled in thoracic aortic disease registries, only 11 (0.15%) had spontaneous coronary artery dissection, indicating that TAD patients are not at markedly elevated risk of SCAD despite the hypothesis.
Among sequenced SCAD/TAD cases, pathogenic COL3A1 variants (associated with vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome) were identified in 3 individuals.
Pathogenic FBN1 variants (associated with Marfan syndrome) were identified in 2 of the sequenced SCAD/TAD cases.
Pathogenic TGFBR2 variants (associated with Loeys-Dietz syndrome) were identified in 2 of the sequenced SCAD/TAD cases.
A pathogenic TGFBR1 variant (associated with Loeys-Dietz syndrome) was identified in 1 of the sequenced SCAD/TAD cases.
A pathogenic PRKG1 variant was identified in 1 of the sequenced SCAD/TAD cases.
Among individuals with heritable thoracic aortic disease, those who also had SCAD showed a significantly higher rate of iliac artery dissection compared to those without SCAD.
Fibromyalgia patients showed reduced amplitude of the P2 laser-evoked potential component compared to controls, with no topographic match to the main site of skin denervation.
Decreased habituation of the P2 wave was more prevalent among fibromyalgia patients with reduced intraepidermal nerve fiber density.
sLORETA dipolar analysis showed activation of the cingulate and prefrontal cortex in the fibromyalgia group that did not correlate with the degree of skin denervation.
Anxiety, depression, fibromyalgia-related invalidity, and pain diffusion were correlated with one another and with LEP findings in the fibromyalgia group.

The authors concluded that LEP amplitude and topography did not coherently reflect epidermal nerve fiber density loss, suggesting LEPs instead reflect clinical pain expression and psychopathological factors rather than small fiber impairment itself.
The paper cites growing evidence that fibromyalgia involves autonomic dysfunction characterized by sympathetic hyperactivity.

The paper describes an immune system alteration with enhanced pro-inflammatory cytokine and chemokine activity as part of a chronic inflammatory state mediating autonomic-immune interaction in fibromyalgia.

The introduction notes that invasive vagus nerve stimulation has previously been shown to be effective in treatment-resistant fibromyalgia patients with a tolerability profile similar to that seen in epilepsy and depression treatment.

A patient presenting with an acute functional neurological disorder and no perception of sleep was found on sleep EEG to exhibit an alpha-delta sleep pattern, in which alpha wave intrusion occurs during slow-wave sleep.

The authors note that alpha-delta sleep pattern is more commonly associated with fibromyalgia than with functional neurological disorder, raising the possibility that this EEG pattern could be a shared biomarker of sleep misperception across conditions.
Adolescents with juvenile fibromyalgia showed reduced gray matter volume in the anterior midcingulate cortex compared to healthy controls, and this region was associated with pain.

Within the juvenile fibromyalgia group, patients with higher functional disability had larger gray matter volume in inferior frontal regions linked to affective, self-referential, and language-related processing.
Gray matter reductions in juvenile fibromyalgia partially overlapped with prior findings in adult fibromyalgia, specifically in the anterior cingulate cortex.
Gray matter reductions in juvenile fibromyalgia partially overlapped with prior findings in adult fibromyalgia, specifically in the posterior cingulate cortex.
Repeated epicutaneous exposure to cockroach allergen extract induced AD-like skin inflammation in mice, including erythema, epidermal/dermal thickening, and leukocyte infiltration, similar to OVA.
Mice sensitized to CRE or OVA showed higher serum levels of allergen-specific IgE and IgG1 compared with controls.
Skin tissues of CRE- or OVA-sensitized mice showed increased transcripts of the inflammatory cytokines IL-4, IL-13, IL-33, and TNF-alpha.
CRE- or OVA-treated mice showed significantly increased skin Th2 (IL-4+) cell percentages, with no difference in Th1 or Th17 cells.
ILC2 cells were increased in CRE- or OVA-treated skin, but the increase for CRE treatment did not reach statistical significance due to limited sample size.
CRE- or OVA-treated mice showed significantly increased skin mast cell numbers by flow cytometry, toluidine blue staining, and tryptase immunofluorescence.
Lesional skin from human AD patients showed increased dermal mast cells compared with healthy controls, alongside increased epidermal thickness.
Mast cell-deficient KitW-sh/W-sh mice were completely protected against cockroach allergen-induced skin inflammation (erythema, eruption, scarring, epidermal hyperplasia).
KitW-sh/W-sh (mast cell-deficient) mice showed significantly lower sIgE/sIgG1 and reduced IL-4, IL-33, and TNF-alpha expression compared with WT mice after CRE challenge, with no change in IL-13.

IgE-deficient mice showed cockroach allergen-induced IgG1, skin epithelial thickness, and Th2 cytokine expression comparable to WT mice, suggesting IgE-independent mechanisms contribute to AD-like inflammation.
DCIR was highly expressed in mast cells and was increased in skin tissues of AD patients compared with healthy controls, colocalizing with tryptase.
DCIR expression was confirmed in human LAD2 mast cells and was increased in the mouse AD model, but this increase was attenuated in mast cell-deficient KitW-sh/W-sh mice.
Recombinant human DCIR showed dose-dependent direct binding to cockroach allergen extract, similar to mannosylated-BSA, indicating CRE contains a natural DCIR ligand.
DCIR neutralizing antibody significantly inhibited FITC-labeled cockroach allergen uptake by LAD2 human mast cells compared with IgG isotype control, showing DCIR mediates allergen uptake.
DCIR-/- mice showed attenuated cockroach allergen-induced skin inflammation, reduced mast cell numbers, lower sIgE/sIgG1, and reduced IL-4 and IL-33 (no change IL-13/TNF-alpha) compared with WT mice.

KitW-sh/W-sh mice reconstituted with DCIR-/- bone marrow-derived mast cells showed attenuated skin inflammation, lower sIgE/sIgG1, and reduced IL-4 compared with those reconstituted with WT mast cells, demonstrating mast cell-intrinsic DCIR is required.
BMMCs from DCIR-/- mice showed markedly reduced CD107a (LAMP-1) surface expression, β-hexosaminidase, and histamine release after IgE/DNP-mediated activation compared with WT BMMCs.
Human LAD2 mast cells with DCIR knockdown by siRNA showed reduced LAMP-1 expression, β-hexosaminidase, IL-5, and IL-13 release after OVA treatment compared to control cells.
DCIR-/- mice showed significantly less Evan's blue dye leakage and less mast cell degranulation than WT mice in both DNP-IgE and CRE-induced passive cutaneous anaphylaxis assays.
DNP-treated DCIR-/- BMMCs released significantly lower IL-6, IL-31, TNF-alpha, and CCL2 than WT BMMCs, although IL-13 was elevated with treatment but not different between genotypes.
Intracellular ROS production was reduced in DNP-treated DCIR-/- BMMCs compared with WT BMMCs, suggesting DCIR regulates ROS generation during mast cell activation.
Allergen-induced CaMKII activity (measured by KTR translocation) was blunted in DCIR-/- BMMCs compared with WT BMMCs after DNP treatment.
DNP treatment induced ox-CaMKII expression in WT BMMCs but not in DCIR-/- BMMCs by western blot, and DCIR-/- mice showed reduced ox-CaMKII in skin mast cells in the AD mouse model.

BMMCs from ROS-resistant CaMKII (MM-VVδ) mice showed reduced β-hexosaminidase and histamine release after DNP treatment, and reduced IL-6, IL-31, TNF-alpha, CCL2 release, compared with WT mast cells, confirming ox-CaMKII's role downstream of DCIR.
Skin tissues from AD patients showed increased ox-CaMKII+ mast cells compared with healthy controls.
Mice lacking IL-27Rα showed increased sensitivity to IgE-mediated skin allergic response and chronic airway inflammation compared with wild-type mice.
Bone marrow-derived mast cells from IL-27Rα-deficient mice exhibited greater FcεRI-mediated activation, with significantly enhanced degranulation and cytokine production compared to wild-type BMMCs.
IL-27Rα-deficient mast cells showed increased activation of the Grb2-PLC-γ1-SLP-76 signaling axis relative to wild-type mast cells.
IL-27Rα-deficient mast cells displayed increased activation of the PI3K/Akt/IκBα signaling pathway.
IL-27Rα-deficient mast cells showed decreased phosphorylation levels of the phosphatase SHP1, consistent with loss of a negative regulatory brake on activation.
Direct treatment of mast cells with IL-27 inhibited their activation, supporting a direct negative regulatory role for IL-27 on mast cell function.
Retrovirus-mediated overexpression of IL-27 in the lung attenuated airway inflammation in mice, indicating a therapeutic potential for IL-27 in allergic airway disease.

A single patient incidentally showed multiple cerebral arterial variations on MR angiography, including anterior communicating artery duplication, accessory anterior cerebral artery, bilateral accessory middle cerebral arteries with bifurcation, right superior cerebellar artery duplication, and left superior cerebellar artery early bifurcation.

Volume-rendering images from MR angiography were reported to be more useful than maximum-intensity-projection images for identifying these arterial variations, particularly the bilateral accessory MCAs that were superimposed with the A1 and M1 arterial segments.

Among 32 patients with clonal mast cell activation disorders (cMCADs) and confirmed COVID-19, only 2 required hospitalization for low-flow oxygen and corticosteroids, with no cases of severe or fatal COVID-19 despite a high prevalence of classic risk factors.
Of 21 patients who underwent genetic testing, 18 (85.7%) carried the KIT D816V mutation, consistent with typical mastocytosis genetics.
20 of 21 evaluated patients with cMCAD developed a specific SARS-CoV-2 T-cell response (IFN-γ ELISpot) against at least one viral peptide pool, indicating an effective adaptive antiviral response.
The T-cell response to the SARS-CoV-2 spike N-terminal fragment (S1 pool) was significantly lower in cMCAD patients than in non-cMCAD patients convalescing from mild-to-moderate COVID-19.
SARS-CoV-2-specific T-cell responses were significantly lower in cMCAD patients than in non-cMCAD patients who had convalesced from severe COVID-19, except for the nucleoprotein (N) pool response.

T-cell responses against endemic human coronaviruses (HCoV-229E, HCoV-NL63, HCoV-OC43, HCoV-HKU1) were similar between cMCAD patients and non-cMCAD controls, showing no antiendemic-coronavirus response defect.

IFN-γ production in response to the CEFX Ultra SuperStim Pool (176 known epitopes from broad infectious agents) was similar between cMCAD patients and non-cMCAD controls, indicating intact general T-cell antigen responsiveness.
Among 15 patients with cMCAD tested by S-flow assay, 14 (93%) were seropositive for anti-SARS-CoV-2 IgG and 7 (47%) for IgA, demonstrating an effective humoral response.
Neutralizing antibodies were detected in 12 of 14 (86%) IgG-seropositive cMCAD patients, and IgG titer correlated with neutralizing antibody level.

All 4 cMCAD patients with serial serology measurements became seronegative for anti-SARS-CoV-2 antibodies after a median follow-up of 33 weeks, supporting a recommendation for post-infection vaccination.
Spontaneous (unstimulated) IFN-γ release from PBMCs in ELISpot assays was significantly more frequent in cMCAD patients than in non-cMCAD controls.

Basal serum tryptase level was positively correlated with spontaneous IFN-γ release in patients with cutaneous mastocytosis, mastocytosis in the skin, or indolent systemic mastocytosis, suggesting mast cell burden is linked to baseline IFN-γ production.
Total serum IgE levels in cMCAD patients were generally low and did not correlate with spontaneous IFN-γ release, arguing against an NK1-cell/IgE-related mechanism for the phenomenon.
Spontaneous IFN-γ release did not correlate with patient age, current symptomatic medications, history of anaphylaxis, or presence of the KIT D816V mutation.
During the COVID-19 episode, 25% of cMCAD patients reported increased signs of mast cell activation while 9.4% reported decreased signs.

Across the total study population, no intracranial hemodynamic parameter (mean flow velocity, pulsatility index, or breath-holding index) in either middle cerebral artery was significantly associated with MoCA cognitive scores.

In participants aged 55-60 years, left middle cerebral artery breath-holding index was significantly and independently correlated with better MoCA scores, a relationship not seen in those younger than 55.
Older age, lower education, and habits of cigarette smoking or alcohol consumption were associated with poorer MoCA scores.
Mutation of the glycosylation site Asn168 on recombinant human diamine oxidase significantly increased its clearance rate in vivo in rodents.
Enzymatic removal of sialic acid (sialidase treatment) from rhDAO glycans also significantly increased its in vivo clearance, similar to Asn168 mutation.
Mutation of the unpaired, solvent-accessible cysteine 123 strongly reduced DAO oligomerization but did not affect enzymatic activity or in vivo clearance.
Recombinant hDAO produced in ExpiCHO-S cells showed a 15-fold reduction in the percentage of glycans bearing terminal sialic acid at Asn168 compared with production in CHO-K1 cells.
Sialic acid capping was also strongly reduced at the other N-glycosylation sites of rhDAO produced in ExpiCHO-S cells compared with CHO-K1 cells.
High abundance of terminal mannose and N-acetylglucosamine residues in the four glycans of rhDAO expressed in ExpiCHO-S cells (versus CHO-K1) resulted in rapid in vivo clearance of the protein.
Screening of human mast cells for metabolite receptors revealed very high mRNA expression of SUCNR1 (succinate receptor 1) compared to other receptors tested.
SUCNR1 expression in mast cells was comparable to that in monocyte-derived macrophages and was upregulated following IL-4 treatment.
Succinate (1 mM) alone induced modest CD63 degranulation marker expression on resting CBMC (from 2% to 5% CD63-positive cells) without significant histamine release.
Pre-incubation of CBMC with succinate significantly enhanced anti-IgE-induced CD63 degranulation and histamine release compared to anti-IgE alone.
The synthetic SUCNR1 agonist cES caused even greater potentiation of IgE-receptor induced CD63 expression and histamine release than succinate.
SUCNR1 antagonists XT1 and NF-56-EJ40 effectively inhibited succinate-potentiated mast cell degranulation and histamine release, confirming receptor specificity.
shRNA knockdown of SUCNR1 in LAD-2 cells attenuated succinate- and cES-potentiated degranulation.
Succinate and cES treatment increased phosphorylation of cytosolic phospholipase A2 (cPLA2) in resting and IgE-activated mast cells, marking early eicosanoid pathway activation.
In IgE-activated mast cells, succinate significantly enhanced production of PGD2, cysteinyl leukotrienes, TXA2 (as TXB2), and arachidonic acid, as measured by LC-MS/MS.
SUCNR1 antagonists dose-dependently blocked succinate-potentiated PGD2 production, and SUCNR1 knockdown attenuated succinate/cES-enhanced cPLA2 phosphorylation, PGD2 and cys-LT production.
IL-8, the most predominant cytokine secreted by mast cells, was significantly upregulated by succinate and cES with or without anti-IgE activation.
Succinate or cES alone induced a panel of cytokines from resting mast cells, most prominently GM-CSF and IL-13, along with TNF-α, IL-6, IFN-γ, IL-5, IL-1β, IL-17A, and MIP1β.
In FcεRI-activated mast cells, levels of IFN-γ, IL-7, MCP-1, MIP1β, and IL-10 were not influenced by succinate or cES, indicating selectivity of SUCNR1-FcεRI synergy for specific cytokines.
mRNA upregulation of TNF-α and IL-8 by succinate was blocked by the Gq inhibitor YM254890 and the NFAT inhibitor cyclosporin A, implicating Gq-NFAT transcriptional signaling.

CD63 expression induced by SUCNR1 activation was blocked by the Gq inhibitor YM254890 but not by the Gi inhibitor pertussis toxin, indicating SUCNR1 signals through Gq to potentiate mast cell degranulation.

SUCNR1 activation enhanced ERK phosphorylation in IgE-receptor-activated mast cells, an effect reduced by SUCNR1 antagonist and genetic knockdown; PKC inhibitors blocked both ERK phosphorylation and PGD2 production, indicating a Gq-PKC-ERK signaling axis.

In guinea pig sensitized tracheal rings, succinate and cES pre-treatment shifted OVA-induced contraction curves leftward with significantly lower EC50, indicating mast cell hyperreactivity in airway tissue.

Increased levels of histamine and cysteinyl leukotrienes were detected in the organ bath fluid of cES-treated guinea pig tracheal tissues, indicating mast cell hyper-reactivity when SUCNR1 is activated.

SUCNR1 antagonist XT1 significantly attenuated succinate and cES potentiation of OVA-induced tracheal contraction but had no effect on OVA-induced contraction in the absence of SUCNR1 agonists, demonstrating specificity.

Succinate and cES had no effect on tracheal contraction induced directly by histamine, LTD4, or U-46619 (which act directly on smooth muscle independent of mast cells), indicating SUCNR1 ligands act via mast cells rather than directly on smooth muscle.
In isolated human small airways, cES significantly enhanced the efficacy and maximal response of anti-IgE-induced bronchial contraction, and this effect was fully blocked by SUCNR1 antagonist XT1.

The paper cites prior studies reporting increased succinate levels in certain asthmatic populations compared to healthy individuals, supporting a proposed role of hypoxia/dysbiosis-driven succinate accumulation in severe asthma pathophysiology.
Bone was the most common anatomic site of involvement in mast cell sarcoma, seen in 9 of 10 cases.
Two of ten mast cell sarcoma patients had a prior history of germ cell tumors (mediastinal germ cell tumor and ovarian dysgerminoma).
Concurrent systemic mastocytosis was present in one of nine evaluable mast cell sarcoma patients.
Serum tryptase levels were elevated in the majority of tested mast cell sarcoma patients (6 of 7).
Mast cell activation symptoms were reported in 3 of 9 mast cell sarcoma patients.
Mast cell sarcoma tumor cells consistently expressed CD43, CD117 (KIT), mast cell tryptase, CD13, and CD33 by immunohistochemistry, with variable expression of CD2, CD25, CD30, and CD68.
The canonical KIT D816V mutation, common in systemic mastocytosis, was not detected in nine mast cell sarcoma cases tested, though two cases harbored other KIT gene mutations.
Chemotherapy with or without radiotherapy given to 7 of 8 patients showed poor response, and 4 of 8 patients died within a median follow-up of five months.
Skin biopsy showed amyloid deposits in 80% of the 183 symptomatic ATTRv-PN patients.
Skin amyloid deposits were detected in 75% of patients at the early stage of ATTRv-PN.
Skin amyloid deposits were present in 14% of asymptomatic TTR mutation carriers, suggesting a subclinical marker of disease onset.
All 183 symptomatic ATTRv-PN patients and 34 of 36 asymptomatic carriers showed decreased ankle intraepidermal nerve fiber density with a proximal-distal gradient.
Reduced intraepidermal nerve fiber density correlated with disease severity and disease duration in ATTRv-PN patients.
Intraepidermal nerve fiber density was below the 5th percentile for age and sex in 82% of the 17 Tarlov cyst patients who underwent skin biopsy, indicating small fiber neuropathy.
Electrodiagnostic (EDX) abnormalities were found in 100% of the assessed Tarlov cyst patients, indicating large-fiber (motor/sensory nerve root) involvement in addition to small fiber neuropathy.
Sural nerve conduction studies were largely normal, with delayed latency in only 6% and low amplitude in only 13% of patients, despite frequent S2 Tarlov cysts.

S1 Hoffmann reflexes were delayed in 25% of TC patients, with only 2 of these 6 patients also showing needle EMG abnormalities in corresponding S1 muscles, suggesting possible sensory S1 radiculopathy.
Anal reflex latency was significantly delayed in 95% of TC patients (38% unilaterally, 57% bilaterally), representing a novel objective EDX finding in this population.

Autonomic dysfunction is highly prevalent across multiple organ systems in MS patients, including cardiovascular, bladder, sexual, bowel, sleep, and thermoregulatory domains.
MS patients commonly experience Uhthoff phenomenon, a transient worsening of neurological symptoms triggered by core temperature increases as small as 0.5°C.

Reduced sweating in MS patients is driven mainly by decreased sweat output per individual gland rather than reduced gland recruitment, and 15 weeks of aerobic endurance training failed to improve sweat function.

Demyelinated axons in MS and its EAE animal model show increased expression and abnormal paranodal/juxtaparanodal distribution of Nav1.2 and Nav1.6 sodium channel isoforms, contributing to hyperexcitability and impaired thermal signaling.

K2P potassium channels on thermal-sensitive hypothalamic neurons are activated by hyperthermia, causing potassium efflux, neuronal hyperpolarization, and decreased action potential propagation, potentially altering thermal sensitivity in MS.

SARS-CoV-2 infection triggers PAMP/cytokine-mediated release of PGE2, which binds EP2 receptors in the preoptic hypothalamic area to raise the thermal set-point, producing fever that can exacerbate thermal dysregulation in MS patients.

MS prevalence is roughly three times higher in women, who differ physiologically (lower blood volume, smaller heart size, higher body fat, hormonal cycling) in ways that may worsen thermoregulatory impairment and symptom severity.
Fatigue associated with heat stress occurs in approximately 70% of individuals with MS, linked to demyelinated lesions lowering central motor conduction and cortical excitability.

Aerobic exercise training for 6-10 days increases plasma volume through increased hepatic albumin production and electrolyte reuptake, and elevated fluid-regulating hormones, contributing to improved thermoregulation.

Exercise-induced increases in nitric oxide inhibit viral replication by suppressing ribonucleotide reductase, and NOS-deficient mice show greater susceptibility to viral infection, suggesting a potential antiviral benefit of exercise-induced NO in the context of SARS-CoV-2.

Cold sensitivity of skin afferents is decreased in MS patients compared to expectations, suggesting MS pathophysiology independently modulates afferent thermosensory function beyond heat sensitivity alone.

Light-to-moderate intensity endurance training (≥50% VO2max) for at least one week is proposed as optimal to stimulate thermoregulatory adaptations and restore body temperature regulation toward healthy levels in MS patients.
In an early heat-stress study, 75% of MS patients showed worsening of neurological signs within 10-15 minutes of heat exposure (55-60°C environment).
Fever occurs as an initial symptom in more than 50% of patients with COVID-19, which poses a particular risk for patients with pre-existing thermal dysregulation such as MS.
COVID-19 patient brain tissue showed markedly increased oxidative stress, with GSSG/GSH ratio elevated in both cortex and cerebellum compared to controls.
Kynurenic acid, a marker of inflammation, was significantly increased in both cortex and cerebellum of COVID-19 brains compared to controls.

Phosphorylated SMAD3, a downstream marker of TGF-β signaling, was increased in COVID-19 cortex and cerebellum brain lysates compared to controls, indicating activation of TGF-β signaling despite absence of detectable virus in brain tissue.
PKA activity was increased in cortex and cerebellum of COVID-19 brains compared to controls, consistent with increased adrenergic activation.
CaMKII activity was increased in COVID-19 brain tissue compared to controls, consistent with heightened adrenergic and calcium signaling.

COVID-19 brain lysates showed normal APP and BACE1 levels compared to controls, indicating that abnormal amyloidogenic APP processing (typical of AD) was not present; abnormal processing was only seen in confirmed AD patient samples.
Phosphorylation/activation of AMPK and GSK3β, kinases responsible for tau phosphorylation, was increased in both cortex and cerebellum of COVID-19 brains compared to controls.

Tau hyperphosphorylation was observed at multiple sites in COVID-19 brains; older patients showed increased phosphorylation at S199, S202, S214, S262, and S356, while younger patients showed increases at S214, S262, and S356 but not S199/S202, and both age groups showed atypical cerebellar tau phosphorylation not usually seen in AD.
NOX2 association with RyR2 was increased in cortex and cerebellum of COVID-19 brains compared to controls, indicating oxidative modification of the calcium release channel.

RyR2 channels from COVID-19 brains showed increased oxidation, increased PKA phosphorylation at serine 2808, and depletion of the stabilizing subunit calstabin2, the biochemical signature of a leaky channel, compared to controls.
RyR2 channels from COVID-19 brain tissue exhibited abnormally high activity (increased ryanodine binding) at resting Ca2+ concentrations compared to controls, when channels should normally be closed.

Ex vivo treatment of COVID-19 patient brain tissue lysates with the Rycal drug ARM210 increased calstabin2 rebinding to RyR2 and reduced abnormal RyR2 channel activity at resting calcium, effectively fixing the channel leak.

Both cortex and cerebellum of COVID-19 patients exhibited reduced expression of the calcium-buffering protein calbindin compared to controls, which could render these tissues more vulnerable to cytosolic calcium overload and tau pathology.
GCPII expression was increased in cortex and cerebellum of COVID-19 brains compared to controls, which could reduce mGluR3-mediated PKA inhibition and contribute to RyR2 PKA hyperphosphorylation.
In addition to brain, COVID-19 patients showed increased systemic oxidative stress and TGF-β pathway activation in lung and heart, correlating with oxidation-driven RyR2 remodeling across organs.
The authors note that cerebellar tau pathology observed in COVID-19 brains could explain a previously reported finding that 74% of hospitalized COVID-19 patients experienced coordination deficits.

The authors propose that leaky RyR2 channels, driven by adrenergic/oxidative stress and TGF-β activation, contribute to tau hyperphosphorylation and AD-like neuropathology in COVID-19 brains, potentially underlying long-COVID brain fog and predisposing to future AD.

Adding purified recombinant SARS-CoV-2 S1 spike protein to normal coagulation-competent plasma is sufficient to induce anomalous amyloid clot formation that resists fibrinolysis.

Fibrinaloid microclots consist mainly of fibrin but sequester many other proteins including alpha2-antiplasmin, viral particles, and elicit fibrin autoantibodies with heightened pro-inflammatory activity.
Amyloid microclots ranging from 1-200 µm can block microcapillaries and inhibit erythrocyte transport, strongly lowering tissue oxygen availability.
D-dimer is a strong prognostic indicator of survival outcome in acute COVID-19.

Standard clotting tests such as INR and aPTT have limited predictive value for identifying bleeding risk in patients with acute and long COVID.

Thromboelastography (TEG) is not useful for determining hypercoagulation status in Long COVID because clotted fibrin already trapped in microclots is invisible to the assay, which measures only soluble plasma proteins.
S1 spike protein can persist within CD16+ monocytes in PASC patients for up to 15 months post-infection, providing a plausible source of continued microclot-triggering stimulus.
Long COVID shows a striking over-representation among women, especially younger women, in marked contrast to acute COVID demographics.
Female sex hormones can induce anomalous (amyloid) blood clotting, offering a plausible mechanism for the female predominance in long COVID.
Endotheliopathy-associated cell death in COVID releases the intracellular iron storage protein ferritin, which can then release free iron contributing to iron dysregulation.

A triple anticoagulation regimen (dual antiplatelet therapy with clopidogrel/aspirin plus the DOAC apixaban, with a proton pump inhibitor for gastric protection) showed promise in clinical practice for treating long COVID, though without treatment-free controls.

Clinical trials of therapeutic anticoagulation (heparin), anticoagulation dosing comparisons, and antiplatelet therapy in acute COVID-19 patients did not show significantly positive outcomes when only one pathology (clotting or platelet hyperactivation) was targeted.
Virus-induced endotheliopathy causing systemic endotheliitis is a key component of severe acute COVID-19 pathological clotting, activating microthrombotic pathways.
Platelets play an important role in acute COVID-19 disease severity, endotheliopathy development, and coagulation pathology through platelet-cell and platelet-molecule complex formation.

Amyloid-type fibrin microclots have also been observed in the blood of individuals with other chronic inflammatory diseases including Alzheimer's, Parkinson's disease, type 2 diabetes, and rheumatoid arthritis, as well as pre-eclampsia.
Coagulopathies, similar to those described in long COVID, have been highlighted as playing a role in ME/CFS.
Ground-glass opacities seen on lung CT in COVID patients are largely composed of fibrin and persist beyond the acute phase, consistent with (though not yet directly stained for) amyloid character.
Highly substoichiometric amounts of bacterial LPS (as low as 1 molecule per 100 million fibrinogen molecules) can induce amyloid 'dense matted deposit' clot formation in plasma.

Tissue hypoxia from microclot-mediated capillary blockage is proposed as the unifying explanation for diverse long COVID symptoms including renal dysfunction, POTS, myalgia, neurological disorders, and lactic acidosis.

A systematic review by Nasserie et al. found fatigue to be the second most common persistent symptom of long COVID (after shortness of breath/dyspnea), with a median prevalence of 40.0% across 25 of 45 included studies.

A retrospective cohort study (Benaim et al.) at a tertiary Israeli center indicated COVID-19 has a partially severe impact on critical functions including the immune system, metabolism, coagulation, cardiac and respiratory function.
The multi-organ presentation and thromboembolic events of COVID-19 suggest SARS-CoV-2 is an endotheliophilic virus, making long-term sequelae more comparable to sepsis than to influenza.

The SARS-CoV-2 spike protein was found to stimulate inflammasome formation and interleukin release, and to cause profound and long-lasting macrophage reprogramming, increasing immunogenicity of the spike protein.

Halpert and Shoenfeld (2020) reported evidence in a subgroup of patients that SARS-CoV-2 has a critical, central effect on human immunity and can trigger autoimmune disease in genetically predisposed individuals, terming SARS-CoV-2 an 'autoimmune virus'.
A post-mortem case series of 43 patients (Glatzel group) most commonly found mild neuropathological changes with pronounced neuroinflammation in the brainstem.

Kedor et al./Scheibenbogen's investigation of a small subgroup of younger patients after mild-to-moderate COVID-19 showed that COVID-19 can trigger a severe chronic syndrome characterized by fatigue and exercise intolerance.
The UK NICE guideline (October 2021) states that graded exercise/activity increase programs should not be offered as treatment for ME/CFS, due to reported harms in people with ME/CFS.

A Norwegian study of 1600 participants found fatigue prevalence of 81% among MS patients, consistent with prior studies reporting prevalence between 50-90%.

Increased inducible nitric oxide synthase (iNOS) activity and reduced antioxidant levels reflect activated oxidative and nitrosative stress (O&NS) pathways proposed to contribute to CFS pathogenesis.

In a prospective observational study of 155 CFS patients, 56% of the 18 participants who used ginseng reported symptomatic improvement in fatigue.
