Across both included studies, no adverse events attributable to ginseng were reported, though safety reporting was limited or absent.
The overall certainty of evidence for ginseng's efficacy in CFS was rated low to moderate, mainly due to inconsistency, imprecision, and risk of bias across the two included studies.

The authors clarify that Siberian ginseng is not true ginseng (it contains eleutherosides, not ginsenosides) and was excluded from this review despite prior literature conflating it with true ginseng for CFS treatment.

Among 72 children referred for suspected EDS, 18 (25%) met the 2017 clinical diagnostic criteria for a specific EDS subtype, and 15 of those (83%) were subsequently confirmed by molecular genetic testing.

Fifty-four patients (75%) had overlapping features with EDS and other hypermobility-related syndromes but did not fully meet clinical criteria, and 12 of these (22%) still received a positive molecular genetic diagnosis of EDS.
Among patients tested with a targeted EDS gene panel, molecular diagnosis was confirmed in 75% of those meeting clinical criteria versus 28% of those who did not fully meet criteria.

Specific clinical features—generalized joint hypermobility, poor wound healing, easy bruising, atrophic scars, skin hyperextensibility, and developmental dysplasia of the hip—correlated with a positive molecular genetic result for EDS.
Arthrochalasia EDS is caused by heterozygous mutations in COL1A1 that result in partial or complete loss of exon 6 during pre-mRNA processing, impairing proper collagen fibril formation.
Heterozygous mutations in COL1A2 leading to loss of exon 6 during pre-mRNA processing also cause arthrochalasia EDS, historically termed type VIIB.
Multiple studies suggest that COL1A1-associated aEDS may be more clinically severe than COL1A2-associated aEDS.
Rolfes et al. investigated whether aEDS causes increased bone fragility in infancy/childhood and did not identify an increased incidence of fractures in children with aEDS.
Basalom et al. observed a very low incidence of fractures in adults diagnosed with aEDS.
Melis et al. described a case of aEDS with progressive cardiac valvular involvement, suggesting cardiac follow-up is warranted for aEDS patients.
Pregnant women with aEDS have been reported to experience complications including breech presentation, polyhydramnios, premature rupture of membranes, and decreased fetal movement.

One reported fatal case involved a baby born at 35 gestational weeks, diagnosed with aEDS post-mortem, presenting with skull fracture and bilateral hip dislocations with metaphyseal sclerosis after an uncomplicated vaginal delivery, with a de novo pathogenic COL1A1 exon 6 skipping variant.

Newborns with aEDS present distinctive dysmorphic features including mild hypertelorism, bilateral epicanthal folds, large fontanels, and pronounced micrognathia, along with severe neonatal hypotonia that decreases with age, while mental development remains normal in all patients.
Approximately 42 patients with aEDS have been reported worldwide to date, reflecting the disease's rarity and unknown true prevalence.
Life expectancy of patients with aEDS is generally not inferior to that of the general population, unlike vascular or kyphoscoliosis types of EDS.

There is currently no specific curative treatment for aEDS; management is symptomatic and focuses on orthopedic problems, including open reduction with iliac osteotomy for congenital hip dislocation, muscle-strengthening exercise, joint protection, anti-inflammatory drugs for joint pain, and psychological support for chronic pain.

Definitive diagnosis of aEDS requires molecular genetic testing, as clinical differential diagnosis (e.g., Larsen syndrome, Loeys-Dietz syndrome, cutis laxa, classic EDS, dermatosparaxis EDS, kyphoscoliotic EDS, musculocontractural EDS) is complex.
SIJ fusion surgery led to reported improvements in pain, quality of life, and disability in EDS patients with sacroiliac joint dysfunction.
The mean patient-reported satisfaction score after SIJ fusion was 78.1 out of 100, with 7 of 16 patients reporting 100% satisfaction.

A diagnostic intra-articular lidocaine SIJ block performed preoperatively in 15 of 16 patients produced significant short-term pain relief, supporting SIJ dysfunction as the pain source before proceeding to fusion.
One EDS patient (case 1) developed nerve impingement due to implant malpositioning after SIJ fusion, which resolved following revision surgery to withdraw the implant.

A second patient (case 8) had no pain relief after initial two-implant fusion despite adequate implant positioning, attributed to persistent instability from insufficient total implant surface area, and achieved an excellent outcome after placement of a third implant.

Postoperative CT analysis showed that implants in less-satisfied patients had less surface contact with the SIJ compared to more satisfied patients, suggesting implant-bone contact area relates to outcome.
One less-satisfied patient was found to have an iliac fracture near an implant on postoperative CT, representing a procedural complication.
Outcomes of SIJ fusion in EDS patients (pain, disability, quality of life improvement) were comparable to previously reported outcomes of SIJ fusion in non-EDS patients with SIJ dysfunction.

Citing external biomechanical work, the authors note that a three-implant construct across the SI joint may be more stable than a two-implant construct, potentially explaining suboptimal outcomes in some EDS patients who received only two implants.

The patient carried a novel heterozygous TNXB frameshift variant (c.12234_12237del; p.Asp4079Serfs*29), predicted to cause premature protein termination and considered likely pathogenic for classical-like EDS.

The patient carried a maternally inherited, previously published TNXA/TNXB fusion gene (CH-1 chimera) with a 120-bp deletion at the exon 35/intron 35 boundary, confirmed by MLPA to include a CYP21A2 deletion, and known to be pathogenic for classical-like EDS.
The proband was heterozygous for the CH-2 missense pseudogene-derived variant c.12174C>G (p.Cys4058Trp) carried on the same CH-1 allele, previously reported as part of a TNXA/TNXB fusion gene.
The authors report that recurrent spontaneous pneumothorax is a phenotypic feature not previously documented in classical-like EDS, broadening its clinical spectrum.

Histological and imaging findings of pneumothorax in this clEDS patient (apical distal acinar emphysema, bullae, pleural scarring without hemorrhage) more closely resemble Marfan syndrome pathology than vascular EDS.
Vascular EDS, caused by COL3A1 pathogenic variants, is associated with spontaneous pneumothorax in 16%-40% of cases, cited as background comparator to the present clEDS case.
The patient scored 8 out of 9 on the Beighton score, consistent with generalized joint hypermobility, alongside recurrent shoulder, jaw, finger, and knee dislocations/subluxations.
Echocardiogram at 33 years detected mild aortic root dilatation at the sinus of Valsalva with a z-score of 2.26, along with borderline mitral valve prolapse and trivial mitral regurgitation.

Approximately 9% of patients with 21-hydroxylase deficiency-related congenital adrenal hyperplasia have an associated connective tissue disorder due to a contiguous gene deletion affecting TNXB and CYP21A2.

Of 15 patients who developed symptomatic craniocervical instability after suboccipital craniectomy for Chiari malformation type I, 12 had a known diagnosis of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, suggesting EDS as a risk factor for this complication.
Occipitocervical fusion performed for symptomatic craniocervical instability following prior suboccipital craniectomy for Chiari malformation type I resulted in good outcomes in all 15 patients.
Clivoaxial angles, measured before and after occipitocervical fusion, were corrected to a more anatomical alignment following surgery.

Symptomatic craniocervical instability is identified as a delayed postoperative complication of suboccipital craniectomy for Chiari malformation type I, with an underlying connective tissue hypermobility disorder such as EDS as a potential risk factor.
Genetic testing confirmed a COL3A1 gene mutation, establishing a concurrent diagnosis of vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome in a patient with Takayasu arteritis.

The patient presented with concurrent Takayasu arteritis and vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, resulting in multi-organ infarction of the brain, kidney, and spleen due to multiple aneurysms and stenosis of the internal carotid artery, representing what the authors state is the first reported case of this combination.
The patient tested positive for HLA-B52, a marker reported to be common in patients with Takayasu arteritis and considered the only definite genetic factor for TAK globally.

Treatment with intravenous methylprednisolone followed by prednisolone and weekly subcutaneous tocilizumab, combined with interventional radiology embolization, led to gradual improvement of inflammatory response and paralytic symptoms with no relapse.

A markedly elevated neutrophil count (99% of a white blood cell count of 38,000/uL) at disease onset was noted as a distinguishing feature, with neutrophils and neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) proposed to contribute to the pathogenesis of systemic vasculitis including large-vessel vasculitis.

Serum CRP was markedly elevated (13.8 mg/dL at outside hospital, then 5.02 mg/dL on admission to the reporting hospital, normal range 0-0.15 mg/dL), supporting the diagnosis of an inflammatory vasculitis (Takayasu arteritis) rather than purely non-inflammatory vasculopathy.

Despite immunosuppressive therapy, follow-up CT revealed new dissection of the celiac trunk and the right femoral artery (the latter associated with the IVR procedure site), illustrating ongoing vascular fragility attributable to the underlying vEDS.

The authors note that only 48.8% of 86 patients who tested positive for COL3A1 mutations in a prior study had a positive family history, indicating that vEDS cannot be excluded based on absence of family history alone, as was the case in this patient.
The clivo-axial angle, measuring craniocervical kyphosis, is normally 145-160 degrees, and values below 135 degrees are considered pathological and indicative of craniocervical instability in EDS.
A pB-C2 line measurement greater than 9 mm is considered pathological and suggests increased risk of ventral brainstem compression in CCI.
The Harris measurement defines normal occipito-vertebral relationships as basion-axial and basion-dental intervals of 12 mm or less in adults, used with flexion-extension dynamics to identify CCI.

Milhorat et al. found reduced basion-dens interval, clivo-axial angle, clivus-atlas angle and atlas-axis angle, along with increased basion-atlas interval in the upright position, distinguishing occipito-atlantoaxial hypermobility in patients with Chiari malformation type 1 plus hereditary connective tissue disorders (including EDS) compared to Chiari-only patients and healthy controls.
Angular displacement between C1 and C2 greater than 41 degrees and/or facet overlap less than 10% is considered pathological for atlanto-axial rotatory instability in EDS.
In a cohort of 12 EDS musculocontractural subtype patients, 2 had atlanto-axial instability diagnosed via an ADI greater than 4 mm at flexion.

Henderson et al. surgically treated 20 EDS patients with cranio-vertebral instability and flexion deformity via occipital to C1/C2 fusion, guided by criteria including kyphotic CXA, cerebellar ectopia (seen in 18/20), and cervico-medullary syndrome symptoms.

Spiessberger et al. found that CXA and pB-C2 line measurements improved after cervical fusion surgery for CCI regardless of the specific fusion technique used, supporting their utility as surgical outcome parameters.

In EDS patients with atlanto-axial instability, C1-C2 fusion led to significant improvement of syncopal, presyncopal, and autonomic dysfunction symptoms, attributed to relief of chronic mechanical stretching of neural tissue and improved vertebral artery blood flow.

Klinge et al. identified laxity of spinal cord suspension ligaments and an associated spinal cord motion disorder as possible pathogenic factors for chronic neck pain and headache in EDS patients even without radiologically proven CCI.

Spiessberger et al. used a 4-6 week trial of hard collar immobilization as a pre-operative selection tool, offering surgery only to EDS patients with suspected CCI whose symptoms improved with immobilization, a novel test-immobilization approach in this population.
Across the 16 included studies covering 695 EDS patients, 78 patients were diagnosed with craniocervical instability and underwent surgical treatment.

Patients with CCI-related cervico-medullary syndrome present with a broad symptom burden including autonomic dysregulation, dizziness, sleep apnea, motor weakness, sensory deficits, balance disturbance, vertigo, and swallowing difficulties.

A 20-year-old male with Ehlers-Danlos syndrome and recurrent extensor carpi ulnaris (ECU) tendon subluxation, who had failed immobilization and autologous ECU reconstruction, was successfully treated with gracilis tendon allograft reconstruction of the ECU sheath plus ulnar groove deepening, resulting in a pain-free, stable tendon at 1-year follow-up.

The patient's autologous ECU reconstruction using extensor retinaculum failed, suggesting compromised connective tissue quality (consistent with Ehlers-Danlos syndrome) may reduce reliability of autologous tissue repairs for tendon instability.

MPFL reconstruction combined with tibial tubercle osteotomy significantly improved Kujala knee function scores from preoperative to postoperative assessment in syndromic adolescents with patellar dislocation.
Lysholm knee scores significantly improved from preoperative to postoperative assessment following MPFL reconstruction and tibial tubercle osteotomy.
Knee flexion range of motion significantly increased after surgical treatment compared to preoperative values.
Knee extension did not significantly change from preoperative to postoperative assessment.

Ehlers-Danlos syndrome was the most common underlying syndromic diagnosis among adolescents undergoing surgical treatment for congenital or habitual patellar dislocation, present in four of eleven patients.
In skin biopsies from patients with Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, Marfan syndrome, and pseudoxanthoma elasticum, the collagen network was structurally altered compared to healthy controls.
The elastic fiber network in skin was structurally altered in patients with Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, Marfan syndrome, and pseudoxanthoma elasticum compared to healthy controls.

In older patients with these inherited connective tissue diseases, the degenerative changes to the elastic network differed qualitatively from the normal physiological aging changes seen in healthy subjects of the same age.

The authors propose that an additional general connective tissue proteolysis process, beyond the primary genetic defect, may explain the distinct degenerative pattern of the elastic network in these patients.
Skin histomorphometric analysis of collagen and elastic fiber networks was used to quantitatively distinguish Ehlers-Danlos syndrome-affected skin from healthy control skin.
The paper states that people with fibromyalgia frequently show impaired memory, attention, processing speed, and executive functions.
People with fibromyalgia have been reported to show altered brain activity at rest and altered autonomic modulation compared to healthy individuals.
Women with fibromyalgia are reported to show lower parasympathetic activity compared to healthy individuals.
Women with fibromyalgia are reported to show higher sympathetic activity compared to healthy individuals.

A previous study cited in this protocol found that women with fibromyalgia showed lower alpha and beta EEG power during dual-task conditions compared to healthy controls, along with a greater impact on brain activity during dual-tasking.
People with fibromyalgia show decreased physical performance when performing two tasks simultaneously (dual-task paradigm), according to prior research cited in this protocol.
People with fibromyalgia have a reduced quality of life and decreased performance in activities of daily living as a consequence of their symptoms.
Prior tDCS studies targeting the primary motor cortex in fibromyalgia patients aimed at pain and sleep showed decreased pain but no changes in sleep.
Application of prefrontal cortex tDCS combined with working memory training has shown promising results for short- and long-term episodic memory and executive functions in fibromyalgia.
A prior study cited found no difference in working memory outcomes between online tDCS at 1 mA versus 2 mA over the DLPFC.
Trigger points are reported to be highly prevalent in the general population, affecting roughly half of adults.
Myofascial pain is estimated to affect 37-65% of the population and costs the US $47 billion annually.
Intramuscular pressure in the trapezius muscle is substantially elevated in fibromyalgia patients compared with rheumatic disease controls.
Capillary microscopy shows reduced capillary numbers with more dilatations/irregular formations and reduced peripheral blood flow in fibromyalgia versus healthy controls.
Fibromyalgia patients show increased ethanol outflow/inflow ratio (indicating reduced blood flow) at rest and reduced nutritive blood flow response to exercise compared to healthy controls.
Interstitial concentrations of lactate, glutamate, and pyruvate are significantly higher in fibromyalgia patients than controls, suggesting a metabolic/ischemic component.
A mitochondrial SNP (m.2352T>C, C allele) is associated with a substantially increased risk for fibromyalgia and reduced mitochondrial membrane potential.
A clinical trial found hyperbaric oxygen therapy significantly ameliorated all fibromyalgia symptoms and improved quality of life.
Fibromyalgia is associated with a DNA hypomethylation pattern enriched in genes related to stress response and DNA repair/free radical clearance.
Fibromyalgia patients show markedly increased muscle damping (a measure of muscle tension), more than twice control mean values, sometimes asymmetrically.
Carpal tunnel syndrome occurs at high rates in fibromyalgia patients, suggesting a compressive/mechanical nerve component.
In a large survey, fibromyalgia patients ranked morning stiffness as more intense than pain itself.
A bidirectional association exists between fibromyalgia and gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD).
High rates of complete resolution of fibromyalgia were observed following laparoscopic Roux-en-Y bariatric surgery.

Parathyroidectomy led to discontinuation of all fibromyalgia medications in 21% of patients and symptom relief in 89%, with rheumatologist-diagnosed patients showing far greater improvement than primary-care-diagnosed patients.
IBS symptoms fell below Rome II diagnostic criteria in 80% of patients after laparoscopic fundoplication for GERD.
TGF-β gene expression in peripheral fibroblasts is significantly higher (two- to three-fold) in fibromyalgia patients compared to controls.
A 1990 study found the majority of fibromyalgia patients tested positive for anti-smooth muscle antibodies.
Ehlers-Danlos/hypermobility syndrome patients show 70-100% prevalence of chronic widespread pain and a close association with fibromyalgia.
A study found much stronger comorbidity associations of fibromyalgia with fasciitis and muscle spasms than with anxiety disorder, based on odds ratios and effect sizes.
Small fiber neuropathy in fibromyalgia patients is accompanied by reduced axonal diameter and Schwann cell abnormalities on electron microscopy.
In vitro co-culture of Borrelia with fibroblasts induces significant upregulation of type I collagen and TGF-β mRNA, suggesting a mechanism for Lyme-associated fibromyalgia-like syndromes.
Fibromyalgia patients show elevated serotonin in myofascial tissue/platelets but decreased tryptophan, serotonin, and kynurenine in blood/brain.
Needling significantly lowers the shear modulus (stiffness) of myofascial tissue as measured by elastography.
Patients with myofascial pain show grey matter changes in the hippocampus, anterior insula, and cingulate cortex.
A high tender point count, but not a low baseline pain threshold, predicts onset of new chronic widespread pain in somatising individuals.
Fibromyalgia patients have higher rates of carpal tunnel syndrome compared to expected/general rates, suggesting a compressive nerve component.
A bidirectional association exists between fibromyalgia and gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD), suggesting shared mechanical/fascial pathology rather than purely psychological overlap.
Laparoscopic fundoplication for GERD relieved IBS symptoms below Rome II criteria in 80 percent of patients, suggesting a mechanical/fascial link between GI surgery and functional GI symptoms.

Tonsillectomy, umbilical hernia repair, and appendectomy are each reported to increase later risk or association with IBS (the latter specifically in fibromyalgia patients), suggesting surgery site-dependent effects on connective tissue/fascia.
Laparoscopic cholecystectomy has been shown to deeply influence (alter) fibromyalgia symptoms, while hysterectomy (with or without oophorectomy) appears to worsen fibromyalgia.
A 1990 study of 20 fibromyalgia patients found the majority had anti-smooth muscle antibodies, offering some support for an autoimmune component.
Studies of Ehlers-Danlos/hypermobility syndrome find that 70-100% have chronic widespread pain, supporting a close association between hypermobility syndrome and fibromyalgia.

Cells from patients with hypermobility syndrome show an increased transition to the myofibroblast phenotype, resembling an inflammatory-like condition consistent with the systemic phenotype of these patients.
Estrogen is suggested to inhibit myofibroblast differentiation and is associated with lower fascial stiffness, and hormonal contraceptives may reduce the risk of fibromyalgia in women.

A study found odds ratios of 5.27 for fasciitis and 6.05 for muscle spasms in association with fibromyalgia (effect sizes 0.92 and 0.99, p<0.0001), both notably higher than the odds ratio of 2.53 (effect size 0.51) found for anxiety disorder.
A study found that the topography of fibromyalgia tender points correlates strongly with the location of myofascial active trigger points (r=0.78, p<0.001).

Wachter et al. quantified muscle damping (reflecting muscle tension) in fibromyalgia patients and found all patients had increased damping, with mean values more than twice and maximum values more than three-fold higher than controls; increased tension was not mediated by extrafusal fibers or alpha/gamma motoneurons and was often unilateral rather than bilateral.
Small fiber pathology in fibromyalgia patients was found to be accompanied by reduced axonal diameter and abnormalities in Schwann cells on electron microscopy.

Borrelia and fibroblast co-cultures show significant induction of type I collagen mRNA after 2 days (p<0.02) and significant upregulation of TGF-β mRNA expression (p<0.01), suggested as a mechanism by which Lyme disease could drive myofibroblast pathology and fibromyalgia-like symptoms.

COVID-19 infection is hypothesized to promote fibroblast-to-myofibroblast transdifferentiation (via immune cell infiltration in the heart and lipofibroblast transdifferentiation in the lung), which the authors suggest could underlie fibromyalgia-like symptoms in post-COVID-19 syndrome.

Fibromyalgia patients show elevated serotonin in myofascial tissue and platelets alongside decreased tryptophan and its derivatives (serotonin and kynurenine) in blood and/or brain, with some patients showing decreased transport of tryptophan across the blood-brain barrier.

A study found placebo had a better outcome than steroids as a treatment for fibromyalgia, cited as evidence against systemic steroid treatment and consistent with the tensegrity model's prediction that systemic drugs distribute unevenly across an imbalanced fascial structure.
A meta-analysis suggests fibromyalgia is associated with a unique cytokine profile (TNF-α, IL-6, IL-8, IL-10 and eotaxin/CCL24), all of which have been implicated in myofibroblast cellular signaling.
Gupta et al. found that a high tender point count is associated with the onset of new chronic widespread pain in somatising individuals, while a low pain threshold at baseline is not.

Obesity-induced connective tissue fibrosis is dependent on mechanosensitive signaling, altering subcutaneous tissue plasticity and increasing connective tissue rigidity/stiffness, suggested as a mechanism linking obesity to fibromyalgia via mechanical compression of fascia.
Younger et al. found that patients with myofascial pain have grey matter changes in the hippocampus, anterior insula, and cingulate cortex, among several other brain areas.
A microdialysis study found interstitial concentrations of lactate, glutamate, and pyruvate were significantly higher in fibromyalgia patients compared to controls.

McIver et al. found that in fibromyalgia patients at rest, the ethanol outflow/inflow ratio (inversely related to blood flow) increased over time compared to healthy controls (p<0.05), and fibromyalgia patients showed a reduced nutritive blood flow response to aerobic exercise (p<0.05), with increased dialysate lactate in response to acetylcholine.

Fibroblasts from fibromyalgia patients show differential expression of proteins involved in ECM turnover and oxidative metabolism, potentially explaining the low-grade inflammatory status of these patients.
A study showed a decrease in transcapillary permeability in fibromyalgia patients, and other scarce studies find abnormalities in the arterial system as well.
Antiphospholipid antibodies (aPL) were detected in COVID-19 patients at rates of 24.2%-57.1% across cohorts, far exceeding the estimated prevalence of aPL in the general population.
Among 159 acute COVID-19 patients, anti-thyroid peroxidase and anti-thyroglobulin antibodies were present in 20% and 11% respectively.
On follow-up of 127 patients approximately three months later, 7 (5.5%) initially anti-TPO-negative patients became positive, while only one initially positive patient reverted to negative.
In the same cohort, 20.1% (41/204) of patients met criteria for 'long COVID-19', defined as persistence of symptoms at follow-up.

In a study of 31 post-COVID-19 patients, all had between 2 and 7 different functionally active agonistic autoantibodies against GPCRs including β2-adrenoceptor, α1-adrenoceptor, and angiotensin II receptor type 1.

The authors' own group reportedly identified close to 20 distinct autoantibodies targeting nervous-system GPCRs and renin-angiotensin system-related molecules significantly associated with COVID-19 clinical severity.
A German study found that 78% of recently recovered COVID-19 patients had a persisting symptom, with myocardial inflammation being the most prevalent abnormality (60%).

An Italian study assessing patients a mean of 60.3 days after symptom onset found only 12.6% completely symptom-free, 32% with 1-2 symptoms, 55% with three or more, and worsened quality of life in 44%.
A study of 355 symptomatic COVID-19 patients found 46% developed post-COVID-19 symptoms, with post-viral fatigue the most prevalent symptom (70%).
A systematic review/meta-analysis compiling over 50 possible long-term COVID-19 effects found that 80% of patients presented with at least one long-term complaint, most commonly fatigue (58%).
Headache is among the most common chronic post-COVID complaints, reported in near 45% of patients according to the meta-analysis.
Neuropsychiatric symptoms including anosmia (21%), attention disorder (27%), depression (12%), and anxiety (13%) were frequently reported post-COVID complaints.

In a web-based survey of 616 COVID-19-recovered patients (6±3 months post-diagnosis), 30.7% met ACR criteria for fibromyalgia, with male gender and obesity as the strongest predictors of post-COVID19 fibromyalgia.

Passive transfer of IgG from fibromyalgia patients into mice increased sensitivity to noxious mechanical and cold stimulation and altered nociceptive fiber responses in skin-nerve preparations compared with controls, supporting an autoimmune basis for fibromyalgia.
Chronic fatigue syndrome has been shown to be associated with higher serum levels of autoantibodies against autonomic receptors, such as beta-adrenergic and muscarinic receptors.

Graded aerobic and strength exercise therapy produced considerable improvements in pain, physical function, and quality of life in CFS and fibromyalgia patients, with adverse effects not consistently reported in controlled trials.

The authors propose that immunomodulatory/immunosuppressive therapy, plasmapheresis, IVIG, rituximab, or extracorporeal apheresis could reduce autoantibody levels and ease post-COVID19 symptoms, though these carry significant potential adverse effects and cost and require formal trials.
Women with FXTAS had significantly higher rates of fibromyalgia than men (26.8% vs 0%).
Migraine prevalence was significantly higher in women than men with FXTAS (43.9% vs 14.5%).
Back pain was significantly more common in women with FXTAS than men (48.5% vs 23.4%), likely related to earlier menopause and reduced bone density.
Allodynia, a hallmark of central sensitization, was significantly more common in women with FXTAS than men (20% vs 2%).
Peripheral neuropathic pain was reported significantly more often by women with FXTAS than men (43.9% vs 25.4%).
Self-reported anxiety symptoms were significantly more common in women with FXTAS than men (82.9% vs 39.7%).
Thyroid problems (largely autoimmune) were significantly more common in women with FXTAS than men (34.2% vs 14.5%).
Osteoarthritis was significantly more prevalent in women with FXTAS than men (65.9% vs 43.5%).
Women with FXTAS were significantly more likely than men to be taking any pain medication (58.5% vs 36.5%).
Women with FXTAS were more likely than men to be taking nerve pain medications, though the reported significance is inconsistent between text sections.
Age of onset of peripheral neuropathy symptoms was positively associated with age of onset of ataxia and tremor, with no gender difference.
No significant associations were found between age of onset of chronic pain or migraine and age of onset of ataxia or tremor, with no gender differences.
Musculoskeletal pain was significantly more prevalent than peripheral neuropathic pain overall in FXTAS patients, and every patient with neuropathic pain also had musculoskeletal pain.
There was no significant gender difference in musculoskeletal pain prevalence between women and men with FXTAS.
FMR1 activation ratio was not significantly associated with either neuropathic pain or musculoskeletal pain in female premutation carriers.
Among participants with autoimmune conditions, females had significantly lower CGG repeat length than males.
Males were significantly more likely to meet criteria for 'Definite FXTAS' while females were more often classified as 'Probable FXTAS'.
Depressive symptoms did not differ significantly between women and men with FXTAS (24.4% vs 25.8%).

FMR1 knockout mice, which produce no FMRP, show decreased neuropathic pain and protection from nociceptive sensitization and IL-6-induced allodynia compared to wild-type mice, implicating FMRP in pain sensitization pathways.

Case report evidence in five females with the FMR1 premutation described an Ehlers-Danlos syndrome-like phenotype, suggesting shared connective tissue pathogenesis potentially via FMRP regulation of elastin, actin, and MMP9.

A controlled trial of CBD in patients with multiple sclerosis, spinal cord, and other neurological conditions found improved pain control, cited as supporting evidence for CBD as a potential chronic pain treatment in FXTAS.
In chronic pain patients, gray matter volume in the bilateral DLPFC, posterior parietal cortex, and other sensory/motor/affective areas increased after an 11-session CBT program.
Left SMA gray matter volume decreased in chronic pain patients following CBT.
Increased prefrontal/parietal gray matter volume after CBT was associated with decreased pain catastrophizing, a key treatment target in chronic pain.

In an RCT of chronic musculoskeletal pain, intrinsic functional connectivity between the anterior DMN and amygdala/PAG decreased after CBT and this decrease correlated with improved self-efficacy for symptom coping.
iFC between the basal ganglia network and right S2 cortex increased after CBT and correlated with decreased pain symptoms.
Increased iFC between the BG network and right S2 cortex after CBT was also associated with increased self-efficacy for pain management.
CBT patients showed increased fractional amplitude of low-frequency fluctuations (fALFF) in the bilateral PCC and cerebellum post-therapy.

In chronic pain patients, abnormal intrinsic connectivity network connections involving the OFC, inferior parietal lobule (DAN), and paracentral lobule (sensorimotor network) normalized after a 12-session CBT program.
Higher OFC intrinsic connectivity network strength was associated with a greater decrease in pain intensity after CBT.
Lower ICN connectivity strength in the dorsal PCC within the DAN was related to positive CBT-related clinical improvements.
In fibromyalgia patients, CBT increased pressure-pain-evoked activation in the VLPFC and lateral orbitofrontal cortex, regions associated with executive cognitive control.
The reduction in anxiety after CBT was significantly positively correlated with VLPFC activation in fibromyalgia patients.

Coherence between VLPFC and thalamus increased after CBT in fibromyalgia patients, suggesting CBT may influence lower brain structures such as the thalamus, which had previously shown decreased activity in fibromyalgia.
In high-catastrophizing fibromyalgia patients, resting-state connectivity between S1 and anterior/medial insula was reduced after CBT, correlating with concurrent reductions in catastrophizing.

In fibromyalgia patients scanned at baseline, post-treatment, and 6-month follow-up, changes in catastrophizing and insula-S1 connectivity occurred after 1 month of CBT, while pain interference improved significantly only by the 6-month follow-up, suggesting a sequential mechanism.

In fibromyalgia patients undergoing an experimental pain protocol, more brain regions showed decreased BOLD activation after CBT for insomnia (8 regions) than after traditional CBT for pain (3 regions), out of 12 regions with significant interactions.

A planned RCT proposes that CBT for insomnia reduces arousal, improves sleep, and reverses HPA axis and CNS changes underlying central sensitization in fibromyalgia with comorbid insomnia, but data collection had not been completed at time of publication.
In adolescents with migraine, an 8-week CBT program with parental involvement reduced headache frequency from 15 ± 7.4 to 10 ± 7.4 per month.

In adolescents with migraine, CBT increased activation of right-sided OFC, VLPFC, and DLPFC, and increased connectivity between the amygdala and paracingulate gyrus, PFC, and occipital cortex, while causing bilateral cerebellar deactivation.
Reduction in headache after CBT in adolescents with migraine correlated with bilateral activation of the occipital cortex, lingual gyrus, angular gyrus, and superior parietal lobule.

Decreased headache after CBT was associated with opposite hemispheric changes: increased connectivity between the left amygdala and occipital cortex, and reduced connectivity between the right amygdala and paracingulate gyrus/DLPFC.

In healthy participants undergoing repeated heat pain, DMN deactivation did not differ between groups before intervention, but after intervention deactivation was significantly lower in the non-CBT control group compared to the CBT group.
In healthy participants, CBT reduced deactivation of the right VLPFC and increased spontaneous functional connectivity between the DMN and right VLPFC during heat pain.
A 59-year-old man developed type III Kounis syndrome (coronary stent thrombosis presenting as STEMI) beginning 20 minutes after receiving the ChAdOx1 SARS-CoV-2 (AstraZeneca) vaccine.

The patient's eosinophil count showed a transient increase-decrease pattern after the COVID-19 vaccine-associated ACS, peaking three days after the event and normalizing by day seven, consistent with a hypersensitivity-mediated process.

In the patient's earlier myocardial infarction (which followed influenza vaccination), eosinophil counts remained within normal range throughout hospitalization, unlike the eosinophilia seen after the COVID-19 vaccine-associated event.

Polysorbate-80 (PS80), a common excipient shared by both the influenza and COVID-19 (ChAdOx1) vaccines the patient received, was identified as the probable trigger of both hypersensitivity-mediated coronary events.
Skin testing with intravenous amiodarone (which contains PS80) was negative, though a negative result does not exclude a non-IgE-mediated PS80 hypersensitivity reaction.
Kounis syndrome is described as occurring due to mast-cell degranulation and platelet cell activation in the setting of a hypersensitivity reaction, driving acute coronary syndrome.
Among Kounis syndrome variants, type I (coronary spasm without CAD) is reported as the most common (72.6%) and type III (stent thrombosis) the least frequent (5.1%).
Kounis syndrome is reported to be more frequent in men and in middle-aged people.
The right coronary artery is reported as the most commonly affected artery in Kounis syndrome, consistent with this patient's presentation.

Systemic hypersensitivity manifestations (skin rash/hives, respiratory symptoms) are uncommon in Kounis syndrome, occurring in only 25% and 15% of patients respectively, so their absence does not exclude the diagnosis.

Serum tryptase is described as the most useful diagnostic marker for hypersensitivity reactions underlying Kounis syndrome, ideally measured at 2 hours (peak) and 24+ hours (baseline) after symptom onset, but it was not measured in this patient.
High-sensitivity troponin T rose markedly from admission to peak, confirming acute myocardial infarction associated with the stent thrombosis event.

Stent underexpansion seen on OCT was not considered the most probable cause of the stent thrombosis, given the patient's good compliance with antithrombotic therapy, supporting a hypersensitivity mechanism instead.

Non-IgE-mediated hypersensitivity reactions, as potentially underlying this patient's events, can occur via complement activation/anaphylatoxin generation or via direct mast cell activation through the Mas-related G protein-coupled receptor X2 (MRGPRX2).
Basophil FcεRI receptor density was significantly higher in patients with CIndU compared with healthy controls.
Basophil FcεRI expression by mean fluorescence intensity (MFI) was also higher in CIndU patients than healthy controls, though the difference was only marginally significant.
Basal FcεRI receptor expression (both MFI and density) did not differ significantly between the different CIndU subtypes.
Total serum IgE levels did not differ significantly between CIndU subtypes.
Higher basal basophil FcεRI expression (both MFI and receptor density) was positively correlated with higher total serum IgE levels across the whole CIndU sample.
The positive correlation between FcεRI expression and IgE levels remained significant when analyzed separately within each CIndU subtype.
Almost three-quarters of CIndU patients (73.8%) responded to antihistamine therapy (licensed or fourfold up-dosing), while 26.2% did not respond.
Baseline FcεRI expression by MFI did not differ significantly between responders and non-responders to antihistamine therapy.
Baseline FcεRI receptor density also did not differ significantly between antihistamine responders and non-responders, though a trend was noted.
Non-responders to antihistamine therapy had significantly higher baseline total IgE serum levels than responders.
Among antihistamine responders, basal FcεRI expression (MFI and density) correlated strongly and significantly with total IgE levels.
Among antihistamine non-responders, the FcεRI-IgE correlation was significant only for MFI, not for receptor density.
Non-responders to antihistamine therapy showed cold-provocation thresholds (CSTT and CTT) indicative of more severe disease compared with responders.
The majority (89.5%) of CIndU patients treated with omalizumab responded to treatment, while 10.53% did not respond.
Baseline FcεRI expression (MFI) was significantly higher in omalizumab responders than in non-responders, suggesting FcεRI as a predictive biomarker for anti-IgE treatment response.
Total serum IgE levels did not differ significantly between omalizumab responders and non-responders, though non-responders showed a numerically higher median.
Cold provocation thresholds (CSTT, CTT) did not differ significantly between omalizumab responders and non-responders.
No significant differences in baseline FcεRI expression, receptor density, or total IgE were found between patients partially versus fully responding to omalizumab.
Basal FcεRI receptor levels did not differ significantly between CIndU patients and a comparison cohort of CSU patients from a related study.
Mast cell-deficient Sash mice (carrying a Kit mutation) showed markedly lower MuLV/Friend retroviral replication in spleen, bone marrow, and blood compared to wild-type mice.
Viral infection increased IFN-γ production in NK and CD8+ T cells of mast cell-deficient Sash mice but diminished it in wild-type mice, while CD4+ T cell IFN-γ was similar between groups.

MuLV/Friend infection increased G-MDSC and M-MDSC accumulation in both WT and Sash mice, but only elevated suppressive markers PD-L1 and iNOS on G-MDSCs in mast cell-competent WT mice, not in Sash mice.

Reconstitution of mast cells in Sash mice via bone marrow-derived mast cell injection restored G-MDSC suppressive marker expression, reduced NK/CD8+ T cell IFN-γ responses, and rescued viral replication in spleen.
MuLV/Friend virus infection triggered rapid mast cell degranulation in splenic, peritoneal, and footpad tissues within 2 hours, similar to the positive control mast cell activator compound 48/80.
Pharmacological induction of mast cell degranulation with compound 48/80 significantly increased splenic viral replication and elevated PD-L1/CD39 suppressive markers on G-MDSCs (but not M-MDSCs).
Exogenous histamine administration (2.5 mg/kg) increased retroviral replication in spleen and increased PD-L1/CD39 suppressive markers on G-MDSCs but not M-MDSCs.

Treatment with the H1-antihistamine mast cell stabilizers Ebastine (5 mg/kg) or Loratadine (10 mg/kg) blocked mast cell degranulation, significantly reduced splenic viral loads, reduced PD-L1/iNOS expression on G-MDSCs, and improved NK/CD8+ T cell IFN-γ antiviral responses.

HIV-1 CCR5-tropic (JRFL) and CXCR4-tropic (HXB2) pseudotyped virus-like particles induced dose-dependent degranulation of human LAD2 mast cells within 15-30 minutes, measured by β-hexosaminidase release.
Replication-competent HIV-1 isolates (CCR5-tropic AD8 and CXCR4-tropic NL4-3) triggered mast cell degranulation with release of histamine and tryptase in ex vivo cultured human colorectal tissue.
FcεRIα protein colocalized with the pan-neuronal marker PGP9.5 in mouse trigeminal ganglion and in conjunctival nerve fibers, indicating FcεRIα expression in sensory neurons.
In human trigeminal ganglion tissue, FcεRIα was expressed in a subset (25.80%) of sensory neurons.

Among conjunctiva-innervating (WGA-labeled) trigeminal neurons, FcεRIα+ cells substantially overlapped with CGRP+ peptidergic nociceptors (58.31%), NF200+ large-diameter neurons (48.91%), and IB4+ nonpeptidergic nociceptors (16.19%), but not with the satellite glial marker glutamine synthetase.
FcεRIα-positive trigeminal neurons and conjunctival nerve fibers colocalized with MrgprA3, a marker of itch-selective pruriceptors.

IgE-immune complex (IgE-IC) directly activated a significantly larger fraction of small-diameter trigeminal neurons from wild-type mice (15.05%) than from FcεRIα knockout mice (1.60%), demonstrating that neuronal activation by IgE-IC is FcεRIα-dependent.
IgE-IC directly activated a subpopulation (24.49%) of MrgprA3+ trigeminal pruriceptor neurons in calcium imaging.

Ocular instillation of IgE-IC (10 and 50 µg/ml), but not vehicle, antigen alone, or monomeric IgE, induced acute eye-directed scratching (itch) behavior lasting up to 3 hours, without inducing wiping (pain-like) behavior.

IgE-IC ocular instillation did not cause immune cell infiltration (neutrophils, macrophages, lymphocytes) or mast cell recruitment/degranulation in conjunctiva or TG at early time points, dissociating IgE-IC-induced itch from classic mast cell/inflammatory mechanisms.

Global FcεRIα knockout mice showed significantly attenuated ocular scratching in response to IgE-IC compared with wild-type mice, while responses to capsaicin (pain) and histamine (itch) were normal, indicating FcεRIα is specifically necessary for IgE-IC-elicited itch.

Mast cell-deficient c-Kit W-sh/W-sh mice showed no significant difference in basal or IgE-IC-evoked ocular scratching compared with wild-type controls, indicating mast cells are not required for IgE-IC-induced ocular itch.

Selective neuronal knockdown of FcεRIα via AAV9-Pirt-shFcεRIα in trigeminal ganglia significantly reduced IgE-IC-induced ocular scratching compared with control-virus-infected mice, without altering baseline responses to capsaicin or histamine.
In an OVA-induced allergic conjunctivitis (ACJ) mouse model, trigeminal FcεRIα protein was significantly upregulated compared with vehicle control-treated animals.
The proportion of FcεRIα-expressing conjunctiva-innervating (WGA-labeled) trigeminal neurons was significantly increased in ACJ mice compared with controls.

In ACJ, a greater proportion of FcεRIα+ conjunctiva sensory neurons co-expressed CGRP, and among MrgprA3+ pruriceptors the percentage co-expressing FcεRIα increased from 13.38% to 28.07%, while NF200 and IB4 co-expression did not differ.

Neuronal-selective FcεRIα knockdown significantly reduced ocular itch in the ACJ model as challenged by OVA, without affecting ACJ pathology, immune cell infiltration (neutrophils, macrophages, lymphocytes), or mast cell number/degranulation in the conjunctiva.
Culturing dissociated trigeminal neurons with isotype IgE significantly increased FcεRIα protein levels without changing FcεRIα mRNA levels, suggesting post-transcriptional regulation.

Blocking new protein synthesis with cycloheximide failed to prevent IgE-induced upregulation of FcεRIα protein in TG neurons, indicating the effect is independent of new translation, consistent with reduced receptor internalization/degradation.

Pre-treatment of dissociated TG neurons with IgE significantly increased both the percentage of neurons responding to IgE-IC and the magnitude of IgE-IC-evoked Ca2+ responses in small-diameter neurons.

In MrgprA3+ trigeminal neurons, IgE pretreatment increased the percentage of neurons responsive to IgE-IC (from 25.22% to 39.02%) and the intensity of the resulting Ca2+ response (from 22% to 30% baseline ΔR).

Using an incremental sensitization protocol, serum OVA-specific IgE and trigeminal FcεRIα protein levels progressively increased with longer sensitization duration (2 and 3 weeks vs control/1 week), and this correlated with progressively worsening OVA-induced ocular scratching behavior.

Bioinformatic KEGG pathway analysis of the CBX gene family and their 246 co-expressed/frequently altered neighbor genes in ovarian cancer identified mast cell activation and mast cell-mediated immunity as the top enriched biological pathways, ahead of response to chemokine.
Healthcare workers wearing N95 masks and PPE for 6 hours showed a significantly greater drop in total brain oxygenation than those wearing three-ply masks.
Baseline (pre-shift) brain oxygenation was already lower in the N95/PPE subject group compared with the three-ply mask control group before further dropping after the work shift.

Cerebral blood flow measured by ASL in the middle cerebral arteries increased post-shift in both groups, but the subject group showed only a modest rise compared with controls, suggesting possible acclimatization to low oxygen.
The cingulate gyri in N95/PPE subjects showed a significantly greater drop in oxygenation than in controls.
Subjects younger than 25 or older than 35 years showed a comparatively larger drop in cingulate gyrus oxygenation than middle-aged subjects.
Among subjects over 35 years with a significant drop in cingulate gyrus oxygenation, 80% reported clinical confusion.
Headache frequency and intensity were significantly higher in HCWs wearing N95 masks and PPE compared with those wearing three-ply masks.
Female subjects wearing N95 masks/PPE reported more headaches than females in the control group.
Greater headache severity in subjects correlated with a larger pre- to post-shift difference in ASL-measured cerebral blood flow.
Overall, the N95/PPE subject group showed a median 15.5% drop in brain oxygenation compared with a 6.7% drop in the three-ply mask control group.
The parietal and occipital lobes were the most affected regions for oxygenation drop, with the temporal lobes affected to a lesser extent.
There was compensatory redistribution of brain oxygenation toward the frontal lobes and anterior cingulate gyri, areas vital for cognitive function.
Seven subjects who showed poor compensation in maintaining anterior cingulate gyrus oxygenation had clinical symptoms of confusion.

Although nausea, vomiting, dizziness, blurring of vision, lethargy, somnolence, and fatigability were seen more frequently in the N95/PPE subject group, none reached statistical significance compared with the control group.
Most healthcare workers in the N95/PPE subject group began showing symptoms, especially headache, around 3 hours after donning the mask and PPE kit.
In the rat stomach, an average of 28.9% of myenteric (Hu-positive) neurons were immunoreactive for nNOS, with similar proportions across fundus, corpus and antrum and no significant sex difference.
The total gastric myenteric neuron population in rat was estimated at 437,591 ± 49,816 neurons, distributed as 67,031 in antrum, 211,778 in corpus and 158,781 in fundus.

Gastric nNOS-immunoreactive neurons had single axons and lamellar dendrites consistent with Dogiel type I motor neuron morphology and did not form pericellular baskets around other myenteric neurons, indicating they function as muscle motor neurons rather than interneurons in the rat stomach.

nNOS-immunoreactive nerve fibres densely innervated the circular and oblique muscle layers throughout their thickness but were rare within the longitudinal muscle layer, which instead was innervated via a tertiary plexus at its inner surface.

nNOS-immunoreactive fibres also innervated the muscularis mucosae (both layers) and formed perivascular networks around small arteries within the gastric wall, but rarely innervated smooth muscle strands between mucosal glands.

The pyloric sphincter region and adjacent antral circular muscle near the gastro-duodenal junction showed markedly denser nNOS fibre innervation compared to antral circular muscle further from the sphincter.
A region along the lesser curvature of the rat stomach, extending 1.5-2 mm laterally, showed a marked paucity of myenteric ganglia compared to the rest of the stomach.
Myenteric ganglion size differed by region, with antral ganglia about 1.3 times larger than corpus ganglia, which were about 2.3 times larger than fundus ganglia.
Submucosal neuron number in rat stomach was about 11,400 ± 2,200, roughly 2.6% of the myenteric neuron number, and submucosal ganglia contained rare nNOS-positive neurons.
Some patients with irritable bowel syndrome have local IgE-mediated food-allergy reactions confined to the intestinal mucosa despite negative serum food-specific IgE and skin prick tests.
More than half of IBS patients report meal-triggered symptoms despite negative serum food-specific IgE and skin prick test results.
Mast cell hyperplasia and higher intestinal mucosal tryptase concentrations are associated with allergic mucosal inflammation in patients with food allergies and IBS.
Histamine released from activated mast cells causes abdominal pain by binding histamine receptors on gut sensory neurons.
In a mouse model of IgE-mediated food allergy, PGD2 deficiency results in mast cell hyperplasia and worsens food-allergen-induced allergic reactions.
A urinary PGD2 metabolite was reported as a useful diagnostic index of food allergy in both mice and humans.
Metabolomic analysis found multifood allergies are associated with altered tryptophan and 1-arachidonoyl-GPD, metabolites upstream of serotonin and PAF production respectively.

MRGPRX2 (murine Mrgprb2) mediates IgE-independent mast cell activation by cationic ligands including drugs, host-defense peptides (LL-37), and neuropeptides, and is expressed on connective-tissue mast cells but not mucosal mast cells.
TGF-β induces expression of mucosal mast cell-specific proteases (mMCP-1, mMCP-2) and the surface marker CD103 in in vitro culture, via SMAD4/GATA2 binding at Mcpt1/Mcpt2 gene motifs.
Notch and TGF-β signaling act synergistically and interdependently, via SMAD-dependent transcription, to induce mucosal mast cell differentiation.

In a mouse model of ovalbumin-induced food allergy, the Notch inhibitor DAPT suppressed intestinal mucosal mast cell expansion and reduced the severity of allergic diarrhea and hypothermia without changing OVA-specific IgE levels.

CD300f-deficient mice showed higher serum mMCP-1 and more severe allergic diarrhea/hypothermia after oral allergen challenge, indicating CD300f normally restrains IgE/mast-cell-mediated food allergy responses.
Pretreatment with ceramide-containing vesicles, which activate the inhibitory receptor CD300f, attenuated food allergy responses in a mouse model.

In a single-cell RNA-seq analysis of one CRSwNP patient before/after six weeks of dupilumab treatment, expression of IL17RB, a marker of human tryptase-only mast cells, was markedly reduced, suggesting dupilumab also targets mucosal mast cells.
A case report describes a 30-year-old woman with severe atopic dermatitis and newly developed corn/nut food allergy who acquired tolerance to these foods after dupilumab treatment.
Combining omalizumab (anti-IgE) with oral immunotherapy reduced adverse events and shortened the time to achieve desensitization in small trials of milk, egg, and peanut allergy.

Oral immunotherapy shifted mucosal mast cells from a pathogenic/pro-allergic status to a regulatory status that releases IL-2 and IL-10, promoting regulatory T-cell expansion and reduced allergen reactivity.
TGF-β stimulation increased CLIC4 mRNA and protein expression in healthy dermal fibroblasts.
Wnt-3a and the Hedgehog pathway agonist SAG each increased CLIC4 expression at mRNA and protein levels in dermal fibroblasts, similar to TGF-β.
CLIC4 expression was upregulated in dermal fibroblasts of TGF-βRIIΔK transgenic (fibrotic) mice compared with wild-type littermates in vivo.
The SMAD3 inhibitor SIS3 prevented TGF-β-mediated upregulation of CLIC4 in dermal fibroblasts.
The β-catenin inhibitor FH535 suppressed Wnt-3a-induced CLIC4 upregulation and reduced CLIC4 protein below basal level in dermal fibroblasts.
GANT61 (GLI1/2 transcription factor inhibitor) prevented the SAG-mediated increase in CLIC4 expression.
α-SMA expression closely correlated with CLIC4 expression levels across all treatment conditions, consistent with CLIC4 being required for α-SMA expression.

SMAD3 knockdown by siRNA or pharmacological inhibition with SIS3 reduced Wnt3a-induced TOP-Flash (TCF/β-catenin) luciferase reporter activity, indicating SMAD3 is required for canonical Wnt/β-catenin transcriptional activity.
Stimulation with TGF-β increased β-catenin protein levels in dermal fibroblasts, providing an explanation for TGF-β enhancement of canonical Wnt signalling.
Wnt3a increased GLI2 transcript levels in a β-catenin-dependent manner, as this upregulation was blocked by the β-catenin inhibitor FH535.
TGF-β-mediated stimulation of GLI2 expression was reversed by β-catenin inhibition with FH535, indicating β-catenin mediates TGF-β-induced GLI2 upregulation.
SAG stimulation of the Hedgehog pathway increased β-catenin protein and transcript levels, and this was prevented by GLI inhibition with GANT61, indicating GLI1/2 drive β-catenin expression.
SIS3 (SMAD3 inhibitor) blocked both Wnt3a- and SAG-induced CLIC4 and α-SMA upregulation, indicating SMAD3 is required downstream of Wnt3a and Hh signalling for CLIC4 induction.
Blocking β-catenin (FH535) or GLI1/2 (GANT61) inhibited TGF-β-mediated CLIC4 and α-SMA expression to a greater extent than the SMAD3 inhibitor SIS3.

CRISPR/Cas9-engineered SW620 colon cancer cells carrying an oncogenic PTCH1 truncation (D1222fs) showed higher mRNA levels of SMAD2, SMAD3, SMAD4 and SMO, lower GLI3, and higher CLIC4 by RNA-seq, confirmed by Western blot for SMAD2/3/4 and CLIC4.
PTCH1mut SW620 cells showed increased GLI1 and CLIC4 mRNA and protein compared with WT PTCH1 control cells, consistent with increased canonical Hedgehog signalling.
Treatment of PTCH1mut cells with GANT61 (GLI1/2 inhibitor) or SD208 (TGF-β receptor inhibitor) reduced GLI1 and CLIC4 mRNA and protein expression.

The β-catenin inhibitor FH535 partially reduced CLIC4 transcript and protein levels in SSc patient fibroblasts (without exogenous TGF-β), but had no effect on basal CLIC4 expression in healthy fibroblasts.
FH535 reduced α-SMA levels only in SSc patient fibroblasts, not in healthy fibroblasts, further supporting that CLIC4/β-catenin signalling is necessary for α-SMA expression in SSc.
siRNA-mediated silencing of β-catenin reduced CLIC4 protein levels in SSc fibroblasts compared to scrambled control siRNA, confirming a role for β-catenin in enhanced CLIC4 expression in SSc.
GANT61 treatment reduced CLIC4 transcript and protein levels in SSc fibroblasts down to levels seen in healthy fibroblasts, with no effect on healthy fibroblast CLIC4 expression.
GLI2 siRNA significantly reduced CLIC4 expression in SSc fibroblasts but not in healthy fibroblasts, confirming a key role for GLI2 in CLIC4 overexpression in SSc.
Inhibition of GLI1/2 (by GANT61 or siRNA) in SSc fibroblasts blocked β-catenin expression, indicating GLI transcription factors regulate β-catenin levels in SSc fibroblasts.
The chloride channel inhibitors NPPB and IAA-94 reduced α-SMA expression induced by TGF-β, Wnt3a, and SAG in dermal fibroblasts, and also reduced TGF-β-dependent upregulation of β-catenin and GLI2.
NPPB and IAA-94 reduced β-catenin and GLI2 protein expression in SSc patient fibroblasts, suggesting CLIC4/chloride channel activity fine-tunes endogenous Wnt3a and Hh signalling strength in SSc.

Chloride channel inhibitors NPPB and IAA-94 reduced α-SMA expression induced by TGF-β, Wnt3a, and SAG in dermal fibroblasts, implicating CLIC4/chloride channel activity in morphogen-driven fibroblast activation.
Chloride channel inhibitors NPPB and IAA-94 reduced TGF-β-dependent upregulation of β-catenin and GLI2 protein expression in dermal fibroblasts.
NPPB and IAA-94 prevented β-catenin and c-Jun (a β-catenin target gene) expression induced by Wnt-3a stimulation in dermal fibroblasts.
Chloride channel inhibitors reduced β-catenin upregulation induced by the Hh pathway agonist SAG, while having no effect on SMAD3 levels in response to Wnt3a or SAG.
Treatment of SSc fibroblasts with chloride channel inhibitors NPPB and IAA-94 reduced basal β-catenin and GLI2 protein expression, suggesting CLIC4 fine-tunes endogenous Wnt3a/Hh signalling in SSc.
The TGF-β receptor inhibitor SD208 reduced GLI1 and CLIC4 mRNA and protein expression in PTCH1-mutant SW620 colon cancer cells with dysregulated Hh signalling.
Inhibition of GLI1/2 with GANT61 in SSc fibroblasts blocked β-catenin expression, further supporting a feedback relationship between GLI transcription factors and β-catenin.

A previous study showed decreased Axin2 (a component of the β-catenin destruction complex) expression in the dermis of TGF-βRIIΔK transgenic mice, consistent with elevated β-catenin potentially contributing to increased CLIC4 expression in vivo.

RNA-seq analysis of PTCH1-mutant SW620 cells (CRISPR-engineered oncogenic PTCH1 truncation) showed higher SMAD2/3/4 and SMO mRNA, lower GLI3 mRNA, and higher CLIC4 mRNA compared to WT PTCH1 cells, indicating widespread TGF-β/Hh crosstalk driving CLIC4.
Using the FiRST screening tool, 45.3% of DGBI patients screened positive for fibromyalgia.
Rheumatological examination confirmed the diagnosis of primary fibromyalgia in all 9 DGBI patients who agreed to be examined after screening positive.
Among DGBI patients, 69.8% fulfilled Rome IV criteria for IBS.
77.4% of DGBI patients fulfilled Rome IV criteria for functional dyspepsia.
Half of DGBI patients (50.9%) met criteria for both IBS and FD simultaneously.
Among IBS patients in the DGBI cohort, constipation-predominant IBS (IBS-C) was the most common subtype.
49.0% of fibromyalgia patients fulfilled Rome IV diagnostic criteria for IBS.
81.6% of fibromyalgia patients fulfilled Rome IV criteria for functional dyspepsia, a notably higher prevalence than previously reported.
44.9% of fibromyalgia patients had overlapping IBS and FD.
There was no significant difference in the prevalence of IBS and FD between patients with primary versus secondary fibromyalgia.
IBS subtype distribution differed significantly between DGBI and FM patients, with IBS-C predominating in DGBI and IBS-M predominating in FM.
FD subtype distribution (PDS vs EPS) did not differ significantly between DGBI and FM patients, though EPS prevalence was notably low in FM patients.

Upper abdominal symptom (epigastric fullness, pain, burning, bloating, distension) frequency-intensity scores showed a graduated increase across groups, with DGBI patients who also had FM scoring highest, followed by FM patients with DGBI, then DGBI patients without FM.
Among lower abdominal symptoms, only abdominal pain differed significantly across groups, with DGBI patients without FM having the highest score.
GI symptom frequency-intensity scores did not significantly differ between primary and secondary fibromyalgia patients.
The observed 45.3% IBS prevalence in FM patients in this study closely aligned with the pooled 46.2% IBS prevalence reported in a 2020 systematic review of 14 studies on DGBI in FM.
